I believe students should design their own summer projects because they tend to be more imaginative, enjoy the work more, and experience less pressure.

When given the chance, students often come up with original ideas by researching experiments or exploring a person’s life. They might look up science activities to try and create something engaging for the class or themselves. Others could choose to write about a famous figure or a family member and explain why that person matters to them. Some students may even invent new projects and present their ideas to classmates, describing how they developed their concept and how it could be useful.

Allowing students to choose their project also makes the process more enjoyable. Pupils are usually more excited to work on something they picked rather than completing a dull assignment set for everyone. With freedom to explore, they can produce more interesting work and take pleasure in tasks that aren’t limited by a strict checklist. They can also collaborate with friends, which adds a social and fun element.

Finally, designing their own project can reduce stress. Students won’t feel pressured to make everything perfect according to a teacher’s rigid rules; instead, they can create their own standards and later share how they organized their work so others might try it too.

For these reasons, I think students should plan their own summer projects.

Homework can be hard most of the time, and you need someone to help you with it. Having an afterschool homework club can be fun and a good thing to do in school. An afterschool homework club can be good for the kids that don't get to finish their homework or don't understand the homework. On the other hand, we have the people that don't have time to do things after school.

An afterschool homework club is good for the kids that don't have nothing to do for the afternoon so they can stay and finish homework from that day or something that they need to finish.

Homework is often challenging, and many students need extra help. While an after-school homework club might seem like a helpful and enjoyable option at school, I believe it is not the best solution for everyone. Some students would benefit from it, but there are several reasons why a regular after-school club would be problematic for many.

First, lots of students already have commitments right after school. They may attend sports practice, dance lessons, choir rehearsals, or music lessons. Because of these activities, they often do not have time to stay after school, and sometimes they cannot even finish their homework at home. For students who have nothing planned in the afternoon, an after-school club could be useful to complete assignments. But that does not apply to everyone, so a one-size-fits-all program does not solve the main problem.

I am personally against an after-school homework club. I often have to go to practice after school, so I can’t remain at school for extra help. I try to finish my work at home and hand it in the next day, but staying after school would not be possible for me. Teachers are in the same position; many of them cannot remain after school every day because they have personal responsibilities, such as feeding pets or looking after their own children. Expecting teachers to stay late regularly is unfair and unrealistic.

Another concern is transportation and supervision. Many students rely on parents or guardians for rides, and those adults might be working, ill, or simply not at home in the afternoon. I do not trust that the school could look after every child who stays late. Also, children might get hungry while waiting; it is unlikely the school would provide snacks for everyone. These practical issues make an after-school club difficult to run safely and comfortably.

If the school wants to offer a structured time for homework, it would be better to schedule it as part of the regular timetable. One option is to make the homework club the last period of the day, so students who need that time can sign up for that block and finish assignments before leaving. Another possibility is to start the day with a homework block as the first period, allowing students who did not complete work at home to do it in the morning. I prefer the last-class option because it gives everyone a chance to rest a little after a long day and still leaves afternoons free for other activities.

In short, while the idea of an after-school homework club sounds helpful, it fails to consider students’ after-school commitments, teachers’ schedules, transportation and meal concerns. Scheduling homework time during the school day would be a more practical and fair approach.

What would you do if you fail your online classes? Some schools now offer online classes to make the student's life easier. I do not agree with the schools that offer distance learning, because it could be difficult for students to understand the online notes or videos, the students always need a teacher to ask questions, and the student's parents need to pay internet at home. Also the internet is expensive and some parents can not afford.

First, it can be beneficial for the students to attend at school because there is more activities and sports, where they can have fun with their friends.

Also, the teachers are always there to help and explain better the subjects. From my own experience, I need to be with a teacher to understand what is the topic about, that helps me to pass my exams and my classes. Even thought, there is some teachers that are very strict and irritate the students but the teachers know that is beneficial for the students future.

Therefore, being at home the whole time it is so boring because the students need to be studding and not having fun. That is why some students cannot develop them knowledge because they do not take fresh air and entertain them minds with someone else. For example, my friend Generic_Name she is at the Community College and the teachers offer some online classes and she decided to take it. But now she is frustrating because she have to watch some boring videos and she have to take quizzes constantly. She told me that she miss all her friends and her classmates.

After all, certain student do not have their mind clear enough attending to school; now imagine how difficult would be for them to take online classes without a teacher. For example, Generic_Name was taking online courses because he got sick so he could not attend to school for one year. Then, he came back to school, he was so disappointed because he mist a lot of stuff from his subject. He had to stayed after school and he had to go to summer school. Well, so far I have not take online classes but I take my friends experiences that is not easy.

Finally, in my opinion is not a great idea that the students take online classes, if they want to move faster and achieve in the future.

I believe requiring these classes is unhelpful, unjust, and not essential for most students.

For students aiming at technical or vocational paths, mandatory arts classes do not increase academic knowledge or improve job prospects. Forcing uninterested students into these courses could also make lessons boring and reduce motivation.

Second, it is unfair to let an unrelated class affect a student’s progress. If a required art or music course becomes a stumbling block, it could lower grades or delay graduation, which is especially damaging if the student needs to move on to college or work. It seems unreasonable to repeat a year or miss opportunities because of a subject that is not important for one’s chosen career.

In short, music, drama, and art should be offered as electives. They can be valuable for those who enjoy them, but they should not be compulsory for every student, since most jobs and future plans do not require these classes.

People should make their own choices instead of relying blindly on other so-called "experts."

First, individuals understand themselves better than anyone else. They know their tastes, limits, and needs—both physically and emotionally. If someone else picked out something for you that you hated or did not want, it shows why it is usually wiser to decide for yourself. You know what fits your life, style, and comfort, so making your own decisions reduces the chance of ending up with something that does not suit you.

Second, making your own choices helps you learn from experience. Many people buy clothing online without trying it on, only to find the size or fit is wrong when it arrives. That mistake teaches them to check measurements or try items in stores first. Similarly, shoppers who do not read product descriptions may receive goods that look different from photos, are smaller than expected, or are missing parts. Those unpleasant surprises encourage better habits—reading details and checking reviews before buying.

Finally, experts are not always right or honest. Hiring a lawyer does not guarantee a win, even if you pay high fees. Doctors sometimes dismiss a patient’s concerns and simply prescribe costly pain medication when different care might be better. Some mental health professionals may also offer medication that a person does not truly need. In these situations, following your own judgment or seeking a second opinion can protect you from poor advice or unnecessary costs.

In short, relying too much on so-called experts can lead to mistakes, wasted money, and wrong treatments. Because people know themselves best, learn valuable lessons from their errors, and may avoid bad or biased guidance, it is usually better to make your own decisions.

I support the idea of an after-school homework club. Many students struggle to finish assignments on their own, and having teachers available to help would likely reduce the number of failing grades. Some children also do not have access to a computer or other devices at home, so a supervised place to work would give them the tools they need. In addition, working together after school lets students interact and see how others approach their homework, which can be a useful learning opportunity.

There are possible problems, however. Some students might try to copy answers and leave early, or treat the club like a social gathering and talk instead of working. To prevent this, the club should set clear rules, such as not looking at others’ work until everyone has finished and keeping conversations quiet and focused. Even with these challenges, many students will use the time seriously and avoid distracting their peers.

In conclusion, I believe an after-school homework club is a good idea because the benefits outweigh the drawbacks. It can help students improve their study habits and raise their grades, especially those who truly care about their progress. With proper supervision and rules to discourage cheating and off-task behavior, the club would give students who need extra support a better chance to succeed and start the next school year prepared.

I want to become a cardiologist because I hope to save lives while making treatment affordable, so that no one has to suffer as my uncle did. He was born with a congenital hole in his heart, but my family could not afford the operation when he was a child, so he grew up with the condition untreated. The problem worsened when he was finishing high school, yet even in pain he continued to study and managed to pass his exams with excellent marks. Many people face similar situations — they need urgent medical care but cannot pay for it. That is why I am determined to change things and help others have at least one chance to live a healthy life.

Cardiology is also a profession that offers good financial rewards. Because my family lacked the money to treat my uncle, I feel driven to build a career that allows me to earn enough to help people in need. By becoming a successful heart specialist, I can provide quality care and still charge patients reasonable fees. I want to ensure that families will not have to endure the same hardship and worry that mine did before I was born. I am ready to work hard and do whatever it takes to bring comfort and security to my loved ones.

There are fewer doctors who specialize in heart conditions than in many other medical fields, and that shortage affects patients everywhere. Many people live with undiagnosed heart problems like my uncle did, simply because they do not have access to a specialist or they are asked to pay fees they cannot afford. When the number of heart surgeons is limited, the cost of treatment often rises, leaving patients with no option but to continue their daily lives while their condition worsens. If this situation continues, many will not get the care they need and could miss out on the chance to enjoy life fully. I plan to become a heart surgeon who charges fair prices so that both I and my patients can be content — I will have a meaningful career and those who come to me will receive treatment they can afford.

In conclusion, becoming a cardiologist is a major goal for me. I want to save lives without placing a heavy financial burden on patients. I will do everything I can to prevent others from experiencing what my uncle went through. Because there are too few specialists and some charge high fees, I hope to offer a different path: skilled, compassionate care at prices people can manage. I dream of making the world a better place where health is not only for those who can pay a lot.

Some people ask if it is better to work with a group or alone? Everyone has different opinions about the benefits of working in a group or working alone, some people prefer working alone and others prefer working in groups. I believe that the best way for the people to improve is by working in groups because they learn more and understand better.

First, working in groups help the people to improve in school or at work because they learn new things. For example, listening other ideas and points of view from their partners. One day my English teacher make groups of four in class and gave each group a piece of paper, then he put some questions in his board and told us that we need it to answer them as a group, when we finish the teacher told us that we were going to discuss it, then when each group discuss their answers with the class we all realized that each group had different opinions, ideas, and points of view. Each group learn something new from each other.

"Everyday we all learn new things in life".

Second, working in groups help the people improve because they will understand better. For example, asking their partners if they have a question or didn't understand really well. My history teacher gave the class an assignment that we need it to completed by the end of the class, when the teacher gave the instructions i didn't understand her really well, then i ask one of my partners if he could explained to me again in order for me to understand it, be able to give my opinions and help my group.

"We could do more if we all help each others".

Many people believe that is better to work alone because they will concentrate more. For example, they will not get distracted with anyone and will finish the work faster. A friend of mine has always work alone because she said that when the people is working in groups they tend to start talking, distract others, don't do their work and by the end of the hour only got a couple of questions done. However, this argument is meaningless because if they don't understand really well, then they would not have a partner who could explained to them what they are doing. For example, not finish their work because they got stuck in a part. Not having someone to discuss the work with could be hard sometimes.

In conclusion, there's a lot of benefits when working with a group. Some of the others benefits that working in groups has are; making new friends, having the opportunity to learn more about your partner, and learn more about yourself. Having to work with someone is a good idea because you don't have a lot of pressure about having to finish the work on time or not having idea what to do. Even though some people say the opposite, i believe that working in groups is better than working alone.

People often debate whether it is better to work alone or in a group. While some prefer working independently, I think collaborating with others is more effective because it helps people learn more and gain a deeper understanding.

For instance, in one English class my teacher divided us into groups of four and gave each team the same set of questions to answer. I remember a history lesson when the teacher announced an assignment that I did not fully understand. In conclusion, group work brings many advantages. Besides learning more and understanding tasks better, it can help you make friends, learn about others, and discover new strengths in yourself. Working with others also reduces stress because you do not have to handle everything by yourself. For these reasons, I believe collaborating in groups is more beneficial than doing everything alone.

Offering distance learning as an option for students to join classes from home through online platforms or video calls might seem useful, but I believe that most students do not gain from studying this way for several reasons.

First, many students are easily distracted at home and cannot concentrate on their lessons. Electronic gadgets, especially mobile phones, often take their attention away from class. In addition, other people in the house can interrupt them — parents, siblings, or visitors — which breaks their focus and slows their progress. When this happens regularly, students fall behind and may even fail courses. For example, my cousin moved to the United States with his brothers and sisters and was allowed to take one subject online. At home he could never find quiet time because of the constant noise and worries caused by his siblings. As a result, his study routine collapsed and he ended up failing that course.

Another problem is that some students struggle to learn independently and find online lessons boring. Without a teacher physically present to explain things and answer questions, many learners find the material hard to understand. Also, virtual classes lack the natural back-and-forth communication of face-to-face lessons, which makes them less engaging. Students who need to be active in class quickly become passive and lose interest. I know a friend who had this experience: he felt bored and could not follow online classes. Even drinking strong coffee did not help him stay awake, so he would often switch off his computer and sleep, which harmed his academic results year after year.

Finally, distance learning can make students exhausted. After a full day at school, some have additional chores or paid work to do before they can attend an online session. This leaves them tired and less able to focus when the class begins. I personally face this: I walk half a mile to get home, finish tasks, do my homework and take a shower before the online lessons start. By then I am often too tired to learn effectively.

For these reasons, I conclude that distance learning does not benefit many students, because the distractions, lack of interaction, and fatigue reduce their academic performance.

Some schools allow students to use cell phones during lessons for educational activities. While some people support this, I think phones should be banned from classrooms. They are a major source of distraction, reduce real learning opportunities, and should be treated as a privilege rather than a right during class time.

First, phones often divert students’ attention from lessons. Instead of following the teacher, many pupils will begin texting, browsing social media, or playing games. Once students get used to taking out their phones in class, they are more likely to ignore instructions and miss important information.

Second, having phones in class can prevent students from learning in the traditional, effective ways. Writing notes by hand helps many students remember material better and perform well on tests. Classes that include hands-on activities or peer teaching give valuable experience that phone use can interrupt. Without active participation, students lose chances to practice skills and discuss ideas with classmates.

Finally, access to a phone should be a privilege, not something expected during lessons. Even with strict rules, some students will find ways to avoid them. Teachers should be able to decide when phones are appropriate, and allowing them freely during class makes that control difficult.

In conclusion, classrooms should remain phone-free. Phones cause distractions, reduce meaningful learning, and are a privilege that can undermine classroom management. Schools should not permit their use during lessons.

I have often judged classmates or coworkers quickly and decided they seemed unfriendly. Sometimes they react the same way, which creates a cycle of coldness between both people.

Their behavior may improve because they finally feel comfortable or find someone to talk to. At the same time, remember that some people simply have different personalities, and you should accept those differences.

In short, don’t judge someone only by the first meeting. If you reach out and try to understand them, you can change the way you see each other and help them grow.

What might happen if older and younger students were paired together? Mixing age groups would be beneficial because younger pupils could pick up new study techniques, receive practical advice about high school, and learn ways to handle stress.

First, pairing students from different grades helps them exchange learning methods. Older students can model how they approach homework, solve problems, and organize their work. Younger students can ask questions when they are stuck, and the older ones can explain solutions step by step or show useful shortcuts. Seeing how a more experienced student studies a subject can give younger learners fresh ideas and strategies they can use themselves.

Second, older students can prepare younger ones for what high school will be like. They can describe how much homework to expect, how classes are different, and which subjects or activities might be fun to try, such as drama or sports teams. They can also point out skills that are important to develop before moving up, like time management or note-taking. Hearing these tips from someone who has recently been through the same transition makes the information more realistic and less intimidating.

Finally, older students can teach younger students how to cope with stress. They can share test-taking strategies, explain how they plan their study time, and show how they set up a workspace that helps them focus. Simple routines and study habits can reduce anxiety and improve performance. Learning a few coping techniques early on will help younger students face heavier workloads and more pressure in high school.

In short, pairing older and younger students has clear advantages: it allows them to learn different study methods, get honest advice about high school, and discover effective ways to manage stress. This kind of cross-age interaction is a valuable experience that can make the move to higher grades smoother and less stressful.

Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home?

Schools should be places where students feel secure and supported, but there are many kinds of schooling. I believe learning from home has both pros and cons. One clear advantage is fewer distractions: without noisy classmates or people who do not take education seriously, a student can focus and finish work on time. In traditional schools some pupils get sidetracked and may have to repeat a year, which can be embarrassing. At home, repeating a course can feel less public and stressful because there is no visible stigma from peers.

Another benefit of home learning is the potential for more individualized attention. With one-on-one instruction, students can progress at their own pace. In contrast, teachers in busy classrooms cannot always give every pupil the help they need. That said, many children would rather attend school in person but cannot for reasons like a physical disability or public exposure as a celebrity. Those students may feel isolated at home and miss the routine and social life of a school, which is important for mental health and social skills.

Home-based education can also be more flexible and sometimes faster. Students who are self-motivated can move ahead without waiting for the whole class. However, there are practical drawbacks: public schools often provide free meals and resources, while homeschooling usually requires paying for internet, a computer, and food. These costs can make home education expensive for some families, even though the long-term benefit of learning and obtaining a diploma may justify the investment.

In the end, whether a student studies at home or attends a school building, both paths offer valuable opportunities. Each has its strengths and weaknesses, but both can help a person gain knowledge and achieve qualifications that will be useful in the future.

Human life today depends heavily on technology; it is hard to imagine getting through a day without it. From the moment we wake up until we go to bed, we rely on devices and systems that make daily tasks easier. Technology has come a long way since the earliest inventions, such as the first telephone, to the advanced gadgets we use now. While there are downsides—like the risk of overuse by young children—technology brings many important benefits that improve our lives.

The story of modern communication began with Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone. His early model looked nothing like the slim phones we carry today. It was large and mainly meant to sit in a home rather than be portable. At first, telephones were not essential for everyone because people were used to living without them. Over time, inventors improved Bell’s idea, making devices smaller, lighter, and capable of more than just voice calls. Competition among inventors and companies led to many different brands and types of electronics. In the early 2000s, Apple introduced the iPhone, which quickly became popular worldwide. Since then, Apple and other companies have produced a wide range of products—smartphones, headphones, tablets, laptops, smartwatches, and portable chargers—that people use in everyday life.

Although technology can have negative effects, especially when children begin using devices too young and become dependent on them, it also offers advantages for young learners. Parents play a key role by deciding whether and how children can use electronic devices. Many families set limits on screen time and restrict content to keep kids safe. When used correctly, educational programs and apps can help children learn colors, shapes, language, and basic social skills before they start school. Resources like ABCmouse are examples of fun, interactive tools that make learning enjoyable and can give children a head start without replacing real-world interaction.

Technology surrounds us at home and in public places. Inside our houses we use security cameras, thermostats that control heating, air conditioners, refrigerators and freezers that preserve food, Wi-Fi routers, televisions, and smart doorbells. Outside the home, technology is visible in the cars we drive, traffic lights that organize flow, and GPS systems that guide us to our destinations. If someone needs information for a class assignment and cannot visit a library, they can find what they need instantly on a phone or computer. Medical devices in hospitals are another vital example: machines monitor patients, assist during surgery, and help newborns survive. These life-saving technologies show how important innovation is for human health.

Technology keeps advancing, and researchers and engineers continue to develop new methods to treat illnesses, understand their causes, and prevent them. As devices and systems improve, we will be better prepared to face future emergencies and reduce risks that once led to serious harm or death. While it is important to manage the negative aspects, the overall impact of technology on the world has been overwhelmingly positive.

In summary, technology has become an essential part of modern life. It connects us, supports learning, keeps us safe, and saves lives. Although we must be careful about dependency and set sensible limits—especially for children—the benefits of technological progress affect millions, if not billions, of people in many useful ways.

They teach us what went wrong, give us experience, and force us to rethink our plans so we can improve. Not giving up and trying again are essential parts of turning failures into success.

One way failure helps us is by showing where our mistakes were. Human history is full of instances where earlier errors led to later improvements. For example, the League of Nations was established after World War I to keep peace, but it failed to prevent another global conflict. Learning from that failure, countries created the United Nations, which has been a much more successful institution for international cooperation. This case shows how recognizing past faults can lead to better solutions.

Perseverance is another important piece of the puzzle. Giving up ends any chance of success. Take the footballer Pelé: many people doubted his potential when he was young, and he faced repeated criticism and setbacks. He also suffered a knee injury during his first World Cup, and doctors thought he might not play again in the tournament. Still, he worked hard every day, kept training, and when given the opportunity later in the competition he proved his worth. Pelé’s story demonstrates how refusing to quit and persisting after failure can lead to great accomplishments.

Trying again after a setback is perhaps the most practical link between failure and success. Once you have analyzed what went wrong, you are in a better position to attempt the task again with improved methods. Space exploration illustrates this clearly. Countless rocket launches have failed—some ended in explosions or mission losses—but engineers studied each mistake and corrected the designs. Over many attempts and refinements, humans have succeeded in sending satellites, probes, and people into space and to other planets. These achievements came only after learning from many earlier failures.

Some people argue that failure is not necessary for success. They say that you can succeed on the first attempt, that failures do not always teach useful lessons, and that repeated setbacks can destroy a person’s enthusiasm. I think these points are mistaken. While first-time success happens, it is uncommon for complicated goals. Most failures do contain lessons if we take the time to analyze them. As for losing enthusiasm, that is often a choice: individuals can decide to keep pushing forward or to stop. Choosing to stay motivated is part of turning failure into progress.

In conclusion, failure is not the opposite of success but a part of its process. It reveals errors, builds experience, and encourages us to make better plans and keep trying. If we maintain our enthusiasm and learn from each setback, Churchill’s idea makes sense: moving from one failure to another without losing hope is often how we finally reach success.

I do not agree with the statement "A problem is a chance for you to do your best." While some people learn and grow from difficulties, many do not, and sometimes problems cause lasting damage. I believe success often comes from making fewer mistakes, not from relying on problems to bring out your best.

First, not everyone learns from their errors. Some people forget past mistakes or repeat them without adjusting their behavior. For example, my brother failed his driving test and then failed again when he retook it. Also, problems can create fear or anxiety that makes it harder to perform well later. I once missed a tackle in a football game and became so worried about repeating it that the next time I hesitated and did not play confidently.

Second, some mistakes have consequences that cannot be undone, so a problem does not always give a second chance to shine. Very serious errors can change a person’s life permanently; for instance, someone who is executed for murder cannot correct that decision. Even less extreme choices can be irreversible: my sister refused to accept an award she was offered, and she cannot go back and accept it now.

Finally, I believe a reliable way to succeed is to avoid making many mistakes in the first place. Repeated errors often lead to more problems and make it harder to reach your goals. My cousin wanted to become a lawyer but encountered so many difficulties that she left law school. When people accumulate failures, they can become overwhelmed trying to fix everything at once. I experienced this during a test when I tried to solve several hard questions at the same time and ended up confusing my answers.

In conclusion, I disagree with the idea that every problem is an opportunity to do your best. People do not always learn from their mistakes, some problems cause irreversible harm, and achieving success is often easier when you minimize errors rather than depend on them to improve you.

A year ago I believed I wanted to study business. At first I tried hard, but the classes were very difficult for me and I failed. I felt terrible and did not know what to do. I began to think that business was not the right choice, but I was afraid it was too late to change. Then I spoke with my counselor and she told me I could switch to a different program. I made that change and now I have found a course of study that fits me better. I might still change again because I can be undecided sometimes, but I also learned that this is normal. I have talked with classmates and friends who had the same experience. Some people claim that it is good for students to decide on a career early because they can choose high school classes that will prepare them. I disagree. I think it is a bad idea for young students to commit to one career because they may choose the wrong path and because many young people are still undecided about what they want to do.

People who support early commitment say it helps students pick helpful subjects in high school. However, many students do not see that this pressure can harm them. I often hear friends say a class is too hard but they keep it because it “matches” their chosen career. These students seem unhappy and stressed. Forcing oneself to stay in a program that does not fit only causes more problems.

First, young students can choose a career that is not right for them. Children often admire their parents and want to follow in their footsteps, even attending the same university. Sometimes parents pressure their children to study a particular subject. As a result, students may pick a field they do not enjoy or where they do not have interest or talent. When they realize the mismatch, they may feel unhappy, stressed, or want to leave school. The problem is not the difficulty of the subjects but the wrong choice of career. This mismatch can lead to low motivation and poor mental health.

Second, many young people are undecided about their future. There are so many careers to choose from that it is hard to pick only one at a young age. Students may discover new skills or interests later that make another career more suitable. Even if someone is good in one area, they might prefer a different type of work after trying other classes. Making mistakes is part of learning; trying different subjects helps students understand their strengths. Some students even study two areas or switch programs and eventually find their path. Experimenting with different options can be very helpful.

In conclusion, I believe it is unwise for students to commit to a career while they are still young. They might choose the wrong field because of family pressure or simply because they are not yet certain about their interests. Allowing students time to explore different courses will help them make better decisions and feel more confident about their future studies.

Working in groups is often better because teachers believe students gain more from projects and class tasks when they collaborate. In a team, people can discuss ideas and help each other solve problems, while working alone can be hard when you face a question you do not understand. Many students feel that group work supports one another and improves learning through conversation. Teachers also think that talking and cooperating with classmates helps students develop skills, since groups encourage more activity and attention during lessons.

This preference for teamwork comes from the idea that people can share answers, explain difficult points, and build more convincing work together. When you do not know how to solve a problem, group members can talk it through and reach a solution, much like a sports team that trains and plays together. Another example is in cartoons such as Looney Tunes, where characters like Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck perform together and create funny scenes by working as a team.

On the other hand, some students prefer to work alone. They believe they can achieve more independently and think more deeply without discussion. Both students and teachers sometimes find that individuals produce better work on their own and only ask the teacher for help when necessary. For instance, some singers choose to work alone because they feel they can create better songs and plan their careers by themselves.

In conclusion, some people enjoy group work while others like working alone. Teachers usually allow either option, so students can choose what suits them best and have time to complete their work whether they prefer collaborating or working alone.

My friend was being homeschooled after she suffered a lot of bullying and felt she could no longer stay at her old school. She wanted to quit, but her counselor suggested online classes instead because her grades were strong and they wanted her to finish and have better prospects. Many schools now offer distance learning, where students join lessons from home via the internet or video calls. I believe homeschooling or online schooling is a valuable option for students who face problems at school, for those thinking of dropping out, and because it can be quicker and less stressful.

First, online schooling helps students who are dealing with difficult situations at school. If you are constantly fighting with classmates, being harassed or bullied, having conflicts with teachers, or feeling that school is a waste of time because you need to work, studying from home can remove you from those negative situations. Taking classes online can keep you safer, reduce stress, and help you stay on track to graduate without further setbacks. If you are struggling, it is important to speak with your school counselor or parents about the possibility of switching to online classes or being homeschooled.

Second, distance learning can help students who might otherwise drop out. Many young people leave school for financial reasons — they feel they must work to support their families — or because of unexpected life events like teenage pregnancy. Without support, these students often give up on their education. Online classes give them a second chance to continue studying while handling other responsibilities, which can improve their job prospects and lift their spirits knowing they can still graduate. I once worked as a student counseling aide and saw this happen: a boy came in, upset and planning to drop out, and was even about to leave his laptop at the office. When a counselor asked him why he wanted to leave, he said he needed to help his family financially. The counselor told him that he could take courses online, something he had not realized was an option. That news made him feel hopeful again.

Finally, homeschooling is often more flexible and faster. You can do your lessons when it suits you, pause if you need a break, and return when you are ready. This flexibility tends to make learning less stressful than attending regular school. A science teacher at SCHOOL_NAME mentioned that a high percentage of students feel stressed by homework and deadlines in traditional schools, while only a small fraction report stress when learning from home. Being able to study in a comfortable environment, organize your day, and avoid commuting gives you extra time and freedom, which many students find attractive.

Some people argue that online learning is bad because you might not have a teacher physically nearby to ask questions. However, many online programs offer one-on-one lessons with an instructor, which can actually improve focus compared with sitting in a classroom full of distractions. For these reasons, I think online schooling is a useful option for students facing problems at school, for those at risk of dropping out, and for anyone who needs a faster, less stressful way to complete their studies.

Haile G/Selasie, one of the most famous long distance runners of all time, did not pave his way to success because he was born with it. He came from a poor family, and walked a long distance to his school everyday. When he started running, he was not good at all. He worked day and night to get to where he is. And when he speaks about his past, he tells the story of how he failed again and again a lot of times but he never lost his passion for his dream. And now he is one of the richest people in Ethiopia and one of the best record holders of Marathon.

Success is a dream for most and a reality for only a few. When it comes to how success is achieved, it creates a great question in all our minds and that is,"How can I be successful?". Some say that success is achieved by going through failures without giving up or without losing hope. That is a truly arguable idea and some might think different. But I fully agree with that idea.

The fact that almost all of the masterminds that are known for their creations of the bulb, physics theories, telephone and many more of the things we take for granted at the moment told the story of how they tried and failed many times than they count. And that is one proof of the point that success doesn't come without failure.

There might be some people that argue this point by pointing out that many people have tried and failed and tried again but it didn't help them achieve their dreams. That is a good point but the fact is that failing is not the only thing that determines your success, but failing and not being discouraged is what really counts. If we plan to achieve a goal, we shouldn't lose our excitement for that specific thing we're doing, we should rather be more encouraged to try harder and to find another way to make it work.

For example, when we first built a rocket,it wasn't done in a day or in the first try. Engineers tried to fix the problem in the mechanical part. Scientists tried to see if their calculations was wrong or if the combination of the chemicals didn't work and many others tried to fix it but they failed more than a couple of times. By not giving up though, it was a success at last.

It might not always seem like it but failure leads to success. The main point is not giving up and not losing our enthusiasm. As the saying goes, "If you fail once, try and try harder". Never give up on your dreams and don't be discouraged by failure.

Did you know that joining after-school clubs and activities can help students learn in many ways?

Whether a student signs up for a sports team, drama, or music practice, these activities teach important lessons beyond the classroom. Many options are both educational and enjoyable, such as athletics, visual arts, and musical groups.

Sports come in many forms—football, basketball, soccer, and more—so students can find something they like. Playing sports teaches about fitness and the importance of staying healthy. It also keeps you active and in shape. For some students, excelling in a sport can lead to scholarships for college. Beyond those benefits, sports are just fun: you spend time with friends, compete against other schools, represent your school, and work toward trophies and awards. Some teams travel to other states for competitions, which gives students a chance to see new places and meet different opponents. Having family and peers cheering at games creates a strong sense of community, even when the contests get intense.

Art activities include drawing, painting, crafting, and other creative practices. For students who find it hard to put feelings into words, art becomes a way to express emotions through color, shape, and hidden meanings in their work. Art clubs often visit museums and galleries, which can inspire students and help them grow as artists. They may enter contests, win prizes, or have their pieces displayed around the school. Creating art based on mood or experience can be enjoyable and help students develop a passion for their skills. Art is deep and meaningful, and experimenting with color and texture lets students explore without strict limits.

Many students choose to join bands, orchestras, or singing groups because they enjoy performing. There are different kinds of musical ensembles—wind bands, string groups, choirs—each offering its own experience and instruments. Music is another form of art that not everyone can master, so playing or singing gives students a special sense of achievement. They might attend concerts, meet well-known musicians, perform on stage at school events, and take part in music competitions where they can earn awards. Over time, students often improve and may be able to upgrade their instruments.

In conclusion, after-school activities are not only fun but also educational. Learning does not have to be only serious or stressful; enjoying the process helps students want to learn more. While education is important, developing a love for learning is even more valuable for success. Clubs and activities teach new skills every day and help build thinking and social abilities, though sometimes it is still necessary to be focused and disciplined.

Some students prefer working alone because they avoid disagreements about project choices and do not have to coordinate with unfamiliar classmates. Even so, most students choose group work since it lets them divide tasks, exchange ideas, and support one another. Group work tends to be more efficient, and for these reasons I would rather work with others than on my own.

First, students often face many projects during a term, which can be overwhelming—especially when a single major project counts for a large portion of the grade. In a group, the project can be split into parts and shared among members, making the overall workload lighter for each person. Everyone brings different skills, so tasks that are hard for one student might be easy for another. This way the team can finish the project faster and with better results.

Second, collaborating with classmates helps develop cooperation skills that are important in the workplace. Many employers expect employees to complete tasks together because different people contribute different knowledge and abilities. Employers often emphasize teamwork to increase productivity. Teachers should recognize this and give students chances to practice working in teams, which also helps students learn from each other.

Working in a group can also increase students’ confidence. Discussing ideas with peers helps clarify understanding and find the best ways to approach a task. Schools frequently allow students to stay after class to meet, which helps groups that cannot meet at someone’s home. Working with others also benefits students who have trouble meeting deadlines, since teammates can offer support and encourage them to finish on time.

In conclusion, students should not be forced to handle large projects entirely on their own when group work is an option. Because companies rely on teams and teamwork usually produces better outcomes, teachers should encourage group assignments to help students improve grades, meet deadlines, and gain cooperation skills. Group work gives a variety of perspectives and makes it easier to do well in class.

If you see someone close to you being a bad influence, then one must learn to not replicate those actions, but instead make good decisions their selves.

In life, people often rely on others to build the person they are, but in reality, it's better to rely on yourself instead of others to make decisions because it makes us rely on ourselves more often than we do, helps us avoid bad influences, helps you grow as a person, and strengthens our minds. All of these things are why we should all grow up by making our own choices and decisions instead of mindlessly doing what everyone else does. People have all the power in themselves to be who they want to be. You're no one other than yourself after all, and that's the most important thing to think about when choosing our own character traits.

John Lubbock, the British naturalist and politician, wrote that a person’s character is something they themselves must decide. I agree with this view because individuals should learn to make their own choices instead of depending on others to choose for them.

From our earliest years we are shaped by family, friends, and society, but that does not mean we should simply accept whatever others expect of us. People are different, and following the crowd without thinking can prevent us from becoming our true selves. Making decisions independently builds resilience and boosts self-confidence. When we rely on our own judgment, we become more capable and less dependent on other people’s approval.

It is also important to remember that influences are not always positive. Those close to us — parents, guardians, or peers — might model behavior that is harmful or wrong. If we do not question what we are taught, we can adopt harmful habits without realizing they are wrong. That is why using common sense and thinking for ourselves is essential: we must evaluate whether actions are right or wrong and choose the path we believe in rather than copying others blindly. When we notice negative examples, we should deliberately avoid repeating them and choose better alternatives.

Some may argue that following others is useful when you feel lost. While guidance can help, attempting things on your own — even if you fail at first — often leads to greater growth. Simply imitating others is like being spoon-fed; it prevents learning and leaves you unprepared to handle tasks alone. By making our own choices and dealing with the consequences, we develop independence and strengthen our mental resolve.

In short, relying on ourselves to form our character helps us resist harmful influences, encourages personal development, and builds mental strength. For these reasons, we should take responsibility for who we become and actively shape our own character instead of drifting along with the crowd.

Students can study alone or in groups. While working alone may help some people concentrate, I believe group work is more advantageous. Teamwork allows students to exchange ideas, improve their performance in class, and learn from one another.

One main advantage of group work is that classmates can share their thoughts. When pupils collaborate on a project or homework, everyone can contribute different opinions and solutions. They can also divide tasks for research, gathering more information than a single student might find. By discussing and combining their ideas, the group usually produces a stronger result than if each person worked alone.

Group work also helps students do better in class. By talking with peers, students can discover what they do not understand and ask questions together, which often makes explanations clearer. Teachers also benefit because answering one question for a small group saves time compared with repeating the same explanation many times. In addition, seeing other students' mistakes helps individuals avoid those errors themselves, which leads to fewer misunderstandings and better grades.

Finally, students learn a lot from the people they work with. If someone struggles with the material, others can explain it in a different way until it makes sense. Working together on research and tasks gives everyone a chance to practice skills and gain confidence. This mutual support helps each member understand the subject more deeply and prepares them better for future studies and work.

In summary, although studying alone has some benefits, working in groups is more helpful overall. Group activities let students share ideas, raise their classroom performance, and learn from each other, which makes school more productive and prepares them for the future.

Should schools switch to a four-day week with 10-hour days? I disagree. This plan would cause problems for students who work, reduce opportunities for supervised studying, and likely increase personal electronics use at home rather than saving energy.

Many students have jobs after school. They need time to commute and change before work starts, and if school days become much longer, working in the evenings would be impractical. Instead of getting a full shift, they might only manage two or three hours, which cuts their earnings. For older students who help pay bills or save for college, losing those hours can be a real hardship. For that reason, keeping the usual five-day schedule and maintaining a reasonable daily length makes more sense.

Teachers often assume that students will use the extra day off to study on their own. But not all students can work independently at home. Some rely on school resources like libraries, quiet study spaces, or teacher help to finish assignments and prepare for tests. If school ends late in the day, those who normally stay after to study will no longer have that option, and this could lead to lower grades and missed deadlines. Schools should preserve the schedule that supports learners who depend on supervised or guided study time.

Supporters argue a shorter week saves energy and money, but they overlook how students spend an extra day at home. With a full day off, many young people will spend more time on phones, streaming services, and gaming — all activities that use electricity. At school, device use is limited to breaks and lunch, so being at school can actually reduce the amount of time students are using personal electronics. Cutting a school day may not produce the expected energy savings if students simply shift their energy use to the home.

For these reasons, I believe schools should keep the current five-day week and maintain typical school hours. This arrangement helps students who work earn more money, gives others a place and time to study with support, and may prevent increased electronic consumption at home. Although the idea of saving costs is attractive, it does not outweigh the practical disadvantages many students would face.

People who value self-reliance define it as the need for each individual to follow his or her own instincts and ideas. There is a quote that says, "If you want to go fast go by yourself, but if you want to far go with someone else". As the quote says, I think that it's very important to have someone to guide us throughout the course of our lives. I agree that seeking for guidance from experts to make wise decisions can have a great impact in our lives. Experts and authorities can provide us with advices to make good decisions in life and accomplish our goals more easily.

First of all, having someone to guide you throughout the decisions you make in life could help you accomplish a goal a lot easier. For example, when I was in middle school I used to think that doing individual work was faster and easier. However, I noticed that most of my classmates who worked in groups finished all the assignments in less time than I did. This experience showed me the importance of always having someone to give you their opinion to accomplish a goal quickly and avoid wasting your time. Thus, seeking for guidance from experts can help you achieve any goal you set in life and avoid wastig your time on making wrong decisions.

In addition, you will learn and gain experience if you have someone expert to guide you. For example, having an expert guiding you will allow you to see his different points of view and learned from his teachings. This will allow you to learn from his teachings and experiences and reflect about them. Furthermore, relying on with an expert will give you the chance to learn new lessons and in the future give you the opportunity to make your own decisions. Finally,

you will learn how to make wise choices by learning from the lessons that an expert or authority could offer you.

For instance, when I was 10 years old I really wanted to make my own decisions that I thought were best for me. In whatever manner, I rarely got to choose my own decisions because my brother was always there telling what decisions to make. As I grew older I understood that my brother was just guiding me through the right path. Because my brother had experienced many of the situations I went through, he was able to help me and in many occasions avoid me from failing. Therefore, experts and authorities will be there to not let you fail and always look for what's best for you.

In conclusion, seeking from guidance from experts may not give you the freedom to make your own decisions, but it will help you accomplish your goals rapidly and efficiently. Since experts have already experienced many rough situations in life, they will know how to make decisions that will benefit us in the best way. Furthermore, in the course of the path with an expert guiding you, you will learn a lot of things that will help you make better choices. Finally, you will avoid wasting a lot of your life's time trying to follow your own instincts and ideas.

Can older and younger students work together? I believe they can, and schools should create programs that pair older students with younger ones. Older students usually have more experience and knowledge, so they can support younger students with classwork. Working together also helps both groups improve their teamwork skills, and they can share useful tips and advice with each other when needed.

One big benefit is help with schoolwork. Because older students have studied topics for longer, they often understand them better and can explain difficult ideas to younger students. For example, my older sister is very good at math. Whenever I have trouble with homework, she sits with me and shows step by step how to solve the problems. After she explains it, I usually know what to do and can finish the rest of the exercises on my own. In this way, older students can act as helpful tutors and make learning easier for younger students.

Another advantage is learning how to work in a team. Teamwork is an important skill because it teaches you how to communicate with others and brings new ideas to a project. When older and younger students collaborate, both sides can improve their ability to plan, share tasks, and support each other. I remember doing a school project with an older student who guided me through the whole process. They helped me decide where to begin and how to finish, and they corrected mistakes kindly while showing me better ways to do things. That experience made the project stronger and helped me learn to cooperate and organize my part.

Older and younger students can also exchange useful life tips and personal advice. I was in third grade when I prepared for my first standardized test and felt very anxious. My older brother gave me advice to stay calm and focus on the questions. He helped me review the material, and his support made a big difference. Older students often know how to handle school stress, and younger students can offer fresh perspectives too. Sharing this kind of advice helps both groups grow.

For these reasons, schools should set up programs that match older students with younger ones. They would support learning, teach teamwork, and provide practical advice when students need it. Pairing students across age groups is a simple way to help everyone succeed.

Choosing a career is an important decision that shapes much of a person’s life. With so many options available, deciding early can feel difficult. I believe students should start exploring and committing to a career at a young age because it helps them understand what the job really involves, lets them discover activities they enjoy, and reduces stress when they become adults.

First, getting involved with a career early helps students learn the true nature of the work. Many young people have only a vague idea of what certain professions require. For example, someone might think being a doctor is only about treating patients, without knowing the years of study, the practical skills needed, or the daily routine. By taking part in internships, job shadowing, or hands-on programs, students can see firsthand what tasks are involved and what skills they must develop. They can also research careers such as dentistry or engineering to learn the educational steps and qualifications needed. Accessing real experiences and reliable information gives students a clearer picture and helps them make better choices.

Second, early career involvement often leads students to find activities that they genuinely enjoy. Many teenagers spend their free time without a clear purpose and can become bored or unhappy. Joining after-school clubs, career workshops, or volunteer positions related to a field can introduce them to hobbies or interests that keep them motivated. For instance, a student who helps in a school science lab might discover a passion for research, while another student working in a community clinic could find satisfaction in helping others. These experiences can turn into meaningful pastimes or even lifelong careers.

Third, deciding on a path sooner can ease future worries. Teenagers commonly feel unsure about what they want to do as adults, and this uncertainty can make finding a job difficult and stressful later on. If students spend extra time while still in school learning about specific careers, gaining experience, and preparing academically, they are less likely to struggle after graduation. Knowing what direction to take reduces pressure during the transition to higher education or the workforce, because students will have a clearer plan and relevant experience.

Some people argue that students are too young to choose a career because they lack enough knowledge. While this concern is understandable, avoiding any early exploration can actually increase problems later. Participating in career fairs, taking relevant classes, or joining practical programs are ways for young people to become better informed and more prepared.

In conclusion, students who begin exploring careers early will understand the realities of different jobs, discover activities that make them happy, and face less stress when starting adult life. Early engagement in career activities gives them valuable information, enjoyable interests, and greater confidence about their future.

Ralph Waldo Emerson famously argued that remaining true to yourself is one of the greatest achievements when society constantly pushes you to be someone else. If you are unsure about that idea, consider why personal freedom and independent thought matter. You ought to be able to choose your own path and act and think for yourself.

Belonging to a group and trying to please the people you care about can be positive. Shared values and behaviors help form a moral framework, and being part of a community gives you a clear identity and a feeling of connection. It can be satisfying when the things that define your community—shared beliefs, interests, or traditions—make the group recognizable. That pride in your community can resemble patriotism or loyalty to a cultural group.

Still, you should feel free to question your community when its views are based on faulty reasoning. When a group treats certain ideas or authorities as unquestionably true, this becomes dogma. In those cases, it is important to challenge assumptions rather than accept them without thought. Likewise, sometimes friends and family may give advice that is mistaken; you should be prepared to think critically about that guidance. That does not mean you should distrust them completely—listen to them and keep faith in your close relationships on most matters—but be willing to disagree when their advice seems wrong.

Ultimately, you should be yourself and use your own judgment. Gather the qualities that make you different from others, and confidently express your own will and character. Independent thinking combined with respect for others gives you a balanced, authentic life.

Because it can be done after a good night's sleep, students rise up in the morning fresh and have a flexible time schedule. The students can work around their parents' schedule instead of the parents working around the students' schedule when it is time to do some distance learning. Some students have trouble working at school because they cannot understand the material at the pace set by teachers; the students cannot always work at that pace. Distance learning allows students to work at their own pace and on their own schedule. Additionally, there are no misguided rules about tardiness or how to dress. Instead of worrying about the rules, the students can focus on their studies. Distance learning can improve certain students' learning process by having a more available schedule and by letting them learn in their own way.

When taking a test or notes at school, there are many distractions that can make students lose focus. This is another reason that learning from home benefits students. Learning from home doesn't have the distractions a classroom has. As a result, students won't lose focus on their work, resulting in better grades. One reason students get distracted is that they are in a class where others are just fooling around, which makes those who want to stay focused feel uncomfortable. If a student learns from home, they will feel more relaxed and comfortable and won't stress about work. In school, you are stuck at a desk listening to the teacher for six hours and have a limited time to eat and take bathroom breaks. But there is another way around it: if you are home, you can eat and do what you want when you want. Because of this, students will feel less pressured and get better grades than they would have if they were in school.

There are still a few reasons not to do distance learning. There are many more opportunities with public and private schools. People from different colleges don't go to students' homes to advertise their career options. Making friends from home would be difficult without social interaction. Public and private schools are great places to socialize during free time. If everyone goes home to attend school, funding for public schooling will fall and teachers will lose their jobs because of budget cuts. In public and private schools, depending on the teacher, cheating is hard to do. On the other hand, in schooling at home students can easily look up the answers on the internet on a different device. So for all that matters, you choose not what you want, but what you need.

Students should be offered classes online or at home because it is less distracting and less stressful. The flexibility of the time students are allowed to complete work would benefit the mental health and grades of students. With a more flexible schedule, students would be more likely to succeed and make good grades. Even though socialization in the school environment allows students to make friends, the conclusion of the argument was that it is highly doubtful that the lack of interaction could affect the student in adulthood. Many students all over the world successfully take some, and even all, classes from home. In the near future, school systems and all districts should provide distance learning.

Would it surprise anyone to learn that studying from home can lower students’ stress levels? Much of the pressure young people feel comes from having too much schoolwork and tight deadlines. Many students complain about the amount of homework they receive, and when they study at home they often feel less burdened by assignments. Letting pupils follow their own schedules can increase their motivation and responsibility. Home education also gives students extra time to study and plan their work, and as a result many achieve better grades than they did in a traditional classroom.

One clear benefit of homeschooling or distance learning is its flexibility. Lessons can be done anywhere and at times that suit the student. After a good night’s sleep, learners can start their day feeling refreshed and choose hours that match their family routines. This can be easier for parents too, since families can arrange learning around each other rather than forcing parents to fit around school timetables. Some students struggle to keep up in a classroom where the teacher’s pace is fixed. Distance learning lets students move through material at their own speed and return to topics they do not understand. There are also fewer strict school rules about lateness or dress, which means students can concentrate more on studying instead of worrying about regulations. For these reasons, a flexible schedule and a personalized learning approach can help some learners improve.

Classroom distractions are another reason home learning helps. In school there are often students who disrupt the class, and noise or activity can make it hard for others to focus. At home, learners usually face fewer interruptions, so they can stay on task and produce higher-quality work. Some students feel uncomfortable or anxious when classmates joke around or misbehave; studying from home can create a calmer, more comfortable environment. In addition, school days can feel rigid: long hours at a desk with limited breaks for food or the restroom. At home, students can take breaks when they need and eat or move around on their own timetable. This reduced pressure often leads to better performance on tests and assignments.

There are, however, some drawbacks to distance learning. Traditional public and private schools offer more opportunities in certain areas. College recruiters and program representatives sometimes visit schools to share information about future paths, and it is harder to receive that kind of outreach at home. Making friends can also be more difficult without regular in-person interaction; schools provide important social time. If many families switch to home study, public school funding could drop and teachers might lose jobs because of budget cuts. In addition, cheating can be easier when students take exams or do work remotely and have access to the internet. Ultimately, families will choose the option that fits their needs, not only their preferences.

Students should have the option to take classes online or at home because these arrangements can be less stressful and less distracting. Giving learners flexible deadlines and schedules can benefit their mental health and lead to higher grades. While school social life has value, the lack of in-person interaction does not necessarily prevent success later in life. Many students worldwide already complete some or all of their studies from home successfully. For these reasons, school districts should consider offering distance learning as a regular choice.

Attending classes from home through online video conferencing is not an ideal approach for students because it does not offer the same learning experience that being physically at school provides. If remote attendance becomes widespread, learners will miss chances to form close relationships with peers and teachers. Online learning also makes it easier for some students to be less committed to their studies, since they lose the direct guidance and oversight that schools offer.

First, studying from home is different from learning in the classroom, and this difference can harm academic performance. In school, students often treat homework, quizzes and exams more seriously than they do at home. When a question arises in class, students can ask their teacher immediately and receive a clear explanation with examples. This immediate interaction helps them understand difficult points and avoid confusion. In-person schooling also allows students to stay after class for extra help, retake quizzes under supervision, or use school learning centers where classmates and tutors can assist with assignments. These options are less available or less effective when classes are delivered entirely online, and as a result, students may leave gaps in their knowledge that hurt their grades.

Second, regular face-to-face classes help students develop communication and social skills that are hard to build when everyone studies remotely. At school, classmates discuss ideas, share concerns and enjoy social moments like lunch. These interactions can inspire students, create friendships, and sometimes lead to strong bonds that feel like a second family. Schools are places where young people can find support not only academically but also personally, from teachers, counselors and friends. Many teenagers face stress, anxiety or depression, and daily life at school can distract them from problems at home and provide access to guidance from caring adults. Learning from home, by contrast, can leave students feeling isolated and bored, without the same opportunities for informal conversations and emotional support.

Third, online classes can reduce students’ motivation and sense of responsibility. At home, there is no teacher physically present to remind them to pay attention, finish tasks or stay awake during lessons. The lack of routine and direct supervision can lead some students to neglect homework or skip studying, thinking they can catch up later. Group work is another example: when students work together in person, they learn from each other, encourage effort and share responsibility; seeing peers work hard often motivates others to try harder. When group activities are handled remotely, this positive peer pressure and mutual support are much weaker, so students who are prone to procrastination may fall further behind.

In conclusion, attending classes online from home is not the best method for most students because it does not replicate the benefits of being at school. Remote learning limits academic support, reduces chances to build social and communication skills, and can lower students’ commitment to their studies. For these reasons, traditional in-person schooling remains a more favorable option for many learners.

I agree with Duke Ellington’s idea that "A problem is a chance for you to do your best" because problems often provide opportunities to learn and perform better in the future.

First, facing a difficulty can help you improve next time. Imagine you are struggling with a subject at school and you work hard on an assignment due the next day. If you receive a low grade and cannot resubmit the work, this experience can teach you what went wrong. You can use that feedback to study differently, manage your time better, or practice the skills you lacked so you will do better on future tasks.

Second, a problem can lead to unexpected positive results. For example, during a group project some members might not participate. In such a situation one student could step up, organize the group, and encourage everyone to share ideas. What began as a difficulty with uncooperative teammates could become an opportunity for leadership and better teamwork. The group might finish the project stronger because someone took the initiative.

Third, problems let you show your best effort by seeking help and finding solutions. If you are stuck on a topic, asking a teacher or a knowledgeable classmate for guidance can give you new ways to approach the problem. By actively looking for help and trying different strategies, you demonstrate commitment and often reach a better result than if you had given up.

In conclusion, I agree with the quote because problems can teach you lessons for next time, create surprising opportunities like leadership, and allow you to demonstrate your best by finding solutions. Seeing difficulties as chances to improve helps you grow and perform at your best.
