We gain more when we act than when we wait for things to happen. When we keep busy and put effort into our goals, we grow and usually receive some kind of return for our work. Many people call this return a "reward." When we work toward something we want, we build self-confidence because we see that effort leads to results. That confidence then encourages us to try even harder. Some people believe that good things can come without any action, but in my experience real achievement comes from doing something — working hard, trying your best, and taking steps toward your goals. If we do nothing, we cannot expect to reach anything important in life.

Taking action leads to growth. I remember when I was in sixth grade and wanted to join the math competition that Generic_Name organizes every year. Only the fastest students were allowed to enter, and Generic_Name held math review sessions after school to help students prepare. I could not attend those reviews because I had paid swimming lessons after school and could not miss them. I was disappointed, but I decided I would do whatever it took to qualify. I began waking up two hours earlier to practice math problems and used my lunch breaks to go to the library and study. That sacrifice paid off: when Generic_Name posted the list of competitors, my name was on it. My mother always told me that failing is part of learning; when you try again you are less likely to repeat the same mistakes. Her words and my effort taught me that persistence and hard work lead to success, and I will remember that lesson for the rest of my life.

Helping others and putting time into good deeds also brings rewards, even if those rewards are not material. When you give patiently and kindly without expecting anything in return, you often gain inner satisfaction and sometimes form meaningful connections. I once saw a hungry child searching for food in the street, and I felt the urge to help. Giving him something to eat made me feel useful and made him happier in that moment. Another time, I helped my mother clean the house of a 79-year-old woman who lived alone and whose only companion was her dog. After that first visit I asked if I could come on weekends to keep her company. I did not expect how special our relationship would become. She was one of the kindest people I have ever met and used to call me her granddaughter. When her son in Generic_City decided to take her away, I was very sad, but she comforted me by saying I would always be in her heart. That experience taught me that small acts of kindness can change your life and leave a lasting impression.

Working toward goals also builds confidence. When you finish a large number of assignments at school or persist through difficult tasks, you realize you are capable of more than you thought. That feeling of self-belief helps you face important decisions and challenges. I remember when my sister was unsure whether she could succeed in the college major she wanted. She was afraid of failing, but she decided to pursue it anyway and worked hard. I admired her determination because she trusted herself and moved forward despite her fear. Her confidence helped her achieve what she set out to do. Sometimes we need to put aside the fear of failure and choose confidence; it can be the difference between staying stuck and making progress.

Overall, doing something produces more than waiting for luck or expecting things to fall into place. By taking action we grow personally, we may bring happiness to others, and we gain confidence in our abilities. People should know that they can improve their lives and reach their goals, but they must be willing to work for them. Hard work, belief in oneself, and consistent effort are the keys to getting what you want in life.

I do not think graduating a year early is a good idea because senior year offers important experiences you can’t easily replace. During that final year students meet with college representatives, learn how to improve resumes, and receive guidance that helps them plan for the future. Many schools organize events, senior activities, and traditions that create lasting memories and help develop social and leadership skills. Losing all of that means missing a chance to get ready for the next stage of life.

Another reason I oppose early graduation is that some students would use it as a way to escape responsibility. Those who choose this path might be the same teenagers who skip classes, ignore assignments, or are often late — in short, students who haven’t shown strong commitment to school. High school is not a race, and success does not come from leaving early but from steady effort. Some early graduates go straight into the workforce and end up in low-paying, unstable jobs, such as entry-level positions in fast-food or retail. A proper education can open the door to better, more secure careers.

Students who consider finishing in three years need a clear plan, especially if they want to go to college. Many colleges expect applicants to complete four years of high school and review transcripts for maturity and consistent effort. This means that some institutions may view a three-year diploma with suspicion. For those not pursuing higher education, they must still have a solid strategy to support themselves. Some young people do not realize how important school is until later, and that understanding is often the key to future success.

If I were to accept early graduation programs, I would only support them for students who are truly ready. Some students may be so focused and prepared that they want to start college or a career sooner; that is a valid choice for a few people. However, this opportunity should be reserved for those with excellent attendance, strong grades, and a clear plan.

In conclusion, school districts should be cautious about allowing students to graduate a year early. Students ought to earn this option and prove their readiness. Senior year provides a final push that helps prepare young people for adult life, and giving it up too soon can limit both experience and future opportunities.

Many people argue that technology is like an extra limb we carry with us everywhere. Devices such as mobile phones are part of daily life and we rely on them constantly. While technology does bring some benefits, it also reduces face-to-face contact and creates constant distractions. Although supporters claim that technology improves our lives, I believe its impact is mainly harmful.

It is true that technology has positive uses. We depend on it for work: many professions require computers and other tools that make tasks faster and more efficient. Phones and messaging apps help us stay in touch, so we can check on friends or arrange meetings quickly. In education, laptops and smartphones give students easy access to information and help teachers prepare lessons and assignments. In these ways, technology has become an important part of modern life.

However, technology often distracts us. In schools, phones can disturb lessons: when students use them without permission, they pay less attention and their grades can fall. For many people, phones are not just a convenience but an addiction—constant checking interrupts concentration. Driving while using a phone is another serious example: texting, choosing music, or glancing at a GPS can take your eyes off the road and cause accidents. These distractions show how technology can make people lose focus and ignore their surroundings.

Mobile devices also reduce real human contact. Many people walk with their heads down, absorbed in their screens, and miss simple interactions. Teenagers in particular may spend more time online than talking to family members or friends, which weakens basic social skills. Some young people struggle to start a conversation in person or feel uncomfortable meeting someone face-to-face. It is worrying that technology can take away our ability to connect normally with others.

In conclusion, despite the clear benefits technology offers, its negative effects are significant. We cannot remove technology from our lives now, but the problem lies in how we use it. If people limited their use to what is necessary, we would likely see fewer distractions and better social relationships. Technology itself is neutral; our habits are what make it harmful.

One goal I really want to reach is losing weight, and I have three important reasons for this. First, I want to improve my health. Second, I hope my success could encourage other people who struggle with their weight. Third, losing weight would likely make me feel better about myself and less self-conscious.

To expand on the first reason: being at a healthier weight would reduce the risk of many medical problems. For example, obesity can lead to conditions like diabetes. Carrying excess weight also makes everyday activities harder; some people find it difficult to walk or move comfortably because of the extra burden. I sometimes struggle with exercises in gym class that others find easy, and I know this is partly because of my weight. For these health reasons alone, I want to make a change.

The second reason is that I want to be a positive example for others who are overweight. If I manage to lose weight, it might give hope to someone else, showing them that change is possible. I believe that helping one person can set off a chain reaction: the person I encourage could then motivate others to try, and so on. Thinking that my success could inspire other people gives me extra motivation. If my efforts not only improve my life but also push others to take healthier steps, I would feel proud.

My third reason is about my self-image. I have some insecurities, and my weight is one of them. When you are insecure about something, you often wish to remove that source of doubt. Losing weight would probably improve my confidence and reduce how self-conscious I feel. I expect that feeling better about my body would positively affect many areas of my life, from social situations to daily moods.

In conclusion, losing weight is one of the main things I want to accomplish. The health benefits, the chance to inspire others, and the boost to my self-esteem are the biggest reasons behind this goal. While there are other reasons I could mention, these three are the most important to me. Achieving this goal would help me and, I hope, might help others too.

School takes up a large part of most people’s days, but extending the school schedule would reduce time students and teachers have for other important activities. For example, at a typical public middle school in Maryland, classes often run from 8:15 a.m. until 3:00 p.m., so students are in school for about 7 hours and 25 minutes. That is already a long day of listening to lessons and concentrating. The school board should not lengthen the school day because doing so would cut into time students need for homework and studying, for after-school activities such as sports and clubs, and for volunteering in their communities.

Longer days would leave students with less time to finish homework or review class material. Most middle school students attend six to eight classes each day, and many of those classes assign work to be done at home. If the school day were extended, students would come home later and have fewer evening hours to complete assignments carefully. As a result, homework might be rushed or left undone, which could lead to lower grades and more missing assignments.

Extending school hours would also interfere with participation in after-school activities. Many young people need at least an hour a day of exercise, but not every student takes physical education, and a typical P.E. class lasts only about 45 minutes. That is often not enough to meet recommended activity levels. If the school day were lengthened by another hour or more, students who are on sports teams would have less practice time and less chance to rest and recover. The same is true for clubs — extracurricular groups let students explore interests they don’t encounter in regular classes, and reducing the time available for these pursuits would limit those opportunities.

Finally, lengthening the school day would make it harder for students to complete required community service. Many programs and graduation requirements include volunteer hours; in my own experience I needed to complete 75 hours of service, doing tasks like helping a teacher with younger students or organizing a classroom before the year began. These activities are often scheduled after school and can take a couple of hours at a time. A longer school day would crowd out the time needed to meet these obligations and could cause some students to miss their required hours.

For these reasons, it is more practical for the school board to keep the current schedule rather than add more hours. Students need time outside of class for homework, exercise, clubs, and community service, and extending the school day would take that time away.

Should schools permit students to use cell phones in class for learning, or should these devices be banned entirely? I believe that phones should be allowed in classrooms for educational uses. Some teachers and administrators argue that phones distract students and therefore must be restricted. While distractions are a concern, I strongly feel that allowing controlled phone use supports learning and offers important practical benefits.

First, cell phones can be useful academic tools when used properly. From personal experience, having a phone in class lets me quickly look up facts, access online resources, and take photos of notes or board work when the teacher agrees. These features make studying later at home much easier and more effective. In contrast, not having a phone can itself become a distraction: students may sit and worry about being without it until the next break, making it hard to focus on lessons. For example, a friend of mine had her father confiscate her phone for an entire school year to force her to study. Instead of improving, she reacted by skipping responsibilities and spending time with friends, and eventually failed her classes. This shows that forbidding phones completely can backfire and harm learning.

Phones also improve safety. In emergencies, a phone can be the quickest way to call for help. If there's an intruder, a lockdown, a fire, a severe storm, or another dangerous event, being able to phone emergency services or family members is critical. Allowing phones makes it easier for students to report problems and let loved ones know they are safe.

Finally, banning phones often makes students hide and use them secretly, which can be more dangerous than supervised use. Given the learning benefits and the safety advantages, I think the positives of using phones in class outweigh the negatives. In short, schools should permit cell phones for educational purposes, since they are convenient learning tools and often faster than other devices like laptops.

Allowing students to consider their future careers early helps them form ideas about what they want from life. When young people start thinking about jobs that suit their interests and strengths, they begin to prepare mentally for the path ahead. This preparation can change their outlook, helping them discover what truly motivates them and where they might find success. Deciding on a direction takes time, but giving students chances to explore career options while they are still young can lead to meaningful choices if they use those opportunities wisely.

Continuing their studies while clarifying their goals is important. Young students are often imaginative and open-minded; if encouraged to reflect on their future, they can make thoughtful decisions for a good reason. In some communities, pupils as early as eighth grade are offered ways to choose a study path and adjust their plans. This marks a shift from a playful childhood mindset to one where teenagers begin to take responsibility for decisions. Through this process, many students learn what they want to pursue and get clearer about their place in life as they prepare to graduate with purpose.

Early career thinking can bring positive change for teenagers. It shows they are capable of making stronger, more constructive choices, and schools can track how ideas develop from middle to high school. While some students pick sensible and promising careers, others find even better fits later on. Choosing a career is not only about selecting a job title; it is about exploring what teenagers imagine for their future and building confidence that they can achieve it.

Still, asking children to decide on a career before high school is not without problems. Not everyone wants to focus on long-term study at that age, and for some it may feel like a waste of time or pressure. Many young people change their minds once they reach high school, and some who once thought they had settled on a direction find they no longer enjoy it. This can lead to dropping out of college or abandoning a field that no longer fits them. Even so, if students discover they can work hard and succeed, they may still build good lives—even in careers different from the ones they imagined in middle school. The process of exploration often continues until they find what truly suits them as adults.

Because of these mixed outcomes, families and teachers should support students thoughtfully. Parents need to listen and understand their children, while teachers should guide them on what skills and subjects they need to reach their aims. When schools and communities provide appropriate courses and advice, students gain the knowledge and confidence to choose paths that benefit them. In the end, careful guidance and opportunities to explore make early career thinking more valuable and less risky for young people.

Some schools now permit students to use cellphones in class for learning activities. Allowing phones in the classroom can benefit students who already use them often. In other words, it can make schoolwork feel more manageable and help learners complete tasks, view their grades and assignments, and improve how they learn.

First, having access to a phone at school can help students finish classwork or homework. Many classes assign a lot of work, and students sometimes need extra time during the day to complete it. Also, personal problems can make it hard to concentrate at home. For example, there are times when I feel distracted or stressed and cannot focus on my homework. Some students also have after-school jobs and are too tired in the evening to study. I work after school sometimes and know how difficult it is to get everything done when you are exhausted. For these reasons, being allowed to use a phone during school could give students the chance to do their assignments when they are more alert.

Second, phones let students check their grades and see which assignments they have missed. When students are absent or busy at home, they may not know about a missing task. Many students forget homework too; for instance, I sometimes start chores at home and suddenly realize it is late and there is no time left to work. If students could look up assignments during class, they could ask the teacher for permission to complete the work or get extra help. I have a friend who struggles with math; he often checks assignments on his phone and then asks the teacher for clarification. This approach has helped him understand lessons better and improve his marks.

Some people worry that phones will distract students because they might text, play games, or ignore the lesson. While this can happen, it does not have to be the norm. If teachers use phones in productive ways, students can learn in ways that feel engaging. For example, some teachers let students play educational trivia on their devices, which makes learning fun and easier to remember. Older generations may worry that more technology harms thinking skills, but when used correctly, phones can support learning rather than replace it.

In conclusion, allowing cellphones in classrooms can have a positive impact by helping students complete work, check grades and assignments, and learn more effectively. As a generation familiar with technology, we can use these tools to gain better knowledge and succeed in school and life. The choice to use technology wisely can make education more accessible and effective.

Having something to do on a regular basis gives us valuable experiences, helps us complete tasks, and provides direction for future goals. The experiences we gain over time keep us motivated and help us decide what we should or should not pursue. By contrast, being idle means missing chances to learn and grow, which can harm long-term plans. I believe that staying active leads to greater achievement and influences how we live our daily lives.

One reason I think regular activity matters is that it exposes you to new knowledge or work that interests you. Formal schooling plays an important role for many people, but it is not the only route to success—effort and commitment matter a lot. In many places, employers value experience as much as formal qualifications, so getting involved in practical work can open doors. Staying busy in this way reduces inactivity and builds useful skills, whether you are helping in the neighborhood, serving meals to the homeless, or mentoring younger children. The key is being willing to put yourself forward and to commit time to these activities.

Another reason is that doing things gives you a sense of purpose and achievement that is hard to get otherwise. From my own experience tutoring children after school, I always left feeling proud and happy that I had contributed to my community. That satisfaction showed me how important it is to teach youngsters the value of effort and persistence. Playing lacrosse has taught me a similar lesson: when I miss my goal time for running a mile, I push myself to improve. Sports have helped me realize that feeling fulfilled takes time and work. These activities motivate me to keep going and remind me that investing energy and time leads to real accomplishment. Doing something you enjoy and seeing progress gives you both personal satisfaction and a clearer purpose.

Finally, staying active shows that you recognize responsibilities and opportunities, though many people do not take them seriously. I feel fulfilled when my actions show others that I care, not just when I try to look good. Many factors affect our choices, but taking part in useful work helps others see your importance in their lives and strengthens relationships.

In conclusion, the more effort you invest, the more accomplished and satisfied you tend to feel. This can boost your self-esteem and demonstrate your dedication to others. Many people I have spoken with say their communities helped them grow and inspired them to give back. Even small actions can make a difference compared with doing nothing. Working toward what you need versus what you want teaches you about both personal fulfillment and social responsibility.

Trying to learn by yourself is less motivating than learning in a group. That is why swimming with friends makes the whole experience enjoyable.

Also, one of the most important things is that you could make a good influence in someone else's life and teach him/her how to find their path in their own way. No matter what happens, you always have to follow yourself.

When you learn more about yourself, it means that you do not just learn things that you already know about yourself; you also learn new things that you did not know about yourself. For example, one day you go to the basement of your house, which is really big, and put on some good music. While you are listening to your favorite songs from your playlist, you are dancing according to the tempo and doing the dancing moves that you usually do. After dancing for a long while, you suddenly let the music take control over you and you make a back flip without practicing it before. You are very surprised because you did something that you did not know you could do, and after that you keep practicing that move and perfecting it until it comes out natural. That is how you learn more about yourself.

You are acknowledging different methods to be better than yourself; this means you will do whatever is right in order to become a better person. For example, Robert Downey Jr used to have a terrible life by consuming drugs and other things that got him in trouble with the law. He even went to court for all the messy things he did. After a long time of taking bad decisions, he finally decided to make things better for the people who cared about him and especially for himself. It took him over 5 years to get back on his feet; with his own effort and the support from his family and friends, he started to make a good difference for the world. Right now, Robert is one of the best actors in Hollywood; he has an excellent life with his wife and kids by his side, and is a great influence for millions of people. That is how you acknowledge different methods to be better than yourself.

Some people say that you are copying someone else when you try to be yourself. However, they are wrong because you actually are listening to those tips that you have heard and following them under your own perspective. That way you are definitely writing your own script while at the same time giving the deserved credit to the person who gave you those tips. For instance, when you are trying to get a girl that you met at a party but you have no idea of what to do in order to get her attention, you ask your friend for some advice to accomplish your goal so you do not go through a bad experience. He tells you what to do exactly and shows you with some women at the party, and now you have some ideas of what you can do. So before you reach out to that girl, your friend tells you "be yourself all the time" and you get the courage to talk to her. After following those examples in your own way, the girl started to have deep feelings for you, everything worked out a lot well, and you made some influence for some of your friends who need that kind of help. That is how you follow your own script with your own terms.

In conclusion, it is very important that you be yourself all the time because it shows that you do not need somebody in order to be somebody. You learn about yourself so you can get to know your own person more than you can know about an anime character. You acknowledge new ways to become better than yourself. Like if you were in a videogame, you are going to the next level slowly. You make a good influence by doing things as right as possible and you give people some benefits out of it. To be yourself you have to do what your gut tells you to do if you think it is going to give some benefits in some way.

Which is better when trying to become someone new: making it up as you go or sticking strictly to a plan? I believe it is more valuable to stay true to yourself and allow some improvisation. This approach helps you discover who you really are, learn different ways to improve, and can also inspire others. No matter what, it is important to act in a way that fits your personality.

First, improvising helps you learn about yourself in ways you could not predict. You do not just repeat what you already know; you sometimes surprise yourself with new abilities. Imagine you are alone in a large basement, playing music and dancing the way you always do. After a while the music leads you, and without having practiced it, you attempt a back flip. You are shocked to find you can do it. Then you practice that move and make it a natural skill. This kind of unexpected discovery shows how trying new things can reveal talents you did not know you had.

Second, experimenting with different approaches lets you improve and change for the better. People who decide to work on themselves choose the methods that suit their lives and goals. A strong example is Robert Downey Jr. He had a difficult period involving drugs and trouble with the law, but he eventually chose to change. With effort and support from family and friends, he rebuilt his life and career over several years. Now he is a successful actor and a positive example for many. His story shows that by choosing to change and finding the right ways to do it, a person can reach a much better place.

Some say using advice from others means you are copying and not being original. That view misses the point. Listening to guidance and then applying it in your own style is not imitation; it is learning. You take ideas that work and adapt them to fit who you are. For instance, if you want to talk to someone at a party but do not know how to start, you might ask a friend for tips. After watching your friend show you some ways to act, you borrow the ideas but speak and behave in a way that feels natural to you. You are not a copy; you are using helpful examples to create your own approach. If things go well, you can even help friends by sharing what you learned.

In conclusion, being yourself and allowing room for improvisation is important. It enables personal discovery, opens up different paths to self-improvement, and can have a positive effect on other people. Using advice from others does not make you fake if you adapt it to your own personality. Trusting your instincts and growing in your own way will lead to the best results.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea because learning to master something can help you move forward in life. When you focus on your goals and follow your own path, you give yourself the best chance to succeed. It is important not to let others make decisions for you, since their choices might not match what you want. If you believe in yourself and keep working, you can achieve a lot—even when people tell you that you are not good enough and should quit.

Mastering an important skill or goal often leads to real opportunities. For example, finishing school is a form of mastery that can open the door to a new job. With a job, you can improve your situation, gain more experience, and grow professionally. For many people, having a supportive family is also a big advantage because they can provide help and open up possibilities. In general, improving what you can and trying your best are key steps to becoming better and reaching new places in life. If you do not try hard, it will be difficult to reach your aims or develop as a person.

Following your dreams matters because it can turn your ambitions into reality. If you pursue your passion, you might become a famous singer or reach a high office, like president. Thinking creatively and taking risks can help you do things you once only imagined. For instance, with confidence and practice, you could become a professional soccer player without showing off or acting overly proud. People may try to bring you down, but if you keep faith in your abilities, you can recover and continue moving forward.

Refusing to accept other people’s decisions for your life is not always easy, but it is necessary. You should try to keep the focus on your own wants and plans, even when others pressure you to change course. Negative comments or bad advice can make you give up on goals you set for yourself. Try not to focus on what critics say about how you should act or what you should try. Instead, work hard to prove your capabilities and make those who supported you proud by achieving what you planned.

When someone offers positive encouragement, it can change how you think and act. I agree that we must keep improving ourselves and not give up on our dreams. Do not simply follow other people’s choices; make decisions based on what you want. If you set clear goals and work to reach them, you will find new opportunities and move ahead in life. It is not easy, and you might need help at times, so accept advice from people who truly want to see you succeed. With determination and the right support, you can accomplish the things you set out to do.

Having a homework club at school is a great idea. I believe every school should offer a homework club at least three times a week. Such a club helps students understand topics better, become more engaged with classmates, and feel more confident about their work. There are many useful activities students can do at homework club, for example finishing a group project, studying for a quiz or test, or getting homework done early.

When more students attend, we can also help each other and share ideas, which creates a friendly learning community. Projects are usually harder when you do them alone, but at homework club you can get the help you need and finish work more quickly. If you are stuck, going to homework club is a good choice to find support.

Many students find it hard to concentrate at home, so studying at school with teachers and classmates can keep you focused. I suggest everyone try homework club at least three times a week to get help before tests or with other difficult topics. With regular attendance, you will be better prepared and more likely to do well on exams.

Finally, homework club helps you finish assignments early. Teachers explain tasks in detail, often giving more examples than in regular class, so students understand the material better. Math, science, history, and English teachers all offer useful explanations that make homework easier to complete. By doing work at school, you can free up time at home and avoid last-minute stress.

In short, a homework club is a very valuable resource. It helps students learn more about subjects, boosts confidence, and encourages cooperation among classmates. Homework clubs support completing projects, studying for tests, and finishing homework early. We can make homework clubs a part of every school, but this requires students to attend and teachers to volunteer their time. With the help of dedicated teachers and motivated students, homework clubs can become a strong and helpful community.

This inner drive helps you form good habits, such as studying more or arriving to work on time, which are important for long-term success.

I have been through a tough six months, but that experience has not made me give up. On the contrary, it has made me more determined and independent, and I want to use that strength to support others.

Even though the world often pressures us to change, maintaining a positive attitude, becoming independent, and believing in yourself are essential. These qualities not only help you succeed but also enable you to lift up others. Stay confident, stay motivated, and never give up.

Many people expect students to decide on a career by the time they start high school, and some even take jobs early to prepare. I believe this is not a good idea. Choosing one specific profession at a young age can pull students away from their schoolwork, interfere with their education and development, and stop them enjoying other activities that are important for their wellbeing.

First, committing to one job while in high school can distract students from their studies. High school becomes more demanding each year, with heavier homework loads and more difficult exams. Students need to concentrate on learning in order to graduate and gain admission to a good college. If they spend a lot of time on an after-school job related to a future career, they may not have enough time or energy left to do homework and study for tests. For example, a student working at a hair salon after classes might arrive home too tired to prepare for an upcoming exam or finish assignments. Over time, this leads to lower grades and can damage confidence and motivation.

Second, teenagers are still learning and growing, so they should use high school to explore and build a strong educational foundation. High school years are a time to discover interests and to gain the knowledge needed for higher education and better job opportunities later on. If a student locks into a particular vocation too early, they may miss chances to study other subjects or to change their plans as they mature. For instance, a young person who chooses a specific career path before fully understanding it might find that their real passion lies elsewhere after attending college or trying different classes. Sticking too soon to one job could prevent them from reaching the dream career they would have preferred.

Third, taking on a fixed job can take away time for hobbies and recreational activities that give students energy and balance. Enjoyable pursuits — such as sports, music, or clubs — help young people stay healthy, reduce stress, and develop social skills. If a student spends most of their free time working, they may have no opportunity to continue these hobbies. Imagine a student who loves playing football and gains confidence and happiness from the sport. If they must also juggle school and a job tied to their future career, they could lose that positive outlet and feel overwhelmed.

In conclusion, high school students should concentrate on their studies and personal development rather than committing to one career too early. By focusing on education, exploring different interests, and keeping time for enjoyable activities, they are more likely to reach a suitable college and later find a fulfilling job that fits their true interests.

I agree with Emerson's idea about the importance of individuality. I feel it is freeing to be myself in a world that often tries to shape me. The world pushes me toward certain identities and expectations, but staying true to who I am lets me choose my own path. For me, that freedom includes exploring beautiful natural places like forests, blossom trees, hills, and other scenic spots.

Even though society frequently attempts to define me, nature offers a chance to be authentic. Visiting a place full of flowers or walking among blooming trees can be an inspiring experience. I enjoy seeing different kinds of flowers and the colours they bring. Watching trees in bloom would be especially pleasing to me and would make me appreciate the simple wonders of the world.

A forest is another place where I can feel myself. At first glance a forest might look like only trees, but when I pay attention I notice small changes and new things. I would observe how life in the forest transforms over time: fresh fruit appearing on branches, flower bushes opening, and young plants growing. These changes remind me that everything is alive and developing, and that encourages me to stay true to my own growth rather than becoming someone else.

There are also times when being myself means seeking wide views from hills. I prefer hills to tall, windy mountains because the gentle slopes give a clear view without the cold. From the top of a hill I can look over open grassy areas and scattered trees. That kind of landscape seems simple and timeless, like scenes from long ago.

Being able to remain who I am in a world that often wants to change me is important. Emerson’s words resonate with me because they capture how the world pressures us to be different, while also reminding us to value our own uniqueness. For these reasons, I agree with his statement.

Some people believe that first impressions cannot be changed. They think we form judgments based on how someone behaves, what they say, and how they look, and these impressions stay with us. I agree with this view because our actions, language, and appearance strongly shape how others see us.

Firstly, behavior when you meet someone for the first time matters a great deal. The saying “actions speak louder than words” is true in many situations. The way you act during an introduction often becomes the image people keep of you. If you are rude or disrespectful, others will quickly decide you are unpleasant to be around. That is why it is important to be polite and calm during first meetings—try not to give a bad impression right away.

The words you use also affect how people judge you. Avoid using offensive language when meeting someone new; it makes others think you lack social skills. You can choose to speak more formally or casually depending on the situation, but speaking clearly and with respect helps build trust. Try not to stammer too much; while a little nervousness is normal, frequent stumbling over words can make people uncertain about you. Some people may allow a second chance if you make a small mistake, but it is better to present yourself well initially. Also, be careful with excessive hand gestures when first introduced; they can distract or confuse the other person.

Appearance is another major factor in forming first impressions. How you look on the outside often influences how people interpret your character. People tend to notice appearance quickly, and a messy or inappropriate look can lead them to assume negative things about you. Conversely, a neat and suitable appearance can make someone more willing to get to know you. In many cases, appearance plays a larger role than words or actions in those first moments.

There are times, however, when people understand that a single meeting does not tell the whole story. Someone might be having a bad day, and friends can see they are not always like that. Still, such understanding is not guaranteed, and many first impressions remain strong.

In conclusion, I believe first impressions are very hard to change. Your behavior, speech, and looks teach others about you, and people learn from these signals. Because you meet new people often, it is important to be careful about how you act, what you say, and how you present yourself.

Which is better: working in a group or working by yourself? I believe working in a group is more useful for several reasons. Group work offers help from others, lets you split tasks so no one carries the whole load, and helps you learn more about the subject. Below I will explain these points in more detail.

One big advantage of group work is getting support from classmates. If you are stuck on something, a teammate can notice and offer assistance. They can explain the problem in a different way and share strategies that make the task clearer. For example, in math class my teacher paired me with a friend for an assignment when I didn’t understand the concept. She sat with me, walked me through different methods, and showed me how to solve the problems. Without her help, I probably would have been confused and unable to finish the work.

Another benefit is that group members can divide the work so the project moves faster. When everyone has a clear role, the workload feels lighter and you don’t have to handle everything by yourself. This reduces stress and makes it easier to complete tasks on time. Last week in history class, I was in a group of four where each person had a specific job. I was responsible for finding the citations, Chloe gathered the main information, Marcus looked for pictures, and Sean searched for videos to support our points. Because we divided the tasks, we finished our project during class and earned an A.

Finally, working in a group lets you discover new information and ideas you might have missed alone. Other members often bring different knowledge or perspectives, which can deepen your understanding of the topic. This shared learning helps everyone, not just for the assignment but also for upcoming quizzes or tests, because discussing the topic together reinforces what you have learned. Group work encourages conversation and new insights that make the subject clearer.

In short, group work gives you extra help, allows tasks to be shared, and exposes you to more information than working alone. These are the main reasons I think collaborating with others is more beneficial than always working by yourself. Group projects give you advantages that are hard to get when you try to do everything on your own.

The school would use more paper and bathroom supplies, and students might need new agendas with additional bathroom passes. With longer days, there could be more conflicts among students; tiredness often makes people more irritable and prone to fights. If the day were extended by one and a half hours, dismissal would overlap with the time elementary students get out of school, which could increase traffic and the risk of car accidents because of more buses and cars on the road.

Students already wake up early, and adding time to the day would make them even more exhausted. For example, a young person who moves out of their parents’ home and starts living independently must look after themselves. Another example is students selecting their subjects for the next school year. Secondly, people who choose their own path are often happier in the long run. Self-esteem grows from real achievement. I believe students should not be rewarded for weak work because that stops them from improving. Teachers exist to help learners develop, and if a student knows they could have done better yet still receives praise, they may decide there is no need to try harder and their confidence will stay shallow.

First, doing well on an assignment and feeling proud of that success builds genuine self-esteem. When a student earns high marks through effort, they see that they are capable, and that strengthens their belief in themselves. Difficult tasks that require persistence should be recognized, because praise in those cases reflects real progress. Students who push themselves to reach a higher standard are more likely to keep growing instead of remaining complacent.

My second point is about how praise affects future effort. If a student hands in work that is below their ability and gets praised anyway, they may assume the same minimal effort will always be enough. That encourages laziness and prevents skill development. Teachers should not give empty compliments for poor work. Instead, they should talk privately with the student, say something like, “This is a start, but it isn’t your best — I know you can do better,” and offer guidance on how to improve.

Some may argue teachers should be strict because otherwise students feel neglected. I agree: letting lazy work slide can make students think the teacher does not care. But if a student brings concerns to the teacher, the teacher can respond and follow up, showing attention and support. This personal engagement helps students learn and motivates them to try harder.

In conclusion, true self-esteem comes from accomplishing meaningful work, not from praise for minimal effort. Praising low-quality assignments keeps students at that low level because they believe it is acceptable. Teachers who challenge students and provide honest, constructive feedback help them build real confidence and improve their skills.

College is something not everyone is looking forward to as a teenager, but some of us are. If we start hanging around with the bad types of people, it can drag us to the deepest part of an ocean; in other words, there's no coming back up to where you used to be. Not saying you shouldn't be friends with that type of people — I mean you can — but in my perspective don't get involved with them as much as your other friends are.

Secondly, tutorials are a big part of Avid. They show your teachers and peers around you how much you know and how strong you are and the effort you put into tutorials. You get in front of the group and explain what you are having problems with, but it also helps you learn from your peers and it's like sharing the brain cells. Online Learning

Who doesn't want to be left in the house all day using an electronic device with online access? Although students save money and time by taking classes from home. It is not beneficial to learn online because students lose focus of what they are learning and tend to easily get distracted when they're in their house, students can't have a one on one conversation with a teacher nor discuss with classmates, and students could also face technical difficulties when attending online classes from home.

Losing focus has a big impact in learning. For example, my friend Generic_Name sent me a text message last month, right when I started studying for my history mid-term exam. I responded back to Generic_Name's text, and without realizing we kept on messaging past midnight. This shows how easily students get distracted at home with a cellular device and how easy it is to lose focus. The next morning I decided to get to school an hour early and review one on one with my teacher.

Secondly, taking classes online doesn't just mean you don't have a physical teacher or instructor that you can question lively, but also means that it will be challenging to find answers to your questions. I remember in my sophomore year a kid in our econ class named Generic_Name was really sick for a while so he had ended up taking classes online. Generic_Name was a straight A student, always was first to answer the teachers questions and he also used to ask questions. Thankfully Generic_Name healed towards the end of the year and I asked him if he benefited and if he recommends attending classes from home. The straight A student Generic_Name said it was a real challenge to take the class online and he finished the class a month after he should have with a B- average. Generic_Name had also said that one of the most difficult parts about attending a class online was his laptop not functioning at all times, and not having a teacher you can talk and converse with one on one.

Finally, using your personal computer and internet connection can always be an issue. You can't always depend on your computer, not just the computers but even people aren't perfect. Another main problem Generic_Name had when attending classes online was his laptop and network connection. Generic_Name explained that he always faced technical difficulties. When his laptop wasn't functioning right, the only thing he could do was to stop the lesson and wait for his dad to get the laptop repaired, which took time. Each month, either his laptop or internet connection would not cooperate, so he finished the class a month later than everyone.

In conclusion, Everyone would like to save money and time by taking classes from home. But getting distracted, not asking your teacher questions when you need to, and wasting money on laptop repair is not worth it at all. Learning from a far distance could also be an option but when asking if it is beneficial, we can say that it is not by looking at the listed reasoning.

Who wouldn't enjoy staying home and using a device with internet access all day? Although taking classes from home can save students money and time, online learning is not truly beneficial. Students often lose concentration and become easily distracted at home, they miss chances for one-on-one interaction with teachers and active discussion with classmates, and they may suffer technical problems that interrupt their studies.

Losing concentration greatly harms learning. For instance, last month I began studying for my history midterm, and right away my friend Generic_Name sent me a message. I replied, and before I knew it we were texting late into the night. This shows how simple it is to be sidetracked by a phone or other devices when studying at home. The next morning I had to arrive at school an hour early to review the material in person with my teacher because I had not prepared properly.

Another major drawback is the lack of direct, live contact with a teacher. Attending class online does not just remove the physical presence of an instructor; it makes it harder to get quick answers or to have a meaningful discussion. In my sophomore year, a classmate, Generic_Name, fell ill and had to join our economics class remotely for a while. He had always been a top student who participated actively and asked questions in class. When he returned to school I asked whether learning from home had worked for him. He admitted it was very difficult. He ended the course with a B- and finished it about a month later than his peers. He said the inability to speak face-to-face with the teacher and the delays in getting help hurt his learning.

Finally, relying on your own computer and internet connection can cause serious problems. Hardware and network issues are unpredictable, and fixing them takes time and money. Generic_Name experienced this firsthand: his laptop and internet often failed, so he had to stop lessons and wait for repairs. A positive mindset alone does not guarantee success; what really leads to achievement is a strong work ethic. Being optimistic does not automatically mean you will reach your objectives, finish high school with an advanced diploma, or secure a job after years spent in a university studying a subject you did not enjoy just because it promised better prospects. To build a successful life you must put in effort, study diligently, and be willing to leave your comfort zone.

Hard work and persistence are what turn goals into reality. If your aim is to own a car next year, optimism by itself will not be enough. You must handle many practical matters: find affordable insurance, arrange financing or save for a down payment, and prepare for monthly payments to the lender or dealership. Earning the money often demands extra work or longer hours, and your take-home pay may change. In short, dreaming about a new car won’t make it appear; careful planning and consistent effort will.

Do you really think a positive attitude will carry you through twelve years of school to graduate with honors? Education requires regular attendance, long study sessions, and persistence through setbacks. Consider the days you were ill but still had to stay at school because nobody could pick you up — your mind was likely focused on getting through the day, not on staying positive. Everyone experiences moments of doubt and exhaustion; relying solely on optimism won’t replace the daily commitment needed to succeed academically.

The same applies to university life, especially when you study a subject you dislike in hopes of a better future. Students often juggle part-time jobs, late nights writing essays, last-minute assignments, group projects, and the stress of paying tuition. Sometimes they struggle to afford the next semester and spend sleepless nights just to meet deadlines. After graduating, they still face the pressure of repaying loans and proving themselves in competitive job interviews. All these challenges require hard work and resilience, not just a sunny outlook.

In conclusion, a fulfilling life usually follows from reaching your goals: completing high school and university and finding suitable employment. Not everyone has the same chances — many people cannot access higher education and must work daily without expecting miracles. Hoping for a sudden windfall, like winning the lottery, is not a strategy for success. A positive attitude can help you stay motivated, but it will not replace the effort, sacrifice, and perseverance required to achieve real results.

I have thought about places such as Calabasas or the Hollywood area, but the final choice would depend on price and the house’s size and style. Owning a mansion there would be proof that my efforts paid off.

Living in California would let me experience those places she talked about and make my own memories.

Character traits can take many forms — being funny, adventurous, cheerful, and so on. Some of these traits come from conscious choices and the actions we take every day. Our behavior often reflects decisions we make about how to act and how to respond to situations. For the most part, people can guide their feelings and reactions, which allows them to adopt and strengthen desired traits over time.

At the same time, there are moments when emotions overwhelm us and traits seem to arise without our consent. Strong feelings like anger, sadness, or depression can cause impulsive or harmful behavior when they are out of control. In such states people may act in ways they later regret, which shows that traits that appear under stress can be dangerous. This is why some qualities can lead to positive outcomes, while others can be destructive if not kept in check.

There are two common opinions about where character comes from. Some people insist we can choose our own traits. They say when they make choices intentionally, their emotions stay under control and their actions match their goals. Others feel their character is mostly shaped by external forces and internal reactions that they cannot control — for example, sudden bursts of anger or deep sadness that change how they behave. Often, when traits seem uncontrollable, negative emotions are involved.

Still, having trouble managing emotions does not mean it can’t be improved. People who struggle with uncontrolled reactions can learn simple techniques to gain better control over their feelings, such as pausing before responding, practicing mindfulness, or seeking support when needed. Year-round schooling gives students more frequent short breaks, but it also reduces the length of the summer holiday. For these reasons, I believe year-round school causes more stress, cuts down on summer vacation time, and reduces opportunities to earn money during the long break.

First, year-round schedules can increase stress. Many students worry about what to wear every day and feel pressure to buy more clothes so they do not wear the same outfits too often. This social pressure can be stressful and expensive. Teachers face stress too: they must plan lessons continuously and have more assignments to prepare and grade without a long downtime to rest and catch up.

Second, year-round schooling means a much shorter summer holiday. Instead of a long three-month break, students may only get three or four weeks off in the summer. That is not enough time for lengthy trips abroad or extended family visits. Parents are affected as well, since some cannot leave their jobs or arrange long-term care for their children, making travel or relocation during the summer very difficult.

Third, shorter summers reduce the chance for students to work and save money. A few weeks of vacation limits the hours available for summer jobs, so students can earn far less than they would during a traditional three-month break. This also affects local businesses that depend on seasonal workers and could reduce economic activity in the community during what used to be a busy summer period.

Proponents say that spreading breaks through the year prevents learning loss and provides more rest. However, even with more frequent short breaks, students still lose a long summer holiday. And constantly studying with only brief pauses can lead to greater stress over time. For these reasons, I think year-round schooling has more disadvantages than benefits.

Most students look forward to a long summer holiday. For many, summer means a welcome break from school responsibilities. Some, however, would prefer shorter summer holidays and longer breaks in winter, spring, or autumn. While there are pros and cons to both options, I support having a long summer vacation with shorter breaks during the rest of the year. My two main reasons are that short vacations make it hard to carry out extended plans, and breaking the school year into many short segments is not efficient for learning or skill development.

First, long vacations allow students to make and enjoy extended plans. Many young people want to travel, visit relatives abroad, or take on projects that need several weeks. If holidays are too short, students must worry about homework, exams, or returning to school early, which reduces the enjoyment of the trip. It is often impossible to see everything you want in a short stay, and that leads to disappointment. The problem is more serious when family members live far away: long visits are necessary to make the time together meaningful, since you might not see each other again for a long time. Being forced to cut a visit short because of school commitments prevents students from spending quality time with loved ones. For these reasons, I believe longer summer breaks are more valuable.

Second, short terms followed by frequent breaks interrupt learning and practice. Sports have seasons for a reason: players train and compete consistently, and long gaps can harm performance and fitness. The same applies to school subjects and activities like music. Regular, steady practice helps students improve; an intense period of effort followed by a long pause rarely leads to lasting progress. For example, playing an instrument every day helps maintain and build skill, while practicing intensely for a few days and then stopping for weeks is not effective. It is challenging to get back into a productive routine after many short terms and breaks. Overall, keeping a longer continuous period of study in the year makes it easier to keep a steady rhythm.

I recognize that some students prefer short, intense study periods with frequent breaks because that pattern suits their habits. They may study hard for a short time and then rest, and it can work for certain individuals. However, this approach carries the risk of forgetting material learned during the cram period, so the gains may not be long-lasting.

In conclusion, summer break is a special time for students to rest, travel, and spend time with family. While changing the school calendar might benefit some, having a long summer vacation gives students more freedom to plan and supports steady learning and skill development. For these reasons, I prefer longer summers and shorter breaks during the rest of the year.

The question of whether students should be allowed to use cell phones in class for schoolwork has many people divided. Some argue phones can help with learning, while others say they lead to distraction. I agree with the latter view. Allowing phones in the classroom will divert students’ attention, reduce their listening to the teacher, and cause them to neglect their schoolwork.

First, phones are a major source of distraction. Students often play music or open social media apps like Snapchat, Instagram, and Facebook instead of focusing on lessons. When a teacher asks us to take out our phones, my first instinct is usually to send a message to a friend. If I do not have my phone, I feel more responsible about finishing classwork and homework. During a group project once, one member kept listening to music on his phone and never paid attention to the task. When it was our turn to present, the three of us who had prepared could explain the project, but the student who had been on his phone could not, and he ended up failing that assignment.

Second, phones make students less likely to listen to the teacher. If many students are using devices, the teacher may become exhausted from repeating instructions, and most of the class will not follow. I admit I would also be tempted to watch a favorite show instead of focusing on the lesson. Only a few students, often pushed by parents, will stay attentive; without that pressure fewer would listen. Not paying attention during instruction leads to misunderstandings and can cause students to fail courses.

Third, allowing phones encourages students to avoid doing their work. Knowing a phone is available creates laziness; students delay or skip assignments and eventually earn poor grades. This hurts their record when they finish high school. I remember being a junior in chemistry: I used my phone during a lab, and a chemical splash ruined the device. When I explained it at home, my parents were angry. They called me irresponsible and said this behavior explained my low grades in the class.

For these reasons, I don’t think cell phones belong in the classroom. They make students dependent on entertainment and weaken our ability to concentrate and complete tasks. Phones will not make anyone smarter; paying attention in class and doing the work will. Education is the path to success, and allowing phones to take away that opportunity is a mistake.

Should schools set limits on how many extracurricular activities students can join? I believe schools should only have limited control. The decision about how many activities a student participates in should mainly belong to the student and their family. The school should step in only in certain situations, such as when grades fall, parents ask for changes, or attendance at meetings becomes a problem.

To begin with, choosing extracurriculars is primarily a family matter. Parents and students know the student’s schedule, study habits, and other responsibilities best. If a family feels the student does not have enough time for homework or to prepare for tests, they should talk with the student and reach a decision together. If parents decide their child should stop attending an activity, they should inform the guidance counselor and the person who leads the activity so everyone is aware of the change.

However, schools should act when academic performance suffers. If a student’s grades begin to drop or they start failing classes, the guidance counselor should meet with the student to find out what is causing the problem. If participation in too many activities appears to be the reason, the counselor can discuss which activities could be paused until the student’s grades improve. This approach helps students understand that staying involved in clubs or teams requires keeping up with schoolwork.

Attendance at activities is another area where schools should have some authority. If a student repeatedly misses meetings or participates inconsistently, they should not be allowed to continue. Missing up to five meetings per month could be acceptable without penalty, but beyond that the school or activity leader should act. The student may be required to leave the club, and parents should be informed of the reasons. In some cases, a temporary suspension from meetings might be appropriate.

In summary, schools should have only a small role in deciding how many extracurriculars a student can take. Families should make most of these choices, except when poor grades or frequent absences indicate the school needs to intervene to protect the student’s academic success.

Students would gain many advantages if they attended classes from home instead of going to school, mainly because they could learn at their own pace. Not having to wake up very early would prevent them from being tired all day; when pupils arrive at school exhausted, they often cannot concentrate or complete their work. With online lessons, students can manage their time more flexibly and avoid rushing to finish tasks before a class ends, so assignments are less likely to be started and left incomplete.

Home-based classes also help when students are ill. If a pupil must miss school for several days or weeks, they can still follow lessons online and stay caught up with the rest of the class. Schools would not need to worry about cancellations for bad weather, such as snow days, because learning could continue remotely. Being at home more often also reduces the need to travel and change location throughout the day.

Another benefit is that learning from home can lead to fewer distractions. Without other students chatting nearby, many learners would find it easier to focus during lessons. Those who often skip school might do better with online options too, because they could complete their work at home rather than miss it at school. As a result, students might earn higher grades since they would be more likely to finish assignments.

If a student does not understand something, help is still available: they can look up explanations online or ask a family member for assistance. Working from home allows short breaks when needed, so pupils do not become overwhelmed by long periods of study. Additionally, taking classes on a computer helps students improve their digital skills, which will be useful later in life.

Parents can check their children’s work more easily when lessons are online, so students can show they have completed tasks and receive rewards at home. Overall, online schooling would be more convenient for those who dislike going to school or waking up early. It would save time for both students and teachers because they would not have to be physically present all day, and it might make school more appealing since lessons can be done at any time before the deadline.

Some people believe students should study from home, while others argue that attending school in person is better. I support the idea that students should go to school for classes. Being at school helps students learn more subjects effectively, and without in-person attendance many teachers and staff could lose their jobs.

One reason in-person classes are better is that students are more likely to focus and cover a wider range of material. At home, learners often get distracted by phones, television, or other devices and may neglect their assignments. There is usually no adult to guide them through their work or to remind them to stay on task. In contrast, teachers at school provide instruction, encouragement, and structure, which help students study more subjects thoroughly and build stronger understanding.

Another important point is that schools support many people besides students. If children stopped coming to school, there would be fewer positions for teachers, administrators, and support staff. This would lead to job losses and weaken the school community. Also, building a relationship with a teacher is easier in person. Face-to-face lessons allow teachers to notice when a student is struggling and to offer immediate help and personal feedback. Such interaction and support are difficult to replicate online.

Some argue that online learning offers benefits and more opportunities for students. They say virtual classes can be flexible and accessible. While online education has advantages, many people still believe that attending school in person provides a fuller learning experience. Schools are designed to teach a variety of subjects in a structured environment where students can interact with teachers and classmates.

For these reasons, students should attend classes at school. Being there helps them learn a broader range of subjects, stay focused, and receive direct guidance from teachers. It also preserves jobs for school staff and allows students to form stronger relationships with educators. Learning face to face remains a valuable part of education that supports students’ academic and personal development.

The benefits of working in as a group or working alone.

I believe working as a group is more beneficial for the students.

My friend Generic_Name is very capable of doing school work by himself.

However, even he needed others help to understand somethings.

I am very capable of doing a school project by myself.

However, even I could use some one else's input in the matter.

I believe working together as a group is beneficial .

For example, my friend Generic_Name he is a very smart person.

He was on the top of the class with grades but, even he could not do it by himself.

One day the teacher assigned us projects.

Generic_Name decided to do it alone.

On the due date, which was later that week Generic_Name turned in the project.

The teacher told him he failed he did not understand why.

The teacher later on the day took him aside and explained that he was not understanding the question.

He asked her how he could make up the points for the failed project.

Two weeks after that she assigned another project.

She took Generic_Name aside and said ' this time work with somebody".

Generic_Name listed so he asked somebody to work with him.

The day the project was due, he was nervous because he does not work with people often.

The teacher told him they got a perfect score.

The teacher took him aside and told him why he passed.

She told him he passed because when you have more than just one persons input.

Things become clear so when you do not understand something that other person's input can help.

The first part I had to do by self.

I got it done when the due date came the teacher told us to pick a partner.

I picked a friend of mine, Generic_Name.

The teacher told us to compare our papers.

However, our paper even though they were on the same subject, they were very different.

She later told us to now write a paper on the same subject but working together.

When we were all done with the two parts she told everyone to rotate their papers to the right once.

Everyone passed them on the teacher then told the whole class to read all three papers and to pick which one made more sense.

When every one was done they all picked the one that made the most sense and gave it to her.

Every single one of those papers she got were all the one people worked on together.

She then asked the class why they did not pick the other one.

They all said because the other papers were one sided as in only one perspective.

Some students may say working alone is better.

However, Generic_Name and I both learned that in some places you need two sides to a story, argument and debate.

If I would have gone on with my life thinking the way I thought before I worked with some one, it would be very different in some perspective.

My friend Generic_Name's life would have been very different too.

Thanks to the team work skill and the skill to listen to other peoples side, Generic_Name and I can make decision with some one instead of just making it alone.

I recommend you talk to your teacher about this and get more group projects going.

Talk to your parents about how you could use those skills in the outside world, become surprised by how much you use them, and by how easier your life become.

When you do not have to make decision alone, decision making becomes much easier.

The teacher explained that having more than one person’s ideas helped identify and fix misunderstandings; a teammate’s input made some parts clearer than they would have been alone.

I couldn’t push myself to study better or to talk more with classmates. Most of the time I only thought about my own problems, and when I got home I felt depressed and ashamed. Things changed when I accepted that I needed help. Over time, people around me encouraged and guided me, and I improved. Living with and learning from others changed me in ways I did not notice at first, and that change was positive. It showed me that if you are open to help, you can improve yourself.

Another negative side of being completely alone is boredom and lack of fun. When you have no one to talk to, life can feel empty. Friends and family bring shared experiences that make life enjoyable — playing games, talking, traveling, and learning together. Some people believe society is cold and nobody cares, but this is not always true. Other people can affect you for better or worse. Constant exposure to negative people can push someone toward harmful behavior and make them lonely, but having supportive people or asking for help can lead to positive change.

In conclusion, strict individuality can sometimes lead people down the wrong path. Having others in your life is necessary because we can lift each other up — no one is worthless. Leaving someone alone can be very sad; offering help makes both the helper and the helped better off. Still, don’t let anyone force you to be someone you are not. Being yourself matters, but being alone all the time can be harmful. You are the main character in your life, and your choices are yours.

Technology brings both benefits and harms to society. While it can make many tasks easier, its growing role in daily life has reduced face-to-face contact and created serious problems. I believe that relying too much on technology hurts people because it can lead to depression and isolation, blur the line between virtual and real life, and damage physical and mental health. Although technology has useful applications, its negative effects are significant.

First, excessive use of digital devices can cause loneliness and depression. Online bullying is common, and many young people suffer emotionally after being harassed on social media. Some become so upset that they withdraw from friends and stop attending school. Video games also contribute to isolation: players who spend long hours online may lose touch with family and community. Many people carry smartphones everywhere and rarely leave the house, which reduces real social interaction. Over time, these habits can seriously affect a person’s mood and well-being.

Second, technology can make people lose their sense of reality. The internet is full of misleading information and persuasive content. Children especially are impressionsable; they often accept what they see on television or YouTube as true. Online videos can present false ideas or extreme viewpoints that some viewers accept without question. Adults are not immune either—people can be influenced by conspiracy theories or manipulated by targeted content. Gamers, too, may start to confuse game logic with real life, leading them to believe unrealistic ideas about behavior and consequences.

Third, the physical and mental health effects of constant screen time are worrying. Eye specialists warn that frequent device use can harm eyesight. The online world also affects how people view themselves: many try to imitate influencers, changing their appearance or behavior to match an online image. In some cases, people copy dangerous stunts seen in videos and get seriously injured when their attempts fail. Additionally, if machines and apps handle most daily tasks, individuals may become less active. Reduced exercise and more sedentary time can cause serious long-term health problems.

It is true that technology can be life-saving and useful. Medical devices, emergency communication, and modern equipment can protect lives and improve efficiency. Technology has also played a role in national defense and made many routines simpler. However, these benefits come with risks. Devices can fail at critical moments, and reliance on technology can cause harm or even death if systems break down. Moreover, many technological processes pollute the environment, contributing to damage to our planet. If people hand over too much responsibility to machines, life could become harder rather than easier.

In conclusion, while technology has clear advantages, its impact on human contact and everyday life is often harmful. I think that reducing personal interaction through constant technology use leads to isolation and depression, distorts people’s connection to reality, and harms physical and mental health. Technology will not disappear, but we should be careful about how much we let it replace real human relationships and healthy habits.
