If I had to choose one subject to teach in elementary school, I would pick science. Children enjoy it because it connects to things they do every day, like turning on a light or throwing a ball. Many students also find science exciting because of the hands-on experiments. I want to teach science because it is enjoyable, relatively simple to present to young learners, and closely linked to everyday life.

First, science is fun for both kids and adults. A big reason for this is the variety of experiments you can do. For instance, to explain kinetic and potential energy, students can watch or participate in activities that show those forces in action, such as tossing a ball and observing how its motion changes. Experiments make ideas concrete and memorable. Also, experiments often involve the whole class at once, so everyone gets to see the same demonstration and react together. Activities like an egg-drop challenge encourage students to compare results and discuss what worked or failed, which makes learning social and enjoyable. For these reasons, science lessons tend to feel lively and engaging.

Second, science is relatively easy to teach to a wide range of students. Unlike some subjects that demand a lot of memorization — such as learning vocabulary roots in language class or many formulas in math — science often focuses on understanding ideas through observation. While students do need to learn terms, much of the learning comes from watching experiments and noticing patterns. If learners pay attention during a demonstration, they can grasp the concepts more directly than by repeating practice exercises like in math. Drawing is another helpful tool in science; when words are confusing, a simple diagram can make a concept clear. Because lessons often include pictures and practical activities, science can be more accessible for students who struggle with purely verbal or rote learning.

Third, science explains many things we encounter daily, so it has clear real-world value. Everyday technology and natural phenomena relate to scientific ideas: lights involve electrical circuits, air conditioners rely on principles of heat and airflow, and a compass works because of Earth’s magnetic field. Knowing basic science helps students understand how household devices operate and how to fix simple problems. Lessons about circuits, forces, or magnetism give practical knowledge that students can use and explore outside school.

In conclusion, I would teach science in elementary school because it is fun, easy to teach through experiments and illustrations, and directly applicable to daily life. I look forward to preparing lessons that let children learn by doing and discovering. Would you teach science? Why or why not?

Although some people argue that remote learning does more harm than good, I believe students can gain important advantages from distance education. People who oppose online schooling have reasons for their view. They worry that students may miss out on face-to-face social skills and become too dependent on virtual life. Critics point to examples like this when they claim remote learning can encourage isolation.

Still, online classes offer real benefits for students with disabilities. When I lived in Honduras, I had a classmate who could not walk. Getting to school was a daily struggle: her mother pushed her wheelchair for the thirty-minute trip, and she had to navigate between classrooms, the restroom, and the playground while at school. Even though she tried to get ready early, she was often late, and some nights she could not sleep well because of the effort involved. As a result, she found it hard to concentrate during lessons. This was not her fault. If she had been able to attend lessons from home, she would have saved travel time and been better rested, which would have made it easier for her to learn.

Distance learning also helps students who don't fit the traditional school routine. Last year my cousin resisted going to school and got poor marks at the start of the year. He complained about being tired because he had to wake up early and often said he felt he was simply not meant for school. After talking to his counselor, he switched to taking all his classes online. His grades improved a lot and he told us the experience changed his view of learning. I believe he was not a bad student; he just needed a different method of instruction. For kids like him, remote classes can make school more accessible and effective.

In summary, distance education can be a valuable option. It makes learning more reachable for students with physical limitations and gives others a new way to study that may fit them better. Offering remote learning helps students overcome barriers and have an equal chance to succeed regardless of how they learn best.

Some people want to shorten the long summer break to just one month and instead lengthen other holidays, but I disagree. First, a lengthy summer break makes it possible for families to take real vacations. Traveling to visit relatives or to spend quality time together often requires several days or weeks, especially when distances are large. For instance, driving from Virginia to Florida takes many hours, and a short break would not give enough time to travel, relax, and enjoy the destination. Some families have traditions or special events that only happen once a year, and those need time to be appreciated. In short, having more weeks off makes it easier to plan and enjoy family trips.

Second, a long summer gives students better chances to work full time and save money. Teenagers often want new things like a car or need to contribute to family expenses, and a part-time job during the school year may not bring in enough income. During a three-month break, students can take full-time positions, learn responsibility, and experience what earning a living feels like. Parents often encourage their children to understand real-life challenges, and a full-time summer job provides practical lessons in budgeting and independence that a month-long break cannot offer.

Finally, a longer summer helps reduce stress for students. School can be demanding, and many students also face difficulties at home. Constant pressure from failing grades, family arguments, or other problems can affect mental health. Having an extended break gives young people time to rest, recover, and deal with personal issues without the added stress of schoolwork. This better prepares them to return to classes refreshed and more able to focus.

In conclusion, although some people think a shorter summer would help students remember more, keeping the traditional long summer vacation is more beneficial. It allows families to travel and keep traditions, gives students the opportunity to work full time and earn money, and provides a needed break from school-related stress. Since most schools and families are used to a three-month summer, it makes sense to keep it as it is.

The claim that "the first impression is almost impossible to change" means different things to different people, but I disagree. While first impressions matter and can sometimes be accurate, they do not fully define a person, situation, or thing. Forming a first impression is a natural, often automatic reaction—like making a quick judgment—but it is not always reliable.

Usually, a first impression does not show the whole truth, so you need to look further before deciding. For instance, when you meet someone you might think she is arrogant or unfriendly. Later, after talking with her, you could discover she was simply having a bad day and is actually warm and friendly. The opposite also happens: someone who seems pleasant at first might turn out to be different once you know them better. Because first impressions are often misleading, it is unwise to base your opinion solely on them.

A person’s appearance, behavior, or mood can easily change how you see them. If someone does not smile and appears rude, you might assume they are unpleasant even if they are very kind inside. That initial judgment can give them an unfair reputation, especially if they generally do not smile often. As a result, you may miss the opportunity to get to know them and be disappointed later when you learn more.

First impressions apply to objects and situations too. For example, when choosing a book in a library, many people pick one with an attractive cover rather than a plain-looking book. If you select based only on the cover and skip the summary, you might find the pretty book boring, whereas the plain-covered one could be much more interesting. Similarly, an object can look appealing but be poorly made. In these cases the first visual reaction—the cover or appearance—does not reflect the true value.

In conclusion, first impressions can sometimes be correct, but more often they are incomplete or wrong. It is natural to form an immediate opinion, but you should not cling to it. Take time to learn more about people, objects, or situations before making a final judgment.

Human beings have survived and advanced because we learned to cooperate and share responsibilities. From this we understand that two heads are often better than one and that some tasks are not meant to be done alone. Over time we have achieved amazing things: we design complex buildings and travel across oceans in hours. It is hard to imagine a single person accomplishing these feats, which is why teamwork matters.

For example, imagine you work for a company that builds websites for government projects and you studied coding and graphic design. If you are hired as a content creator, you become one part of a larger system, fitting carefully into a role that supports the whole project. When every member performs their job well, the team operates smoothly without creating extra strain on anyone else.

Another advantage of working together is that tasks can be split fairly so no one is overloaded. In a construction crew, workers often measure and mix cement in portions to avoid waste. Similarly, a team assigns each person a share of the work they can handle to prevent burnout. Think of a busy kitchen: one person chops carrots, another prepares the cake batter, and someone else decorates the final dish. Each person focuses on a specific job, and the end result comes together faster and better.

In conclusion, teamwork offers many benefits for everyone involved. Like a well-oiled machine, good teamwork depends on clear communication and trust. When each member knows their role and understands what others are doing, the group functions as one. Teamwork is one of the most important lessons we can learn, because there will always be tasks that are too big to do alone.

Many people today like to offer advice about life, work or personal relationships. The question is: is example not just the main way to influence others, but the only way? I believe it is, for two reasons.

First, when you talk to someone you often share stories about other people’s experiences. For example, you might describe someone who behaved poorly in the past but later changed. Such stories show that relationships and personal habits can be repaired, and they give a concrete model for change. By using examples, reasons and visible actions, you can encourage another person to alter their behavior—if they choose to do so.

Second, we always persuade others with reasons, whether good or bad, and that is essentially how influence works. Changing someone’s view is not easy; you must come prepared with the kinds of examples and explanations they need to hear.

In conclusion, influencing people depends on examples, actions, reasons and your personal advice.

Should students have shorter summers and a longer winter break? Why change the current schedule? Would most students welcome it, and would it help their learning?

If students do go outside in freezing temperatures and get sick, they could miss school days and fall behind in their classes. Summer also allows for more freedom to visit places, enjoy sunshine, and be active, which many students value.

On the other hand, some young people might prefer more winter vacation because summer can become uncomfortably hot. Heat can cause dehydration and make outdoor activities tiring. Still, summer offers many advantages: going to the beach, visiting amusement parks, camping, traveling, and swimming. Longer summer break gives students more days to relax, enjoy good weather, explore nature, and reduce the time they spend on phones and computers.

Personally, I would not support cutting summer vacation in favor of a longer winter break. I enjoy warm weather and dislike having fewer summer days. I also find snow days less fun because they interrupt routine for reasons beyond our control. I believe most students would rather keep the current schedule so they have the vacation time they prefer.

In conclusion, it is unlikely that changing vacation dates would be popular among students. People want to enjoy their time off, not regret it. If authorities consider adjusting the calendar, they should ask students for their opinion first and try to find a solution that most of them accept.

People everywhere make plans for what they want to do in the future. Some never find the time or energy to follow through, while others work steadily toward their goals. A few remain passive, but many take concrete steps to reach what they want. As Thomas Jefferson advised against idleness and pointed out how much can be achieved through constant effort, I firmly agree that we accomplish more when we keep working.

First, taking action helps you reach your goals faster. If you are given a task, you cannot expect it to finish itself or wait for someone else to do it for you. For example, if your aim is to graduate high school and earn a college scholarship, you must study hard and prepare for exams. If you want a stable, well-paying job, you need the right education and a strong resume. Doing the necessary work speeds up progress and makes you more efficient at completing each assignment.

Second, being active motivates you to improve. When you fail a test, it is not enough to ignore the result; you should respond by studying harder for the next assessments. In my own experience, when I do poorly on a quiz, I prepare more for upcoming units instead of waiting to catch up in class. I often study before lessons because I do not always understand everything during class time, so preparing in advance helps me follow along better. Taking notes, planning study time, and reviewing material regularly all encourage action rather than passivity, and they move you closer to your goals.

Some people argue the opposite: that staying calm and avoiding constant effort reduces stress. They point out that many high school students push themselves so hard to get into good colleges that they use stimulants or pull all-nighters, and some become ill or dependent on pills. While this concern is valid, it does not mean effort itself is wrong. Working toward your goals helps you build responsibility, gain experience, and become better prepared for the job market. Employers often look for people who have shown initiative and relevant experience, so being active now can make future opportunities easier to attain. Because no one can predict what the future holds, it is wise to be prepared.

In short, I prefer to set clear goals and study ahead of class. Regular action keeps you involved in important tasks, leads to new discoveries, and improves your performance in school. Over time, this approach increases your chances of success, earns the respect of teachers and colleagues, and can help you reach the college and career you hope for.

I want to talk about the importance of showing kindness. Small acts of kindness can really change people's lives because they make others feel better in different ways. For example, you can show kindness by picking up litter or by returning something someone dropped. These simple actions can support others and help them succeed in their daily lives.

Being kind also matters even when you are upset with someone. You can still treat them kindly and speak to them in a gentle way. Talking nicely to a person can lift their mood and calm a tense situation. Another helpful example is assisting someone with their homework; offering a little time and patience can make a big difference for a student who is struggling.

Helping others in small ways makes you a more caring person because you are actively giving support. You might help by translating English into Spanish for a classmate, or by explaining a difficult idea. These modest gestures show that you care and can really improve someone’s day.

Kindness can include everyday chores too. Washing dishes together or helping family members clean the house are simple tasks that make home life easier and show you value others. Even petting someone’s dog or taking care of their pet for a while can be a kind and thoughtful act.

Showing kindness affects both the giver and the receiver. When you help another person, you often feel better about yourself, and the person you help may feel happier or less alone. Talking with someone who seems lonely, even for a short time, can make them feel noticed and appreciated.

In many situations, a small act is enough to change someone’s mood or outlook. Picking up trash, returning a lost item, speaking kindly, helping with homework, translating, cleaning, or spending time with a lonely person are all ways to be kind. These actions are simple but powerful, and practicing them makes you a kinder, more helpful person while improving other people’s lives.

For example, some students always play some unappropriate songs very loud while everybody else is taking the test. This situation always happens in every school. The second reason is the person who is with a cell phone can attract the other one who sits beside, and interrupt other students' business.

Finally, schools should not allow students to use cell phones in classroom because they will cause the laziness, lack of knowlegde, and procrastination to students. Students will keep messing on their cell phones, and ignoring the education, causing the lack of knowledge. Students will not absorb enough knowledge into their brain because they can just easily search for information on their cell phone without thinking critically of what they are doing. They can have the good results but actually they have nothing in their brain from school. The more schools allow students to use cell phones, the more they are worsening their students.

Cell phones should not be allowed for students to use in classrooms because cell phones are the huge distraction in classrooms. Even in other public places, students will have an opportunity to cheat on the test or the exam using the cell phones, and cell phones will cause the laziness, lack of knowlegde, and procrastination to students. If the cell phones are allowed in every school, students will not need to go for education because everything is available to use on cell phones. Schools only need the real hard working, and the real quality from students, not from websites on cell phones. Every school should always have to think critically about the effects of allowing students to use cell phones in classrooms.

If students were allowed to use cell phones in class for learning, they might find it easier to look up information. Despite this potential, I believe schools should ban cell phones during lessons. Allowing them would create distractions, make cheating easier during tests, and encourage laziness, gaps in knowledge, and procrastination among learners.

Some people argue that phones belong in classrooms. They say students could use them after exams to relax, play games, or listen to music that helps them concentrate. Others point out that phones are useful for researching projects or checking facts quickly. Some foreign students could benefit from translation or dictionary apps. Supporters also note that phones can be used for educational activities such as Kahoot quizzes or learning apps that reinforce school subjects.

Nevertheless, the risks are too great. First, phones make cheating much simpler. If students are allowed to keep phones with them, it is very likely some will use them during tests. They can take photos of exam questions and send them to friends, or store answers to copy later. Because information is easy to access and save on a smart phone, some students may choose to rely on their device instead of studying. This undermines the purpose of assessment and weakens academic honesty.

Second, phones are a major distraction in class. A single ringtone or a short video can break the concentration of everyone in the room. Students who play loud or inappropriate music during exams or lessons spoil the learning environment for others. Even when only a few students use their phones, their activity can spread — classmates get drawn into chatting or watching, which interrupts lessons and reduces productivity for the whole class.

Finally, regular phone use in school encourages laziness, shallow learning, and procrastination. When students can quickly look up answers, they may stop thinking deeply or developing problem-solving skills. They might get good grades by using devices, but still lack real understanding. Constant phone use also makes it easier to put off assignments and study until the last minute because quick answers are always available online. Over time, these habits erode students’ work ethic and knowledge base.

For these reasons, schools should not permit students to use cell phones in class. Phones create distractions, facilitate cheating, and promote lazy study habits and incomplete learning. If phones are allowed everywhere in schools, students may rely on devices instead of learning. Schools must prioritize true effort and genuine understanding, and carefully consider the harmful effects that allowing phones in classrooms can have on students’ education.

In high school I once had a teacher who looked unfriendly and seemed uninterested in talking with students or repeating explanations. I asked the school counselor if I could switch out of his class, but she said it was not possible. After a while in that class I discovered I had been wrong about him. Whenever I asked for help, he did his best to explain the material and helped me prepare for quizzes and tests. This experience showed me that first impressions can change. People sometimes judge others quickly, but those initial feelings are not always accurate.

One reason first impressions can be wrong is that everyone has bad days. Life includes both good and bad moments, and when someone is upset or stressed they may not behave their best. Problems at home, work, or school can affect a person’s mood and how they treat others. If you meet someone while they are having a difficult day, they might seem rude or distant even though they are usually kind. For that reason it is important to avoid deciding a person’s character from one short meeting.

We should also avoid judging people by their appearance. Many cultures use the saying "don’t judge a book by its cover" to remind us not to decide who someone is just by how they look. Some people look friendly but can betray trust, while others may seem cold or strict but are actually caring and helpful. If you rely only on first impressions, you might miss out on reliable friends or unfairly trust someone who is not good for you.

To form fair opinions, it is better to get to know someone over time. Only after seeing how a person acts in different situations can you really understand their character. In conclusion, first impressions can change because people sometimes act differently when they are having a bad day, and a deeper knowledge of a person usually gives a truer picture. It pays to withhold judgment and learn more about people before deciding what they are like.

Some students also miss cousins or other family members and want to reconnect when possible. Because family opportunities can be rare, young people often choose to use their spare time to be together rather than extending the school day.

Second, many students must leave school early to take care of other important duties. For example, some have sports practices or rehearsals right after classes and cannot afford to stay two extra hours. Others must go home to babysit younger siblings because their parents are working, or they need to go straight to a job. If the school day were lengthened, these students might be late for work, miss practices, or get in trouble at home. For these reasons, staying at school longer is not realistic for everyone.

Third, free time is important for students’ well-being. After a full day of classes and sometimes work, young people want a chance to relax and hang out with friends. Some enjoy shopping, others prefer to spend evenings with their parents while they still can. If students are forced to be at school or work for most of the day, they lose the only moments they have to unwind and do things they enjoy. This can make them feel trapped and unhappy.

For these reasons I believe we should not add extra hours to the school schedule. We are still young and should be able to use our free time before adult responsibilities increase. Adding more time to the day could also overload students, causing some to lose motivation and give up on their schoolwork. For example, when I finish school I often have to go home and look after my little sister because my mother is at work. If I also had a long work shift, I would be too exhausted to do homework and might simply fall asleep.

I would not like being stuck at school for two extra hours. If I worked a four-day, ten-hour week too, I would struggle to complete my school assignments at home because I would be very tired after work. Overall, keeping the current school hours lets students balance family, jobs, activities, and some free time, which is better for their health and motivation.

Many people believe that distance learning is an excellent choice for students. It can improve attendance, reduce conflicts at school, and support learners who have disabilities or health issues. Others argue that studying from home may encourage laziness and a lack of responsibility. Despite this criticism, I remain convinced that distance learning offers important advantages for both pupils and schools.

One clear benefit is better attendance. When students can take classes from home, they are less likely to miss school. Getting up very early, commuting, and spending long hours on campus make some students exhausted and more likely to skip classes. Learning remotely removes those obstacles and helps students stay engaged with their lessons.

Distance learning is especially valuable for students who cannot be in a regular classroom because of a disability or medical condition. These young people deserve the same educational opportunities as their peers. By offering lessons online, schools allow such students to follow the curriculum without facing physical barriers. For many families, this equal access to education is the most important advantage of remote learning.

Another benefit is a reduction in negative social issues. Face-to-face schooling can expose pupils to bullying, peer pressure, and unnecessary drama. Studying from home can shield students from these harmful interactions, letting them focus more on their work and less on social conflicts. This can create a safer, calmer environment for learning.

Critics say remote education makes students irresponsible. However, students should be free to choose how they learn. If a student becomes less motivated while studying at home, the root cause is personal habits, not the learning format. With proper guidance and self-discipline, distance learning can help students develop independence and good study routines.

In short, distance learning brings real benefits—improved attendance, accessibility for those with health needs, and fewer social problems—while concerns about laziness can be addressed through student support and responsibility.

Choosing a career while still in high school can help students get ready for life after school. In some places, young people are expected to decide on a career path before they start high school. I believe making that choice early is beneficial.

First, deciding on a career in high school can let students reach their goals sooner. If they focus on a particular field and take related classes, they may not need the usual four years of college. With the right background from high school courses, some students could finish a college program in one or two years. This shortens the time and cost needed to enter the workforce.

Second, picking a career early can encourage students to act more responsibly about their future. When they follow courses linked to a chosen profession, they often become more motivated to study and plan ahead. This can change the mindset of students who might otherwise avoid studying, helping them understand that their choices now affect their later life. Learning to take charge of their education is an important step toward adulthood.

Some people disagree and think choosing a career so early is not a good idea. They say it adds extra pressure because students must study more and pass additional classes. This workload could lead to stress and fatigue, so those critics prefer waiting until college to make a decision.

However, postponing the choice until college can be risky. By then, students have less time to explore options and may feel forced to pick a major quickly. If they choose something without real interest, they might spend extra years changing direction or even drop out. That can make it harder to find good jobs later.

In conclusion, committing to a career during high school is a sensible decision. It helps students prepare earlier, reach their goals sooner, and enter college with clearer expectations. While it requires effort, the advantages for a student’s future make it a worthwhile choice.

Some research suggests that students who decide on their dream job before high school end up more successful in that field. Even so, choosing a profession so early can create a lot of pressure and stress. Committing to a specific career before you really know yourself often makes students focus more on meeting that goal quickly than on enjoying school or exploring other possibilities. Because high school is a time of growth and change, I believe young people should not be forced to pick a career path that early.

The first reason is that early commitment can increase stress throughout high school. At first it might seem helpful to set a clear goal, but the pressure to reach it fast can become overwhelming. When you concentrate on only one future, every class and decision starts to feel like a test of whether you are still on the right track. That single-minded focus can make it hard to study other subjects well or to keep up a healthy balance between work and personal life. In many cases students lock themselves into choices they later regret, which only adds to anxiety.

Pressure from family, teachers, or schools is another major problem. Saying you must commit to a career can feel like you are trying to prove something to other people—to make your parents proud, to show teachers you are serious, or to meet expectations at your school. Over time, that constant need to please others can raise stress levels and lead to sadness or even depression. Instead of choosing a career for yourself, you may end up following a plan meant for someone else, which is harmful to your well-being.

High school itself is a strong reason not to decide on a career too soon. The jump from middle school to high school brings tougher classes and many new subjects to try. Electives give students chances to discover talents and interests they did not know they had. When you haven’t experienced these options yet, you cannot be sure what you really enjoy. High school changes many students’ views, so making a fixed career choice beforehand ignores the natural process of learning and growing.

From my own experience and what I have seen in others, I would advise against committing to a career at a young age. Use high school to take different classes and find what you like. If a subject appeals to you, pursue it; if it doesn’t, try something else. Real life rarely matches the neat pictures we see on TV, and careers are not the only measure of success.

Everyone develops at their own pace. A career is not a final label you must accept early. Don’t force yourself to decide a life path before you have tried enough options and understood what matters to you.

Education shapes how people think, solve problems, and prepare for the future. Skills learned at school—like math and language—have helped generations achieve remarkable things. Because schooling is so important, decisions about its structure deserve careful thought. I believe the school day should not be lengthened. The current schedule already allows for significant learning and personal growth, adding time would likely increase stress and unproductive behavior, and it would create conflicts for students, families, and staff.

A regular seven-hour school day is already full of demands. Students arrive with different challenges: some rushed from a late bus, others dealing with personal issues before class even begins. Once school starts, they juggle learning new concepts, finishing homework, and preparing for the next lesson. Between classes and lunch there are practical concerns—locker organization, catching up with classmates, or handling group projects. By the end of the day many students still have assignments and responsibilities at home. All these tasks can make a long school day feel overwhelming, even without adding more hours.

Lengthening the day could increase several negative effects. More time at school might mean more homework, longer assignments, and higher expectations for in-school work, leaving students with less energy and motivation. Some lessons could become dull if students are expected to concentrate for much longer periods; attention and engagement naturally decline. To fit an extended schedule, schools might shorten individual classes or rearrange the timetable in ways that reduce the quality of instruction. Overall, extra hours do not guarantee better learning; they may simply create more opportunities for boredom, fatigue, and incomplete work.

A longer day would also cause practical conflicts for many families and staff. Students often rely on after-school activities—sports, clubs, music lessons—that require adequate time for practice and travel. Extending the school day might force them to miss those activities or reduce their effectiveness. Parents and guardians who work scheduled hours might find it harder to coordinate pick-ups, supervise homework, or attend to their jobs, creating stress at home and potential economic strain. Teachers and other school employees could be required to stay later to finish planning, grading, or cleaning, which would lengthen their workdays and complicate personal obligations. In short, extending school hours would upset the balance of several connected schedules and responsibilities.

It is true that a longer school day could offer some benefits. Students might have more time to study difficult subjects in class, complete homework during school hours, or socialize during longer breaks. These potential advantages are real for some students. However, they do not outweigh the drawbacks. Even with more time, unproductive routines and increased pressure could remain. Not all students would profit equally; those already struggling might be further overloaded rather than supported.

For these reasons, I am against increasing the length of the school day. The current timetable already contains many educational and social opportunities, and adding hours risks greater stress, reduced focus, and clashes with extracurricular, family, and staff commitments. While extending the day could help some students, the possible negative effects on wellbeing and daily logistics make such a change unwise. Before making any lasting adjustments, decision-makers should carefully weigh these consequences.

People often argue about whether genuine self-esteem comes from being praised or from actual accomplishments. Some claim that praising subpar work lowers standards and harms learning, so they insist that achievements are the real foundation of self-worth. I disagree. I believe that receiving praise for a student's efforts builds true self-esteem because it encourages independence. Compliments, when given appropriately, help students work more effectively on their own, boost their confidence, and improve their learning.

First, positive feedback helps students become more efficient and independent. When teachers acknowledge good work, students see that they can complete tasks successfully without constant supervision. Praise makes students feel proud of what they have done, which increases their willingness to take on new tasks and to keep working. Of course, praise should reward real effort and results; praising work that shows no effort can make students complacent and unfairly equate their performance with those who tried hard.

Second, praise strengthens self-confidence, which in turn leads to more steady effort and better outcomes. Students who believe in their abilities are more likely to invest time and energy into their studies. When teachers recognize and praise this effort, students gain a stronger sense of competence. That inner belief becomes a motivator: confident learners persist longer, take on challenges, and complete tasks more carefully.

Third, students who consistently pay attention, meet deadlines, and put in real effort should receive recognition because it reflects maturity and a goal-oriented attitude. Praising these behaviors shows that teachers value commitment and preparation, and it encourages other students to adopt similar habits. Some young people focus more on popularity than on learning; positive reinforcement for responsible work helps shift attention back to education and personal growth.

In short, praise that acknowledges real effort and achievement supports independence, builds confidence, and promotes better learning. When teachers show appreciation for students’ work, it communicates care and encouragement, which makes students more eager to attend class and to continue improving. For these reasons, praise is a key source of true self-esteem.

I believe students benefit more from attending school because it encourages them to be active, provides access to information and support, and gives chances to share ideas with others.

Schools help students stay physically and mentally active. Teachers organize activities that get students moving and involved, and they try to make learning enjoyable. For example, physical education classes let children exercise and learn teamwork through games or sports. Even students who are shy or reluctant often take part when teachers lead group activities. These opportunities to participate help pupils build confidence and keep a healthy routine.

Public schools also offer important information and support that can improve learning. In the classroom, teachers explain subjects clearly and give examples that help students understand lessons. If a student struggles, they can ask for extra help, such as staying after class for additional tutoring or attending review sessions before exams. Teachers are available to answer questions and guide students, so learners do not have to find everything on their own.

Another big advantage of school is the chance to exchange ideas with classmates. Group projects and class discussions allow students to hear different viewpoints and learn how to work with others. When pupils solve problems together or debate opinions, they learn to listen, explain their thoughts, and adjust their ideas. Working with peers makes tasks more interesting and teaches social skills that are important later in life.

Because schools encourage activity, give access to knowledge, and promote idea-sharing, they are often a better choice than homeschooling for many children. For these reasons, I strongly disagree with adding one and a half hours to the school day.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators think that summer break is too long and students do not retain information as easily as they would in the fall. Because of this a lot of educators think we should have year- round school years. This would be shorter breaks in the summer (3-4 weeks) and longer more spread-out breaks throughout the year. I disagree with this statement and believe that summer break should stay the way it is.

The first reason I disagree with this statement is that it would ruin certain summer activities or even business plans. Think about all the activities in the summer that kids usually take part in, this could be sports, some sort of trip, etc. All of these activities students would preferably do during summer break. They have this preference because they see the summer as a perfect time to do all these activities without having to balance their education as well. They can put most of their time on this activity. The same preference applies to things like summer jobs or internships. During the summer they can learn important values like how to save and earn money. Or if a certain student has a chosen career path they can explore this career path by going in a internship for that spesicifc job. For all of these activities students at the very least would be discouraged to participate in if there was a year-round school year.

The second and probably most important reason is pertaining to the students mental health. An article, by Complex News writing about kids mental health stated, that over 40% of kids by the end of their freshmen year in high school are depressed or overall feel exhausted and depleted mentally. The article continues to say that this number from the time of their freshmen year only increases after each school year. Students use the summer break as a way for their brain to refresh from the long almost ten month school year. Students need this time to relax their brain and get ready for the next year of education. As a student, I can say that during school my brain goes into this state where I am mostly just focused on school work. And I can admit that my brain at multiple points during the year is worn down and damaged by always be in this state. My brain does not get a chance to heal from this until the summer, when school is over. So if we were to hypothetically have a year-round school year, this would mean that the brain would also be in this damaged state year round. If this were the case than the brain of the student would eventually just break and shut down. No student should have to experience that because of a year- round school year.

Although the strongest reason for this year-round school year is that students cannot properly retain enough information for the next school year, I think I have a much stronger counter claim and solution to this problem. A very simple way to take care of the problem of retaining information, is to make mandatory (but simple) assignments from the previous year for the student to complete so that they don't forget this information. This way students can have their long summer break to refresh their brain and do their activities, without them having to forget any information. You get the best of both worlds with no need for a year-round school year.

In conclusion I think my assertions for the summer break to stay the way it is is much stronger than year-round school year argument. Having a year-round school year would be unnecessarily tedious and dangerous as it would negatively affect summer activities and mental health. As someone said once upon a time "Don't fix it if it ain't broke."

Many students look forward to summer vacation, but some educators argue that the break is too long and that pupils forget too much over the months away from school. For that reason, they suggest moving to a year-round calendar with shorter summer breaks (around three to four weeks) and more frequent breaks spread through the year. I disagree with this proposal and think the long summer holiday should remain.

First, changing to year-round schooling would disrupt many summer activities and plans. Summer is the time when students can take part in sports, family trips, camps, and other activities that require several weeks at once. These activities fit best into a long break because students do not have to juggle classes and can devote most of their time to what they enjoy. The same is true for summer jobs and internships. Working during the summer teaches young people how to earn and manage money, and internships give them a chance to try out a career path. If the school year were spread evenly across the calendar, students would likely be less willing or able to accept these kinds of opportunities, which could hurt their personal growth and future plans.

The second, and to me most important, reason is student mental health. According to an article by Complex News about young people’s mental well-being, more than 40% of students feel depressed or exhausted by the end of their freshman year in high school, and that number grows with each year. Summer gives students a necessary break to recover from almost ten months of continuous study. Speaking from my own experience, during the school year my mind becomes so focused on classes and homework that it feels worn out at times. The long summer break allows me to rest and recharge so I can return refreshed. If we switched to year-round schooling, students would have much smaller breaks and might not get enough time to recover. Over time, being constantly stressed and tired could seriously harm a student’s ability to learn and their overall well-being. No one should have to face that risk.

Although supporters of year-round school say it helps students retain information, I believe there is a simpler solution that keeps summer intact. Schools could set short, required review tasks for students to complete during the summer. These would be light assignments designed to refresh key material from the previous year so students don’t lose what they learned. This approach preserves the long break for rest and activities while still helping students remember important concepts.

In summary, keeping the traditional long summer break is better than moving to a year-round system. A longer vacation supports valuable activities, part-time work, and crucial mental recovery, and a few simple summer review tasks could address concerns about memory without overhauling the school calendar. There’s no reason to change something that works for students.

I think genuine confidence comes from achieving something, so it is wrong to reward those who are not truly trying.

My first objection is that excessive praise for minimal effort creates dependence on others. If children become used to being praised for small or careless actions, they may always look for someone to lift them up. In the real world, you cannot rely on others all the time. If constant encouragement is always available, students may not learn to push themselves. Without outside praise, they may stop trying altogether because they expect someone else to cheer them on.

The second reason is that this habit prevents real accomplishment. Finishing a task brings a satisfying sense of achievement. But if students receive praise simply for trying, they might feel as if the job is done and not complete the work properly. This false sense of success can harm them later. In future classes or in jobs, they may fail because they believe their initial effort was enough, even when it was not.

I do recognize that encouraging students can have benefits. Praise can boost confidence and help students who need a push, and those students might later inspire others. My point is only that teachers should be careful not to overdo it. Praising a child for basics—like just writing their name—goes too far. Sometimes firmness is necessary; it may be uncomfortable at first, but it usually leads to better results.

For these reasons, I do not support blanket praise for students who do not try. Students should learn to work independently, though I do not oppose helping those who truly need support. Teachers should concentrate their encouragement on students who show effort and willingness to improve.

Many middle schoolers imagine high school as a time when we can do whatever we want and a final stop before college. In reality, high school is full of required courses meant to guide us toward future goals. Yet classes like art, music, and drama offer something different from the usual academic subjects. They provide a break from constant essays and long math problems, giving students a chance to relax, enjoy singing, painting, or performing, and connect with classmates. These creative subjects also help pupils build social and communication skills that are hard to learn in other classes.

High school is often more stressful than people expect. Students juggle passing courses, preparing for standardized tests, and beginning college applications all at once. Creative classes can give students a needed breather from that pressure. The atmosphere in these rooms tends to be light and encouraging, and students learn by interacting and collaborating. Sometimes a student who never thought they liked music discovers a real passion after a few months in class and decides to pursue it further. The value of these courses goes beyond a short rest; they can teach unexpected lessons and point students toward new interests.

Consider a very shy student who never speaks up in math class, not even to ask a question. Many of us have asked at least one question in math, but some students always remain in the background. If that hesitant student never learns to express themselves, how will they later give presentations or take risks at work? Even the most intelligent person will struggle if they cannot communicate their ideas. The ability to speak up and share thoughts is a social skill that helps people advance; it is essential for moving forward in life.

Some people argue that arts classes are a waste of time and that students simply use them to hang out for 90 minutes. I believe that offering distance learning as an option for students to take classes from home through the internet or video calls is mostly a bad idea. I do not base this on the fact that I go to a public high school; there are several reasons why I disagree with this approach.

First, online classes can damage students’ social skills. When lessons happen at home, you are not physically with classmates and only interact with the teacher through a screen. Although I have not personally experienced an online class, I think being in the same place as other students helps you learn how to communicate and work with different people. Classmates can explain things in a way you understand or help with problems during breaks or group work. That kind of peer support is hard to get when you are not in school with them.

Second, distance learning can reduce participation in practical activities. In school we do many tasks and projects that are linked to what we study, and doing these in person helps ideas stick in your mind. It is usually easier to ask questions during class and get clear explanations from the teacher on the spot. If you have trouble understanding something online, you might have to send an email or a message and wait. This can slow down learning and make it less effective. Teachers also might not reply right away, which could affect your homework and even your grades. For these reasons, I prefer face-to-face instruction for better understanding and participation.

My final concern is that studying from home can encourage laziness and missed classes. Being at home makes it tempting to skip lessons, oversleep, or get distracted by other things. If you are not very disciplined, remote learning can seriously harm your academic performance. I admit that I would struggle with online classes because I tend to be lazy and could easily miss sessions. On the other hand, there are organized and motivated students who can succeed with distance learning. For those people, studying online can work well because they are committed and responsible.

In conclusion, while distance learning can be a helpful option for students who cannot attend school for good reasons, I generally disagree with it as a replacement for in-person classes. I think it weakens communication, reduces practical participation, and can lead to poorer attendance and lower grades for many students.

Have you ever met someone and immediately formed a positive or negative opinion of them? Many people believe first impressions can be corrected because everyone deserves a second chance. Others insist they are permanent because first meetings reveal who you really are. I agree with the latter: first impressions are very hard to change because they reflect your personality, your attitude, and your true character.

To begin with, the way you present yourself shows your personality and is difficult to undo. A friend of mine once went to a job interview wearing inappropriate clothes. She was surprised when she did not get the position, and later she found it hard to find work elsewhere. This suggests that how you dress, how you speak, and how you behave at first contact matter a lot. People notice whether you seem respectful, responsible, or mature, and those early signals shape their opinion of you. Because those cues are so visible, it is not easy to erase the impression they create.

Next, the attitude you display in your first encounters tends to stick. When I was younger, I often reacted with insults or anger when someone upset me. Once an old woman asked me for help and I rudely refused and insulted her. She warned me that I would have a difficult life, but I ignored her. Later, when I tried to change, the memory of that incident followed me—people still brought it up and connected that behavior to me. I wanted to apologize, but by then the woman had passed away. That experience taught me that disrespectful actions at first meetings can leave a long-lasting mark, even if you try to improve afterward.

First impressions also reveal who you are to a wider audience. I remember a news story about a woman who took an ice cream from a store, licked it, and put it back without paying. That single act destroyed her reputation in public. Everyone who saw the story now has a negative view of her; she not only embarrassed herself but also brought shame on her family and community. Such incidents show how quickly a first impression can define a person in other people’s minds.

Some argue that people can change and should be given second chances, and that is true to an extent. However, once an initial opinion forms, many will continue to see you through that first image. Some may accept your change, but others will always remember what they first saw. For these reasons, I believe first impressions are usually very hard to alter.

In short, your appearance, behavior, and attitude at the first meeting often determine how others see you. Will your first impression be respectful or rude, appropriate or careless, responsible or thoughtless? Think carefully because it is not easy to make people forget.

I believe working with a team is more advantageous than working alone because tasks can be completed faster, ideas are shared, and it demonstrates effective teamwork. Collaborating with others also helps meet deadlines and reduces the workload on one person.

To begin with, teamwork often speeds up the completion of tasks. When several people work together, each member can handle a different part of the project at the same time. Doing everything by yourself can slow progress and make it hard to finish on time. In a group, the workload is split, so everyone can focus on a specific task and the overall project moves along more quickly. Working alone can cause stress because you must generate every idea and manage every detail, whereas in a team you benefit from others handling parts of the job.

Another advantage of group work is the exchange of ideas. Collaborating with others brings different perspectives and creativity to the project. One person might have an especially original idea that improves the whole task. If you work alone, you miss out on this kind of input and may not notice problems or better solutions. Being part of a team also makes it easier to get help when you are unsure about something; teammates can offer advice and feedback. Working by yourself often forces you to multitask and can be tiring, while a group can support each other and reduce that strain.

Finally, working in a group shows good teamwork and can make the process more enjoyable. Teamwork lets each member act as a leader in their area, taking responsibility for their piece of the work. Group projects are a chance to meet new people or collaborate with familiar classmates, which can make the effort feel more motivating. When everyone knows their role and completes their share, the whole project progresses faster and more smoothly.

In conclusion, I prefer working in a group rather than alone because teamwork makes tasks easier and less overwhelming. Without teammates, there is no one to discuss ideas with or to offer feedback, and carrying all the responsibility yourself can be difficult. A group provides a variety of ideas, divides the workload, and creates a more enjoyable working environment. For these reasons, collaborating with others is, in my view, the more beneficial option.

In today’s competitive world people need a range of skills, but many prefer to stay where they feel comfortable. Most do not try unfamiliar tasks and stick with what they already know. What is the best advice for personal and professional growth? I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea: people cannot develop if they always do the same things.

First, many professions require branching out to advance. For example, a photographer who mainly takes still images can also learn how to shoot video. They might move into cinematography or even work as a visual journalist. By exploring related fields, they increase their opportunities and grow as professionals. Likewise, leaving the comfort zone promotes personal development: a student who goes abroad to continue studies gains new perspectives, and a doctor who studies different areas of medicine may discover treatments for illnesses. Both know that trying activities outside their usual routines will help them improve. In short, exploring new fields is a key part of getting ahead.

Also, growth demands change. Skilled craftsmen, like carpenters or construction workers, often consider starting their own businesses but fear failure. Even though they are excellent at their trade, they hesitate to take on unfamiliar responsibilities such as managing a company. Entrepreneurs should be willing to take calculated risks, invest in new equipment, and try new approaches to expand. If they keep doing the same thing without investing or adapting, their business will stagnate. Some argue that doing the same task repeatedly makes you an expert — for instance, a professional athlete who trains the same way. Yet even top athletes vary their routines and constantly work to improve; repeating only one method prevents them from becoming the best. This idea applies across many fields where people want success.

In conclusion, Emerson’s statement is correct: people fail to reach their goals if they keep repeating the same actions. To grow, individuals must go beyond familiar activities and be willing to try new things. Change often brings benefits, and being skilled in several areas is more valuable than mastering only one.

I support the proposal for a 10 P.M. weekday curfew and a midnight curfew on weekends. This change would ease parents’ constant worry, help teenagers concentrate more on school, and encourage young people to act more responsibly. Most teenagers enjoy going out and spending time with friends, and they often become livelier and less attentive to rules when in groups. If parents refuse to let them go out, teens can react badly or seem ungrateful. A clear curfew law could remind them to appreciate the freedoms they already have.

Parents are often anxious about where their children might be because the world feels less safe than it used to. For many families, city officials putting a curfew in place would be reassuring. When teens are allowed to go out, parents usually set a return time, but teenagers do not always follow those limits and come home late. A legal curfew gives parents extra support: if young people know there is a rule enforced by authorities, they are more likely to respect the agreed time. Given the real risks today, such as abductions and violent incidents, a curfew could make parents feel relieved knowing that police will intervene if children are found outside past the allowed hour.

A 10 P.M. curfew would also help teens get home earlier and sleep sooner. More sleep means better attention in class and less chance of dozing off during lessons. Teenagers sometimes act as if school is unimportant and choose social activities over rest, forgetting that school prepares them for the future. By encouraging earlier bedtimes and limiting late-night outings, a curfew could improve students’ focus and academic performance. Making smarter choices about time and priorities would benefit their education and future prospects.

Curfews can teach responsibility and time management. When teens must be home by a certain hour, they learn to plan their evenings and judge whether they can finish activities and still meet the deadline. If they break the rule, there are consequences, and that understanding helps them mature. Being out on the streets after 10 P.M. often suggests risky behavior, and the simplest way to avoid trouble from police or dangerous situations is to go home on time. While some young people learn only after facing consequences, a curfew offers a safe framework for them to practice following rules and protecting themselves.

In conclusion, implementing a 10 P.M. weekday curfew (and a midnight curfew on weekends) could encourage teenagers to be more respectful of their parents’ wishes, improve their school performance, and help them become more responsible with their time. It would also reduce parental anxiety about their children’s safety. Overall, this measure aims to protect teenagers from harm and guide them toward better habits without taking away the support families need.

Debate over remote learning has attracted a lot of attention recently. Many educators now back online education and it is becoming widely accepted in different communities. While some argue that studying remotely can make learners less responsible, I maintain that taking classes from home is advantageous because it cuts out travel time and strengthens students’ digital skills.

First, attending lessons online saves the hours students would otherwise spend commuting. For many pupils, the journey to school lasts from ten minutes to over half an hour. Those minutes add up each day and reduce the time available for study, rest, or family. By removing the need to travel, remote learning helps students use their day more productively instead of losing it on buses or cars.

Second, online education encourages students to become more capable and efficient with technology. Those who regularly learn through digital resources become familiar with software, online research, and virtual communication. As a result, they can complete tech-related tasks faster than peers with little exposure. This experience also eases the transition to college and workplaces, where digital tools are commonly used.

In summary, remote classes offer clear benefits: they reclaim travel time and build valuable technological competence. Given these advantages, schools should make distance learning available as an option so students can choose the mode that best fits their needs and prepares them for the future.

Many people think it is better to get advice from experts or authorities when facing important life choices. Others feel they should decide for themselves. I believe people benefit more from making their own decisions. By choosing for themselves they learn from mistakes, develop resilience, and become more independent. Asking for advice can be useful sometimes, especially from those with more experience, but it should not replace personal decision-making.

First, making mistakes is one of the best ways to learn. If someone always follows instructions from others, they may never understand why a choice was wrong or how to avoid the same error in the future. When people make decisions on their own and face the results, they learn to reflect, correct their behavior, and not repeat the same faults. This process teaches responsibility and helps people become wiser.

Second, too much guidance from parents or other helpers can cause problems later. If children grow up having others make all their choices, they may struggle when those guides are no longer available. In difficult moments, those who are used to being directed may not know how to act or how to solve problems by themselves. Relying entirely on parents or mentors prevents people from developing the skills needed to stand up on their own.

Third, taking responsibility for decisions helps people accept consequences and grow. Some avoid making choices because they fear possible negative outcomes, but facing those fears is part of maturing. When someone chooses for themselves and deals with the results, they gain confidence and learn how to handle challenges. This experience makes them stronger and better prepared for the future.

In conclusion, people learn most effectively when they make their own decisions. Mistakes are valuable teachers, and independence is essential for dealing with life’s difficulties. While it can be helpful to seek guidance from experienced people at times, it is unhealthy to depend on others for every choice. People should practice deciding for themselves, accept the consequences, and use those lessons to become more capable and mature.

Students should be allowed to use their cell phones for learning because phones can make schoolwork easier and more engaging. A mobile device can serve as a calculator in math lessons, help students look up facts in history class, and support teacher-led activities that require online or app-based participation. Allowing phones in class can increase student participation and make lessons more interactive.

In math class, phones are especially useful as backup calculators if a handheld calculator runs out of batteries. Many phones also have tools like measurement apps, levelers, or simple drawing apps that can help students draw straight lines or organize their work when time is limited. Teachers can ask students to take photos of the board or important notes so they have a clear reference for homework or review the next day. These practical uses show how phones can assist students when they need a quick, reliable tool.

For subjects like history, phones allow students to check facts, visit recommended websites, or access short news programs to connect past events with current affairs. If a student must leave class early, taking a picture of the board ensures they do not miss key information. Teachers can also use phone-based activities, such as quizzes on Kahoot, to create a lively classroom atmosphere and encourage teamwork. Programs like CNN10 offer brief news summaries that help students understand what is happening in the world, which supports lessons about timelines and causes of events.

Some people worry that phones will distract students or encourage cheating on tests. Others argue that students should practice finding answers in books rather than online. These concerns are understandable, but they do not apply to every student. With clear rules and supervision, phones can be used responsibly for learning. Teachers can set boundaries during exams and guide students on when and how to use devices for schoolwork.

In conclusion, permitting cell phones for educational purposes can make lessons more active and interactive. When teachers allow controlled use of phones, students gain helpful tools and new ways to participate. Used properly, cell phones can improve learning, increase engagement, and even make school more enjoyable through activities like Kahoot that motivate students.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to share my opinion about changing the school lunch menu to healthier options. I strongly support this idea because it would reduce students' intake of unhealthy foods, help them stay physically well, and encourage better eating habits.

Many students eat unhealthy meals at school almost every day. Replacing those items with healthier choices would lower how much junk food they consume. Regularly eating poor-quality food can harm young people in several ways. For example, it can increase the risk of obesity or long-term illnesses like heart disease. A healthier menu would not only benefit students but also teachers and other school staff who eat on campus.

A better lunch selection would also help students maintain good health because they would get necessary nutrients, such as proteins, that support growth and development. This improvement in nutrition can lead to better performance in sports and in class by increasing energy, concentration, and recovery. Another benefit is that new, varied meals would give students the chance to try different foods instead of eating the same dishes year after year. Over time, they may see the change is not meant to force unwanted food on them but to promote well-being.

Some students might worry that this plan would remove their favorite meals. While that concern is understandable, I believe the change would be positive overall. Encouraging healthier eating habits now can protect them in the future, and students who adapt may persuade friends and family to make healthier choices too. This ripple effect could help prevent diet-related illnesses beyond school.

In conclusion, I think switching to a healthier lunch menu is a good move because it would decrease unhealthy eating, support student health, and motivate better long-term habits. I hope you will consider implementing this change to improve our school community. Thank you for your time.

Smooth Sails do not make Skillful Sailors!

In my opinion, anyone can succeed if they work hard and strive for what they want to achieve. Nothing is a piece of cake. There is handwork and determination behind every successful person. One should have a specific aspiration in their life, and should not do something because they are forced to. There will be a satisfaction if we make a mistake in the work we like to do. We try to find solutions and solve the problem, but if we do something our parents want us to, there will be no contentment.

School life should be the time where all the students should relax and have fun in addition to studying. It is not supposed to be a burden to anyone. Every kid has a right to receive the same education and programs. Discrimination should not be shown to anyone. They should be allowed to do whatever they want to, but should be taken care of so that they do not do something wrong. American school systems are perfect for students because they get to study and at the same time they can take courses they are passionate about. They have a chance to learn new things about the career they want to pursue. The balanced system helps them to manage stress level and also concentrate on how their future will unfold.

Some schools in the United States also allow high school students to graduate in three years instead of traditional four years. There is no point in students graduating one year early to work or enter to college soon. How does graduating one year early matter? This increases nothing but stress and restlessness.

Some students wish to do that not because they want to, but their parents force aspirations on their children. I do not say that it is wrong whatever parents do, but I say that this is not a right way to expect their kids to be successful. All the students need recreational time where they can forget all the school stress and enjoy their time, but parents desire to see their kids as the most successful person, is not letting them to be happy like other kids. Higher grades always does not matter. All that matters is that how can we use in ow much knowledge we attained from the school and how can we use that knowledge in the future. In order to finish high school early, the kids are required to take summer classes and spare their time in the evening. This is not something that is useful for a kid. They need some time to relax their mind, so that concentrate in their studies. They should be able to take their favorite electives as those classes can help them to be successful in the future.

I know an incident where one of my cousin graduated early from high school in order to attend college early. He was really smart until high school junior year. He had a great knowledge of what is happening around the world. He would share those with everyone and help us gain some knowledge too,but at the end of the junior year, he was so into graduating early that he did work hard and finally got into a college. He regrets that decision now as he did not learn so many things in the last year of high school that are stressing him now. If everyone finish high school in the traditional way, they will know everything about college and how it works. Then they can do whatever they want to and have at least some knowledge about it. We often hear news about how students commit suicide as they are stressed about academics, so I think they should not do whatever they do not like, and instead work on what they desire for.

Hard work is the key to success, but that does not mean that everyone should work hard on something they do not like. instead they should really work hard to achieve what they want. Our aspirations should not be impacted by anyone. If we have our own goal and ways to succeed them, we should follow that way and make sure that we become the most successful individual in that particular field.

Smooth seas don’t make skilled sailors. I believe anyone can achieve success if they put in effort and are determined to reach their goals. Behind every achievement there is dedication and hard work. People need to have clear goals and not do things just because others tell them to. Making mistakes is easier to accept when you enjoy the work; you learn from them and look for solutions. But if we follow a path chosen by our parents or others, we are unlikely to feel satisfied.

School years should be a time for learning and enjoyment together. Education should not be only a burden. Every child deserves equal access to education and opportunities; discrimination has no place. Students should be free to follow their interests, while adults guide them so they avoid harmful choices. I think the American school system works well in this respect because it allows students to study required subjects while choosing electives they care about. This balance helps reduce stress and lets young people explore possible careers.

Some U.S. schools allow students to finish high school in three years instead of the usual four. I do not see the benefit of graduating early merely to enter college or the workforce sooner. Graduating one year early often brings more anxiety than advantage. Many students decide to speed up their studies not out of their own wishes, but because of pressure from their parents. I do not mean to criticize parents’ intentions, but forcing children to rush through school is not the best way to help them succeed. Young people need free time to relax and enjoy life, like other kids. Parents’ desire for perfect grades or early achievement can stop children from being happy. What matters is not just high marks, but how students use the knowledge they gain and how it helps them later.

To graduate early, students usually take extra classes during summers and use evenings for schoolwork. This routine leaves little time for rest, and that is harmful. A child needs periods of rest to return to studies refreshed and able to focus. Elective classes, which students choose because they enjoy them, are important too; these can guide young people toward future success and keep them motivated.

I have a cousin who graduated from high school early to start college sooner. He was very intelligent and well informed up to his junior year. He used to discuss current events with family and helped others learn. But by the end of his junior year he had become obsessed with finishing early. He worked hard and entered college ahead of schedule, but later he regretted that choice. He missed important lessons and experiences from the final year of high school, and now he finds himself under pressure. If everyone followed the normal school timetable, they would be better prepared for college life and decisions about the future. We often hear about students suffering from extreme stress and even taking their lives because of academic pressure. That shows how important it is not to push children into paths they do not want.

Hard work is essential for achievement, but it should be devoted to things we truly care about. People should be allowed to set their own goals and follow the path that fits their dreams. When we choose our own direction and work for it, we are more likely to become successful and satisfied in what we do.

This shows that courage can praise someone to keep going.
