For example, at my school, students like to stop by the library before classes because the librarians are welcoming. They always smile and help anyone who asks. A simple friendly greeting in the morning can make you expect a good day, and that cheerfulness can spread to people you meet afterwards. Life can be stressful, but a positive outlook can make it much more pleasant.

Also, if you want life to go smoothly, you must use the right attitude to find the best path. People sometimes lose direction because they react negatively when things do not go as planned: they become discouraged, lose motivation, and give up. A short story about two friends shows how attitude can affect outcomes. Lina and Sara had been friends since they were five and both loved collecting shoes. One afternoon, Lina planned to wear a sparkly pink sandal but could not find it. She immediately thought Sara had taken it because Sara had mentioned wanting the same shoe the day before. The two had a terrible argument and their friendship broke for a long time. Later Lina found the sandal hidden in a drawer. Instead of continuing to ignore Sara, Lina tried to explain and rebuild their friendship. This shows how a quick negative reaction can destroy something valuable, while a positive choice can repair the mistake and restore success in relationships.

Finally, a positive attitude shapes how others see your character and abilities. People do not automatically think someone will succeed; they judge you by your behavior and effort. A student who shows enthusiasm for learning and a willingness to help others is more likely to be seen as hardworking and valuable. That recognition can lead to chances to prove yourself and move toward success.

In short, a positive attitude is essential for success. It helps make your days better, guides you toward the right path, and influences how others view you—creating opportunities for achievement. If you want to be successful, cultivate a positive outlook.

People who believe in being self-reliant should still turn to experts and authorities when facing important life choices instead of deciding everything on their own. By experts I mean people who know much more about a subject than we do — for example a teacher compared with a student. Teachers study and train for years to gain their knowledge, so it makes sense to value their advice when a decision matters.

Self-reliance is about making choices, and everyone wants to be able to decide for themselves. Yet no one is perfect, and we all make mistakes. This is especially true for teenagers, who are more easily influenced and often need guidance. Parents are usually the first experts young people trust; they want their children to do well and will often point out what is best out of love. Of course, not every parent is attentive, but when they are, their experience is very helpful. Besides family, professional experts with formal training and diplomas can provide reliable, informed advice. Consulting such people can help us make better decisions and succeed in life.

Bad choices can harm us deeply. Some decisions may seem attractive at first but have serious consequences if we do not think them through. For example, someone might decide to invest their savings in opening a restaurant because it looks like a profitable idea. Many fail to consider the full costs, the market risks, and the work required. If the business fails, the person could lose all their money, become deeply depressed, or worse. This is the kind of situation where expert help — such as advice from business consultants, accountants, or experienced entrepreneurs — can make the difference between success and disaster. Experts understand the details and long-term risks, so their guidance can protect us from costly mistakes.

Some people argue that making decisions on our own is better because we learn responsibility and cannot blame others if things go wrong. It is true that personal experience teaches lessons. However, it is wiser to seek advice before taking large risks. Experts can help us avoid errors and teach us what to expect. Combining our judgment with outside knowledge is often more effective than relying only on ourselves.

In conclusion, asking experts for help is usually the best course when important choices are at stake. We should accept that we cannot know everything and use the knowledge of parents and professionals to improve our decisions. Being self-reliant does not mean refusing help; it means using available resources and advice to make wiser, safer choices.

This essay examines the advantages and disadvantages of working in groups compared with working alone, focusing on how these modes of work affect an individual rather than the team as a whole. First, I will outline what a group is and explain the concept of group dynamics. Then I will consider how being part of a group can influence a person, sometimes positively and sometimes negatively.

Think back to the last project you had to complete. You probably weighed different ways of tackling it and quickly considered whether to work by yourself or join others. Most people understand what it means to handle a task alone: one person is fully responsible for planning and doing the work. But what exactly is a group, how does it form, and what are the forces that shape its behaviour?

A group can be defined as a number of people who come together to achieve a common purpose. Groups differ in their structure, how they operate, and the processes they use to reach goals. These processes—collectively called group dynamics—help explain why groups form, how they develop, and how members interact. Group dynamics are important in both formal and informal settings, and studying them is a key part of understanding behaviour in organisations.

Group work brings many benefits, but it also has drawbacks. For an individual, one downside is that you may have less control over the task than when working alone. Some members may dominate discussions and decisions, while others contribute very little, which can limit learning and personal involvement. On the positive side, teams often accomplish more than individuals working separately. Combining varied skills and perspectives can improve practical results, and exchanging ideas can deepen each person’s understanding of a subject.

Being in a team also helps you build interpersonal skills, such as clear speaking and active listening, and teamwork abilities, such as leadership and motivating others. These are valuable throughout your academic life and beyond.

To gain the most from group work while avoiding its pitfalls, it is important to manage teams carefully, making sure roles are clear, contributions are balanced, and communication is effective.

Is setting an example by your own behavior the best way to influence other people? Sometimes it is not the best idea to mirror other people's behavior because some people do not always have a positive behavior. There could be time's that someone could be in a negative place of mind, reckless, and does a lot of horse play; other time's people can be charming, properly mannered, and influential.

Growing up in the Generic_City area, I have been able to witness a lot of drugs, gangs, and violence. The example these group of people decide to display is not a very positive act on their behalf; this is not a pathway you would want to be taking because of the bad outcomes from it. I remember I had a friend who's father shot himself due to the poor choice he made which made him reflect and he figured that was the only solution.

On the other hand, some people decide to be very influential to society in a positive manner. Out of my three years of high school I was able to see some students making their way for others by not being selfish; a lot of them did volunteer work as well to help the community and to hopefully inspire others to do so as well. In conclusion, I am mutual about examples being the best way to influence other people because of it not always being a positive thing due to the poor decisions some people choose to make. Truthfully I think it is a better idea to be the best you that you can be because at the end of the day there is only one of you and so many of us; it is best to stay unique.

Most high school students choose to spend the usual four years in school, then apply to college during their senior year with guidance from counselors and teachers. Graduating early can be hard for teenagers because everyone learns at a different pace; some students need more time to understand material while others move faster. School districts should allow students to decide for themselves whether to finish early, but generally giving young people more freedom to plan their future is important. Many students stick to the traditional schedule because trying to graduate sooner often adds pressure and worry, requires extra coursework, and limits the chance to take elective subjects.

All students know it is important to pass classes and keep track of the credits needed for graduation. Trying to leave high school early can make this situation risky, because the added stress and rush may cause anxiety. When pressure and worry build up, mental health problems can follow. Some parents become strict about grades, frequently checking progress and restricting privileges if results fall short. This kind of parental control can be very frustrating and difficult for teenagers, who may feel they have little freedom if they must meet intense expectations.

Fear of falling behind and getting low marks is common among students, but those who follow the regular four-year path often feel less of this worry. Teachers sometimes suggest that students take extra classes in the summer or in the evenings to move ahead, but if you plan to stay in school for four years you usually do not need to overload yourself. Of course, you still must complete regular assignments, but you won’t be racing against time as early graduates often do. Every student should take responsibility for their work, and having more time can make that responsibility easier to manage.

High schools also offer the chance to try new subjects through elective courses. Students who take four years can choose electives and explore interests they might not otherwise see. In contrast, those who rush to graduate early usually miss these opportunities because schools may consider such classes unnecessary for a quick diploma. Being able to take electives lets students challenge themselves, learn new skills, and discover subjects they enjoy.

In conclusion, it is generally better for students to complete the traditional four years of high school. During this time they can get help from teachers and counselors, avoid some of the anxiety and pressure linked to early graduation, and have space to do regular assignments without extra strain. Elective classes are also valuable because they provide a break from core subjects and allow students to learn new activities and interests. For most teenagers, the full high school experience offers a healthier balance of support, learning, and personal growth.

Picture yourself leaving high school a year early and moving on to college or a job. It might seem thrilling because all the effort finally paid off, but getting there would require giving up a lot of free time and activities you enjoy. For this reason, I believe students should not be encouraged to finish high school in three years and start college or work one year sooner. Doing so often forces students into summer or evening classes, cuts out elective courses, and increases stress.

To complete graduation requirements in three years, many students would need to take classes during the summer or after regular school hours. Summer is a common time for teenagers to work and earn money or relax before a new school year. If they have to attend classes, they would lose those job opportunities and the chance to rest. Evening classes can also conflict with after-school commitments like sports practices and club meetings, preventing students from participating fully in extracurricular activities.

Another problem is that rushing through the required coursework can leave little room for electives. Students must complete certain core classes to graduate and to meet college admission standards. When the schedule is tight, there is often no space for subjects that help young people explore their interests, such as art, music, drama, or photography. Missing out on these electives limits personal development and makes the high school experience less well-rounded.

Finally, finishing high school in three years can be very stressful. Students would have to juggle heavy course loads, regular homework, projects, and presentations without the usual breaks or downtime. The pressure to keep up can harm both academic performance and well-being.

For these reasons, schools should not promote finishing high school in three years and entering college or the workforce a year early. The drawbacks—lost summer jobs and extracurriculars, fewer electives, and higher stress—outweigh the benefits.

Many schools partner with businesses so students can try out different jobs through internships or shadowing. I believe this is a valuable opportunity because it helps young people find out whether a particular career suits them. By visiting workplaces and gaining firsthand experience, students are more likely to understand what they want for their future and later secure well-paying employment.

The first reason I support internships is that they help students clarify their goals and build a solid path forward. For example, a cousin of mine was selected to attend Liberty University some years ago to see if the courses matched his interests. After a few months he committed to his studies, earned excellent grades, and completed his degree. Today he runs his own business and seems very satisfied with his life and work.

A second reason internships are useful is that they can lead to stable, better-paid jobs. Another cousin joined the Air Force because his family could not afford college at the time. Although he found military life difficult at times, the experience did not go to waste. Later he enrolled at Liberty University, graduated in 2015, and now works for the FBI. He told me that, though his military service felt hard while it was happening, it ultimately opened doors and helped him reach a place he is proud of. He also earns a good salary and dreams of buying a large home. Seeing how far he has come made me feel proud and inspired to aim high as well.

Some students say they do not care about college, and that attitude is understandable in certain cases. I remember a friend who dismissed higher education, asking why anyone would bother and pointing out that her parents did fine without it. She even said she preferred remaining in a job like the one she had at Wendy’s. Hearing those remarks upset me at first, but it also pushed me to work harder and focus on my studies so I could have more choices later.

In conclusion, giving students the chance to explore occupations through internships is an excellent idea. It helps them discover what they want to pursue and can guide them toward rewarding careers. My cousins’ stories have encouraged me to improve myself and aim for success. Perhaps one day I will work for the government and be able to give my own children a comfortable life.

No, I believe that first impressions are not impossible to change because when you typically meet someone for the first time many people just try to " fit in " or be someone who they really aren't but within time the perspective of how you are viewed can be changed and the first impression you made of yourself the first time won't matter. Also, when you first meet someone , typically you are nerves and you can be seen as a quiet and closed person when in reality you are really outgoing but it just takes you time to adapt to someone and many people don't act like themselfs.

After a while of me being around her she started to see me as a different person/much better person than i was and she started to see how outgoing I was and how I was nothing like the first impression I gave her and her view of me changed.

Another example I have of how first impression can be changed is the from the first time i met one of my best friends. The principal’s choice to require students to take part in extra activities is wrong. Many students already have heavy workloads at school, and adding compulsory programs can interfere with their academic progress.

If students are pushed into these activities, they will have less time for their regular assignments. Homework and projects need attention, and extra commitments can reduce the hours available to complete them well. This also cuts into time families spend together, which can create tension and weaken home relationships.

Being forced to join additional programs increases stress. One more obligation in a student’s daily schedule means extra tasks they did not choose. That pressure can lead to poorer sleep and other unhealthy effects, since students may stay up late trying to manage everything.

Too much stress and less time for study can lower academic performance. When young people spend time on activities they do not want to join, their focus shifts away from schoolwork and grades can suffer. Mandatory participation risks causing exactly that result.

For these reasons, it is clear that making extracurricular activities compulsory can harm students. Joining such programs should be an option students choose freely, not a requirement imposed on them.

Your character is shaped by the choices you make, but it can also be affected by forces outside your control. I think people do have the power to decide who they want to be, yet influences from friends, family, and even strangers can change the traits they develop. Some influences push individuals toward harmful habits or attitudes, while others encourage positive behavior and success. Ultimately, whether you become a better person or not depends on how clearly you recognize good and bad influences and how you respond to them.

First, many negative traits come from the people around you. If you grow up in a difficult home or spend time with friends who make poor choices, it’s easy to pick up those same habits. People who do not wish to see you succeed may try to hold you back, and their opinions can affect your decisions. At the same time, a supportive family or honest friends can teach you values and habits that lead to success. The environment you live in and the company you keep play a big role in the character traits you develop.

Second, personal traits often show in real-life outcomes. Those who adopt disciplined, positive behaviors are more likely to achieve stability and success, for example in their careers and possessions. On the other hand, negative traits can lead to failure and unhappiness. Relationships can be especially powerful: a harmful romantic relationship may cause arguments, blame, and emotional damage that leave long-lasting effects. But relationships can also have the opposite effect, helping you grow and making better choices for the future. It depends on whether you let someone else control your actions or keep control of yourself.

Finally, not everyone is easily influenced. Some people have strong self-awareness and resist attempts by others to drag them into harmful patterns. If others are jealous or try to sabotage your progress, you must protect yourself by recognizing those intentions and keeping distance. My advice to anyone who feels pressured by outside forces is simple: decide what kind of person you want to be and act according to those values. Your character will be what you choose to make of it, so think carefully and pick traits that lead you toward a positive life.

In several cultures, teenagers are expected to decide on a career path as they begin high school, and their classes are arranged to point them toward that job. However, many adolescents are not ready to make such an important decision at that age. I believe students’ views about work evolve over the course of high school. They should not be forced to pick a career when they first enter high school because they lack the experience to know what they really want, they may choose a career that does not suit them, and they could end up unhappy after spending time on a field they later abandon.

At around fourteen, most young people have little idea of what they want in the long run. Their interests and priorities change during their teenage years as they learn more about themselves and the world. High school is a period of growth and discovery; students often only begin to understand their strengths, weaknesses and preferences toward their mid-to-late teens. Expecting them to decide their whole professional future at the start of this journey ignores how much they can change. Choosing a career too early therefore risks being based on incomplete information and temporary tastes.

If students are required to commit to a single career path when they enter high school, they may pick the wrong direction. A decision made at fourteen or fifteen may reflect a passing hobby, pressure from family, or a misunderstanding of what the job actually involves. If later they realise their chosen field does not match their abilities or interests, they will face the difficult prospect of changing course. That can mean extra years of study, additional expenses, or the discomfort of starting over, all because they were pushed into a premature choice.

Spending time on the wrong career track can also lead to unhappiness and wasted effort. People usually do better and feel more satisfied when they work in areas they enjoy. When a student is locked into a stream that does not suit them, motivation falls and performance suffers. Reversing that path takes time and energy, and many young people may feel frustrated at having to undo work they could have avoided with a later, better-informed decision. Careful planning and research, performed when students have more maturity, will likely lead to more considered and lasting choices.

In short, high schools should allow students more time to explore their interests before demanding a firm career choice. Young people need experience and knowledge to pick a path that fits them; forcing the decision too early increases the chance of mistakes and unhappy, costly detours.

Many students go straight from high school into college, but I believe finishing high school in three years and spending a year working is better. Graduating early and entering the workforce before college lets students save money, become more mature, and develop strong time-management habits. These advantages give them a head start when they finally begin their college studies.

First, working for a year gives students the chance to earn money for college. Not every family can pay tuition, and many students end up borrowing through loans that must be repaid later. If a student leaves high school after three years and works for a year, they can build savings and reduce or avoid borrowing. Earning their own money also teaches responsibility and independence, and it eases financial pressure on parents. Showing that you can support yourself and manage money well is an achievement that makes both you and your family proud.

Second, a year of work helps a young person become more mature. Many students who graduate early are still only about 17 years old. Spending a year in a job exposes them to adult responsibilities and the real world, which can make them more prepared for college life. Maturity matters: it helps students meet deadlines, communicate with professors, and act responsibly. It also can change how others treat them; being older and more responsible makes people take you seriously. For students who might feel isolated because they are younger than most classmates, working for a year means they will enter college at the same time as their peers and are less likely to feel alone.

Third, holding a job teaches valuable time-management skills. Work requires showing up on time, completing tasks by set hours, and organizing daily routines. These habits transfer well to school: turning in assignments on time, attending classes punctually, and keeping a healthy sleep schedule. Good time management also means planning time for studying, working, rest, and leisure, so nothing is neglected. By practicing these routines during a year of work, students arrive at college already used to balancing multiple responsibilities.

Some people will argue that going straight to college is better. With respect, I disagree: a year of work can open many opportunities and prepare students for success. Without enough maturity and practical skills, starting college right away can be difficult.

In conclusion, I believe graduating in three years and working before college is beneficial. Students who do so can avoid large loans, become more mature, and gain strong time-management skills, all of which help them succeed in college and in life.

People want independence for many reasons, but the main one is the chance to make their own choices. Deciding for yourself shows responsibility and maturity. Some people use that freedom to make wise choices, while others make poor ones. When choices are bad, they can hurt not only the person who made them but also the people around them.

Examples of harmful choices include using drugs, driving while intoxicated, and joining gangs. These decisions carry serious risks. Joining a gang can put your life in danger for reasons that often seem meaningless, and if you are killed, your loss causes deep pain for your family and friends. Drunk driving endangers both the driver and other road users; a single decision to drive after drinking can lead to accidents, injuries, or death and leave families grieving or caring for someone in the hospital. Drug use is harmful in many ways and hard to stop once it starts. It damages relationships and disappoints loved ones. Avoiding these behaviors in the first place is the safest choice.

At the same time, making good decisions helps shape a successful future. Thinking carefully about life after high school—such as which career to pursue, what to study in college, or whether to start a family—can lead to better outcomes. Jobs can be difficult to get without the right education or experience, and employers usually prefer people who are prepared and willing to work. Going to college with a clear idea of the career you want lets you focus on the subjects you need. That preparation makes it easier to earn a living and support a family when the time comes.

While young people are learning to make these choices, parents often watch and decide how much freedom to give. Many mothers and fathers want their children to try things for themselves so they can learn and grow. Letting kids make their own decisions helps them think independently and become more capable. It also reassures parents that their child can handle responsibility when they are on their own.

In short, making choices is not always easy, but it is an important part of becoming independent. Good decisions open doors and provide stability, while bad ones can cause lasting harm. Independence is something many people want—once you have it, the next step is to use it wisely.

Can people achieve more by staying busy all the time? As Thomas Jefferson suggested, we should avoid idleness because a great deal can be accomplished when we keep working. Sitting around doing nothing will not produce results. In contrast, staying active helps us learn new skills, connect with people who support our goals, and realize how much is possible when we make consistent efforts.

I studied until I memorized them and was able to do well on the exam. These experiences show how doing something—even when it feels uncomfortable—leads to real progress.

Keeping busy also opens doors to meet people who help us reach our aims. I’m usually more comfortable staying indoors, but during soccer season I had to work with teammates and coaches. Through those interactions I learned teamwork, got tips to boost my speed, and developed a stronger attitude toward improvement. Similarly, when I struggled with a math problem, I approached a new teacher for help. He explained the steps clearly and has continued to support me whenever I need assistance. Building relationships like these makes it easier to move toward our goals.

Think about the possibilities if people used free time productively rather than watching TV all day. Small efforts now can pay off later by improving our abilities and sharpening our thinking. Sometimes we might feel we don’t need help, but asking others can break a fixed mindset and speed up learning.

Of course, not everyone can stay constantly active—some people are short on time, money, or transportation, so they may appear inactive while working toward long-term goals. Still, passivity alone won’t create opportunities; waiting for good things to happen is rarely enough.

In short, keeping busy with purposeful activities helps people accomplish more. As Jefferson advised, avoiding idleness and staying engaged makes it surprising how much we can achieve.

I oppose the proposal to extend the school day. Right now, the hours we spend at school are enough. If the district tacks on an extra 90 minutes, students will be more exhausted and less able to absorb lessons. Longer days combined with regular homework would increase stress for many pupils. For a lot of students the current schedule already feels demanding; adding more class time could make school unpleasant and might lead some to lose interest, skip assignments, or even drop out. Many students also juggle part-time jobs, so a later dismissal would leave them very little time to prepare for tests or complete major projects at home.

Young people need free time for their well-being and physical health. Speaking as a middle school student, I can manage my studies and have leisure time now, but I worry that an extra hour and a half would cut into the time I use to relax, see family and friends, and do hobbies. Losing that downtime would affect my mood and energy. Students who work after school would suffer even more: they would struggle to spend time with family, rest, or exercise. This would hurt their mental and physical health and reduce their overall happiness.

Teachers who rely on part-time work would also face problems. Many educators take additional jobs to support large families or to supplement modest salaries. If school ends later and teachers must stay after school to help students or give retakes one or two nights a week, they would have less opportunity for outside employment or for caring for their own families. That could force some teachers to leave the profession or else require the district to raise pay so they no longer need second jobs.

School bus drivers already face risks driving early in the dark mornings. Pushing schedules later is not what they need either — the real concern is the late afternoons. Currently some after-school programs run about two hours; if the school day were extended by 90 minutes, dismissal plus after-school activities could end up about three and a half hours later than usual, often in much darker conditions. That would make transporting students more dangerous for drivers and riskier for everyone on the bus.

After-school programs are important for helping students make up work, retake tests, and improve grades. They also let students complete service hours or receive extra help. But with later school hours, fewer students and teachers might be willing or able to stay, and bus difficulties would make attendance harder. As a result, schools might be forced to cut these programs, which would harm many learners.

For these reasons, I believe adding 90 minutes to the school day would do more harm than good. It would increase stress, reduce free time, strain teachers and drivers, and threaten valuable after-school support.

Can extending school hours help save energy? One plan suggests moving to a four-day school week while adding two extra hours to each remaining day. I disagree with this change. It would create real difficulties for many students and teachers who depend on the current schedule.

Adding two hours a day would cause many problems. Students who work after school or take part in sports and clubs would find it harder to manage their time. Longer days would leave them exhausted and with less chance to relax or see friends. Some students also have family duties, such as picking up younger siblings, and a longer school day could conflict with those responsibilities. Teachers would be affected as well. Many live far from their workplace or have children to pick up, shop for, or care for after work. Changing the day’s length could make it impossible for them to keep family routines. Overall, this plan could disrupt the daily lives of both students and staff.

There are some benefits to having longer school days and a shorter week. More class time could allow students to finish assignments during school hours, spend extra time on tests, and cover more material in class. Teachers might give less homework, and students could take additional courses or even finish their studies sooner. A four-day week also means a longer weekend for rest and personal time. These advantages could help learning and reduce evening workloads for students.

Despite these possible benefits, I still oppose the idea. The practical difficulties for many families and staff are too great. Students who rely on after-school jobs, sports, or caregiving would struggle with the new hours. Teachers with long commutes or family duties could also face serious inconvenience. School is the main daily commitment for young people, and extending it by two hours would change their whole routine.

For these reasons, I hope schools do not adopt the proposed plan. While energy savings are important, any schedule change should consider the many students and adults whose lives would be negatively affected.

Scientist Albert Einstein once said, "Imagination is more important than knowledge." Now imagine yourself as a beginning engineer, sitting at your desk, aggravated because you can't come up with a new invention. All you have around you are textbooks but no image or thought of what your invention may be. If only you could imagine a new invention of some sort then maybe you could build something. But with no imagination, how can you build knowledge? I agree with Einstein's quote. I believe imagination is more important than knowledge.

I agree with Einstein's quote because having imagination is how we've had all our inventions yet. Without imagination how were many of the things we own invented? For example, the telephone. The telephone couldn't have been invented without someone imagining a device where you could communicate without leaving your home. You need imagination in order to make new things. Another example would be the camera. Whoever invented it, had to have imagination in order to think of a device that captures any moment almost in an instant. Even I, as a student, need imagination in order to make new things. For example, when making an essay, such as this one, I need to imagine of a good story hook that goes along with the prompt.

Furthermore, I believe in Einstein quote because without imagination, knowledge is almost useless. For example, when learning a new vocabulary list. You may know all the definitions but you can't put them in your own words or use the words in different instances. Why? Because you can't imagine it. You can't picture it, you just know the definitions. Another example is when reading a book. Knowing how to read isn't even near of what you need to fully comprehend a book. You need to imagine it. Picture the story in your mind in order to fully understand the book's theme, setting and tone.

Lastly, I agree in Einstein's quote because without imagination, all our decisions would be made carelessly. For instance, before you speak or move, most of the time you imagine what the outcome of that action will be. If not, the outcome won't be for the better. Another instance is when in an experiment, you hypothesize what the result of the experiment will be. That takes imagination. When signing a contract, it's needed to imagine the consequences of signing and not signing the contract. In other words, you need to imagine things before you decide to take them on. Knowledge isn't the only thing that will help you when making decisions.

In conclusion, Einstein's quote is correct in my perspective. Knowledge isn't the most important factor to have, imagination is key to everything you do and will do. You can't fully understand most things without imagining them. Can't go on inventing things before imagining them first. Also, you won't be able to make good decisions before imagining the outcome. All in all, imagination is also how you'll enjoy your life. Knowledge is great and all but it can't bring others as much happiness as imagination can. It's how we've been happy for all these years. Imagination is how we have gone so far in this world and how much we've survived.

Albert Einstein once claimed that "Imagination is more important than knowledge." Picture yourself as a new engineer at your desk, frustrated because you cannot think of any original design. You have books full of facts, but no image of what your creation could be. If you cannot imagine a concept, how can you turn it into real understanding or a product? I agree with Einstein: imagination matters more than knowledge.

First, imagination is the driving force behind inventions. If people had not pictured new possibilities, many objects we take for granted would not exist. Take the telephone: someone had to picture a way to speak with another person over a distance without seeing them face to face. The inventor first imagined that connection before learning the technical details needed to build it. The same goes for the camera: its creator had to think of a tool that could capture a moment instantly. Even as a student, my imagination helps me create new work. For this essay, I had to come up with an opening idea that fits the topic. New things start as images or ideas in the mind.

Second, knowledge by itself can be limited if imagination is missing. For example, learning a list of vocabulary meanings is not the same as being able to use those words in different situations. Without imagining real contexts, the words remain abstract definitions. Similarly, reading ability alone does not guarantee full understanding of a book. To grasp a story’s mood, setting, and themes, you must picture scenes and characters in your mind. Imagination turns stored facts into deeper comprehension.

Finally, imagination is essential for making careful choices. Before we act or speak, we often imagine possible results and choose the best option. If we never do this, our actions might lead to poor outcomes. In science, formulating a hypothesis requires picturing potential results before testing them. When deciding whether to sign a contract, you mentally play out the consequences of both signing and not signing. Knowledge provides information, but imagining the future is what guides wise decisions.

In conclusion, I believe Einstein was right. While knowledge is valuable, imagination is the key to creating, understanding, and choosing well. We cannot invent new things or fully understand complex ideas without imagining them first. Imagination also adds joy to life in ways facts alone cannot. It has pushed humanity forward and helped us survive and thrive. For these reasons, imagination deserves the higher place Einstein gave it.

Are vacations a necessity to us and to our success? Why do we need them? While some say that inactivity gives us time to reinvent ourselves. Others believe that it instigates procrastination. Inactivity serves a purpose because it keeps us from giving up and it allows us time for new ideas.

Inactivity serves a purpose because it keeps us from giving up. For example, I was once taking a very long test that lasted around 4 to 5 hours. At first, I was just guessing my way through it because I was very tired and ready to give up. Then, we were given a five minute break so I got up and walked around a bit. After walking for a few minutes, I was energized and ready to finish the test. With my new found energy, I was very content with the test and my score. In fact, students who take mental breaks during long testing periods score 31% higher than the ones who did not take any breaks. In conclusion, inactivity keeps us enthusiastic about our work.

Inactivity serves a purpose because it allows us time for new ideas. For example, one of my friends named Generic_Name once did not go to school for three days. During these three days, she organized her school essentials and cleaned up her room. Since she was working on a project before the break, she had time to finish it and she even had another project idea for her science class. She obtained a good grade on both projects. In fact, students who have taken breaks during long tests, like the SOL, say that after their break they had a better understanding of the test. Even the workforce workers are encouraged to take a few days off. It helps the worker get more creative. Even the owner of a business need a vacation. In fact, around 56% of entrepreneurs say that they came up with at least one new idea after a vacation. Inactivity helps prepare our minds for when we are active.

Inactivity serves a purpose. Inactivity keeps us from throwing in the towel. it gives us a mental break; which, creates time for new ideas. Some believe that inactivity encourages laziness. However, it gives us time to rejuvenate our attitude and our mindset. If we take more breaks, to let our mind wonder, we would be more effective in anything it is we are doing.

Have you ever faced a major choice and felt unsure which direction to take? It can be stressful to decide alone, but turning to others for advice often eases that pressure. Because important decisions come up many times in life, gathering opinions from several people can give you a wider range of information and help you reach a better conclusion. Asking multiple people for their views is a practical way to improve your decision-making.

First, consulting several people brings more information and perspectives. When you talk to a number of people, you collect different ideas and suggestions you might not think of on your own. Some of those people may also have more experience with the issue than you do, which can be especially useful. For instance, a student choosing which colleges to apply to might ask parents or older siblings for guidance because they have gone through the process before. By hearing many viewpoints, the decision maker can compare options and slowly form a clearer plan based on the accumulated advice.

Second, seeking multiple opinions helps reduce bias. If you only listen to close friends or family, their views may be influenced by their relationship with you. Adding input from people who are less personally involved—such as classmates, teachers, or coworkers—gives a wider, more impartial set of ideas. For example, a person trying to pick a school sport could ask friends and family, but they should also ask teammates or PE teachers who can give practical, less biased feedback. Hearing different, independent perspectives makes it easier to avoid one-sided thinking and lets you judge the choices more objectively.

Third, talking to several people can make you feel more prepared and confident about your decision. With many pieces of advice to consider, it becomes easier to decide because you have examined the situation from different angles. This reduces anxiety and helps you focus on what matters most. For example, someone choosing a new car may feel overwhelmed at first, but after consulting friends, family, and perhaps mechanics, they can better understand the trade-offs and choose a model that fits their needs. That preparation leads to a calmer, more confident final decision.

In short, getting advice from multiple people can lead to better choices. It brings more information, limits biased views, and increases confidence in the final decision. When faced with an important choice, asking several people for input is a smart way to make the best possible decision.

What are some fun activities to do outdoors at parks? There are plenty of options, and what you can do often depends on the park’s facilities. Three popular choices are playing golf, walking along a trail, and taking part in sports on an open field.

Parks often have trails of different lengths, so you can choose a short stroll or a longer hike depending on your time and fitness. Many people prefer walking in state, local, or national parks for the scenery and fresh air.

Finally, playing sports on a field is a popular way to have fun and exercise. If you like team games, you can play soccer, basketball, volleyball, football, and more. Some parks even supply balls and basic equipment, which makes it easy to join in.

In summary, parks offer many enjoyable outdoor activities like golfing, trail walking, and field sports.

Imagining the future fills a part of me that often feels empty and keeps me motivated every day.

I want to begin with a question most of us rarely consider: how is technology affecting our health? This is an important issue that deserves an honest answer.

Technology is now woven into almost every part of our day. From the moment we wake up until we go to bed, we interact with phones, computers, and apps dozens of times. These tools let us do many things without meeting other people face to face. We can borrow books, buy clothes, play games, and even talk to relatives online without leaving home. But reducing real human contact because of technology brings serious downsides.

Some people argue that less face-to-face contact has benefits, such as convenience or safety. However, many others believe—and I agree—that this reduction in personal interaction has mostly harmful effects. When I compare two people, the difference is clear: someone who relies on devices for almost everything is more likely to develop health problems sooner than someone who still prefers in-person activities. The person who uses technology constantly may shop online, read e-books, play video games, do homework on a laptop, and keep in touch with friends only through messages. This lifestyle encourages sitting for long periods and poor ergonomics, which often cause neck strain, back pain, and other musculoskeletal issues. Over time, these problems can become chronic and difficult to treat.

In addition to physical problems, heavy technology use can damage other aspects of health. Staring at screens can cause eye strain and worsen vision, while loud audio or frequent use of earbuds may contribute to hearing damage. Constant connectivity and notifications can increase stress levels, too. Many technology users also experience loneliness and depression because they lack real social support. Humans are social creatures; research shows that having friends to talk to is important for mental well-being. When people spend most of their time alone with devices, they miss out on those important connections and are more likely to feel isolated and unhappy.

Returning to the original question—how is technology impacting our health?—the answer for many is clear: it often does more harm than good. Technology can increase stress, harm eyesight, cause back and neck problems, and contribute to hearing loss. It can also reduce meaningful social contact, which raises the risk of depression.

If we do not learn to control our use of technology and balance it with real-life interaction and physical activity, the next generation may face the same problems or worse. We live in a world where technological progress is constant, so reversing these trends will be difficult. Still, change is possible if people work on managing their time better and make room for face-to-face relationships and healthier habits. Without that effort, more and more people will suffer from pain, illness, and loneliness because of excessive technology use.

Students know their own strengths and preferences, and when they are trusted to make choices, they often commit to doing well. Allowing choice supports their ability to succeed if they put effort into their studies.

If counselors assign students to classes they dislike, those students may avoid attending or put in little effort. It makes more sense to encourage students to enroll in classes that fit them personally. I urge school leaders to give students this responsibility and let them select electives that match their goals and interests.

I believe adding two more hours to the school day would be a bad idea. Schools already put a lot of pressure on students, and longer days would only increase stress. With more time in class comes more assignments and less chance to finish homework at home. Students would become exhausted and have trouble concentrating, which could lead to headaches and other health issues. Pushing children to stay alert and active for longer periods is not healthy, and many students’ bodies and minds would struggle to cope.

I prefer keeping a five-day school week rather than switching to four longer days. Extending each school day to make up for a shorter week would steal time from students’ lives outside of class, including hobbies, family time, and extracurricular activities. That extra time in school would feel unnecessary and unhelpful. For me, longer days mean more work and less rest, so I would feel more stressed and worn out. Many students would carry heavy mental loads, worrying about unfinished tasks and deadlines, and this constant pressure would cause frequent stress and headaches.

There are better ways to save energy and protect resources than simply increasing school hours. For example, we can encourage recycling, improve water treatment, and promote energy-saving habits. Teaching students how to care for the environment is important, but it doesn’t require extending the school day. Volunteering in clean-up efforts, learning about renewable energy, and taking part in local conservation projects are practical activities that help the planet and can fit into existing schedules. People should think creatively about global problems and work together to find solutions that do not sacrifice students’ well-being.

Many people would be unhappy with longer school days because it takes away time they need for other responsibilities. Overworking students can make them lazy or burned out, which hurts both individuals and the community. Another serious risk is tired driving: if students or parents are overly fatigued, the chances of accidents increase. Overall, forcing everyone to work longer hours would likely cause health problems and lower quality of life. If I were faced with that change, I would not accept it; it would be too much to handle and could make me sick. For these reasons, extending school hours is not a good idea.

What are the benefits of working with a group and working alone? Some school systems now let motivated students finish high school in three years instead of the usual four. I support this idea. Graduating a year early can help young people begin college sooner, give them more time to decide on a career, and encourage them to use their time wisely and work more efficiently.

When people face an important choice, they usually think carefully and weigh their options. If students complete high school in three years, they gain an extra year to reflect on what they want to study and to choose a college that fits them best. This matters because one decision can shape many future experiences. With that additional time, students can focus on their real interests, reconsider their plans if necessary, and make a better-informed choice about a career path. One year may not seem long, but it can be enough for a young person to discover a meaningful major or job they had only dreamed of before.

Time is an investment, and students should make the most of it. Some parents, teachers, and classmates worry that finishing early will take away free time for hobbies, family, or relaxation. In my view, however, this option can actually improve students’ performance. Knowing they have a shorter timeline often helps young people set priorities and stay focused. Of course teenagers still need free time, but parents also have a role in teaching them responsibility and how to balance obligations. For example, I enrolled in English 10 during summer school while living in Generic_City. I drove for an hour each morning to get there; waking up early and making that trip was difficult, but now I see that it was the right choice because I am close to graduating. People should remember that achieving great rewards sometimes requires extra effort.

Opponents argue that students are not mature enough or prepared to leave high school early. They believe finishing all four years helps young people be ready for college or work. Some parents also object to the demands of taking extra classes, evenings, or summer courses, calling these options “additional pressure” on students. These concerns are understandable. Many think it is better for students to follow the traditional four-year path.

Still, this program does not force anyone to rush; it gives motivated students a chance to accelerate when they are ready. For those who choose it, the extra work and occasional sacrifice can pay off by opening opportunities sooner. Rather than prolonging a student’s journey, the three-year path can shorten the time to reach higher education or a career start, which may be the right move for some families.

In conclusion, pressure can sometimes be a useful tool that helps people push toward their goals. When students take calculated risks and work hard, they often reach achievements they did not expect. The three-year high school option offers valuable support for motivated students, helping them prove they can meet their aims. By setting clear academic goals and committing to them, a single extra year gained can bring a student closer to the future they want.

Technology has become powerful, letting students and teachers give and receive classes online. Disadvantages or advantages of taking classes online? These questions are faced today by students deciding to take online classes. Often students work part- or full-time jobs while going to school or college, so their time is valuable. These students want to make the right decisions in choosing classes, so knowing the disadvantages and advantages is important. I believe that online classes are a good opportunity for students as they give flexibility; they often offer any type of class desired, provide access to faculty, and often offer accelerated courses.

To begin with, one of the best advantages of online classes is flexibility. A student can usually take the course at any time during the day or week. While there are custom essay writing and researching assignments to complete, the precise time to take the class often depends on the student's desire. Students who work are able to take the class based on their schedule, since many work in the afternoon. The flexibility makes it possible for a person to complete the course when attending school or college courses in person might be impossible due to their work schedules.

Secondly, another great advantage of online courses is that almost any type of course can be found online. Distance learning courses are often available from a number of colleges. A person can simply use Google to find a class. While most people believe a disadvantage of taking online courses is that students cannot have access to a faculty member, the fact is that many online courses offer greater access to faculty. Shy students are able to ask questions and receive the answer back almost immediately.

Lastly, online courses are convenient for most undergraduate and graduate students who can study when they want and finish writing or researching assignments based on their own personal schedules. The fact is online classes offer flexibility and convenience that are often vital to students who work and have families. In addition, many students are looking for classes that are advanced to complete the course faster. The best way to advance in the class is to make it online, because in regular schools it takes a long time as there are students who get behind and the teachers wait for them since everyone has to go at the same time.

To conclude, with online classes, students do all the work at their own pace, as long as they meet their deadlines and participate appropriately online. Also, studying online requires more self-motivation and time management skills because students will spend a lot of time on their own without someone physically close to keep them focused on deadlines. Online courses will not only teach students geology or poetry, but will also help them become more self-motivated, a trait that will make them stand out in the workplace and beyond. It will teach educators to be mature in choosing right decisions, as it will make them explore more and be students with an open mind.

Technology has made it possible for teachers and students to meet and learn without being in the same room. Many students today must decide whether to take classes online or in person. This choice is especially important for those who work part- or full-time while studying, because their schedules are limited. I believe online courses are a valuable option because they offer flexibility, a wide range of subjects and access to instructors, and opportunities to complete studies more quickly.

First, flexibility is one of the clearest benefits of online learning. Many online courses let students study at times that suit them, whether early morning, late at night, or during breaks at work. Although assignments and deadlines still exist, the exact hours for reading lectures or watching videos are usually up to the student. For people who work afternoons or have other obligations, this flexibility makes it realistic to keep studying, something that in-person classes with fixed meeting times might prevent.

Second, almost every kind of course can be found online. Colleges and training providers post a huge variety of classes, and a simple search often reveals many options. Some people worry that online learners have less contact with instructors, but often the opposite is true: electronic communication—email, discussion boards, and messaging—can make it easier to ask questions. Students who are shy may find it simpler to write their questions and get a quick response, improving their access to faculty.

Third, online programs can allow students to move through material faster. In traditional classrooms, the pace is shaped by the whole group, and teachers sometimes slow down for those who fall behind. Online courses frequently let motivated students progress at their own speed, which helps those who want to finish a course or degree sooner. This convenience is especially helpful for undergraduates, graduate students, and anyone juggling family responsibilities, because they can plan study time around their lives.

In conclusion, online classes let students manage their learning on their own schedule while still meeting deadlines and participating as required. They demand stronger self-discipline and time-management skills, but they also help learners develop these traits. Beyond teaching a subject like poetry or geology, online study can encourage independence, maturity, and an open mind—qualities that benefit students in their careers and personal growth.

Many schools offer a range of extracurriculars, and one popular option is learning to play an instrument. Playing music opens up many possibilities. For example, marching bands perform impressive routines at football games that take a lot of practice. Orchestras fill a hall with flowing classical pieces and sometimes play bold, energetic works too. Being involved with an instrument can be fun in many ways, especially when you get to hear yourself play well, take enjoyable trips, and explore lots of different kinds of music.

Playing in a band or orchestra exposes you to a wide variety of pieces, and mastering a song can give you a real confidence boost. When you and your classmates perform a piece successfully, it feels great and reassures you that your concert will go well. Knowing you can play music that some people cannot is satisfying. Auditioning for a particular ensemble and then being accepted is exciting — it proves you reached a goal. These chances to improve and succeed are part of what makes playing an instrument so rewarding.

Another big perk is the chance to go on field trips. Often, schools reserve special outings for students in band and orchestra as a reward for their dedication. These trips are more fun because you share them with friends from your class. Joining a music group is a good way to make new friends who enjoy the same things you do. Some schools plan more trips than others, but when they do, students might visit places like Kings Dominion, Busch Gardens, or Hershey Park — all full of roller coasters, water rides, and games. Those kinds of trips are memorable treats for young musicians.

In addition, almost any movie or show has music that your group can perform. You can usually find sheet music for popular songs, or you can create your own arrangements. With an instrument, you can bring to life the tunes you’ve always wanted to play, including favorite movie themes. Although arranging some songs for an ensemble can be challenging, it’s almost always possible to turn a beloved song into playable sheet music.

Learning an instrument takes practice, and improvement comes from working hard. Playing isn’t easy, but the effort is satisfying. Doing well makes you proud, and others will be proud of you too. Being part of the music community is a privilege that not everyone experiences, but there’s nothing stopping someone from joining. The friendships, trips, and musical opportunities that come with band or orchestra make the experience feel limitless.

First impressions are a natural and almost immediate way people respond to new situations, and they are very hard to change. These quick judgments depend on how surprising, frightening, or amusing something is and on a person's feelings at the moment. Because they happen so fast and automatically, people often have little control over them. The mind forms these first impressions without warning, and once they appear they are difficult to reverse.

First, first impressions form automatically and we cannot easily control them. For example, when you meet someone for the first time, you quickly form an impression of that person, regardless of who they are. These judgments appear without deliberate thought. A second example is when people move to a new town or visit a different region; their immediate reactions to the place and its people arise on their own. Third, students often develop early ideas about a class or teacher before they know much about the subject. Even without planning to do so, they create impressions of what the course will be like, and those early views are not easy to change.

Second, the mind plays a central role in creating these instant impressions. Our brain gathers information and produces judgments very quickly. For instance, when shoppers compare prices at different markets, their minds immediately form opinions about value and quality based on what they see. Another example is hospital staff who regularly care for seriously ill patients; after repeated exposure, their minds form habitual impressions about illnesses and how to respond. Similarly, people who move to the United States from another country experience many new impressions as their minds adjust to different customs and ways of life. In all these situations, the mind is actively shaping the first impressions that guide reactions.

Third, people are usually unprepared for the first impressions they receive because these reactions appear suddenly. For example, when someone goes to the cinema to watch a new movie about the world or society, they may have no expectation about the film’s content, but as the story starts they quickly form impressions of the themes and characters. Technology is often called the crowning achievement of the 21st century. Most people admire it, but is it truly all good? When I was younger, I heard warnings that technology would harm our social lives. At the time I shrugged them off, yet now I understand what they meant.

At its core, technology is meant to make everyday tasks simpler, not to isolate us or make us unhealthy. I believe it has enormous potential, but we frequently misuse it. Instead of preparing meals at home, many choose to order takeout, which is often far less healthy. Another serious problem is that people organize their lives around devices; when a phone or an app stops working, some act as if their world has ended. The widespread use of social networking apps is a major factor in this shift. Too many people prefer scrolling through feeds to having real conversations in person.

That said, technology also brings clear benefits alongside its drawbacks. A key advantage is that it saves time in many routine activities. For example, sending a letter used to take days or weeks, while today a message can reach someone in seconds. Technology also enables cleaner ways to power our world: electric homes, vehicles, and aircraft can replace fossil-fuel machines that damage the environment. We can generate electricity from solar panels, wind turbines, and hydropower. These sources are effectively renewable, barring catastrophic events like the Sun disappearing or all winds stopping. For normal circumstances, they offer a much cleaner alternative.

Overall, I view technology as a remarkable human achievement. It has harmful effects, but many of them can be controlled. If we avoid making social media the center of our lives and treat devices as tools rather than masters, the negative impacts will lessen. Technology has come a long way — it started by lighting a bulb and now it powers cars, buildings, phones, and entire cities.

Being true to yourself helps you become the best version of who you are. When you act like yourself, you are honest about your values and habits instead of pretending to be someone else. It is okay to grow and improve, but you should not lose the core of who you are just to fit in or please others. People often change because they want to be better or because they are tired of being quiet and alone. However, changing the way you act can be hard to undo, because it means altering habits and parts of your personality that define you.

First, being yourself makes you original. You do not need to change just to prove something to others. Your behavior — whether kind or rude, quiet or outgoing — comes from who you are now. Life events can cause people to change: the loss of a loved one, abuse, or depression can all affect how someone behaves. Still, if you decide to change, do it in a way that improves you rather than erases you. Your family and close friends know you for who you are; sudden changes can confuse them. If you want to become better, aim to build on your strengths instead of copying someone else. Remember that other people's opinions should not completely control who you are.

Second, changing for the wrong reasons can make you lose your inner self. Many people try to be someone they admire, or they change to gain approval. But if you change only for friends or to avoid criticism, you may end up unhappy because those changes are not true to you. My grandmother used to tell me not to change for anyone because family will love and respect you in ways others will not. No one should be forced to hide parts of themselves to be accepted. Even if you are sometimes rude or annoying, you still deserve respect and the chance to show the best of yourself. Keep the parts of your character that matter, and bring out the positive sides that others might not have seen yet.

Third, your personality reveals your character. People do not like someone who acts superior or pretends to be better than everyone else. Be proud of where you come from, even if you do not have much wealth or live in a fancy house. Showing confidence in who you are signals that you do not care too much about others’ judgments. If friends or family react badly to a change in you, do not meet their distance with a mean attitude; that will only push them further away. Take advice from others when it helps you grow, but do not become a copy of someone else. Stand out for being genuine, not for imitating others.

Fourth, trying to return to an old version of yourself after changing can be hard. Once you push away the person you used to be, it may take a long time to regain that identity. Some people who moved away from you may never come back because of the changes you made. If you choose to change, accept your decision and focus on growing into that new person. You changed for a reason, so embrace and love that growth. The person you become is someone you will continue to develop as you live your life.

In the end, be yourself and avoid changing into someone you are not. Let any change come from your own desire to improve, not from pressure or the desire to impress. Being authentic will guide you through life and help you become the person you want to be.

Many people argue about whether it is better to set very ambitious goals or to aim lower. Some fear that reaching too high only leads to disappointment and giving up. However, this view misses an important truth: goals and successes come in many forms. Setting ambitious targets is worthwhile because it often leads to greater achievements, stronger motivation, and a stronger sense of accomplishment.

Critics say that aiming too high can be discouraging. If someone sets a difficult target and fails, they may lose confidence and stop trying. This fear of failure makes some prefer safer, lower goals that seem more likely to be reached. While that concern is understandable, it overlooks other important outcomes of aiming high.

Ambitious goals help people accomplish more. When you push yourself, you often end up pursuing several objectives rather than just one. Working toward a big aim can break down into many smaller milestones, and completing those gives a person multiple successes to be proud of. Even if one particular target is not met, the effort usually produces other results and skills that count as real achievements. Not every goal will be reached, but aiming higher increases the chance of achieving difficult, meaningful things.

High goals also boost the feeling of success. Finishing a challenging task produces a deeper sense of achievement than ticking off an easy objective. Succeeding at demanding goals builds confidence and reduces anxiety about future challenges. Over time, these successes add up and help people believe they can handle more. That growing self-assurance can be useful in many areas of life, making people feel that their time and efforts had real value.

Finally, setting ambitious targets tends to increase motivation. Big goals require focus, dedication, and hard work, and having something important to strive for channels a person’s attention and energy. This focus creates drive — a mental push to keep going and to overcome obstacles. For many people, the process of working toward an inspiring goal is what keeps them committed and productive.

For these reasons, aiming high is generally beneficial. Yes, failure is possible, and the risk can be scary, but nobody is perfect. People will make mistakes and fall short sometimes; what matters is learning from those experiences and continuing to reach for greater things. Ambition, when balanced with persistence, can lead to more accomplishments, stronger motivation, and a real sense of success.

Can people who have already mastered a skill continue to develop if they never try anything else? Some believe that being very good at one thing is enough. It is true that someone can become an expert in a single profession, but if they refuse to explore other areas, their growth will be limited. Choosing to focus on one specialty is fine, yet that person’s knowledge will only expand within that narrow field. If a person’s mindset is fixed on what they have already mastered, they will not gain new understanding.

People who remain only in their comfort zone cannot grow much further. For example, Ms. Generic_Name ran a plant shop and taught customers about gardening. One day she explained to some children that plants don’t thrive by themselves — people help them grow. She took the kids to the back of the shop to show them an apple seed and admitted that she used to care for the seedlings but stopped because she thought her job was done once the plants looked healthy. She believed they would continue to develop without attention, so she left them alone. Because of that attitude, the plants did not grow as well as they could have. The same thing happens to people who stop learning once they feel competent: they remain steady but do not improve. Therefore, if someone assumes their current skills are enough and never tries anything new, their personal growth will stall.

Knowledge is closely tied to growth. At first, Ms. Generic_Name knew only the basics about her plants and did not realize how much ongoing care they needed. Over the years, though, she kept learning and broadened her understanding. She went to college to study different species from other countries and, thanks to her dedication, Estency Generic_Name became a leading specialist in her field. This shows that nobody should be satisfied with only what they already know; people should pursue more learning related to their interests, just as she did.

For instance, Generic_Name finished college and became a constructor, though he had once dreamed of being an architect. He chose a simpler path, but even after reaching mastery, people should stay open to new knowledge. Being skilled at one thing is valuable, yet continual learning keeps growth alive.

In conclusion, people do not grow if they never try new things. Knowledge increases with time and effort, and it plays a key role in personal development. It is better to keep learning than to stop after achieving one success.

Students work hard there is no arguing that. They have schoolwork, homework, extracurricular and maybe work, all these things make a students life stressful so it is important that they get a break every once in a while. I believe that students should get a long summer break, instead of a year-round school year, because, firstly, there are other activities that can be done during the summer that keep students minds active, secondly their health is at risk and lastly, summer break is beneficial to school staff as well.

From time to time, people need to get a break from their day-today life they need to take a moment to relax and enjoy their life and maybe discover an interest that they may have. Although school is important and necessary for success later on in life, so are outside experiences that can contribute to the development of a student's 'real life skills'. During summer break there are multiple activities that can be done in order to keep a student's mind active, whether it may be sports, summer camps, summer jobs etc. All these activities allow for their minds and bodies to stay active. Eventhough, they are not keeping their brains engaged in terms of school work and studying they are exposing themselves to new activities that might require them to think critically, open-mindedly and collaboratively; which I feel is essential for real life. For example, a student might be at summer camp and they are put in a group with four strangers and are given a challenging task that requires them to collaborate with the other member of the group, critically analyzing the situation and coming up with solutions and be open-minded to listening and trying to understand the perspectives of their peers. This also reflects their environment in school therefore, it can be said that they are keeping their minds active while outside of school.

Although, not all students might be involved in activities outside of school, some are taking a break from the stress of life itself. Due to all the demands in their life during the school year summer break is a good way to take a breather and take care of themselves mentally. Depression has been very common in teenagers in recent years, and although it may not be entirely due to the stress of school, school does contribute to the detirriation of their mental health. In addition, over-working ones self has negative impacts overall whether they are depressed or not. Too much stress in ones life can have negative effects on their health overall. High blood pressure, hypertension, severe weight loss are a few examples of the effects stress. Furthermore, when stressed our body releases a neurotransmitter called Cortisol, this neurotransmitter in excess can impair a persons thinking and reaction time; which is very important for students as they are required to think in order to complete school work and homework, therefore, if they dont take breaks their grades are probably going to drop due to their inability to think effectively, further contributing to their detirriating mental health.

Lastly, summer break is and essential time for everyone that is involved in schools, such as teachers, administrators, councilors etc. Although schools are intended to educate students, its the school staff that make this possible. This is why we need to give our school staff a break because all the points I stated above also applies to them. In addition, with a long summer break teachers are able to have more time to thoroughly think about their lesson plans for their students as well as have an extended amount of time to live their lives and enjoy time with their family and friends, after all, teachers are humans too and they need to be able to life their lives and forget that they are required to do so much for such little pay.
