Students today juggle many responsibilities: classwork, homework, clubs, and often part-time jobs. All of these demands make school life stressful, so occasional periods of rest are essential. I support a long summer holiday instead of a year-round school calendar because, first, summer offers activities that keep students’ minds active; second, long breaks protect their physical and mental health; and third, teachers and other school staff also benefit from extended time off.

Everyone needs a pause from their daily routine to relax and explore new interests. School is important for long-term success, but learning also happens outside the classroom. During the summer, students can take part in sports, camps, volunteer projects, or work. These experiences engage both mind and body. Even if they are not doing formal academic work, students often face situations that require problem-solving, teamwork, and open-minded thinking. For example, at a summer camp a group of students might be given a difficult challenge that forces them to communicate, evaluate options, and cooperate to find a solution. Such activities mirror the social and cognitive skills used in school, so students continue to develop while enjoying their break.

Not every student will be involved in organized programs, but for many a summer break is a chance to step away from stress and recover. Teen depression has become more common, and although school is not the only cause, academic pressure contributes to poor mental health. Chronic stress can harm the body too: it is linked to high blood pressure, unhealthy weight changes, and other medical problems. When we are stressed, our bodies release cortisol; in large amounts this hormone can reduce clear thinking and slow reaction times. For students who must concentrate to do well in class and on exams, impaired thinking can lead to lower grades, which then increases stress—so taking a proper break can help prevent this negative cycle.

Finally, long summers are also important for the adults who work in schools. Teachers, counselors, and administrators play a central role in education, and they need time to rest and restore their energy. A lengthy break gives teachers the opportunity to plan lessons more carefully, pursue professional development, or simply spend quality time with family and friends. Like students, school staff can suffer from burnout, and a sustained holiday helps them return to work refreshed and better prepared to support learners.

For these reasons, I believe schools should keep a long summer vacation rather than switching to year-round schedules. Summer activities can keep students mentally active, extended time off protects physical and mental health, and school personnel also need the break. All of these benefits support the idea that a long summer holiday is valuable for the whole school community.

Aiming low might look like it's the simple and easy way that's safer, but what's really the danger is for people to forget to aim high and believe they can achieve great things. The best is to make a decision that won't make you regret and making the best aim you can make. No one has to be excellent or perfect, but everyone should try their best in their short life so they can die with no regret.

Many people have heard a famous idea often linked to Michelangelo: the real risk is not aiming too high and failing, but aiming too low and succeeding. I agree with this view. Setting ambitious goals offers greater benefits. People who aim higher reach larger achievements, develop more original thinking, and open up more opportunities than those who settle for modest targets.

First, aiming high creates many more possibilities. When you limit your goals before you begin, you narrow the paths available to you. For instance, consider job hunting: is it better to only apply for easy, low-skill work like washing dishes, or to try for every role you are qualified for? The second choice obviously gives you more options. The same idea applies to education. A young person unsure about a future might choose military service because it seems straightforward, or they might go to university where many fields and careers are possible. Attending college often expands employment prospects and may lead to better opportunities than taking the simpler route.

Second, higher goals encourage more original thinking and fuller use of one’s abilities. People who set low expectations often hide their true ideas or may never explore them, because they do not push themselves. In contrast, those who aim higher take on tougher challenges and think more deeply about how to achieve them. This kind of effort develops the mind and can lead to unique solutions. Famous artists, for example, did not limit themselves; they pushed boundaries and produced remarkable works. If they had accepted small goals, those creative achievements might never have appeared.

Third, aiming high helps you reach greater results instead of settling for the minimum. Think about schoolwork: doing the least to meet the requirements will not get you as far as putting in extra effort to produce excellent work. A low aim may cause you to give up when tasks become difficult, even if those tasks are important. With higher goals, people are more likely to persevere and complete meaningful objectives. Therefore, choosing harder targets usually brings better outcomes than always picking the easiest path.

Some may argue that very high ambitions cause suffering and stress. While this is sometimes true, it does not mean people should set small goals instead. Balance is important: know your limits and choose aims that are challenging but attainable. People often tell children to eat balanced meals; the same idea applies to setting goals. Also, avoiding stress completely is not always desirable. Some stress can motivate and push a person forward. I remember when I was a student in Japan and did not want to study. I felt anxious and stayed home, but that did not make me feel better. Returning to school and confronting the challenge improved my situation. Though stress can be harmful, it can also produce positive change when managed well.

In short, taking the easy route and lowering your aims is rarely the best choice. Aiming low may seem safe, but it risks keeping people from realizing their potential. We should choose goals that challenge us and avoid living with regrets. Nobody must be perfect, but everyone should try their best while they can.

Some people claim that first impressions are permanent and cannot be altered. I disagree. First impressions can change over time because people grow and develop, because the behavior of those around us influences us, and because life events can change how others see us.

People often alter others’ views as they mature. My mother often reminds me that I am different from the child she raised. When I was seven or eight, I was quiet and nervous speaking to strangers; I would try hard to be polite and avoid attention. As I grew older I became more confident in how I looked and how I acted in public. I stopped doing things I once did as a child and learned new ways to express myself. This kind of personal growth shows that first impressions based on youth or inexperience do not have to last.

Other people also play a big role in changing impressions. For instance, my younger brother used to be very shy and rarely spoke to others. He began to see how I interacted with people—calmly and confidently—and he copied that behavior. Over time he became more outgoing and now talks to many different people and enjoys social situations. Our actions can serve as models for those close to us, and a supportive or negative influence can change how someone is seen by friends and acquaintances.

Life’s challenges and events can also reshape how people perceive us. I remember a few days before my fourteenth birthday, my father was arrested. I felt that everything was unfair and lost interest in celebrating. At school I usually laughed and joked, so people thought I was always happy. After my father’s arrest, I stopped making jokes and became quieter. My classmates noticed the change and began to treat me differently — giving me space and taking my feelings more seriously. That situation made them see me in a new light, not as the cheerful teenager they assumed I was. A major life event revealed a different side of me and altered their first impression.

In conclusion, I believe first impressions can be changed. Maturity, the influence of others, and events that shape our lives all affect how people view us over time. Because people and circumstances change, initial opinions are not fixed and can be revised.

Many people claim that a positive attitude leads to success, and I agree. Keeping a hopeful outlook can support you throughout your whole life. It helps you notice the good in difficult situations, improves your character, and even boosts your chances at work.

A positive mindset makes it easier to avoid dwelling on the worst part of a problem. Instead of focusing on failure, you look for what can be learned and how to move forward. For example, if you fail a government test, thinking positively will help you study harder and believe you will pass the next time. This kind of thinking turns setbacks into steps toward improvement.

Maintaining an optimistic attitude can also make you a better person. There are many people around us dealing with money worries or family difficulties. If you stay positive, you are more likely to offer help, comfort, or practical support to those in need. Helping others not only benefits them but also gives you a sense of pride and personal growth.

A good attitude is important at work, too. Employers often prefer workers who are friendly, cooperative, and willing to help customers or teammates. If you do not have a job, showing a positive approach during interviews can make you stand out. In the workplace, a constructive attitude improves communication, customer service, and team spirit.

In conclusion, a positive attitude really is a key to success. It guides you through problems and poor choices, encourages you to support friends, and makes your daily life more enjoyable. By staying optimistic, you increase your chances of achieving success and leading a happier life.

Many people today think it is wiser to choose a modest, achievable goal than to aim for something grand and risk failing. I disagree. Michelangelo, one of history’s greatest artists, warned that setting our sights too low can be dangerous. He spoke from experience, having made mistakes and faced failures before he became famous. He preferred to risk failure by pursuing ambitious work rather than settle for small, safe achievements. I side with Michelangelo because aiming high teaches us from our mistakes, encourages us to take risks, and pushes us to grow.

Failures offer important lessons. When we try difficult things, we can study what went wrong and work to improve. For example, the cooking competition MasterChef eliminates one contestant each week. Although being sent home can be disappointing, many of those chefs use the experience to recognize their weaknesses and return stronger. Another everyday example is taking a driving permit test as a teenager. I failed mine by only one question because I was nervous, but by reviewing the errors and studying, I passed the next time. These situations show that making mistakes while reaching for something challenging helps us learn and become better.

Taking risks is a key part of tackling large goals. Big choices often involve career moves, educational decisions, or launching a business, and they push us out of our comfort zones. The television show Shark Tank illustrates this: entrepreneurs must persuade investors to support their ideas, and many do not receive offers. Still, those who are turned down often continue to take risks—seeking different partners, refining their product, or self-funding—and sometimes succeed later. Learning to take chances also improves confidence and communication. For instance, meeting an employer in person instead of doing a remote interview can be more demanding, but it gives you a better chance to connect and demonstrate your abilities. Facing these challenges makes you stronger and more prepared.

Overall, I agree with Michelangelo that aiming high, even if you fail, is preferable to choosing small, safe goals. Larger ambitions demand more effort and force you to confront mistakes, learn from them, and develop resilience. Small goals may be completed easily, but they can also encourage complacency. By striving for greater achievements, you expand your skills and knowledge and become more capable.

In short, setting ambitious goals is worth the risk. Failing while trying to reach a high aim teaches valuable lessons, builds the willingness to take risks, and promotes personal growth. It is better to challenge yourself than to settle for what feels safe and simple.

First impressions often vary from person to person. Everyone reacts differently when they meet someone or see something for the first time, and these initial thoughts can change later as you learn more about that person. First impressions are important because they are our immediate response, but they can shift after an hour, a day, or more time.

For example, you might find a class boring on the first day and form a negative opinion. If the next lesson is more interesting and the teacher makes it fun, your view can change. Your attitude also affects how you judge things at first. If you are negative or closed-minded, your first impressions will likely be negative too. Sometimes a bad first impression reveals more about your own mood than about the other person.

There are cases when first impressions do not change. Many people keep their first judgment and refuse to reconsider it. However, a good first impression can be ruined if the person later does something wrong or shows a bad side.

Another example is starting a new job. On day one you may like the work because it seems easy and you meet friendly coworkers. But if you soon discover your boss is rude or unfair, your opinion of the job can go down. First impressions matter because they influence whether you become friends with someone or stay distant.

In conclusion, first impressions can change depending on the individual and their attitude, but they do not always change. It is important to try to learn more about others before making a final judgment, because otherwise you may miss the chance to understand them better.

Eighty-nine percent of students at Generic_School oppose the school board’s plan to add an extra hour and a half to the school day. Most students work after school or need to get home quickly to look after younger siblings and finish homework. For these reasons, extending the school day would cause real problems for many of them.

A lot of students have parents who work full time, so someone must care for younger brothers and sisters when the parents are away. Older children often feed, change, and watch their siblings to keep them safe and out of trouble. Taking on this responsibility is important: younger children need supervision so they don’t get hurt, and someone has to make sure they are fed and clean. Sometimes older students also do household chores while the little ones sleep so the house will be tidy when the parents come home. If school finished later, parents would worry about who would look after the children.

High school brings a heavy workload. There are regular homework assignments and larger projects that take much more time and effort. Homework helps students keep good grades, but when there is too much work, it becomes overwhelming. Projects can be especially demanding and often require help from classmates. Studying with friends is useful because it makes learning more enjoyable and lets students support each other. Graduating from high school is a major goal, and students want to protect their grades to make their parents proud.

Many students also have part-time jobs. Earning money gives them independence and helps pay for clothes, food, and other needs without always asking parents for money. Working after school can be tiring, since students are already worn out from classes, but the extra income is important for their families and themselves. Some students even work with friends, which makes the job more pleasant.

For these reasons, most students at Generic_School disagree with adding extra time to the school day. With jobs to attend and siblings to care for, extending school hours would make life harder for many of them.

For instance, when you support your colleagues and perform your duties well, your supervisor is likely to notice and reward your dedication. In the same way, being warm, confident, and loving makes it easier to find a partner who returns your feelings and treats you in the same way.

First, a good attitude is one of the most effective ways to advance at work. Employers and coworkers usually prefer to work with people who are agreeable because they make the team function more smoothly and increase overall productivity. For example, last year my uncle was one of three candidates considered for a promotion. Most of his colleagues voted for him because they said he was the friendliest and most suitable person for the role. This shows that when you have a likeable attitude, others will support you and trust your leadership.

Second, strong relationships depend largely on attitude and communication. Most successful couples share mutual respect and open dialogue, which helps them solve problems calmly. My parents rarely argued; instead, they talked through their disagreements and taught me that a calm, cooperative attitude is better than anger. Their example shows that maintaining a positive attitude can prevent love from fading and reduce the chance of separation.

Some people argue that a pleasant attitude is not always necessary for success. There are well-known figures who have achieved power despite being unpopular. For example, the president of my country has an unpleasant manner but has built a powerful political career and still holds office in El Salvador. Still, many people say, “He is president because the country needed him, not because people like him.” This proves that while success and authority are possible without being well-liked, an unpleasant attitude makes it hard to earn genuine respect and affection.

People with a friendly personality generally find it easier to build helpful relationships, while those who remain distant or strange often struggle to make friends. In conclusion, being charismatic and respectful improves most areas of life and makes achieving your goals smoother.

I agree with being an individual. I like when people choose what they want for their own lives. It feels great to make your own decisions. I have many friends who copy what others do. I prefer to do what I decide and what I enjoy, even if sometimes I am not sure what I want.

My family can be very negative at times and they do not listen to me. That frustrates me because I want to speak up and be heard. I value individuality because I hope others will listen to me and let me do what I want.

I have seen a lot of people who depend on others, and I think that is not good. In my history class we learned that in the past people had much less individuality. Today I believe many people want attention, so they follow others instead of thinking for themselves.

Life now is different from before. People often care too much about what others say about how they look or who they are. I like who I am because I consider myself kind and good, so I do what I want and I don’t worry too much about other people’s comments.

I will tell you about my life because I do not know what else to write. I arrived from Puerto Rico two years ago and since then everything has changed. I started to appreciate every little thing I get because now I know the value and the sacrifices people make to achieve things.

Even though it is hard, I still want to improve and work on many parts of my life. It is not easy because the language and customs are very different. But I am still here and I will keep going because I believe in myself and I know that when I set a goal I achieve it.

When you arrive, you meet many people from different places — some are very nice and others are not. I enjoy learning new things and visiting new places. One thing that annoys me is that, even though Puerto Ricans are part of the United States and I am not undocumented, some people treat us like we are because our first language is Spanish.

These two years have not been easy. School has been one of my biggest challenges because it is difficult to walk into a classroom and feel completely alone. When you cannot ask or talk to anyone, you just sit and watch while others do well and you cannot. A few months after I arrived I began skipping school and making bad choices because I had no support at home or anywhere else.

Today I sometimes feel like I do not belong here. The only reason I stay is my mother. I want her to succeed and to be able to give her everything she deserves. She was always there for us in Puerto Rico and tried to give us the best despite how hard life was.

Some people argue that students should be allowed to use cell phones in class because they can access the internet for schoolwork. However, I believe students should not use phones in the classroom because they cause disruptions and encourage chatting while the teacher is speaking.

First, phones often create disturbances during lessons. When students play music, watch videos, or browse social media, they distract others and stop doing class activities. This makes it hard for teachers to keep the lesson focused and wastes time for the whole class. If a student insists on listening to music and the teacher asks them to stop, this can lead to arguments. Repeated disturbance can become a serious problem, and schools may have to take strong measures, such as warnings or suspensions, to keep order.

Second, phones promote chatting and rude behavior that ruin the learning atmosphere. If students are texting or messaging during class, they do not pay attention to the teacher and miss important information. Sometimes classmates share inappropriate or insulting pictures and laugh, which hurts the person who is targeted. A student who is mocked or shown a bad image can feel ashamed and lose confidence, and this may make them reluctant to come to school.

Third, cell phones make it easier for students to cheat on tests. A student with a phone can look up answers during an exam and get an unfair advantage. This is not fair to other students who work honestly, and it damages the cheater’s learning because they do not practice doing the work themselves. Relying on phones for answers reduces real knowledge and study habits.

Fourth, cell phones reduce class participation and can harm health. When students focus on phones instead of joining activities or answering questions, class interaction declines. Time spent watching videos or always listening to music can be a large waste of study time. In addition, constant screen use is not good for the eyes and can lower concentration. If students are always focused on their phones, they miss chances to listen to others and take part in meaningful discussions.

In conclusion, although phones might help with internet access, students should not use cell phones in the classroom because they disrupt lessons, encourage chatting and bad behavior, enable cheating, and reduce participation while harming health.

It's really hard to make the selection of which advice you're gonna pick.

When you need guidance, you usually do not rely on only one person. Most people prefer to ask several people so they can compare different viewpoints and reduce the risk of missing a better option. Getting many opinions helps avoid putting all your trust in just one person’s judgment.

One advantage of asking more than one person is that you receive a wider range of possible choices. If you consult several people, you are more likely to find alternatives you had not thought of before. This can be good, but it also means you face trade-offs. Every choice has consequences: it might affect your future, change your mood for the day, or influence your personal growth. Because different advice can lead you in different directions, you should expect a variety of possible outcomes.

Another positive aspect is learning from other people’s experiences. Hearing how others handled similar situations lets you recognize which paths worked well and which went badly. You can adopt parts of their advice or avoid mistakes they made. Later on, you can use that knowledge to help people in similar circumstances or to handle the same situation better yourself. In that way, asking around can improve both your judgment and your ability to support others.

However, there are downsides to getting multiple opinions. Hearing many different suggestions can confuse you and even change your original plan. Sometimes the new advice is better, but other times the conflicting responses make the decision harder. Choosing between several courses of action can create extra stress and pressure. And no matter which option you pick, it could turn out to be a great decision or a bad one. That uncertainty is what makes selecting the right piece of advice so difficult.

Some schools let students learn from home through online classes or video calls, while others choose not to offer this option because they believe it is not an effective way to study. I agree with the view that distance learning is not the best choice for most students.

First, when students study at home they often lack immediate support. If something is unclear during a lesson, there may be no teacher or classmate nearby to explain it right away. This delay can make it harder for students to grasp new ideas and stay confident in their work. In a classroom, teachers can notice confusion and give extra help on the spot, which is difficult to reproduce through a screen.

Second, the school environment plays an important role in learning. Being at school helps students develop routines, discipline, and social skills that are part of being a learner. Classrooms give structure and a place dedicated to study, with fewer everyday interruptions than home. This structured setting helps students focus on what they need to learn and maintain good study habits.

Third, studying from home often brings many distractions. Electronic devices, family members, children, or other household tasks can easily pull attention away from lessons. Even if a student can access the same material at home, these interruptions make it harder to concentrate and complete work properly. For many young learners, the calm and consistent environment of a school is more suitable for productive study.

I do recognize that distance learning can be useful for some people. Students who must work after school, those who have caring responsibilities for young children, or newcomers to a country who need flexible schedules might find online classes helpful. For example, parents who need to stay home with their baby can use online courses to continue their education. Immigrants who juggle jobs and language study may also benefit from being able to learn at times that fit their lives. In these cases, distance learning gives a chance to study that might not exist otherwise.

Despite these advantages for particular situations, I believe that, overall, attending classes in person is the better way to learn. Face-to-face lessons provide immediate help, disciplined routines, and fewer distractions. Going to school and working hard every day remains the most reliable path to reach our goals and prepare for the future. Experienced people often encourage students to keep going and remind them that with effort they can succeed.

Thomas Jefferson once asked whether people achieve more by always being busy or whether inactivity has value. Many disagree with his view. Some prefer a relaxed life and avoid effort, while others push themselves to create new chances. I agree with Jefferson’s idea because being active helps us struggle through problems, make the most of our time, and keep seeking new opportunities.

Not everyone believes we can improve our situation. Some people feel they cannot change the options they already have. For example, many face hard lives and do not have money to try something different. Still, I think we must accept that nothing valuable comes easily. My grandfather told me about his early years. Life was very difficult for him; his family was poor and his five children sometimes had only one meal a day. Even so, he always said, “One day everything will change.” He never stopped believing that, and after those hard years he found chances to give his family a better life. His example taught me that if you want something, you have to work and struggle for it.

Also, we can reach great goals if we use our time well. People who work hard can achieve dreams they once thought impossible, such as owning a nice car, a large house, or other comforts. With effort, you also gain the ability to help others and change their lives. People who keep working and do not give up usually accomplish many things. Consistent effort leads to more opportunities, and those who act are more likely to succeed than those who wait.

Finally, being active and always looking for more is important. If you stay in the same place, you will not find new paths. I remember thinking about how to reach my dreams more quickly and deciding that searching for different options would help. If we are curious and willing to try new directions, we increase our chances of success. Time passes fast, and if you do nothing, nothing will happen. That is why it is important to move forward and explore possibilities rather than remain passive.

In short, this idea shows how many opportunities you can create by moving from one side to another and by working hard. People who never try to go further will miss chances and never know what they could have achieved. On the other hand, those who struggle, use their time wisely, and keep looking for new options will get closer to their dreams. Work hard, search for opportunities, and you will improve your life.

From my experience, I do not agree with the idea that a first impression cannot be changed. People can grow and behave differently over time, so an initial judgement is not always reliable.

Often a poor first impression happens because the other person seems uninterested or distant. If someone appears not to care about the conversation, it is easy to assume they are unfriendly. However, that attitude might just be a temporary reaction, not a true reflection of their personality.

Another reason a first impression can be misleading is that the person you meet might be having a bad day. Feeling stressed or uncomfortable can make someone quiet or rude in a particular moment, but that does not mean they will always act that way. It would be unfair to label them forever based on one brief encounter.

For example, when I first met my best friend in math class, he did not want to be my partner and ignored my questions. At the time I thought he was unfriendly, but later we started talking more and became close. In my circle there are even two friends who did not give me a good first impression, yet now we are good friends.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement because first impressions can change as people reveal more of themselves over time.

Students’ self-esteem can grow from both praise and personal achievements. While pupils usually work hard, recognition from teachers or peers can encourage them to keep trying. Even when their work is not perfect, positive feedback helps them do their best. Praise is often given to those who succeed, and these successes also strengthen a student’s confidence. In short, self-esteem can come from being praised and from achieving goals.

Praise plays an important role in encouraging students. When learners put effort into a task, compliments or supportive words lift their spirits and increase their confidence. This boost motivates them to continue working hard and try new challenges. Praise can also influence classmates: when one student receives recognition, others may feel inspired to improve their own work. Feeling appreciated makes students happier and more willing to take part and learn. In many cases, a kind comment is enough to help a student grow both academically and personally.

Achievements themselves are another major source of self-esteem. When students complete a project, get good results, or reach a goal, they gain a sense of success that proves their ability. These accomplishments show them that their effort pays off, which builds lasting confidence. Students who have done well often feel proud and more secure, and their example can encourage others to aim higher. Achievements can come from school tasks, events, or personal challenges, and each success contributes to a stronger belief in oneself.

In conclusion, both praise and achievement are valuable for students’ self-esteem. Recognition helps learners stay motivated and feel supported, while real accomplishments give them concrete reasons to feel capable. Together, praise and success create a cycle: encouragement leads to effort, effort leads to achievement, and achievement increases confidence. By valuing both, teachers and peers can help students grow and keep improving.

Failure is an important part of becoming successful. When people fail, they learn what not to do and how to improve. This learning process helps them avoid repeating the same mistakes and gives them a clearer path toward their goals.

Imagine I wanted to be a professional soccer player. I had played for top youth clubs, earned the title of best player on my team, and never been dropped. One day my coach told me about a professional tryout happening next week and asked me to prepare. He gave me a schedule to follow: eat properly, train every day and work on my fitness. Most days I followed it, although there were moments when I felt tired and ate poorly. I pushed myself through those bad days because I wanted to be ready.

On the day of the tryout I was as prepared as I could be. We began with warm-ups and moved into drills. I performed well and felt confident on the field. At the end they announced the players who made the cut. I was not chosen. I failed to get into the professional team.

This is where enthusiasm and determination matter. After failing, I had two options: give up on soccer and pick a different path, or pick myself up and try again. Failure reveals how patient and committed we are. It tests whether we are willing to keep failing and learning until we succeed.

A well-known example is The Pursuit of Happyness. The main character makes a device he hopes to sell, but buyers refuse to buy it. He becomes homeless and struggles to care for his child, yet he continues to try selling the machine. After many setbacks, someone finally buys it and later tells others, which leads to more sales. His success came because he never gave up despite repeated rejection.

In short, failure is not the end but a step toward success. It teaches lessons, builds resilience and, when combined with persistence, becomes the key to achieving your goals.

I believe working ten hours a day is preferable to an eight-hour day because it can save energy, reduce electricity use, and free up time. If people work four days at ten hours each, they still reach a 40-hour week. Those who need extra income can always take overtime on Fridays or Saturdays.

The same idea could work well for schools. If school days were extended by two hours, students could finish classes in four days instead of five. This change would allow longer rest periods at home, so pupils could get better sleep and also have time for part-time jobs. Cutting the week to four school days would reduce school energy and water use and give teachers an extra day off each week as well.

Many students struggle with early mornings and then have little time to complete homework. With more sleep, they would be more alert and able to concentrate during lessons. Having a longer block of time during weekdays and an extra day off would also free up weekends, so students could use that time for important assignments. Better-rested students are likely to stay more energetic and focused in class, which helps them reach their goals in high school.

A lot of high school students already work long hours outside school—many report working around 32 to 38 hours a week—which leaves them with barely any time for homework on weekends. Extending school hours by two each day and moving to a four-day week would give both students and teachers more balance. In my view, longer days and shorter weeks would be a practical way to improve rest, reduce resource use, and help students perform better.

Many people believe that doing nothing can sometimes be justified, but in reality people need to keep themselves busy and have meaningful activities in their lives. Being active gives direction and purpose. A motivated person can achieve success and improve not only their own future but also the prospects of younger generations in their family. On the other hand, inactivity is linked to laziness and a lack of concern for personal goals or for others.

There are many who are unemployed yet do not look for work. They prefer to remain idle and let time pass without taking steps to improve their situation. Because of this, they remain poor and miss opportunities that might lead to a better future. In some countries lazy people sit on the streets asking for money instead of seeking jobs that would allow them to support themselves. Even when chances arise, inactive people often do not consider them; they may simply value free time above having responsibilities. This lack of purpose can harm their children as well. When parents do not work, their young children sometimes have to work or beg alongside them, losing a normal childhood and limiting their own future chances.

Laziness can start early. Many students show inactivity at school: they pick only the easiest parts of group projects or avoid effort altogether. This habit makes life more difficult when they become adults, because they expect everything to be easy as it was during school. Work opportunities may be available, but if a person is unwilling to take the effort, they ignore them. Some people look for the simplest possible jobs or find other ways to waste time at home instead of being productive. Young people should learn to be active and purposeful, because inactivity during youth can have long-lasting negative effects on their futures.

On a larger scale, widespread inactivity affects the economy. High unemployment and a culture of laziness can hold back national development. If fewer people were inactive, countries could reduce poverty and improve economic conditions. Working people contribute to their families and societies, and this collective effort is important for a country’s progress.

In conclusion, living without activity gives no real purpose. People should always try to do something meaningful to shape their future. Active individuals work with goals in mind and are more likely to succeed. In contrast, inactive people lack direction and miss chances to improve their lives. Everyone should try to be more active so they can achieve greater success and build a better future for themselves and their families.

I wrote a short piece to try to understand why some people are bullied. It is surprising how differently people behave once they get to know someone. I have tried hard to get along with others, but not everyone is kind. Some people judge and hurt others without even trying to meet them. That is why I often feel alone: too many people talk about others and spread gossip, and I dislike when people speak badly about someone behind their back. Those who are victims of bullying sometimes do not defend themselves because they are afraid of the bullies, and this makes the situation worse.

I try not to pay attention to what others say; they are free to talk, and that is their problem. But when people who criticized you later need help, they sometimes come looking for you. When I am upset or sad, I like to play soccer because it helps me forget my troubles for a while. If I could do something to help, I would organize soccer games so anyone who wants to play can join and forget their problems for a bit. Sports give people a chance to have fun together without fighting. We can also go to the movies or watch football, basketball, or volleyball matches with friends. These activities help people meet and learn about each other.

I believe every problem has a solution, but we need more respect for one another. If we respected people more, life would be very different. We all want to feel safe in our neighborhoods and not be threatened by gang members who often make life harder for families. Families should get involved in protecting their children and working together to stop those who harm others. Many young people study hard because they want a better future for themselves and to help their families escape difficult situations. Finishing high school can already open the door to decent jobs, even if it is not the dream job, it can still provide stability.

If someone takes your things, you can go to the police and report it so they can try to help and recover what was lost. People should not be afraid to ask for help, because showing fear sometimes encourages others to take advantage of you. We are smart, and we should use that intelligence in all situations. Just because someone is clever in some areas does not mean others must treat them badly. Also, showing anger or weakness can make you vulnerable, so be careful about revealing your most sensitive points to others.

Most people are kind, but when they become angry they can change a lot. To avoid conflicts, invite people to play sports or hang out with friends at the beach or elsewhere. Sharing positive experiences can turn strangers into friends. However, do not expose your greatest weaknesses, because friends and enemies might use them against you. This is my reflection on bullying and how to face it.

Self-confidence is essential for people to feel positive about themselves. For many students, developing confidence can be difficult because of how they were raised or how others treat them. Still, young people need to cultivate self-esteem for their own benefit. Learning often seems challenging at first, but with steady effort it becomes manageable rather than impossible.

Some argue that praising poor-quality work harms learning by lowering expectations. Students should be encouraged to tackle tasks they truly understand and take responsibility for improving, rather than relying on empty praise. True self-esteem, I believe, comes from achievements — from the risks taken and the hard work put into reaching goals at school and in life.

It is important to acknowledge that building confidence is not easy. There will be times when a student feels like giving up or doubts their ability to continue. Facing and overcoming personal struggles, however, is exactly what strengthens confidence. When students push through difficulties and accept the risks involved in learning, they gain real achievements and a more solid sense of self-worth. In the end, confidence grows through effort and accomplishment, not through unwarranted praise.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea that we must attempt things beyond what we already master. If we only repeat tasks we know well, we cannot improve or move forward. Growth comes from facing unfamiliar challenges and learning along the way.

When people stick to the same activities, they remain comfortable but stagnant. Doing what is already familiar does not build new skills or open opportunities. To progress, we need to try different tasks and accept the mistakes and lessons that come with them. That process is how we advance.

Spending time practicing only completed tasks can be a waste. The hours used to repeat the known could be used to explore new areas and develop abilities that matter in the long run. Many people stay where they are because they avoid stepping outside their comfort zone.

For these reasons, I support Emerson’s view. Taking on new challenges is important because it leads to learning, improvement, and real personal growth.

Ralph Waldo Emerson praised the importance of individuality, but I disagree with his view. Life often requires help from others, and being truly independent also means knowing how to manage your relationships and time. In this essay I will discuss three areas where cooperation is important: work, society, and decision-making. These examples show that strict individualism is neither realistic nor always desirable.

At work, there are many situations that require collaboration. You may have colleagues whose behavior you dislike, yet learning to cooperate with them can be useful because you might need their support later. Trying to build bridges instead of insisting on standing alone can improve results for everyone. Also, many of us do not have our dream job at first. That does not mean we should accept it passively, but working with others in the company often helps us advance toward our goals. Most businesses rely on teams to reach objectives, so isolating yourself can limit your progress. Teamwork and mutual support are practical parts of professional life.

People also react differently to social life. Some prefer to be alone and feel comfortable that way; others enjoy being the center of attention and act independently. These behaviors can come from personal history or upbringing, and they are not always fixed. Living in society can be complicated, especially when personalities clash, but people can change when they receive understanding or help from others. Some who seem solitary actually look for support in subtle ways, and others become more open when someone close helps them grow. So social interaction and cooperation matter for personal development.

Finally, the choices we make shape who we become. Becoming someone else is not simply a wish; it is the result of decisions. You can let outside forces dictate your life, or you can make conscious choices about your path. Many take the easier option of following what society expects because it seems safer. Even leaders cannot act alone: a president may try to make choices independently, but must cooperate with congress and advisors to achieve change. Similarly, individuals must decide whether to work with others or be pushed by external pressures.

In conclusion, we all choose how to act, but life often requires cooperation. I have shown this through examples at work, in society, and in decision-making. For these reasons I believe Emerson’s idea of constant individuality overlooks the importance of working with others to become who we want to be.

John Lubbock once wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make." I agree with this idea because, although our past experiences influence us, we still have the power to decide who we become. We are not passive products of what happened to us; our actions and choices play the biggest role in shaping our character.

Take a person who grew up with abusive parents. That background can lead them to repeat the same behavior, but it does not have to define them. Many people use painful experiences as fuel to become stronger and kinder. Instead of becoming what hurt them, they can build resilience, learn empathy, and create a better life. Others might label someone as "mean" or complain that they do not share, but that could be more about personality or temporary reactions than the person’s character. In the end, only the person themselves decides which qualities to keep and which to change.

When someone close dies, the pain is real and the sadness can feel overwhelming. At first, a person might be depressed or deny what happened, and that is a natural response. Over time, however, grief can become a source of strength. Choosing to carry on, to honor the memory of the lost person by living well, shows courage and builds character. Friends and family often notice that inner strength and wonder how someone became so independent or brave. When you explain the steps you took and how you kept going, others usually feel proud. That recognition is a sign that your choices shaped something valuable.

Everyone faces moments of doubt and hears negative thoughts that say, “You can’t do this,” or “This is impossible.” If you let those thoughts control you, they will stop you from growing. But if you decide to face challenges, push through obstacles, and ignore the inner critic, you strengthen your character. Life will throw many "brick walls" in your path, but only you can decide to break them down. Trust your instincts, make choices that feel right, and do not let other people’s opinions determine your future.

Your life is not a list of options someone else chooses for you. It is yours to shape. Lubbock’s phrase reminds us that, while our past leaves marks, we hold the main power over who we become. Live boldly, enjoy the journey, and make choices that build the character you want to leave behind.

People are free to make their own choices because they decide what they want to do with their lives. Most people do not like doing things they dislike, so they choose paths that match their goals and interests.

Some choices lead to a difficult route while others seem easier. The hard route often means studying and working steadily to reach long-term goals. The easier route can look like finding a quick way to start a future plan, for example by using money or connections to shorten the path. That shortcut may seem attractive, but it can be risky and not everyone can take it. A person’s financial situation often affects which option they pick. Those with plenty of money can afford to make quicker choices because they do not worry about debts or basic expenses. People with less money usually need to take a slower path: they must save, manage bills, and often work harder to reach the same results.

I know some people who made choices that changed their lives. One friend left high school because he thought working would earn him more than studying. He now does nails for a living. Sometimes he makes a lot, sometimes very little, and he did not want to try harder in school, so he lost the chance to go to college and aim for a more stable career. My brother also left college after two years to start working. If he had stayed, he might have qualified for a better job. These examples show that people should think carefully about how their choices affect the future.

Although everyone can decide for themselves, many people need help to make good choices. Some are unsure about their interests or what career suits them best and feel stuck. Advice and support from family, teachers, or friends can make a big difference.

Dear Principal,

I believe changing the cafeteria menu to include healthier lunches is an excellent idea. New and healthier options would give students the chance to try foods they may never have tasted before. As a student, I welcome this change because it would provide more nutritious choices for everyone.

Introducing a new menu would make many students happier. Some of us are tired of eating the same meals almost every day, while others still enjoy the current menu and would not mind keeping some favorites. To satisfy most students, it would be wise to work with the cafeteria manager to collect information about which meals are most and least popular. With that list, you and your team could decide which items to keep and which to replace with healthier choices. Removing only the least-liked dishes and swapping them for new options would allow students to keep their favorite meals while bringing variety to the menu.

This change could benefit several groups at once. Students would be pleased because the cafeteria would still serve dishes they like while adding different and healthier options. Trying new foods can be exciting and help our school stand out. Other schools may notice our effort and copy the idea, which would be good because many students in other areas face the same problem with repetitive or unhealthy cafeteria food.

A better menu could also help parents save money. When students dislike the lunch offered at school, they sometimes ask their parents to buy food from outside, and this can be expensive. Some families cannot afford this extra cost. If the cafeteria serves meals that students enjoy and that are healthy, fewer students will need to buy food outside. This would also reduce the number of students who leave school during lunchtime to get something to eat, which can be unsafe and cause worry for parents when their children are missing. Reducing absences for this reason would help students stay in class and protect the school’s reputation.

Many students enjoy trying different kinds of food — I am one of them. The current cafeteria menu includes both good and less healthy items, and the balance is not equal. We need more nutritious choices so that students can eat well at school. Some students have allergies and cannot eat certain cafeteria dishes, so they miss meals or get sick. If healthier and more varied options were available, those students would have better chances to eat safely at school, especially when they cannot go out to buy food.

In conclusion, asking the cafeteria manager to gather a list of the most and least liked meals would help make the change acceptable to most students. Keeping popular dishes while replacing the least popular ones with healthier alternatives would reduce the number of students leaving school at lunch, ease parents’ financial concerns, and improve student health. Healthier lunches mean better nutrition, less unhealthy fat, and more protein for growing bodies. Changing the school menu is a great idea that most students will understand, and those who need time to adjust will soon accept the new options. Other schools may follow our example, which could help many more students. I hope you will consider students’ opinions and take steps to improve the cafeteria menu for the benefit of everyone. Thank you.

Michelangelo’s remark about aiming too low prompts mixed feelings for me. On one hand, I agree that being the absolute best is not necessary; what matters more is trying hard and giving your best effort. If you work sincerely, you can accomplish many things even without being perfect. This idea encourages people to focus on effort and progress rather than on being the top in everything.

On the other hand, I disagree with the implication that people should always lower their expectations. Goals can be ambitious, and aiming high can push you to grow and learn. At the same time, having a modest aim does not always stop you from succeeding. For example, I am preparing for a SOL exam. If I set my goal very high—passing and moving on to 12th grade to earn my diploma—I might fall short, but I can still reach a simpler target if I try hard. In other words, both high and low aims can lead to achievement depending on the effort and path you take.

I also think the quote points to a common human tendency: many people choose low standards for themselves. In everyday life—at work, at school, and elsewhere—people face choices about how high to aim. No matter which route you take, trying is essential, and often you can reach your goal through persistence.

Some people fail to complete tasks when they are already occupied with something else because being busy can leave them no time to finish additional assignments. Others, however, find that having free time is useful: if they are not currently engaged, they can use that time to get work done and meet their responsibilities.

One reason inactivity can be useful is that people who are not busy should be able to finish outstanding tasks instead of claiming they had no chance to do them. When someone is already working on a long or difficult assignment, it is understandable that they might not have time to take on more. But those who have completed their tasks and still have spare time should be expected to do more until they are out of hours at school or at their job. This prevents unfair excuses and helps keep things moving.

There are also reasons why people do accomplish work while they are occupied. Some stay focused and do not waste time, so they manage to finish their duties even with other responsibilities. Yet being busy can also stop people from completing everything: they may run out of time or rush through additional work, which leads to careless errors and lower grades or poor performance reviews. That is why multitasking sometimes harms the quality of the work.

In conclusion, both situations happen: some people finish their work and some do not. Periods of inactivity can be valuable for those who have free time to catch up, while people who are already busy may need careful scheduling to avoid mistakes. When someone is done early, they should not simply sit idle; giving them extra tasks until the end of the class or shift is a reasonable approach.

Still, I support Churchill’s view because success rarely happens without effort and persistence. Life is hard, and achieving goals usually needs work and resilience. There are many people who struggle with unemployment, homelessness, or hunger because they were not able to find success. Often you learn from each failure, improving bit by bit. No one is born already successful; progress normally comes after several attempts.

In conclusion, while failure is painful and sometimes costly, it can also teach lessons that eventually lead to success.

Yes, I agree with this statement because believing in yourself makes many goals reachable, like applying for your first job or building the career you want. Self-confidence is especially important when you enter college: it helps you make better choices, manage your resources, and move closer to what you want to achieve. When you trust your abilities, you also develop skills and learn more about who you are, which helps you find work where you feel comfortable.

A confident attitude affects how others see you. First impressions are powerful and often hard to change, so presenting yourself positively from the start can leave a lasting impact. When people notice your confidence and competence, they are more likely to form a good opinion of your personality and abilities. Over time, this positive impression becomes part of the experience you build for yourself.

Not everyone has the same first impression because people have different personalities and beliefs about themselves. Some never try to change how others see them, and this holds them back. By contrast, those who work on improving their image and skills often change their lives for the better. They gain self-confidence and are willing to use their time productively instead of wasting it.

If someone does not care about their future or refuses to put in effort, their impression will stay the same and they are unlikely to succeed. In short, believing in yourself is a key step toward shaping your image, gaining skills, and reaching your goals.

I understand why some people avoid honesty: they do not want to hurt someone’s feelings. But sometimes you have to be honest, because leaving someone with false hopes will hurt them more later. Overall, honesty has both good and bad sides, and I see both. Even so, I prefer to have honest people around me. Some people think the current summer schedule should be changed because the break is too short. I agree with this view and believe schools should remove spring break and move the summer vacation to run from June through August.

If spring break were removed, the week could be used for SOL testing and review. That extra time would let teachers give more practice and assessment without interrupting the school year. In April, classes could include more engaging activities and focused preparation so students are better ready for the exams. Using the former spring break for testing would also free up time later in the term for instruction and help from teachers.

Summer should start in June and end in August rather than beginning in May. May is often too cool to feel like summer, and cancelling classes then seems unnecessary. Beginning the holiday in June means students can enjoy warmer weather and plan vacations with family and friends when conditions are better for outdoor fun.

Removing spring break and shifting the summer months has other benefits, too. Students would gain more classroom time to study for finals and receive support from teachers. Schools could organize an educational week in April with activities that are both enjoyable and instructive. More time in the school year would allow for extra sports, new skill-building opportunities, and trips to concerts, universities, or museums.

For these reasons, I support changing the calendar so the summer lasts three months (June–August) and spring break is eliminated. This would give students more school time for tests and learning while still keeping a full, warm summer holiday.

I disagree with school district plans that require students to finish their high school diploma in three years. Three years is too short and would force students to study much harder than is healthy. Compressing the curriculum means many young people would need to take classes in the evenings and over the summer, leaving little time for rest. This constant pressure would make them tired and reduce their ability to learn well.

Another problem is that a faster schedule would limit students’ choices. Elective courses and important non-required classes might be removed or become optional only if students have time, which many would not. Losing these classes would prevent students from exploring different interests and developing skills that help them choose a future path. Although finishing high school sooner might seem like an advantage because it saves time, it would not help most students if they must sacrifice balance and variety in their education.

If students are pushed to complete school in three years, they will have to work very hard during evenings and summers. This continuous workload can lead to burnout and reduce focus, making it harder to prepare for university. Having four years provides more time to strengthen knowledge, improve study habits, and decide what direction to take after graduation. It also gives students chances to take part in activities, jobs, or personal projects that teach responsibility and planning.

In short, a four-year high school program is better for most students. It allows time to learn deeply, try electives, rest, and get ready for college or a career. Rushing through high school in three years would likely do more harm than good.

I believe students should not attend classes from home through online or video conferencing. In my view, learning at a distance does not benefit most students.

First, home environments are full of distractions. With videos, games, and other activities nearby, many students try to do other things while joining a lesson. When classes are held in person, pupils pay more attention because the teacher is physically present and can guide them directly. This face-to-face interaction helps students understand lessons more clearly and makes learning more effective.

Second, the option to study from home is impractical for many families. For example, I live with three brothers and a sister, so it is hard to find a quiet place to concentrate. The noise and interruptions at home prevent me and others from focusing on classwork.

Finally, I also think learning at certain times matters. Students are usually more alert in the morning and learn better then, while evening online sessions make memorizing harder. For these reasons, attending school in person seems far more useful than taking classes from home. Many parents share this opinion because they see better progress when children go to school instead of studying remotely.

Some people choose a four-day school week because they believe it will save energy and resources. I disagree with this idea because longer school days would actually increase consumption.

With a four-day schedule, each school day would be extended by about two hours, so students would spend around ten hours at school. Longer days mean students use more energy overall, simply because they are in the building for a longer time each day.

Schools would also need to use more materials to support those extra hours. We could see higher use of paper and greater water consumption during longer breaks and lunchtime, which would strain natural resources.

In addition, extra time at school would raise electricity use. Classrooms would run computers, monitors, tablets, and lights for more hours, which increases power demand unless specific measures are taken to cut usage.

In conclusion, these points explain why the four-day model, as described, would not effectively conserve energy or resources in schools.

I agree with Churchill’s idea that success often means moving from one failure to another without losing enthusiasm. We cannot be perfect all the time, and setbacks are part of the path to achievement.

For example, last year I took an important English test. I studied hard and hoped for an A+ or at least a B+, but I failed the first time. I felt very disappointed, yet my teacher offered me a second chance. I took it and earned an A-, which made me very happy. Failing that first test taught me that the number of times we fall does not define us; what matters is staying determined and continuing to try.

Another example comes from my aunt, who planned a trip to El Salvador. At first the airfare was too expensive, so she waited. Months later prices rose again, but she decided not to wait any longer and tried to buy a ticket. Then she discovered her ID had expired and she could not complete the purchase. She felt upset because she had forgotten to renew her documents. She applied for a new ID, which would take about three months, but even after that time passed she still had not received it. Despite these problems, she has not given up on her plan to visit our family. Her persistence shows how maintaining enthusiasm can help us keep working toward a goal even when obstacles appear.

Some people disagree with Churchill’s view. They say it is not true because some who fail many times lose hope, become discouraged, and are judged negatively by others. In my view, those negative outcomes happen because people allow failure to defeat them; they lose their motivation and become weaker emotionally.

In conclusion, experiencing failures is a normal part of trying to succeed. My own test and my aunt’s travel problems show that setbacks can teach us lessons and make us stronger if we do not lose our enthusiasm.

Many people feel the same: doing their own projects often leads to better outcomes because personal responsibility creates stronger commitment.

Competition is another factor that drives individual performance. Although rivalry can sometimes reduce teamwork, it often pushes people to improve. Imagine a factory where one worker performs noticeably better and receives extra pay or time off. Other workers may feel upset at first, but that can lead them to find new ways to raise their own output so they can earn the same rewards. For example, staying true to ourselves demonstrates our inner strength and helps us continue developing in the way we believe is right.

When we see people around us change, we should still have confidence in who we are and not follow every trend. If someone or a part of society pushes us to become something bad or to behave in a way we do not agree with, we should refuse to change for the worse. Keeping our faith in ourselves and continuing to improve in our chosen direction can show others how firmly we hold our beliefs. In this way, we protect our values and may even encourage others to believe in themselves and follow their own paths.

If society changes in ways we think are wrong or disrespectful, we should not accept those changes. Instead, we should remain true to our principles.

In conclusion, I believe it is good to be ourselves and do the things that make us happy and help us grow. When society or some people try to change us in ways that do not feel right, we should stand by our choices and continue to improve in the ways we believe are best. Overall, staying true to ourselves leads to personal progress and can inspire others to do the same.

Today’s technology has made learning more convenient. In the past, people had to go to a physical school because there were no alternatives. Parents may worry about bullying or bad influences and feel powerless to protect their child.

With home-based online schooling, parents can be present during study time and monitor progress directly. If a parent’s schedule does not allow that, they can hire a trusted tutor or helper to assist their child. At home, a child is less likely to be surrounded by peers who might cause stress or depression, and parents can follow their academic development more closely.

Because of these benefits, I believe enrolling a child—or even yourself—in online classes is a smart choice. Online education offers flexibility for adults who want to finish their studies or improve their qualifications. People can study when it fits their routine and do it in a comfortable environment. For me personally, I would prefer taking online classes instead of traveling to a school every day.

Overall, online schooling opens doors for many learners, provides a safer and more manageable option for families, and lets people continue education at any stage of life.

If you need guidance, would you ask just one person or seek opinions from several people? I believe asking multiple people is better because it gives you different views on the situation.

First, hearing more than one opinion helps you understand the problem from several angles. Each person notices different details and may suggest solutions you had not thought of. This wider perspective makes it easier to weigh the pros and cons.

Second, different people have different attitudes toward risk. For example, if you are considering a risky choice and ask your mother, she might advise against it to protect you. But a friend who likes taking chances could encourage you to go for it. Comparing these responses helps you decide which path fits your own values and goals.

In conclusion, asking more than one person for advice helps you see both the risks and benefits and makes it easier to choose the best course of action.

Do you make your own decisions or ask experts for advice? I think people should be able to make their own choices. There are several reasons for this. First, others are not always correct, and their advice can be wrong. Second, only you truly understand what you want and what fits your life, so those choices belong to you. Third, you should not simply copy what others do; following someone else’s path can lead you into problems that are not right for you.

One reason I believe people should decide for themselves is that trusting others completely is risky. Would you want your best friend to decide everything for you? Maybe not, because even someone you trust can be mistaken or have their own motives. People make wrong decisions all the time, and doing what they suggest could get you into trouble or cause harm. When you make good decisions, you can also set an example and help others learn from you. That is why it is important not to let others control your choices — their advice might lead you into situations you did not want.

Life offers many options, but the final decision is yours. You should not let other people judge or control your choices because everyone has different goals and values. If you make a poor decision, you must accept responsibility for it instead of blaming someone else. For example, students sometimes get into trouble because they follow peers who make bad choices. This can harm their education and waste time. Children who avoid negative influences often stay out of trouble and do better in school. So following others without thinking is not a good idea.

When deciding, think carefully about what you want. If you do not feel comfortable doing something, don’t do it just because others expect it. Ask yourself whether the choice is wise and what the consequences might be. You are the one who will live with the results, so it makes sense to weigh options before acting. Also, be careful about the friends you choose. I picked my friends at school so I would not be pressured into making harmful decisions. People around you can influence your behavior a lot, so choose friends who support your values.

In conclusion, remember that you should pick your own decisions. It is true that nobody is perfect, and everyone will make mistakes sometimes. But taking time to think about your choices helps you avoid regrets. Don’t put all the responsibility on others, and don’t let their actions decide your life. Trust yourself, think before you act, and accept responsibility for the path you choose.

Showing examples is one of the best ways to teach people. When a teacher or anyone wants to help, demonstrating how to do something makes the lesson clearer and shows care.

As a child, my grandmother taught me many practical skills by showing me how to do them. Because of that, I enjoy helping my friends and teaching them things they do not know, whether it is how to play soccer or how to find information. I prefer to show and explain rather than only give instructions.

Over the years I have learned surprising things, such as repairing toys, fixing computers, and other small maintenance tasks. These skills came from watching others and practicing myself. I appreciate teachers who explain well and give examples, because they make learning easier. In contrast, some teachers seem angry or uninterested, and then students often say they dislike that teacher. Clear teaching and patience help students learn and feel more confident.

Behavior is another important part of learning. How we act at school or at home affects how others see us and whether they want to help or advise us. If someone has good manners and listens, people are more willing to show them how to do things. Giving examples and modeling good behavior are effective ways to teach both skills and values.

Watching others is not the only way people are influenced, but it is a strong one. I learn many new tools just by observing how others use them. Right now I do not have a definite plan after high school, but I am interested in technology and electricity. These subjects appeal to me and I want to learn more because life is short and opportunities can disappear quickly.

Everyone makes mistakes — me and you — and the best way to fix them is to learn from them or accept help from someone who can show you the right way. Other ways to learn include reading newspapers, watching the news, asking people questions, and being curious.

A good example also shows what a person can do, regardless of their skin color or background. Everyone, from the youngest to the oldest, can offer some knowledge. Many people come to me for advice because they trust me and know I will listen. I try to be a supportive person.

We all have family, friends, and neighbors who care, and perhaps a purpose in this world that we discover over time. Finally, I try to have a good day and be on time for class every day because punctuality matters to me. My goal this year is to pass the SOL and finish the class, and my teachers are good examples of how people can positively influence others.

In some places, young people are expected to decide on a career by the time they start high school. I agree with this idea because choosing a career early can help students focus on their future and support their families.

Firstly, when students pick a career path while they are still young, they are more likely to plan and work towards clear goals. Knowing what you want to become makes it easier to choose the right subjects, internships, or training. Many students feel this is important because they want to have better lives and sometimes they hope to give their parents financial support as their parents grow older.

Secondly, thinking about a career early helps students find the right route among many options. There are many professions to choose from, such as technology, teaching, technical trades, or police work. Some of these paths are more demanding than others, but any stable career can lead to improvement in life. By deciding early, students can prepare for the specific skills and qualifications needed for their chosen field.

On the other hand, some students prefer not to decide so soon. They feel they are too young at school to choose a single career and want to enjoy time with friends, relationships, and social activities. This attitude can sometimes lead to bad choices, like drinking, drugs, or fighting, which can harm their future job prospects. Because of that risk, it is better for young people to start thinking about their future careers while they still have time to prepare.

In conclusion, I support the idea that students should identify a career by high school. Making this decision early helps them study with a purpose, gain the right experience, and increase their chances of a stable and supportive future for themselves and their families.
