Some schools should offer distance learning so students can attend classes from home by video or online platforms. Many people support this idea because online classes bring several benefits: learners can study more effectively, produce better work, and spend more time with their families. If students can take courses online, they will have greater opportunities to follow their goals and do the things they want.

One main reason online classes are useful is the flexibility they provide. When students study from home, they can arrange their time to complete both school tasks and other responsibilities. For example, I want to finish my studies but it is hard because I have to work to pay for my living costs, and I often do not have time for homework or to prepare for quizzes. With online classes I would save time on commuting and early mornings, so I could work and study at the same time. This balance helps people continue their education without giving up their jobs or family duties.

A second reason is that students can often do better work and get higher grades in online courses. Having more time and a quiet place at home allows students to concentrate on assignments and projects. They can use the internet to find a lot of information and prepare more complete homework. When students are relaxed and have enough time, they can focus on learning for a few hours rather than being tired from many classes and early starts at school. As a result, they are able to submit higher-quality projects and understand the material more deeply.

Some people argue that online classes are a waste of time because students may be distracted at home by their phones or other activities and not study as much as they would at school. It is true that distractions exist, but online learning can also improve family life and allow students to enjoy free time with relatives. For example, being at home makes it easier to play sports with family, watch a movie together, or go out on weekends. These moments are important for well-being and do not have to conflict with study when students manage their time responsibly.

In conclusion, offering online classes is beneficial because students can learn more, produce better work, and have extra time to spend with family. Distance learning helps people balance study and work and supports their goals, such as finding a good job and completing their education. For these reasons, schools should provide the option of studying online.

As far as I know, music, drama, and art courses are not part of the required curriculum; they are elective options that students can choose. In other words, these subjects are available for those who want to study them, but they do not count as mandatory credits needed for graduation. For example, if a student takes an art class, they usually do so by choice to explore an interest or earn extra credit. If someone replaces one of their four required classes with an art class thinking it will satisfy a graduation requirement, they may end up taking the wrong courses because art is not generally required for finishing school. Therefore students should be careful to enroll in the classes that meet graduation rules.

Sometimes schools allow seniors to pick art or music when they have fewer required courses left. In those situations, seniors choose these electives, and younger students such as juniors might take them as well to gain additional credits or pursue their interests.

Required classes typically include subjects like English 11, geometry, math, CIS, world history, and similar core courses. These are the classes students must complete to earn school credit and be eligible for graduation. Each required subject usually has its own SOL test. When students reach those courses, they must pass the SOL exams, which are an important part of the required classes and are given twice during the year. Students need to reach the passing score (often around 300) or they must retake the test. In short, art, drama, and music should be seen as elective choices rather than compulsory classes for graduation.

I completely agree with Winston Churchill. Feeling enthusiasm for what comes next in our life is more exciting than we all think. As humans, if we start to believe in ourselves, stay positive, start to dream, and understand that failure is part of our daily life, we will become more successful with the knowledge of how life really works and that life is not as hard as we have all been thinking.

"Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." Although failure means not reaching a goal, it does not have to mean losing the ability to move forward. As people, we sometimes stop trying and lose the energy to begin again. Winston Churchill's words remind us not to give up our enthusiasm.

First, failing is part of life. At different moments we all experience setbacks; they appear in many forms and often at important times. When something goes wrong we tend to ask why it happened: did we do something wrong, or did we not try hard enough to get the job, pass the test, or solve a problem? Failure can feel overwhelming, which is why many of us treat it like a great obstacle in daily life.

However, failure is more than simply not succeeding. It is a chance to examine what went wrong and to improve. Failing teaches us valuable lessons and helps us avoid repeating the same mistakes. Each failure can become a source of experience and guide us toward later success.

Take scientists for example. They often run many experiments that do not work before finding the result they want. Even when experiments fail, researchers frequently discover unexpected things that add to knowledge. This demonstrates that no matter how many times you fail, there is often a useful outcome or a new idea to explore.

At the same time, keeping a positive attitude can be difficult. People try every day to stay hopeful and see mistakes as opportunities, but after a setback this can become more stressful. Feeling anxious or insecure after failure is normal. Our emotions make us human and can even make us stronger. Yet some people fall into depression after failing: they lose hope, stop pursuing their goals, and become tired and uninterested in trying again.

A good example appears in a book the students at Generic_School read last year called "The Life of an Indian." The story follows a poor boy living on a reservation who seems to have no future until his teacher shows him a different world and encourages him to believe in himself. He fails many times, but instead of giving up, he faces his problems and slowly finds hope and direction.

This example shows that remaining positive after setbacks is possible, even for someone with few advantages. Not everyone can respond in the same way, but most of us want happiness, and learning from failure can bring us closer to it.

In conclusion, learning from our mistakes is one of the best paths to success. Every failure can offer a lesson and a new perspective. I agree with Winston Churchill: keeping enthusiasm for what comes next is powerful. If we believe in ourselves, stay optimistic, and accept that failure is a normal part of life, we will grow wiser and become more successful.

Many schools now let students join lessons from home through online video platforms. Is it a good idea to study this way? I believe it is, because distance learning can save time and make education more practical for many people.

First, online classes fit better with different work schedules. Many students have jobs with irregular hours and cannot rely on employers to give them a convenient timetable. Studying from home after work means they do not have to rush or miss shifts to attend classes. Being at home also helps tired students relax, have a proper meal and concentrate more during the lesson.

Online learning also frees up time for other useful activities. When students do not need to commute, they have extra hours for hobbies, exercise, or meeting friends. This balance can improve their wellbeing and prevent burnout. For example, someone who finishes a shift in the evening can join a live class from home and still find time to rest or play sports the next day.

Health and transport problems are another good reason to offer online options. If a student is ill, they should not travel to campus and risk infecting others. Remote classes allow sick students to continue studying without endangering classmates. Likewise, not all students can drive or afford parking; paying for a parking space or facing bad weather can make attending campus difficult. Online lessons remove these barriers and make education more accessible in bad weather or when public transport is unreliable.

Family responsibilities make distance learning especially valuable. Some students are parents or carers and need to be available for young children or family members. Studying from home lets them combine caregiving with learning: they can attend classes while still looking after children or helping a relative. Disabled students often face physical challenges getting to campus; online classes reduce these obstacles by bringing education directly into their homes. This flexibility can prevent dropouts and reduce stress, because students know they do not have to miss important lessons if something comes up.

Finally, modern technology has made remote learning easy and effective. Video conferencing, recorded lectures and online resources save time and let students study at a pace that suits them. For busy people, the ability to access learning materials from anywhere is a clear advantage.

In short, online classes offer practical benefits: they accommodate work schedules, ease health and transport concerns, support family and disability needs, and use technology to make learning more flexible. For these reasons, I think taking classes online is a very good idea.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." I agree with this idea because society often pressures people to change their views, beliefs, or traditions. Staying true to who you are is difficult but important. There are three main reasons I support Emerson's claim: keep trying, love and accept yourself, and remember where you come from.

First, do not give up on being yourself. The world may push you to behave differently or hide parts of your identity, but you should keep going. It is essential to feel comfortable with who you are, even if others disapprove. Second, love and be proud of yourself. Everyone makes mistakes, but those errors do not have to erase your identity. Learn from them and continue to value your qualities. Your traits and personality make you unique, and accepting them builds confidence.

Third, never forget your roots. If you move to a new place or face people who expect you to change, resist the pressure to pretend to be someone else. Your background and traditions are part of what defines you, and honoring them shows strength.

In short, don’t let the world force you to become someone different. Keep trying to be yourself, cherish who you are, and stay connected to your origins—these are the signs of a true accomplishment.

In conclusion, adding two hours a day to the school schedule would create valuable opportunities to educate students about saving energy and resources and to carry out real projects that improve our community. When people become more aware and take action, we can hope for a better world in the future.

For these students, being allowed to follow their own interests is more enjoyable and less stressful.

Because of these reasons, making every student take part in a school activity is not a good policy. If I were the principal, I would give students the choice: they could join an activity or spend time inside relaxing or taking part in a club that fits their interests. This respect for variety and rest would make school better for everyone.

When a baby first enters the world, the immediate reaction is usually a loud cry. If a newborn does not cry, doctors often stimulate the baby to elicit that sound. From that first cry we begin to show small signs of individuality — each child develops their own pitch and pattern of crying. We also receive fingerprints, unique to each person; even identical twins do not share the same prints. These early differences are small, but they point to the fact that we start to form our own identity from the beginning.

As infants, our brains begin to work quickly, learning simple ways to get what we need. Babies cry to signal hunger, discomfort, pain, or a desire for attention. As we move into the toddler years, we pick up basic skills by watching the people around us. Children learn to walk by observing others, learn to speak by listening, and learn to use utensils and other tools by copying daily routines. Much of what we can do comes from seeing and imitating those around us.

Between ages six and twelve we become more aware of social groups and want to belong. We are exposed to television and public figures, and we learn about many possible roles in life — musicians, athletes, doctors, police officers, chefs, and many more. These influences show us potential paths, but they do not decide who we will become. During the teenage years, roughly thirteen to nineteen, people start developing their own voices and making more independent choices. Parents can offer guidance and share their experience to help avoid mistakes, but ultimately teenagers begin to make their own decisions.

Making mistakes can be useful. Failing at something teaches lessons that advice alone cannot. When young people take responsibility for their actions, they learn whether they are dependable, patient, forgiving, or the opposite. Entering adulthood means taking on new responsibilities at work and in life. The safety net of living with parents often disappears, and adults must shape their behavior and character through daily choices and responsibilities.

Our environment affects us, but it does not fix our character. Someone living in difficult circumstances can still be cheerful and resilient, while someone with many privileges can be unhappy and ungrateful. A person who sees themselves as a victim will often act helpless, while someone with determination and a positive mindset tends to develop strength and respect. Mindset plays a large role in how people behave; a defeatist attitude usually brings negative results, while a strong will produces better outcomes.

In short, I believe we are not born with fixed labels that determine our lives. We learn, copy, fail, and decide for ourselves. Through these experiences and our own choices, we build and shape our character rather than accepting a fate predetermined by anyone else.

People often ask whether reduced face-to-face contact because of technology is good or bad. I think the answer varies — for some people it helps, for others it causes problems.

On the positive side, technology can be a real lifeline for those who feel lonely. When someone is alone, having entertainment and connection at hand can make a big difference. I have seen people who would rather avoid uncomfortable social situations and instead read books online, shop, play games, listen to music on apps like Pandora, or watch shows on YouTube or Netflix. These options give comfort and distraction and can prevent the deep sadness that comes from feeling isolated. Technology also makes communication simpler, keeps us informed about world events (even news from space), and saves time by allowing online shopping, food delivery, and quick answers without reading a whole book.

However, there are downsides. As my grandfather used to say, good things often come with negatives. Because devices can do so much, some people lose interest in ordinary activities and in real social gatherings. Family get-togethers can suffer when relatives are more focused on their screens than on each other. I used to prefer being with close friends rather than sitting through dull conversations at home, but now it is often hard to have a simple talk because people are busy on their phones. To me, that feels disrespectful and can make others feel ignored or offended.

The convenience of technology can also encourage laziness. People may ask themselves: why go out and meet someone when I can talk through my phone? Why talk in person when a device offers endless entertainment? If we keep answering those questions the same way, we risk ending up more isolated in the long run.

In conclusion, technology is a powerful and useful tool when used appropriately. It becomes harmful only when it replaces real human contact or takes over our attention. Use it when needed, but don’t let it control your life.

I think one of the best ways to enjoy the outdoors is to spend time with family and friends having a cookout—grilling hamburgers, hot dogs, carne asada, tacos or barbacoa. You can play sports like soccer, football or baseball, go for a bike ride, or organize running races with your friends. Play some music but keep the volume down so you don’t attract unwanted attention from the police. Invite your son or daughter’s partner and their parents to join, and bring snacks for the afternoon.

Being outside with loved ones can feel like a day of camping. If there is a river where fishing is allowed, it’s fun to try catching fish to cook and eat. But more than food or activities, the main goal is to enjoy time together. You can admire the beauty of nature, forget your worries for a while, and listen to the birds. These moments help you reconnect with family, remember how important their love and support are, and feel grateful for the people who care about you—especially because some people do not have that support and can feel very alone.

At night you can make a small, safe fire to roast marshmallows and then sandwich them between two cookies—one on top and one on the bottom—so everyone can enjoy a sweet treat. Around the fire people can gather to tell scary stories or jokes. The best part of being outdoors is the shared fun with friends and family, and also the chance to breathe fresh air and relax.

Community parks, state parks and national parks are very important for people. They are places where you can celebrate with friends, spend time with a partner or family, have a small party, go for a run, walk your dog, or just take a quiet walk to clear your mind and think. Parks also need our care because they are the homes of many birds, animals and plants. Looking after these places helps ensure that everyone can continue to enjoy nature and the company of others.

Technology makes it possible to do many everyday tasks without having direct contact with other people. We can borrow books, shop, and play games online, which has changed how often we meet face to face. While some argue this reduces human contact, I believe the effects of technology are largely positive because it lets us keep in touch across long distances, work from home without commuting, and meet new people and cultures.

First, technology helps families and friends stay connected even when they are far apart. Video calls, messaging apps, and social media let us share daily moments and important news instantly. Without these tools, it would be difficult to speak regularly with relatives who live in another city or country, and over time we might lose touch. Technology also helps in emergencies: if someone has an accident, family members can be contacted quickly and the location can be shared. Even simple things like notifying your employer when you are sick become much easier with a phone or internet access. For these reasons, communication technology improves our safety and keeps relationships alive.

Second, working online has clear advantages that improve people’s lives. Remote work removes the need for a daily commute, which saves time and transport costs. This is especially helpful for parents who want to spend more time with their children while still earning a living, or for people who are unable to drive. Working from home can make balancing family and job responsibilities easier. It also gives the freedom to travel and continue working from other places, which can increase income or create new opportunities. Overall, online work makes life more flexible and can reduce stress connected to travel and time management.

Third, technology opens up chances to meet new friends and learn about other cultures and languages. Social media and online communities connect people from different countries, so we can ask questions about traditions, beliefs, and daily life. When visiting an unfamiliar place, apps can help with directions and translation, making it easier to communicate with locals and find your way. For example, a phone translator lets you ask questions even if you don’t speak the language, and maps help you avoid getting lost. These tools make travel and cultural exchange safer and more enjoyable.

In conclusion, technology has brought many positive changes to our lives. It keeps us connected with loved ones, enables flexible and remote work, and helps us discover new people and cultures. Used well, these tools are valuable resources that improve communication, safety, and opportunity.

What does self-reliance mean? In short, it is the ability of students and adults to make their own decisions and take responsibility for their actions. This idea matters now more than ever because many of the problems we face affect not only individuals but the whole country. For example, a government shutdown hurts everyone — workers, businesses, farms, and stores. That is why relying on yourself does not mean refusing help; it also means knowing when to seek guidance and gather information so better choices can be made.

Good decisions usually come from more than one point of view. When people discuss problems together, they can share ideas and find better solutions than any one person could alone. We should not teach children only to follow others; we should teach them how to think independently and lead. True leaders also ask for help. They begin with small steps, learning and gaining experience over time. Even when someone becomes knowledgeable, asking questions and learning from others continues to be important.

Self-reliance is useful in many parts of life: family, work, and everyday routines. It is not just students who need these skills. In the workplace, being able to find information, ask for advice, and make smart choices improves performance and helps a career grow. At home, these skills help when making financial or personal decisions. Self-reliance is similar to leadership: it means standing up for what you think is right while also being open to other opinions. Seeking advice and considering different options prevents mistakes and gives you more paths to choose from.

The military shows how important self-reliance and training can be. Service members must be ready to make quick decisions that may affect many lives. Basic training and ongoing practice prepare soldiers mentally and physically so they can act when needed. Even there, commanders and teams share information and advice. This combination of personal responsibility and teamwork is exactly what we need in civilian life too, where important choices can involve our children, jobs, or future.

These skills are important for everyone, regardless of age, race, gender, or background. Learning how to find information, ask questions, and cooperate with others will help both now and in the future. If we all pay attention to what is happening in government and society, and speak up when needed, we can help prevent economic problems like market crashes and support our communities.

Finally, remember that our jobs often depend on larger systems, including government decisions. When those systems fail, many people and businesses suffer. So instead of worrying only about small personal wants, focus on what matters and seek advice when you need it. Do not be afraid to ask questions — we all learn every day. Keep searching for answers, share your ideas, and teach these habits to the next generation. In short: practice self-reliance, seek guidance, and never stop asking questions.

As education develops, schools increasingly offer subjects that let pupils explore their natural talents, and many students who enjoy the arts can freely join those lessons to discover their strengths. Besides helping students follow personal interests, art classes give a useful break after two or three consecutive hours of study. These activities allow learners to relax and regain energy for the next study period, although for pupils who have no interest in practicing an art, such classes can feel like wasted time.

High school can become dull for many students because they do not always know where they fit or what excites them at school. In this situation, finding enjoyable activities is one of the best ways to fight boredom and lower stress. Options such as joining a band, taking part in a drama group, or attending a drawing class can restore students’ motivation and make studying more bearable. Students should be encouraged to take these classes because they help maintain interest and give a balance to academic work.

Art lessons not only refresh the mind but also improve the ability to absorb new information. After a heavy, information-packed session, doing something creative like singing, acting, or sketching calms the brain and makes it easier to take in more material afterward. The benefit depends on personal taste: when students engage in an activity they enjoy, their body and mind relax and they return to study more ready to learn.

We support the idea that students should have art classes in their timetable, but those courses should be chosen to match each pupil’s natural preferences. If attendance in a particular arts class is forced on uninterested students, many of them may become disruptive — sleeping, chatting, or otherwise disturbing others — and this ruins the experience for those who want to benefit from the break.

In conclusion, art classes are valuable because they refresh students after long study periods, boost learning capacity, and create motivation at school. However, to avoid wasting time and causing distraction, these classes should be elective so students can pick the creative option that suits them best.

Technology is an important tool in our lives because it helps people in many ways: with tasks, communication, and entertainment. Today technology develops very fast and we can access news, contact family and friends, or do schoolwork using a phone, tablet, or computer.

Technology has a positive effect on society because it makes shopping easier, offers many entertainment options like games and music, and gives us access to useful apps and functions such as GPS, translators, and e-books. Many of these services are affordable or free, so most people can use them.

One reason technology is essential every day is the practical help it gives. For example, if someone is lost in an unfamiliar place, a smartphone’s GPS can guide them to their destination or to the nearest store or supermarket. This kind of support is useful in many situations and makes life simpler.

Another benefit is entertainment. When someone feels bored, technology offers many choices: streaming music from any artist or genre, downloading games, or finding e-books. It is often easier to find a book on a phone or tablet than in a physical bookstore because you only need to type the title and get many options. The internet also provides thousands of games for all kinds of people, from sports and adventure fans to puzzle lovers.

Communication is a major advantage of technology. No matter the distance, people can stay in touch through apps like Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger. These platforms are simple to use and let families and friends share photos and videos, helping people feel closer even when they are far apart. If used properly, these apps can be a valuable way to keep relationships strong.

Technology also helps solve practical problems. If you need to cook a new recipe or fix something at home, you can find step-by-step videos and tutorials on sites like Google and YouTube. These tutorials explain tasks clearly and give tips, and they can save time and money. Sometimes you can also find professionals or mechanics online who offer help for more complex issues.

Finally, technology can help people find jobs. Many companies ask applicants to fill out online forms, which is fast and convenient if you have a phone or computer. Businesses also use the internet to show their products and services and reach more customers. This makes it easier for a local company to become known in other places and grow its profits.

In conclusion, technology is a valuable tool that supports communication, entertainment, problem solving, and job searching. With many apps and services available on our devices, people can access information, contact loved ones, and improve their daily lives. When used responsibly, technology brings people together and helps them in many practical ways.

Asking several people for advice can help someone make a wiser decision. I have seen this in my family and among my friends. In one case, my uncle had one hundred dollars in his wallet. He gave me ten and kept the rest. I told him to save the money because he might need it the next day, but he ignored my advice. Instead, he spent everything on shirts, pants and hats. The following morning he asked me for money to pay for gas. He was happy when he bought the clothes, but because he did not listen, he had nothing left when he needed it.

Another example happened with a friend who had some money in his pocket and wanted to go to the cinema. He said, "Let's go watch a movie," but the rest of us said no. We explained that the same movie was available on CD and that would cost much less. After hearing our opinions, he understood a different point of view. Even though he wanted the cinema experience, buying the cheaper CD was a better choice for his budget. In the end he bought the CD.

I also remember a time with my dad giving me money to buy whatever I wanted. I knew I would need a white shirt the next day for a special place we had to go, but I spent the money on a game because I wanted it. My dad had warned me about the shirt and told me where we would be going. The next day I had to ask for money to buy the shirt, and he reminded me, "I told you to buy it yesterday." I learned from that experience and later made sure to save some money for similar situations.

These stories show how important it is to listen to people around you. Getting different opinions lets you see things from other perspectives and often leads to better choices. What about you — do you sometimes listen to more than one person before deciding?

Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, "Unless you try to do something beyond what you already mastered, you will never grow." I agree with this idea for several reasons. First, if people never prepare themselves to learn more than one skill, they will not develop. Second, having a wider range of knowledge gives a clear advantage over others. Finally, without attempting tasks that are more difficult than what we already know, we cannot progress.

For the first reason, when people limit their lives to only one area of knowledge, they often lack direction and face fewer chances in society. Employers usually seek candidates with varied abilities, so someone who has not gained additional skills may find it hard to get better jobs. For example, a person searching for new work experiences may be passed over because they do not have the qualifications required for the position. In this way, they cannot contribute as much to their workplace or community if they remain unprepared for important tasks.

Second, having different kinds of knowledge makes life easier in finding suitable work. Knowledge is a powerful tool that people cannot simply buy; it must be developed. Those who focus on learning more will have a stronger position to grow in their careers and personal life. 

Finally, taking on harder challenges brings new experiences that lead to growth. For instance, a university graduate who becomes a teacher but never seeks further responsibility will not advance to roles like principal or administrator. 

In conclusion, I support Emerson’s statement because trying beyond what we already know is essential for gaining opportunities, power through knowledge, and personal development.

Taking courses online or through video calls is a great option for students who cannot afford to attend campus and for older adults who missed earlier chances to continue their education due to money problems. Today many people face financial difficulties that make campus living costly. Students often struggle to pay for on-campus or off-campus housing, which forces some to leave their dorms. Many have part-time jobs to cover these expenses, and juggling work with classes is challenging because it requires careful planning to balance both responsibilities without becoming overwhelmed.

Transportation and parking also cause problems, so some learners prefer studying from home to avoid being late. Even large colleges sometimes lack enough parking spaces, and not every student owns a car or another vehicle. Being able to join classes from home means they can begin lessons at times that suit them, especially after a tiring day, which reduces stress and removes the pressure of commuting.

Studying online helps students be more productive and finish tasks more quickly. With fewer disruptions, they can follow lectures more easily and stay focused on the material. Online formats make it simple to ask questions during or after class, and recorded lessons allow students to review difficult parts until they fully understand them. Teachers often adjust workloads for online learners, giving fewer projects so students can concentrate on core assignments and manage their time better.

Overall, online classes and video conferencing give people the freedom to handle other responsibilities, arrive for lessons punctually, and support those who otherwise could not attend college. This approach saves money, improves organization, and helps students develop better time-management skills while still allowing them to reach their educational goals.

In some cultures, young people are expected to pick a career path as early as high school. Many think choosing a direction sooner helps: students can get guidance from counselors, prepare for college courses linked to that field, and secure employment after graduation so they do not have to worry later. However, deciding on a career at a very young age is often unwise. It can lead students to drop classes, cause excessive uncertainty and thinking, and waste valuable time.

First, early career choices can make students abandon their studies. For example, teenagers who enroll in a course and attend for only two or three weeks may quickly lose interest and stop going. Once they give up, catching up becomes hard and their schoolwork suffers. This lack of commitment often comes from choosing too soon without fully understanding what the course involves. Therefore, it is better for young people to reflect carefully before signing up for a specific career track.

Second, picking a career early can create a lot of unnecessary worry. Even adults take time to decide on a career because they must weigh factors like job prospects and income. Young students, however, may feel pressured to choose before they are ready, which leads to overthinking and stress. Many teenagers focus more on earning money or spending time with friends and decide on their professional plans later in life, after gaining more experience.

Third, early decisions can waste time. Children sometimes treat career forms as a school task and write "don’t know" or return to hobbies like video games instead of seriously exploring options. Without a clear plan, their time is spent on distractions rather than useful preparation for the future. Planning carefully before committing helps avoid this loss.

Choosing a career at twelve or younger is generally premature because it can cause students to quit courses, create excessive doubt, and lead to wasted time. Young people should be encouraged to plan thoughtfully and not rush into a decision they may soon regret.

Technology has changed how people relate to one another, and one important consequence is the reduction of face-to-face contact. I believe technology has mostly positive effects, but it also limits direct human interaction in many ways. Below I explain some examples that show both the benefits and the drawbacks of this change.

First, technology plays a large and helpful role in daily life and work. Many people rely on devices and the internet to do their jobs. If technology did not exist, they would have fewer chances to learn new skills and earn a living. In schools, teachers and students often use computers to complete and submit assignments online, and they search the internet for information instead of using only books. In medicine, doctors depend on advanced tools for diagnosis and surgery, which saves many lives. Factories use machines that make production faster and easier, so people do not have to do heavy manual labor the way they did before. These examples show why technology can be a powerful positive force.

At the same time, technology can be used for harm. Although most users use it for good—such as doctors, teachers, and office workers—some people use digital tools to cheat, steal, or hurt others. Fraud, hacking, and online scams are common problems; criminals can steal money from bank accounts or trick people through social media and games. Also, in many families technology acts like a "babysitter": parents give children phones or tablets to keep them quiet while they do other tasks. This may be useful, but it also reduces real interaction between parents and children. In some cases, young people are exposed to strangers online who can take advantage of them. These negative uses show that technology is not always harmless.

Technology has also changed how people think and feel. It can make people feel safer at home because of security systems and monitoring devices. Social media and platforms like YouTube allow people to share their talents and earn a living without meeting audiences in person. Older generations have adapted too: instead of writing letters, they now send texts or make video calls. Online gaming and messaging let friends in different countries communicate instantly, creating connections that were impossible before. In these ways, technology reduces the need for face-to-face contact and alters social habits.

However, the loss of direct contact can cause problems. In the workplace, good relationships with coworkers often depend on talking in person and building trust, which is harder when everyone communicates only through screens. Romantic relationships can also suffer if partners rely only on text messages instead of real conversations. School students may accept quick answers from classmates or the internet without discussing ideas in person, and technology does not always provide accurate or deep information. For many situations, human contact remains important for understanding emotions, resolving conflicts, and creating strong bonds.

In conclusion, technology brings both advantages and disadvantages for human contact. It makes life easier, improves many jobs, and connects people across distances. But it also encourages less face-to-face interaction and can be misused in harmful ways. Because of this, I think we should value real human communication more and try to balance our use of technology with opportunities for personal contact.

I agree with the idea that a positive attitude is essential for a successful life. To me, success is not only about material things but also about making life easier by showing kindness and calmness to others. No matter what people say or think about you, it is important to stay composed when problems come up and try to solve them with a good attitude. Getting angry rarely leads to a good solution. That is why being respectful and peaceful with everyone, keeping inner calm, and building strong relationships with the people around you are so important. Try to face what comes to you with a friendly expression.

Being kind to others makes them feel valued and makes you feel good too. When you treat people well, you show that you are different in a positive way. It is true that many people can be selfish or rude, but that should not stop you from being a nice person. If someone has a bad attitude, you do not need to become like them; instead, keep your distance and look for people who think and act similarly to you. Those people can feel like family and improve your life and chances of success. For example, I am kind to my family and my friends. I spent time getting to know my friends—their interests, how they spend their free time—and they appreciate me for being reliable. They think I am a person with a good attitude, and I want them in my life. I also believe they will be successful because I can see their qualities.

Having peace inside is a very important part of living well. When you are peaceful, you receive many positive feelings that make you comfortable. Of course, sometimes events or people will make you feel uncomfortable, and finding peace can be difficult. But not having inner peace can affect many areas of your life. To feel calm, try to do things you love and find activities that do not bore you. Also, do not let small problems turn into long-lasting anger. For example, when I was 12 my younger brother did something that upset me, and I remembered it for a long time. I am 20 now and I still sometimes think about that moment, but I try not to focus on it. When I do remember, I tell myself that I love him and that we are close. He listens to me and when I share my thoughts with him I feel peaceful again.

Good connections with people around you help keep a positive attitude. If you meet people who are optimistic and focused on things that improve life, they can influence your future in a good way. These people are interesting to talk with, and you can learn from them and exchange ideas. On the other hand, some friends will invite you to parties or activities that might harm your future. Sometimes those who try to help you are not the ones who seem fun at first, but they offer things that are better for your life. I remember a classmate who was hardworking in seventh grade, but in ninth grade he began to spend time with students who did not care about studying. His grades dropped and he got involved in bad habits with his new friends. I think he may not have gone to college because of that choice. That story shows why it is important to be with people who support your goals.

In short, being a good person to others, keeping peace in your heart, and choosing the right people to be around are three key elements for having a successful life. Showing a good attitude to everyone, no matter what is happening, can make a big difference.

First impressions can be changed. Not everything is what it seems at first glance, and many things turn out differently from our initial thoughts. Too often people decide something is bad or unpleasant simply because that idea came to them immediately when they first encountered it.

We should avoid making quick judgments about people or situations, because those first reactions are often incorrect. We form opinions about others without really knowing them or understanding their background, and that can lead to unfair conclusions. I have been guilty of this myself. In tenth grade I judged a classmate too quickly. Although we shared several lessons, I kept my distance because I believed he showed little respect to students and teachers. I assumed he would be rude to me, so I did not try to get to know him.

Later I discovered how wrong I had been. He became one of my closest friends — a kind, reliable person I could trust and enjoy spending time with. That experience taught me that initial impressions are not fixed; they can change as we learn more about someone. Even if your first thought about a person feels strong, it is worth giving them a chance. With time and more information, your view may shift, and you might find that your first judgment was not accurate.

Some people disagree, but I believe it is better to begin with modest goals because this approach helps you notice and correct small mistakes early.

People should consider aiming lower at first so they can focus on the things that need improvement. These small corrections are what make you stronger and allow you to handle many future challenges more effectively.

Those who start from a modest position often end up surpassing their expectations. By setting achievable targets and learning from errors, they grow in ability and confidence. Mistakes along the way build character and teach skills that make a person more capable in the long run.

Many people set very high goals, thinking they will automatically reach the top without much thought or effort. This can be dangerous because such ambition sometimes ignores the careful planning and steady work needed to succeed. It is wiser to begin a bit lower so you can develop the habits and resilience required to reach bigger aims. For example, someone who risks everything for a huge plan may lose that chance after a single wrong step because they did not think things through. Starting with small, safe moves lets you avoid unnecessary risks and learn progressively as you go.

Choosing low-risk aims also helps protect what you have already achieved. Understanding this allows you to move forward without losing important progress. Taking the time to consider your options and improve what you already possess is often more effective than chasing a dramatic leap forward. While it can be valuable to challenge yourself sometimes, you should not put everything at stake without careful thought. A single impulsive decision can undo months or years of hard work.

In my view, people should think carefully before acting. That thoughtful approach, starting with manageable goals and growing step by step, is more likely to lead to lasting success than taking reckless risks. If you do decide to challenge yourself, plan and reflect beforehand so you do not lose what you have already built.

I agree that being honest all the time is the best approach because honesty means telling the truth and not deceiving others. When I am honest, people can trust me. That trust matters when someone asks me a question or when I need help with schoolwork or other tasks. Even if others are not always truthful, my honesty makes it easier for them to rely on me.

Honesty is a core trait I want to keep in my character from the beginning. As I grow older and gain more experience, being honest will remain important. It gives me confidence: for example, if I tell myself I will not fail a test, that honest intention drives me to prepare and try my best. Similarly, being truthful helps prevent problems like bullying, because people who are honest tend to create clearer, more respectful relationships.

Of course, being honest can sometimes lead to problems. If I tell the truth, some people may get upset with me, especially if they expected something different or wanted to be reassured. They might stop trusting me and decide never to trust me again. That would be painful, especially if I had been sincere just to cheer them up rather than hiding difficulties. A negative experience like that could damage a friendship or a family relationship.

However, relationships can heal. People may realize later that I was honest and apologize for losing trust. We might rebuild our connection and agree about the value of honesty again. On the other hand, sometimes a friend may find other people they trust more than me, which could lead to ongoing arguments or distance between us. To avoid those big conflicts, it is better to talk face to face, calmly explain my position, and listen to theirs. A direct conversation is less likely to hurt someone's feelings and can prevent long-term separation.

Honesty can also help others move away from negative thoughts and dangerous behavior. If I and others around me are honest and supportive, it may reduce stress and stop people from feeling hopeless or turning to drugs or risky actions. Even if someone tells me they no longer trust me, I would not lose hope or consider harming myself. I would keep standing by honesty, even if I have disappointed people before. I believe that failing a test is more often a result of not studying than of being honest. If I guessed on many answers because I did not prepare, that is my responsibility, not honesty’s.

I will use honesty as a tool when I need it to succeed, and I plan to remain honest throughout my life. I want everyone to make honesty their top quality because it can help resolve many difficult problems and reduce conflicts. Some people think being honest all the time is unrealistic and say they must first learn what honesty truly means. They may also assume that intelligence and honesty are connected—that smart people are more honest. I disagree. Honesty is not tied to how smart someone is. Less intelligent people can be honest and grow, while intelligent people might change and begin to lie if they are not guided properly.

If someone loses honesty, the people who can help them return to it are often family members or teachers, since they usually care enough to correct that behavior. Friends can sometimes lead someone away from honesty by encouraging bad choices, which is why it’s important to be careful about who you spend time with. When a person changes for the better and becomes honest, others will notice and wonder how that change happened. They may share that story with others and be surprised by the difference.

In the end, honesty should be a top priority for everyone. It builds trust, helps solve conflicts, and supports personal growth. For these reasons, I believe honesty is the best policy and should stay at the center of my life.

The national park is a great place for both children and adults to enjoy the outdoors with friends, family, and pets. Throughout the park there are many activities to join: board games, toys for kids, picnics, sports, and other fun attractions. We also run a campaign to feed people who are homeless. If you donate to this cause, you will receive an exclusive T-shirt as a thank-you for your support.

If you are tired of staying at home, come to our national park for a day of enjoyment. We will host a soccer match between two teams; the winning team will receive a prize at the end of the day. There will also be a boys-versus-girls tug-of-war to see which side wins — come and watch to find out. A pie-eating contest will take place to crown the champion on March 21, 2019.

Our events run from March 21 to March 29, 2019. On March 22 we will hold a chess tournament, and ice cream will be available with a buy-two-get-one-free offer. March 23 is the day for a team race: twenty teams will compete in a three-hour challenge that tests cooperation and endurance. The entry fee is ten dollars per person.

On March 24 we will focus on collecting donations to support people who are asking for help so they can survive another day. Please join us and contribute so that our community can move toward a more peaceful and hopeful future. March 25 will bring a new dog adoption center where animals in need can find loving families; we hope many dogs will be given a second chance.

March 26 is dedicated to cleaning our town and its surroundings to make our environment nicer for everyone. We would be very grateful to see over one hundred volunteers come out to help with this project. On March 27 we will hold a celebration for families and friends to honor the hard work of everyone who helped with the clean-up, donations, and adoptions — we aim to rehome over one hundred dogs in a single day.

March 29 will be our final day of festivities, with giveaways for people who have spent time with us during the week. The community park will also have information tables where you can sign up for various clubs and activities. The national park is a lovely place for people of all ages to spend time outdoors, take part in events, and support one another. Come join us and be part of the fun.

Dear council,

I believe the city should introduce a 10 P.M. curfew for teenagers because it would help keep them away from trouble. Some young people stay out late and cause problems for others by loitering or making noise. A law requiring teenagers to be home by 10 P.M. would encourage those who are likely to get into trouble to return home earlier. At the same time, many teens need rest for school the next day, so a curfew would help students get enough sleep and be ready for their classes.

Late nights also increase the chance that young people will meet others who carry weapons or belong to gangs. Even if a teen is not involved in crime, being out on the street at night can lead to bad situations and even arrest because of who they are with. A curfew could reduce these risky encounters and lower the number of teens who end up in trouble with the law.

Some people say a curfew interferes with young people’s freedom. It is true that it limits what teenagers can do at night, but many of those activities are unsafe. The curfew is meant to protect them, not punish them.

Overall, I support a rule that teens must be off the streets after 10 P.M. because it would help keep them safe and reduce trouble in the city.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote that unless you try something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow, and I agree with him. To understand this idea, recognize that mastering something means you can do it reliably. Growth comes when you set new goals and challenge yourself beyond familiar abilities. Even tiny steps forward move you along the path to bigger achievements.

Learning takes time and rarely happens overnight. Some skills require years of practice, but with determination and self-confidence you can reach a higher level. For example, if you can ride a bicycle, try learning to ride a motorcycle; if you can bake a cupcake, aim to make a whole cake; if you can float in water, teach yourself to swim properly. These small challenges build on what you already know and help you expand your skills.

Unless you push yourself, you will stay where you are. With steady effort and dedication, the goals you set become reachable and you can go beyond your current limits. Failing at a small task now does not mean you will never master it — you must keep practicing until you improve. Ultimately, it is your choice: either keep growing by taking on new challenges, or remain the same and miss the chance to achieve your goals.

I believe that first impressions can be changed. People react differently to those first impressions, and not everyone ends up with the same attitude.

Some people never change because they simply do not care, while others adjust their views depending on past experiences. For some, a first impression will not affect them at all and they continue their normal routine without paying attention to what others say. But when someone receives a strong negative impression, they may begin to reflect on their behavior and think about what they did wrong. Change usually happens when a person feels it is necessary, and it often takes time. Many people repeat the same actions without thinking, so change does not occur quickly.

Relationships are a common area where impressions shift, especially when there is betrayal. Couples often face problems like jealousy, toxicity, or bad influences. Young people can be particularly vulnerable; sometimes they react so strongly to suspected betrayal that it causes serious harm to themselves. Being in a relationship should not be about making others jealous. Although changing is difficult, it can help build healthier connections.

I can relate to this from my own life. At first, when people told me I had disappointed them with my behavior, I felt crushed and thought I could not change. I believed I could not do what others did because I was used to my own habits, even if those habits were not good for other people. Eventually I decided that I would try to change no matter how hard it was, and I believed I could improve with or without help.

In conclusion, first impressions can lead people to change. Changing shows others that you are not the same person you used to be, and it helps prevent repeating past mistakes. It may be hard to forget what happened before, but with daily effort we can improve. Nobody is perfect, but we can work on our behavior and be more careful about who we trust.

Many people argue that students should pick a career when they start high school and choose classes to support that path. I disagree with this idea. I believe it is unwise to force young teens to commit to a specific profession because they are often too young and inexperienced to make a firm choice.

First, high school students usually do not have enough knowledge about different jobs to know which one suits them best. Most teenagers have little or no work experience, so they cannot fully understand the reality of a career. Choosing too early may lead to a decision based on incomplete information.

Second, teenagers sometimes act without thinking and change their minds. If a student picks a specialized set of courses in their freshman year, those classes might turn out to be useless later if they decide to follow another interest. For example, a friend of mine took a technology course in ninth grade. After researching typical salaries and day-to-day tasks, he realized it was not what he wanted. He later switched to a materials and processes class to learn construction skills like cutting and building houses.

Finally, making a career decision while young increases the chance of choosing poorly. For me, the smarter plan is to wait until junior or senior year to select classes that will prepare me for a particular field. By then I will know more about life and careers and be more responsible in my choices. Meanwhile, students should concentrate on doing well academically and exploring different subjects.

In conclusion, requiring students to decide their career path at the start of high school is not a good idea. It is better to focus on learning and grades, then pick a direction later when you have more experience and clearer goals.

I believe students would gain a lot from being allowed to attend classes from home. Learning online can make it easier for students to be ready when class begins and help them concentrate better on their work.

One reason is that some students feel embarrassed at school and hold back. They may be afraid of classmates who put them down, for example someone saying “you can’t do this” or “your English is bad.” At home, shy students do not have to worry about other people’s reactions, so they are more likely to try and participate. When a student studies alone and has questions, they often try to find answers on their own, which builds independence.

Also, studying from home gives practical flexibility. If I am working on new material all day and become hungry, I can quickly go to the kitchen, prepare something, and return to my studies without losing much time. If I need help, I can message a teacher. For many students who need one-on-one explanations, online classes can feel less stressful and more comfortable than a crowded classroom. People who prefer not to get up early can choose to study later in the day, which can improve their learning when they are more alert.

I also think of students who face special challenges, like pregnancy. I have a friend who continued attending school while pregnant. It was clearly difficult for her to come to campus tired and uncomfortable, and after her baby was born she found coming back to school hard because she did not want to leave the child at home. When she started taking some classes from home, it helped her keep studying without the stress of being away from her baby. Stories like hers make me feel that, if I had the choice, I would prefer learning from home rather than always going to school.

Of course, there are problems to solve. Not every family can afford online classes or the equipment needed. Some students must work to support themselves or their families, and that can mean missing school or feeling too tired to pay attention. For students who need to earn money, online learning can be a good option: they can work a few hours and then study at home, or arrange alternating days of work and study. Still, online study requires discipline. Students must keep trying, seek help when they do not understand, research, and study regularly. With effort and support, it is possible to reach goals even when others doubt you.

Online lessons and video conferences can explain math problems or other topics clearly. Benefits of attending classes from home include spending more time using educational technology, concentrating better on homework, accessing information on a phone whenever needed, studying at convenient times, avoiding gossip or interruptions from friends during class, and finishing tasks faster without distractions.

In cold weather, students would not need to worry about the cold or special school clothes. They also would avoid uncomfortable encounters or conflicts with other students. Many young people suffer from low self-esteem, and being able to learn from home could protect their mental health. Overall, I think giving students the option to attend classes online would be very helpful for many of them.

Can you truly be yourself all the time and still reach the highest goals in life?

I believe you can. When you stay true to who you are and keep faith in your abilities, the path to great achievements becomes easier. If you trust yourself and work consistently, many things that seem impossible can become possible. As the saying goes, the sky is the limit. Confidence and faith give you strength; with them, obstacles feel smaller and less important.

Martin Luther King is a clear example. He dreamed of equal rights and a society where people were treated fairly, regardless of their skin color. He had strong faith in his vision and kept a positive attitude even when the struggle was hard. Because he believed in himself and never stopped working for his dream, he was able to turn that vision into real change. His determination helped bring people together in powerful events, like the March on Washington, and made lasting progress in civil rights.

Cristiano Ronaldo shows the same idea in sports. He grew up facing hardships and his family had limited resources, but he did not give up. From a young age he practiced a lot, balancing training with other responsibilities. His passion and self-belief pushed him to improve continuously. Over time, his hard work paid off and he became one of the best football players in the world. His story proves that belief plus effort can overcome difficult beginnings.

Even when you doubt yourself, remember that persistence and faith can change things. If you start working toward your dream and keep being yourself, you can reach your goals. Don’t give up when problems appear; keep believing in your dreams and acting on them. With confidence and steady effort, what you imagine can become reality.

When parents cover for their children—paying fines or defending them to others—teens may not learn from their mistakes. Graduating sooner can push them to face consequences and learn what behavior is acceptable and what is not.

Another example is when parents handle all the practical matters like car insurance or legal trouble. If parents always step in and say their child is innocent, the teenager may never accept responsibility. Finishing school earlier can encourage them to be more aware of their environment and the effects of their actions, because they have to stand on their own feet.

The second reason is that young graduates must manage their own finances and daily bills. Paying rent, electricity, and phone bills teaches people to budget and care about how much they use. For example, if a parent pays the phone or utility bills, teenagers often do not notice how their habits affect the total cost. When they must pay these expenses themselves, they become more careful and responsible.

Some people argue that graduating in three years is harmful because you might miss out on enjoying teenage life and feel more stressed. While that can be true for some, the benefits of becoming independent and responsible often outweigh that downside.

In conclusion, graduating in three years can be a good idea because it helps young people grow up faster and take full responsibility for their lives. They learn how life really works and what it means to be independent.

That is not acceptable because sometimes the person who picked it up didn’t need it — they just wanted it. There is a difference between needing something and wanting it. If you need something, it is important to you and you might struggle without it. But if you really need it, you can usually buy a replacement from a nearby store. Wanting something is different: you don’t have to have it, you just want it to show off or have fun. If you took something that you only want, you might not be struggling at all — you just decided to take it.

If someone drops something, give it back to them.

Be helpful and kind.

This lesson matters because many people today ignore it and take things, and some parents do not correct that behavior anymore. That leaves schools responsible for teaching children right from wrong. Think about how you would feel if you dropped your favorite toy or important item and someone else took it. You would probably feel angry, sad, or upset because that item might be special and hard to replace. Now imagine someone saw you drop it and quickly returned it to you. You would feel relieved and grateful because they didn’t even think of keeping it; they knew it belonged to you.

I lost my iPad years ago because someone who saw it didn’t give it back. I don’t know who took it because I wasn’t paying attention. I was happy at the time when someone picked it up and gave it back — I didn’t expect anything bad, so I didn’t watch what happened next. When I realized it was gone, I was very upset and had to use my mom’s phone until my dad bought me a replacement phone. That experience taught me why this lesson is so important: if you take something that doesn’t belong to you, someone else could do the same to you later. You might never find the item again.

If my phone were stolen, I would be angry and sad because it would be hard to replace and I would feel the loss.

That is why we should always return lost things when we find them. Taking items that don’t belong to you is not smart or fair. Teaching kids to be honest and helpful can stop many of these problems before they start.

I believe that students develop real self-esteem through their accomplishments. When students work hard and earn awards or other recognitions, they feel proud of themselves and that pride helps form genuine self-worth.

There are many students who put in effort, finish assignments on time and even hold part-time jobs after school, yet they still struggle to feel truly self-assured. For these students, building confidence is essential because without self-confidence it is difficult to turn achievements into lasting self-esteem.

On the other hand, some students attend school and have free time after class or on weekends, and they are confident, but they lack the achievements that would strengthen their self-esteem. This shows that both effort and confidence are important; achievements give a concrete sense of progress, while confidence lets students accept and build on their successes.

Students should aim to earn accomplishments because achievements motivate them and help them grow in self-respect. Self-esteem can be built through personal effort: studying hard, being punctual, and organizing tasks with a checklist or a calendar can make a big difference. Simple routines and planning show students what to do first and help them reach goals step by step.

I worry that many students today do not work as hard as they could. Maybe technology makes life easier or more distracting, or perhaps they lack the desire to try. I get frustrated when I see students who never open their backpacks; if they spent just two hours studying at home, they would likely earn many accomplishments and move closer to their goals.

To build true self-esteem, students need to pursue achievements and grow their self-confidence. Teachers also have a role because students often spend more time with teachers than with their parents during the week. I do not expect teachers to teach self-esteem directly unless a student asks, but teachers can guide students toward methods for achieving success. Showing the right path and encouraging goal-setting can lead students to think about how to earn achievements and build confidence.

When I first came to the United States in 2017, I did not speak English and I had no friends at school. I was shy and my face would go red when someone talked to me. Over time I worked hard to learn the language and to make friends. Now I can read, write and speak well, I feel much more confident, and I enjoy school.

In short, working hard for achievements and developing self-confidence are key to building students’ self-esteem. Parents and teachers should encourage students to focus on their studies and take steps toward success so they can become the best versions of themselves.

I agree with Emerson’s idea because having a master’s degree helps people perform better, opens more doors, and usually leads to higher positions than for those without this qualification.

Some people disagree, arguing that people without degrees can sometimes do a job better than those who hold a master’s. While this can happen, it does not change the general advantages of formal advanced study.

First, earning a master’s means you have spent years learning and practicing, so you usually work more effectively in that field. For example, in a restaurant a chef with a master’s-level education in culinary arts will already know many techniques and recipes. Other staff may need extra time to learn ingredients, tools, and kitchen equipment.

Second, a master’s degree often creates better opportunities because it is a clear sign to employers that you are prepared for the role. Many companies set a degree as a requirement for certain jobs. For instance, some restaurants ask for a master’s when hiring a manager, and those managers generally receive higher pay than staff without advanced degrees.

Third, people with a master’s frequently obtain higher positions than those without one because the degree shows experience and training. If a restaurant needs staff for kitchen roles, management, and dishwashing, someone with a master’s is more likely to be chosen for management. Someone without the degree is more likely to start in a lower job and must work longer and harder to reach the same level.

In conclusion, a master’s degree tends to lead to better performance, more opportunities, and higher positions, so I agree with Emerson’s statement that without advanced study it is difficult to grow professionally.

Thomas Jefferson once said, "It is wonderful how much may be done if we are doing." He meant that steady effort leads to achievement. This raises a question: do we accomplish more by staying active, or can inactivity sometimes be useful? Some people argue that rest is necessary to recover and stay effective. Others believe that constantly working brings results and benefits society.

Every day millions get up to work hard and give their best. But what about those who are not formally employed? Even without a paid job, you can still contribute to society and develop personally. Volunteering, helping neighbors, or learning new skills are ways to remain active and useful. Everyone needs rest sometimes, but if you rest too much you may never reach your ambitions.

Being consistently productive is valuable when your actions are positive. People work for different reasons: to achieve goals, to earn money, or to support family. These motivations push people to keep going. My mother always told me, "If you want something, go after it." That advice captures why many of us stay busy—because we want a better future. This is why doing something is usually preferable to doing nothing.

From a societal perspective, staying active is important. Most people need a job to pay for food, housing, bills, and taxes. Work helps meet these basic needs. Besides paid jobs, there are many ways to stay involved, such as community service or helping others. Whether you are paid or not, doing meaningful work helps you grow and contributes to the community.

In short, activity drives progress for individuals and society. Rest and downtime are useful, but they should not become an excuse to abandon goals. Jefferson’s words encourage us to consider how we use our time: balance rest with effort, and keep working toward the things that matter.

Thomas Jefferson warned against idleness, noting that constant effort can produce surprising results. Staying active—by setting career aims, learning new skills, or helping others—clearly supports physical and mental wellbeing, while prolonged inactivity often brings many problems.

Do people achieve more by following their interests, or can doing very little also lead to success? In practice, being inactive rarely helps. Long periods of inactivity can harm health, reduce motivation, and leave people without a clear purpose. Someone who stays at home all the time, avoids work, or leaves school early may increase the chance of poor health and limited opportunities later. Cutting oneself off from everyday life and social contact is unhealthy both physically and emotionally.

On the other hand, taking action gives direction and benefits in many areas. Working toward a job, studying at school or university, or developing new abilities improves both career prospects and personal wellbeing. Volunteering or helping others adds meaning and social connection. Even small steps—spending part of each day on a goal or a hobby—can lead to steady progress and better health.

Joining activities and being involved in the community tend to make life more successful and satisfying. Different people will have different views on how active they should be, and not everyone follows the same path. Still, Jefferson’s idea that avoiding idleness leads to greater achievement remains a useful reminder.

Some people argue that every student should be required to take an art class, while others think students should be free to choose their own electives. I believe students must be allowed to pick the electives they prefer. Letting young people select subjects they enjoy helps them discover their strengths, gain useful skills, and prepare for the future.

If students are forced into classes they do not like, they will often lose interest. A bored student is more likely to skip lessons and stop trying, which leads to lower grades. When grades fall, motivation drops and some students give up altogether. Without enough course credits, a student might not graduate high school, which makes college and good job opportunities much harder to reach. In the worst cases, this can lead to long-term unemployment and serious financial struggles. For these reasons it is important that students can choose electives that match their interests.

Another point is that everyone has different talents. Electives give students the chance to explore what they are good at. When a student finds a subject they enjoy and understand well, they are more engaged in class and tend to perform better. Good performance earns credits and opens doors. Developing skills in an area can also create concrete opportunities after school. For example, a student strong in drama might pursue acting, join a theater company, or even work in film and earn a living from it. Also, people do not need just one skill. Students can try several electives and build a range of abilities, which makes them more attractive to employers later on.

Choosing electives also supports a smoother transition into adult life. If students have practiced skills and followed their interests in school, they are more likely to find a clear direction after graduation. This makes planning for college or a career easier and reduces the shock of entering the working world. Even when life is difficult, practical skills and real experience help people cope and keep moving toward their goals. Electives can be the start of a student’s dream career or a path that leads to stability and satisfaction.

Some argue that students might not be motivated and could treat electives lightly, as if they were a joke. While that can happen, the solution is to guide and encourage students to try different subjects until they find something meaningful. Overall, letting students choose their electives gives them the best chance to learn, grow, and succeed.

Many businesses and some schools have switched to a four-day week to save energy and other resources.
