Ralph Waldo Emerson said, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." I agree with this idea because your actions, achievements, and attitude reveal who you are. When you stay true to yourself, people notice something special in you. They may try to follow your example, learn from you, and be inspired to change. I believe being yourself matters for three main reasons: others will imitate you, you become a source of inspiration, and your accomplishments can influence how people think.

First, being authentic can lead others to copy your behavior. When you go the extra mile—helping others even when it is not required—people see that and often repeat it. For instance, if you are a student who takes the time to explain a difficult math problem to a classmate, you are acting beyond your role. Helping in that way shows kindness and responsibility, and others may begin to do the same. Small acts like this can spread because people like to follow positive examples.

Second, staying true to yourself makes you an inspiration for the people around you. Whether at home, in the neighborhood, at school, or in a community group, your honest efforts can motivate others. For example, if a neighbor keeps their yard clean and helps others with tasks like mowing the lawn, that neighbor becomes a model for the community. Seeing someone do simple, helpful things can encourage others to act similarly. Your behavior can lift others’ spirits and push them toward better habits.

Third, your achievements can change how people think. When others notice your progress and wonder how you reached it, you have a chance to share your story. That message can show them what is possible. In families, for example, some members may have low-paying jobs while others run their own business. If you support and help your family, you pass on confidence and positive energy. People can adopt your attitude and try new paths because they saw your example work.

In conclusion, Emerson’s idea is true: being yourself in a world that pushes you to be different is a great accomplishment. Most people recognize the value of helping others, and when you act from your true self, you set an example. Your behavior can make others want to follow, inspire those around you, and change how people think about what is possible.

The idea of switching to a four-day school week raises many arguments for and against, but I support the change because its benefits outweigh the drawbacks for most students and teachers. Instead of attending classes five days a week, schools could concentrate instruction into four longer days and free one weekday for other important activities.

Removing one school day reduces total weekly hours, but this can be solved by lengthening the remaining school days by about two hours. That change would allow teachers and students to spend more time on each subject, finish projects, and get extra help. With longer periods, students who are struggling could meet with teachers and classmates for support, making it easier to improve grades and understand difficult material.

Those extra hours could also be allocated to libraries, sports, or after-school clubs. Students who enjoy reading or want more time for athletics and arts would benefit from structured blocks for those activities. Having dedicated time for extracurriculars during the school day makes them more accessible to everyone, not just those who can stay late.

The freed weekday would be useful for appointments and personal business that now force students to miss class during regular hours. Parents often write notes excusing absences for doctor visits or other errands; scheduling those things on the non-school day would reduce missed lessons. Families would avoid pulling students out of important class time, which improves continuity of learning.

Teachers who are parents would also gain a valuable day for family responsibilities and household tasks. Many educators juggle childcare and schoolwork; a regular weekday off would help them balance work and family life better.

High school students, especially seniors, face critical decisions about college, jobs, and internships. A free weekday would give them time to visit campuses, attend interviews, and research future options. Freshmen transitioning from middle school also need time to adjust to new routines and extra commitments; the extra day could ease that change and reduce stress.

Schools could turn the free day into opportunities for community service or work experience, with parental permission and adult supervision. Students could help clean local parks or partner with companies that offer job training and part-time positions. This would allow young people to gain practical skills without interrupting academic time.

Some details must be decided by each school: which day becomes free, whether it is Friday or Monday, and how to use the extra time. A three-day weekend gives families more time together, reduces early mornings, and offers chances to rest and catch up on assignments.

There are disadvantages to consider. Students with part-time jobs might find longer school days harder to combine with work schedules. However, the free weekday can be used for paid work or internships, helping to offset that issue. Also, doing school and work in one day can be tiring—so schedules need to be managed to avoid burnout. Overall, though, many of these problems have practical solutions.

In conclusion, a four-day school week with longer days offers more focused instruction, time for extracurriculars, easier scheduling for appointments, and better work–life balance for teachers and students. I believe most students would benefit from a three-day break each week, and together we can advocate for this change in high schools and colleges.

My special talent is drawing. When I draw, I enjoy sketching the stars, the moon, forests and the ocean. Drawing is a way to show who you are and share many kinds of art. There are so many styles, but my favorites are drawing and painting. With drawing you can create anything you imagine, and if you make a mistake you can usually correct it. Painting is also one of my favorite ways to make art because it lets you show emotions. If you are sad, happy, angry or calm, a painting can express those feelings.

Art is something I love because it gives freedom to create, and people often value good work very highly. Some paintings and drawings sell for huge amounts of money because they are beautiful and meaningful. Many people have artistic talent, but some are so critical of their own work that they throw it away. They do not realize that someone else might like their piece and be willing to buy it. Other artists keep their work for memories or to share with family, and they do not want to sell those pieces for large sums because they are personal. Still, sometimes family members buy these artworks simply to keep them in the family.

I believe artists should try to sell their work, because it can bring them income. Making art is not an easy job. It takes patience: you might make mistakes and need to start again. Many artists do not throw their mistakes away. Instead they change them into something beautiful. Art is about seeing something imperfect and turning it into something attractive.

Some people think art is boring, but that is not true if you love it. When you enjoy making art, it never feels boring. Sometimes I feel so excited that I stop thinking too much and just let my body and hands make the painting. In those moments I do not worry about whether the result will be perfect; I just enjoy the process. It feels good and gives me energy.

Other times, I feel stressed because my drawing does not look the way I wanted. That is normal, and it is why patience is important. Art is hard at first, but it becomes easier with time. I am good at drawing, but I am still learning. Practicing regularly helps a lot; practice teaches you and improves your skill. With patience and effort, anyone who loves art can get better and maybe even sell their work.

Do students really gain from being allowed to join classes from home? I believe they do not. From my experience, when a friend switched to remote learning she stopped doing most of her schoolwork. She treated online classes as an opportunity to do other things and ended up learning very little. In my view, students generally would not benefit from remote attendance because many of them exploit the situation, fail to complete their tasks, and ultimately do not learn.

First, some students use attending class from home as a chance to handle non-school matters. For instance, they turn in assignments late or neglect long-term projects, thinking no one will notice. Not every student behaves this way, but those who do often take freedom to an extreme: they prioritize social plans or personal errands over class responsibilities. They also make excuses for unfinished work, blaming technical issues or claiming they forgot, rather than facing the consequences. This misuse of flexible schedules means coursework gets delayed or ignored.

Second, many students simply do not do the work they are supposed to when they are at home. Given less direct supervision, they become lazy about assignments and projects. Instead of completing tasks, they spend time on activities like parties or hanging out with friends and partners. Even if they know the material, they choose not to put in the effort. Teachers are less likely to check on every student during online lessons, so some learners rely on that gap to avoid doing homework or preparing for exams.

Finally, attending classes from home often results in little actual learning. Some students copy answers from others or look them up online rather than understanding the subject. Instead of using class time to study, they treat it as a break from school and focus on entertainment. When students consistently play around during lessons, they miss important explanations and practice, which harms their overall progress.

In conclusion, I do not think students benefit from attending classes from home. Many take advantage of the flexibility to do other things, neglect their assignments, and fail to learn the material. As a result, remote attendance can do more harm than good for students who are not disciplined.

It is true that having several people contribute ideas often produces more creative results than working alone.

A school survey found that pupils prefer online lessons because they can sit or arrange themselves in ways not allowed at school. I agree with this view — I like to choose how I sit, but school rules usually limit that.

Safety is another important reason to support home-based classes. In recent years there have been more than a hundred school shootings, showing that being on campus can sometimes be dangerous. Gangs and other harmful influences at school are also risks that can affect a child’s life.

Allowing students to attend classes from home can also ease parents’ worries about their children’s well-being.

In conclusion, while it is true that remote schooling can make group work more difficult, the comfort and increased safety that home learning offers make it a valuable option for many students.

I disagree with the idea of extending school hours to save energy because it would create extra pressure on many students. For some young people this change would mean being at school for ten hours a day, which is exhausting and could harm their well-being. Several students rely on after-school jobs, and shortening those work hours would reduce their earnings. That income often helps support their families, so cutting it could cause real financial trouble at home.

Many students also have responsibilities at home, such as looking after younger brothers or sisters, doing household chores like cleaning, washing dishes, or preparing meals. These tasks help their families function and allow parents to work. If school finishes later, students will have less time for these duties, which would make life harder for their households.

Extracurricular activities and free time would be affected too. Students who play sports — soccer, basketball, tennis, and others — would lose practice time. Others need a little quiet time to read or walk and relax after a busy day. Losing those moments can make a student’s life less enjoyable and more stressful. If school hours are simply pushed later, many students would still need to work the same number of hours each week, which means they would have to spend even more of their day away from home to meet their obligations.

We should remember that many students work to help provide food and support for their families. In the past, mothers often did this kind of work, and today some students take on similar responsibilities. These young people and their parents sacrifice a lot to give them a chance at a better future. For these reasons, extending school hours would do more harm than good for many students and their families.

I believe many students misunderstand what really matters for success. They often think that self-confidence and visible achievements are the only proof of truth and value. I disagree with the idea that short-term results are everything. Some young people do not plan for the future; they focus only on the present and treat life as if it were only about getting by. In my view, students should look ahead and think about long-term goals, not just immediate rewards.

Students often mix up confidence and trust. Being confident means showing you believe in your own abilities. Trust or confidence in someone else means relying on that person. Many students are confident about learning and improving, and they push themselves hard to get better. They sometimes see order and discipline as strict commands, but these can also be helpful ways to stay focused. Learning requires effort, skill, and persistence, and when students put those in, they can achieve meaningful results.

Achievement comes from working hard and using skills well. Completing a task successfully gives a sense of satisfaction and shows real progress. Life should also offer chances to improve and to enjoy moments with family and friends. Work is important, but it is not everything. Students must find time to rest and reflect so they can plan a better future and appreciate life beyond just a job.

What is the future? It means a time that lies ahead, and making plans for it requires thought and patience. Students should not make their future depend only on a single profession. A profession needs training and education, and it is a long-term path. A career involves a series of jobs with increasing responsibility over time. A trade is often practical work done with the hands and requires specific training. Some young people feel they lack work experience, but experience can be gained gradually if they are willing to start and learn from mistakes.

Experience teaches many lessons. When students try and sometimes fail, they gain knowledge and skill. Sincerity is important too: being honest and true to your feelings builds trust and respect. Praise and recognition are valuable, but students should also be careful and take precautions to avoid risks. Planning ahead and protecting what matters helps prevent problems later.

Tolerance and compassion are also necessary. Accepting different opinions and treating others with consideration make teamwork easier and life richer. People should think carefully before making important choices and evaluate whether risks are too large. Students need respect and should not be judged only for their lack of experience. Intelligence and courage come together when students feel secure rather than insecure. In my opinion, a balance of confidence, hard work, careful planning, and kindness will prepare students better for the future.

Many schools run programs that pair older students with younger ones. These schemes exist because they help both age groups learn important lessons. Older students learn responsibility by guiding the younger ones, while younger students get a chance to see what being older will be like and to receive support. At the same time, younger children can teach older students new things and help them grow.

Older students can show younger pupils how to avoid common mistakes. Everyone makes different errors, and older students can share their experiences so the younger ones know better choices to make. By explaining what went wrong for them and how they corrected it, older students give practical advice that teachers or parents might not always provide in the same way.

Younger students also benefit by being able to ask for help when they need it. Older students can visit classrooms, answer questions, and work directly with younger pupils on problems. This contact lets younger students learn from the older students’ past mistakes and understand how to act responsibly. In many cases, older students explain everyday life skills and social rules that help the younger ones do the right thing.

The relationship can be similar to the one between an adult and a child. Younger pupils need guidance, and older students can fill that role by reminding them of what not to do and suggesting better choices. If a younger student has trouble with schoolwork or with language, for example, an older student can explain things in a simpler way. Older students can also ask younger ones for help when they do not know something, so both groups benefit from cooperating. They can work together on many activities and stop problems such as fights by calming things down and encouraging better behavior.

However, there are some challenges. Sometimes older students are not willing to help, or younger students refuse to listen. This lack of cooperation creates difficulties for the program. Older students may also ignore advice from their teachers or parents and still make poor choices. Because of this, it is important to encourage respect on both sides: older students should take their role seriously, and younger ones should try to learn from them.

I remember my father telling me that when he was young he needed help but did not want to ask an adult. He said it would have been easier if an older student had been there to guide him. He advised me to ask older students for help when I need it so I can learn from my mistakes. Overall, these programs are valuable because they teach responsibility, support learning for younger pupils, and strengthen good behavior when both groups work together.

Can technology affect people’s lives and human contact? I agree — technology is not always a positive thing. Many people say technology breaks family ties or that they dislike how it changes relationships. I think these concerns are valid. Here are some reasons why technology can harm our lives and reduce real human contact: addiction to phones and games, online shopping dependence, and a decline in communication between people.

First, people can become addicted to their phones or video games. When someone is focused on their device, they often think only about themselves. For example, if a person nearby needs help, someone absorbed in their phone may ignore them because their device seems more important. This can happen to both adults and children. We should try to be kinder and ready to help others instead of being lost in technology.

Second, online shopping can become an addiction, especially among women. Many women enjoy the convenience and independence of buying clothes and other items online. However, some buy too much and develop a habit that is hard to control. While shopping online can be useful, it becomes a problem when it replaces healthy spending habits or affects daily life.

Third, when people stop talking to others, they lose motivation and inspiration. A person who rarely communicates or takes part in activities that encourage growth may struggle to find purpose for their future. Communication with others helps build ideas, goals, and encouragement, so its absence can make life feel empty.

Some people say success means moving from one failure to another without losing spirit, a view often linked to Winston Churchill. I disagree. While failure is a common experience on the road to a goal, success does not simply come from repeating failures. You must keep trying, work hard, and remain enthusiastic if you want to reach your dreams.

First, almost everyone faces failures at least once. People make mistakes in many parts of life — at work, in school, or in relationships. It is normal to miss a job opportunity or get lower grades than expected. Very few people never experience any setbacks; exceptions are rare. For example, my cousin always did very well in school, earning high marks and a scholarship. She did not disappoint her parents and was accepted to Virginia Tech. Her case shows that some people achieve success without a long trail of failures, often because of consistent effort and strong results.

Second, hard work and persistence are essential to reach your goals. If you fail, don’t let it make you give up or fall into despair. Instead, treat failure as a reason to try again and search for new chances. Life offers other opportunities, so you should not stay stuck on one failure. Make a new plan or look for different paths that might suit you better. Keep fighting for what you want and stay determined; this attitude increases your chances of succeeding.

Finally, enthusiasm plays a major role in achieving success. If you are passionate about something, pursue it and do not let others take that chance from you. Enthusiasm gives you motivation and energy to work harder and to keep going when times are tough. People who lack interest or drive often accept things as they are and do not push themselves. I experienced this myself: when I moved to the United States as a child, I had to start over because I did not know English. To improve, I had to put in a lot of effort and remain motivated, and that determination helped me succeed in learning the language.

In conclusion, I do not agree that success is just a series of failures without loss of enthusiasm. Although failure happens to most people, success comes from hard work, persistence, and keeping your passion alive. If you continue to try and maintain your enthusiasm, you can reach your goals even though the journey is not easy.

One skill I use a lot is reading aloud. I do this because it helps me understand the text better. When I say the words out loud, the ideas stay in my mind and I can talk about them more clearly. It also makes it easier for me to write an essay about what I have read.

Reading aloud improves my comprehension. I can hear how I am reading and notice if I hesitate or mispronounce words. This tells me when I need to say a word slowly or look up its meaning. Saying the sentences gives me a clearer sense of the text than just moving my eyes over the words.

Another reason I read aloud is that it helps me explain the story. When I speak the words, more details come to mind and I can describe what happens. After I finish, I remember the material better. If I read silently, I often forget parts of the story and miss important points. I have also seen that other people understand a text more easily when they read it out loud.

Reading aloud also helps me prepare for essays. While I read out loud, I collect many ideas and phrases that I can use later. This makes it easier to write because I already know the main points and details. I feel less nervous about writing since the story is already fixed in my memory from reading it aloud. It also helps me check that my essay matches the book’s ideas.

In conclusion, I read out loud because it helps me understand the book, keeps the information in my head, and makes essay writing easier.

Every student puts effort into their studies at some point. They can learn to keep working even without regular compliments, sometimes over months or years. Constantly praising a student for every good mark or for completing a minor assignment is not helpful. I think genuine self-confidence comes from personal achievement and hard work. This kind of confidence is shown through the quality of a student’s work, it prevents them from becoming arrogant, and it teaches them not to rely on praise. It is true that occasional recognition feels nice, but it should not be the main goal.

When students really try, that effort becomes clear in their work and in how they carry themselves. Many learners give their best without needing applause. A student must be motivated from within if they truly want to succeed. If praise is given for every small success, what lesson do they learn about effort? They might start expecting a reward for every positive action instead of valuing the work itself.

Sometimes praise can create arrogant behavior. Students who receive a lot of recognition may act superior, even though others may have worked just as hard and not received the same results. This can hurt classmates who feel they put in the same effort but did not get similar grades. When peers show off their marks, it can damage someone else’s feelings. Some students prefer to keep their achievements private for this reason.

If praise becomes the main reason to study, students will do tasks for the reward rather than for personal growth. They won’t understand the importance of persistence and discipline and will believe that every success must come with external approval. In contrast, finishing difficult work and feeling satisfied without constant compliments builds stronger self-respect. Students who learn to appreciate their own effort do not depend on others to feel good about themselves.

In conclusion, I believe true self-esteem is earned through hard work, not through constant praise. Feeling proud of your own progress and not expecting rewards from others shows real maturity. Students who focus on their efforts and personal achievements are the ones who deserve praise.

Working in groups has many advantages

I believe working in groups is better than working alone for several reasons. When students work together, they can support one another, produce higher-quality work, and learn useful skills. Group projects also help classmates get to know each other, share ideas, and improve communication. Teachers should give students more chances to work in teams because this practice benefits them both in school and later in life, such as at work or with family.

One important benefit of group work is that having multiple people involved brings more and often better ideas. If a student is unsure about how to complete a task, a classmate can explain it and show them how to do it well. Group members can discuss different approaches and reach a stronger result than someone working alone. Also, cooperating with others helps students understand the subject more clearly because they talk through problems and learn from each other. In many cases, working in a group helps students pass assignments and avoid failing, since they can rely on the support of others.

Another advantage is learning practical skills, especially communication. In teams, students practice speaking clearly, listening, and giving feedback. These skills are useful every day: if you do not understand something, you can ask someone in the group to help. Students who are more confident or who understand the topic better can support classmates who struggle, whether because they do not understand the material or because language makes it harder for them to follow. Regularly working in groups gives everyone more chances to practise, improve, and become better at both written and spoken tasks.

Group work also helps students build friendships. When the teacher divides the class into teams, you might meet classmates you would not usually talk to. Over time, you can become friends with people you met only for a project. This social connection is important because it improves the classroom atmosphere and makes learning more enjoyable. In addition, learning how to cooperate and maintain good relationships is useful outside school — at home and at work. For example, in a soccer team, players share strategies and help each other to win. In the same way, students working together share skills and ideas that lead to better outcomes.

Good communication within a group is essential. When everyone understands each other and treats one another kindly, the team can achieve excellent results. Helping others is generous, and when you assist classmates, they are more likely to help you later. If you work alone and get stuck, there is no one to ask for help. In a group, other members can explain and guide you, which speeds up learning and makes the work easier.

I know there are some disadvantages to group work. Sometimes students can become distracted by their peers, and teachers worry that group members might copy each other’s work. Working alone can give better concentration and prevent cheating. However, these problems can be reduced if teachers organize groups carefully, set clear rules, and encourage fair participation. Overall, the benefits of teamwork — more ideas, better grades, stronger communication, and useful life skills — outweigh the negatives.

In conclusion, I think teachers should encourage more group activities because they help students learn more, share ideas, and build good relationships. Students who know more can help others, and those who need extra support can improve with help from teammates. Learning to work with others prepares you for future jobs and daily life, where teamwork is often required. I enjoy working in groups because when I do not know what to do, other students help me, and together we can create better work than we could on our own.

Albert Einstein once claimed that imagination is more valuable than knowledge, and I fully agree with him. Imagination can bring personal joy, help other people, and even lead you to the job you want. In the paragraphs below I will explain these points.

First, imagination can increase your happiness. By picturing things you enjoy, you can feel better even when they are not real. For instance, many people dream of flying like a bird, and though this is impossible, imagining the sensation of soaring can give a sense of freedom and pleasure. You might also picture yourself at an older age and find comfort or amusement in that image. These mental images are a simple way to lift your mood.

Second, imagination can be useful when helping others. Imagine a child crying in a busy shopping center because she feels embarrassed by her unusual clothes. Instead of joining the crowd, you could use your imagination to change her perspective. You might say, “Think of everyone as guests at your royal party — they are looking at you because you are the princess.” Such a playful idea may calm her and change how she sees the situation.

Finally, people often say imagination won’t get you a good job, but I disagree. In creative fields, imagination is essential. A home designer without imagination will produce dull or ugly spaces and may lose clients. In contrast, a writer who can create many vivid stories could publish numerous successful books and earn a good living. Imagination helps you create work others value.

In conclusion, I believe Einstein was right. Imagination not only makes life happier and allows us to help people, but it also opens the door to satisfying careers. For me, imagination is a powerful and important ability.

I find science experiments one of the most enjoyable activities at school. They feel different from the usual assignments. For instance, math or language arts projects often mean doing a set of problems or writing an essay. Science projects, however, let you actually see and touch things. One memorable example was when we dissected a frog. It might sound gross to some people, and the smell certainly was unpleasant, but the experience fascinated me.

During that dissection I learned that frogs do not have as many organs as humans. Either they simply lack some of the organs we have or they are much smaller. I was also surprised by the colors inside the frog — there were blues and pinks, while human organs are mostly red. Our teacher had warned us that the frogs had been frozen, so their tissues looked dry, but that actually made cutting easier. Since we were allowed to investigate freely, my group tried to explore every part. There was one rather disgusting moment when we found flies in the frog’s stomach. That grossed me out, but it didn’t make me want to stop.

After we had examined everything we could, the teacher explained the names and functions of the frog’s organs. At one point a friend of mine thought it would be funny to poke the frog’s eye. I still don’t know why he did it. The eye wasn’t completely frozen, so fluid shot out and soaked him. Fortunately it didn’t reach me, but it definitely hit my classmate, and the teacher sent him to wash up in the bathroom. After that incident the teacher decided to end the activity early. Even so, it had been a lot of fun.

Another project I remember was part of our unit on light. The teacher turned off the lights and asked us to spray a mist in front of a flashlight. The idea was that the droplets would let us see the path that light travels along. The demonstration was simple and less exciting than the frog dissection, but interesting in its own way. At first I couldn’t see anything and felt disappointed, but after a few seconds faint patterns appeared. They were hard to notice and lasted only a short time, yet I still enjoyed watching them. The downside was that the teacher spent a long time explaining the theory, while the actual demonstration was quite brief.

By sharing these two examples, I want to show that science experiments are not always boring. You might not like every experiment you do, but it’s worth trying them. At least one of the projects will probably capture your interest. They make class more engaging and teach in a more direct, hands-on way. That is why, in my opinion, experiments are the best activities in school.

Working in a group is more beneficial. Why is it better to work with others? Because a team can give you ideas, help with writing, offer examples, and share information. If you work alone, you do not have anyone to support or improve your ideas.

There are several advantages to group work. When you are in a group you can discuss the task, ask questions, and compare examples. Group members can explain how they would approach the work and give feedback. This kind of support often makes the task easier and leads to better results.

Working alone has some advantages too, but they are limited. You can use your own ideas without interruption and nobody will distract you. However, it is harder to find all the information by yourself and you will not have anyone to check or support your thoughts. This can make the work more difficult and slower.

For example, in high school the English teacher might ask students to form groups of four for a project. The students usually agree because they can divide tasks: one person collects information, another writes the report, a third chooses examples, and the fourth prepares the presentation and reads in class. Doing the project this way can be more comfortable because the group members help each other and the work is shared.

On the other hand, if a student chooses to work alone after the teacher offers group work, they might like working without interruptions and can use only their own ideas. But that student will not have classmates to talk through the project with, and they may feel nervous, bored, or distracted when they present or study alone.

Some people do not like group work because they have conflicts with others, feel uncomfortable speaking in a group, or prefer quiet, private work. Still, most people enjoy working with others because they like cooperating with friends, feel good talking about the task, and appreciate answering questions and receiving feedback. These reasons explain why group work is often more beneficial.

People often talk to more than one person because they need help solving problems. Getting several opinions can lead to better decisions and prevent bad choices like stealing or selling drugs. Advice from others can guide someone toward doing the right thing.

One person alone may find it hard to pick the best option, while a group of people can offer different ideas and viewpoints. If you rely on only one suggestion, it might be difficult or not work for you. For example, when solving a math problem, using just a single method could leave you stuck; trying different approaches makes it more likely you will find a solution. The same idea applies to life choices: compare ideas and pick the one that fits you best. Children who do not follow directions at school can also benefit from advice. When teachers, parents, and classmates share ideas about rules and good behavior, the classroom becomes safer and better for everyone.

Not following rules or ignoring advice can cause problems. Young people especially need guidance, because they sometimes make poor choices like stealing or getting involved with drugs. Advice can help them understand the consequences and find safer alternatives. Some people prefer to speak with just one trusted person, and that can be helpful when the issue is simple. But when someone keeps making bad choices, it is better to talk with several people to get stronger support and different perspectives. For instance, a person who repeatedly steals money needs more than one voice to help them change their behavior and find better options.

In short, advice is useful for making good decisions and improving behavior, especially in schools. Listening to others is like following rules: it helps people choose wisely and stay safe.

I agree that first impressions are very hard to change, and I have three reasons for this.

First, when you meet someone for the first time, their behavior and manner can immediately create strong feelings of liking or disliking them. Those first reactions are emotional and often happen quickly. Second, you might never meet that person again, so the way they behaved in that single encounter becomes the basis for your judgment of them. If there is no second chance, your first opinion stays the same. Third, even when you see someone often, their repeated actions can reinforce your original view. If their behavior continues in the same way, your first impression is confirmed and it becomes difficult to change.

For example, I once talked to a person I had not met before. His way of speaking and his attitude made me uncomfortable, so my impression was negative from the start. I never met him again, and my opinion never changed. That shows how a first meeting can fix an idea in your mind.

In short, first impressions tend to stick because they form quickly, may be the only meeting, and are often reinforced by later behavior, making them hard to change.

Although it may seem that "unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow," it is actually right. Having something you have mastered doesn't mean that trying something new will make you fail. Giving up is what would cost you growth. For example, changing your lifestyle by eating right and going to the gym is not going to be easy, but you are still going to give it a try. The reason is that we want to challenge ourselves in a new environment that we never thought we would challenge ourselves in. Another reason is that trying something new means we are looking for something we would enjoy or like.

For example, we teach ourselves how to cook even though we know we never knew how to cook, but that doesn't mean we are not going to give it a try. That's why we try new things: we want to challenge ourselves in a situation we never knew we could solve or in which we might give up. Another reason is that we love trying new things because we are curious if we can master them. Another example would be raising a kid, wondering if we have everything and teaching them what is right and what is wrong. That is why we love trying new things: to see if we can do it or not. That is more important—trying new things and seeing if we can master them—because we are capable of doing things a computer can't do, and that is trying to learn new things.

We can master anything in our way because we are willing to find out if we can do it. If we cannot, we should not fear it. If we got this, give ourselves ideas that anything we do is possible when we put our mind to it; nothing can stop us. For example, we got our freedom from England a long time ago, we ended slavery, and we ended racism which was big in the United States. Those are the reasons why we can master things even if they are hard. We do it for a reason, and the reason is that we love to try new things even if they are bad. Every challenge we are given, we master. But there is no doubt we would fail those challenges that the world has given us. Mastering is a challenge that is difficult because in our lifetime there are times when we give up and don't want it anymore. Where our mind and our body just don't want it and don't keep trying, at some point we start calling ourselves losers, quitters.

We bring ourselves down because that is how we punish ourselves without physical pain but emotional pain. In our lifetime on this earth, the most pain that brings us down is emotional pain when we give up in life and haven't mastered it. That is the big challenge we haven't tried to complete because it has been beating us since the beginning. Since we were born we haven't controlled our emotions, and that is the challenge we haven't mastered.

For that, we have issues that we aren't able to figure out because it's hard for us to figure what makes us mad, sad, or happy. But people who have mastered it did give it a try, and they successfully master those emotions that give us a hard time in life. Those people are therapists who want to understand those types of emotion because they want to help people who don't understand why they react like that.

That is what makes us try new things in life: we are curious about what interests us as human beings and want to see if we can master it. So, "unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, keep trying new things that you would be able to do and get your attention to it."

I agree with the idea that you must try things beyond what you already know in order to grow. Knowing how to do something does not mean you will fail if you try something new. What stops growth is giving up. Changing your life, for example by eating better and going to the gym, is difficult, but many people still try because they want to challenge themselves in situations they have not faced before. Another reason for trying new things is the search for activities we enjoy.

Take learning to cook. Even if you have never cooked before, that does not stop you from trying. We test ourselves in new situations because we want to see if we can solve problems we once thought were impossible. Curiosity also drives us: we wonder if we can master a skill. Raising a child is another example. Parents worry whether they are teaching right from wrong, yet they try anyway to learn and improve. These examples show that trying new things is important because it reveals our capabilities — things a computer cannot do — and helps us learn.

If we are willing to try, we can master many things. Believing in ourselves and not being afraid of failure helps us push forward. History gives examples of people overcoming huge challenges: gaining independence from England, abolishing slavery, and working to end racial discrimination in the United States. These achievements were hard, but they happened because people kept trying. Still, failure is possible. Mastering something is not easy; there are times when we feel exhausted and want to give up. At those moments we may call ourselves losers or quitters.

Giving up often brings emotional pain. In life, emotional suffering from failed attempts can be worse than physical pain. Many people struggle with their emotions because they never learned how to manage them, and this is a challenge that some never overcome. On the other hand, there are people who have learned to understand and control emotions because they made an effort. Therapists are an example: they study emotions to help others who cannot understand their own reactions.

This is why we keep trying new things — curiosity, the wish to improve, and the desire to master difficult tasks. If we continue to push beyond what we already know, we increase the chance of learning and growing. In short, unless you try something beyond what you have already mastered, you will not grow. Keep trying new things and you will find what you can do.

I have tried many things in my seventeen years of being alive, and I can say I have grown to be the person I am now. Many people don't try new things only because they are quick to judge the presentation of the new item or new person, but if people actually gave the new experience a chance, it could be life changing for better or worse.

If I wish to try something new and be a better person in society, I will, but if I wish to not try anything at all and just do the same boring routine day after day, sooner or later I will get bored of everything. Even though some may argue by saying, "that's how I got successful in the first place by doing the same routine over and over." In some cases that may work; for example, in sports the athlete must do the same thing over and over until they get better at the sport, or like a dance, they practice the same dance over and over until it's ready to be shared with the world how well one can dance. And for others, trying a new routine can lead them to success (well, maybe not everyone is talented).

In conclusion, trying something new does change who you are a bit by either helping or destroying yourself. People do grow to be wise and old, and others don't grow old wise, just young and reckless. The saying "Unless you try something beyond what you have mastered you will never grow" sounds wise at first, but wise words often lose power when few people are willing to act on them. I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea: if I never step outside my comfort zone, can I really say I have grown?

If I stick to the same habits and never experiment, I will not move forward. I cannot imagine a strong reason to disagree with this idea. In my seventeen years, I have tried many new things, and those experiences have helped shape who I am today. Too many people avoid new experiences because they judge something—or someone—by first impressions. Yet if they gave new opportunities a chance, those experiences might change their lives, for better or for worse.

Still, whether you grow depends on your choices. If I choose to try new activities to improve myself and contribute to society, I will develop. If I refuse and continue with a dull routine, I will likely become bored and stagnant. Some will say that repeating the same routine is how they achieved success, and that can be true in certain fields. Athletes repeat drills over and over to build strength and skill, and dancers rehearse the same choreography until it is perfect. For others, trying a different path can open opportunities they would never find by staying in one place—although talent and effort still matter.

In conclusion, attempting things beyond what you already know can change you — it can help you grow or, in some cases, lead to setbacks. Some people grow older and wiser; others remain young and reckless. Emerson was right to highlight the importance of pushing beyond your mastery if you want to grow.

I believe students should join clubs or sports at their own school because taking part in activities you enjoy makes school life better. My first reason is that people should spend time doing what they love. Second, being active in sports or clubs helps you build skills and discipline. Third, joining activities keeps you away from screens too much and gives a healthier routine.

First, if you really enjoy something, you should try it. Too many students doubt themselves and never sign up because they think they are not good enough. But if you love an activity, practicing it can make you improve and feel proud. Following your passion at school can lead to confidence and success. Instead of wasting time on things you dislike, focus on what excites you. School activities are a good place to test your interests and grow. Believing in yourself and trying is the first step to becoming better at anything.

Second, being involved in sports or other active programs prevents laziness and keeps your body healthy. Sports teach discipline, teamwork, and commitment. If you work hard, a hobby could even become something more important in the future. The habits you form through regular practice will help you in life, not only in physical fitness but also in time management and responsibility. Joining a team or club helps structure your free time so you are doing something useful instead of sitting around doing nothing.

Third, taking part in school activities is a good way to reduce the time spent on phones and other electronics. When students are on their devices all day, they miss chances to practice, play with friends, and make real memories. Too much screen time can make you tired and unfocused in class or at practice. By going outside, meeting teammates, or planning weekend activities, you can enjoy life more and feel better physically and mentally. It is okay to use electronics sometimes, but balance is important.

In conclusion, I think everyone should try an activity at school that they care about. Trying new things takes effort, but it can help you grow and give others someone to admire. Don’t just follow others—be willing to lead by doing what matters to you. Life is short, so make the most of your time at school by joining activities that help you become the person you want to be.

Have you ever found that examples help you learn, or do you prefer other approaches? I agree with the idea that examples are not the only or always the best way to influence someone. There are other methods that can work better in many situations.

One effective way to help people learn is through direct support rather than just giving examples. In my ceramics class, for instance, the teacher often shows one demonstration and then leaves us to work alone. Because she rarely helps students individually, many of us struggle to recreate the techniques she showed once. When she does spend time guiding a student step by step, that person’s work usually turns out much better than the others. Personal assistance can correct mistakes in real time and build confidence more than a single example can.

Examples can also sometimes create confusion instead of clarity. Imagine a teacher asks you to draw something from your imagination to express your own ideas. If she then offers specific examples of what to draw, students may change their plans and feel they must copy those suggestions rather than use their own thoughts. In cases like this, examples limit creativity and make the task unclear.

Some people argue that examples are useful because they demonstrate experience and show how to do something, and that is true for many learners. Still, I believe that in some situations stronger approaches—such as hands-on help and encouragement of original thinking—make examples less necessary. For these reasons, I think there are better ways to influence others without relying on examples.

Many students would welcome a longer summer holiday because it gives them more time to be with family and friends. An extended break can also feel like a deserved reward for those who worked hard all year. Time away from school lets students step back from the pressure of exams and assignments, which can reduce stress and help them recharge. Learning to balance work and rest shows students the value of education and prepares them to face future challenges independently.

Some educators worry that pupils forget what they learned during a long vacation and come back to school having lost knowledge. It is true that students often focus on fun and relaxation instead of studying while away from class. However, not all time away is wasted: many young people are quick learners and may keep important facts in mind, and others read books or follow the news during the break so they do not fall behind. Whether students forget depends largely on how they spend their time off.

Travel is another advantage of a longer holiday. Many families travel out of state or to other countries during the summer, and extra days make it easier to explore new places without rushing. Visiting different regions can teach students about history, culture, and everyday life in other communities. Those experiences can be shared later with classmates and teachers, adding to students’ knowledge in ways that classroom lessons alone might not.

Not every student treats a long break the same way. Some use the time to earn money to help pay for their needs, while others take on family responsibilities that leave little time for rest. There are also students who volunteer or join community activities to keep busy and learn new skills. So the effect of a longer summer vacation varies depending on each student’s situation and how they choose to spend it.

Overall, I believe a longer summer vacation is beneficial because it offers more chances to reconnect with family and friends, especially for those who live far apart. It gives students time to relax, gain new experiences, and return to school refreshed. For many people, not only students, extra time at home or traveling is valuable in ways that go beyond the classroom.

Many people claim that having a positive attitude helps you succeed in life, and I agree with this view. An optimistic outlook opens doors in different areas and makes it easier to meet and work with others.

First, being positive often brings more opportunities. When you approach situations with confidence and hope, you are more likely to speak to new people and build useful connections. Employers and colleagues prefer to be around someone who is cheerful and motivated, so a person with a good attitude will often be offered more chances to grow.

At work, a positive mindset improves both feelings and behavior. If you go to your job with a hopeful outlook, you usually feel better throughout the day and handle tasks calmly. You also communicate in ways that do not upset or discourage others, which helps maintain good relationships with friends and coworkers.

I see this in my own family. My grandparents achieved a comfortable life largely because they kept a positive approach. They believed in the value of their efforts and often said that having the right mindset was essential in both life and work. Their confidence helped them try new things, even when they were unsure, and in many cases that willingness led to success.

When faced with uncertainty, a positive attitude can be the push you need to take action. Instead of letting doubt stop you, optimism can encourage you to try, learn, and improve. Simple habits, like smiling in the morning, can start the day with energy and make a real difference in how you face challenges.

Of course, some people do not have this optimistic view and think differently; they may feel lost or unsure about how to become more positive. Despite this, I believe a positive attitude will continue to grow in importance for individuals and society.

In conclusion, having a positive attitude helps people succeed by creating opportunities, improving work and social interactions, and giving the courage to act even when things are uncertain.

I agree with the idea that gaining new experiences is important. Many people spend their whole lives doing the same thing and never try anything different. They may think new skills will not be useful later, or they simply do not feel the need to change. However, trying different things helps you grow as a person because experiences teach you lessons you cannot learn any other way.

When you grow up and face new situations, you learn things that make you more mature. Even young people who seek new knowledge can act more like adults than their peers who do not learn. Knowing more gives you responsibilities and changes the way you make decisions. The things you learn affect your life choices and the opportunities you create for yourself.

School is a clear example of where we gain knowledge and prepare for the future. The more you learn, the more chances you have to be successful. I agree with this point because many people never step outside their comfort zone. For instance, a teacher who has taught the same subject for five years might feel bored or stuck. If that person tries a different job or studies another field, they can expand their skills and become richer in experience. People often remain trapped in one routine, but there are always solutions if you are willing to work for your goals. Reaching those goals usually requires sacrifices, and it is not easy.

You may need to give up some hobbies, time with family, or other comforts, but in the end, hard work often leads to the things you want. When you achieve success, you can look back and see that the risks and sacrifices were worth it. That success comes from the experience you collected along the way. Nothing is impossible if you apply what you have learned and keep trying new things.

For example, imagine you own a small restaurant and want to expand. If you studied business and also worked as a manager in another restaurant, you already have useful experience. Knowing how to manage money and creating a good marketing plan can make your business grow. Using past experience helps you make smarter choices and improve as both a person and a professional.

In conclusion, I believe that learning more and trying new challenges leads to personal growth and better opportunities. Unless you go beyond what you already know, you will not develop. Experience is the key to becoming more capable and successful in life.

Over the past several years, students have been using mobile phones far more than they did before. When phones first became a common part of everyday life, they were usually banned in class. Today, however, many schools permit students to bring and use their phones in lessons. In this essay I will consider the question: what are the effects of letting students use mobile phones in the classroom?

Allowing phones in class has some clear advantages. It can make tasks easier for both teachers and pupils. Students can quickly look up information on a topic using their phones, which is helpful when there are not enough school computers for everyone. Teachers can also take advantage of mobile apps to present material or organise activities in ways that might not be possible on a desktop computer. These tools can support learning and save time.

Yet this change also brings problems. Many students begin to use their phones irresponsibly during lessons. They may check messages or social media while the teacher is explaining, or use their device in ways that distract classmates. Such behaviour reduces attention and interrupts the flow of the class.

These examples show both the positive and negative effects of allowing mobile phones in classrooms.

I agree with Churchill’s idea that failure is an important part of reaching success. Failure matters most for people who want to change their lives and are willing to learn. It helps in three main ways: it teaches us lessons, it reveals who truly supports us, and it forces us to stop repeating the same mistakes.

First, every mistake can teach something useful. We are all human and we will make errors, but those who pay attention to what went wrong improve faster. People who have learned from their own failures can also guide others who face similar problems, because life will bring new challenges and mistakes later on.

Second, failure shows who your real friends are. When you go through a setback, some people will stay and help while others will disappear. Sometimes someone you expected to avoid you will be the one who supports you, and a trusted person might not be there. For example, a true partner would not abandon you after your first failure.

Third and most importantly, do not repeat the same failure many times. Repeating mistakes destroys your motivation. If you keep failing in the same way, it becomes harder to keep trying. It is better to learn from one failure so you do not lose your enthusiasm for the next steps.

In conclusion, everyone experiences failures, but their value depends on how we respond. The most successful outcome is turning a setback into learning and deciding not to make the same mistake again. Change is possible, but the person must want it and be ready to act.

The question here is whether summer vacation should be shortened because students forget what they learned over a long break. I disagree with reducing summer holidays and believe they should stay as they are.

Summer break gives students time to travel and relax with their families without thinking about schoolwork. After many months of classes, young people need a longer break to recover from school stress and focus on other parts of life. Families who live far apart can use the summer to visit each other and reconnect, something that is harder during the busy school year. The long break also lets students do activities they cannot fit in when they have daily lessons and homework — it’s a rare chance to enjoy things freely for about two months.

There are practical benefits, too. Some students take summer classes to make up credits or to improve grades, and a full break still allows them to do this without interfering with the regular school year. Athletes can train, play, and maintain fitness more easily when they have more free time, and they can enjoy their sport without juggling school obligations. Students who love reading can spend large amounts of time at libraries or at home with books, catching up on many titles they could not read during the year. Those who travel often can collect experiences, keep journals, and take photos to share with classmates when school resumes, which also enriches their learning and social conversations.

If summer break were shortened, school time would increase and many opportunities would disappear. Families might not be able to travel together, and students would face more pressure with less time to relax. Losing a long break would likely raise stress levels for many young people. Summer is also an important period when classmates and friends meet up and enjoy activities together; without enough free time, those social gatherings would be reduced and the season would feel less fun.

For these reasons, school boards should not cut summer vacation. The break is important for family time, rest, catching up on classes if needed, practicing sports, reading, and traveling. Reducing it would take away valuable experiences and likely increase stress for students. I support keeping summer as a long break so students can recover and enjoy time outside of school.

I believe curfews are necessary because they help protect young people, especially at night. Curfews are meant with good intentions: to keep teenagers safe. In the end, the main people who benefit from these rules are the young themselves.

At night, teenagers can get into trouble more easily. Without adults around, they might do what they want and take risks. A curfew gives a clear rule to follow, so young people are less likely to be out where problems can start.

Also, most adults stay at home in the evening, resting or spending time with family, and it makes sense to expect teenagers to do the same. Empty streets and late hours make it easier for crimes like theft or attacks to happen. A teenager might get hurt simply because they were in the wrong place at the wrong time or tried to help someone and were attacked.

Some people say that going out at night is harmless fun, for example visiting clubs. But nights out can be dangerous—there have been violent incidents at night that cost lives. For these reasons, curfews are a sensible way to look after young people and reduce risks to their safety.

Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend class from home? I believe that while distance learning can help some students, overall I do not agree that it is better than going to school in person. In my view, attending school offers important advantages: students can take part in sports, avoid feeling bored and isolated, and choose from many elective classes or vocational programs. Still, I recognize that for some people online learning is the only way to get credits and finish their studies.

First, schools give students the chance to play sports and join teams. Many young people enjoy physical activities and schools provide the space, coaches, and equipment for that. Sports are more than a hobby: they make me feel happier when I am sad, they keep me focused, and they give me a way to share something I love with others, like playing soccer with friends. Being involved in sports also helps students stay away from harmful activities, such as drug use or gangs, because it offers a positive community and goals to work for. Young people need places where they can explore their interests and work toward their dreams.

Second, attending school in person helps prevent boredom and isolation. Most students prefer a learning environment that is active and social, not sitting alone all day in front of a computer. At school you can meet friends, make new acquaintances, and feel more motivated. When I am confused about homework, I can quickly ask a teacher or partner for help. Schools also organize trips to universities, museums, and historical sites, which make learning more interesting and help us understand our history and culture in a deeper way.

Finally, schools offer many elective classes and academies that help students find their future path. In my country, schools often provide options like cooking, piano, cosmetology, art, fitness, medical assistant training, dental care, band, police or detective programs, electrician courses, and emergency medical training. These classes let students discover what they enjoy and gain practical skills. Schools also support students with information about university applications, scholarships, and how to get student loans or credits. For example, my school helped me decide what to study and assisted me in getting a loan for university.

In conclusion, although online classes are useful for some people, most students benefit more from being at school. In-person learning allows students to practice sports, avoid boredom through social contact, and try a wide range of elective courses that prepare them for the future. However, I understand that some students cannot attend school because of family responsibilities, work, or lack of transportation, and for them distance learning is a necessary and valuable option to finish their education.

I agree with the idea because first impressions are very hard to erase, even when someone makes an effort to change them completely.

A first impression is something people remember—whether it is our behaviour, the way we speak, or our feelings toward someone. These initial views often stay with others. For example, the habits that show us off—how we talk, walk, or eat—are difficult to alter quickly. If a man has been in love with a woman since childhood, his first image of her will influence how he sees her forever, and even a new person entering his life will not easily replace that first feeling.

People sometimes try to copy or change an impression, but usually they cannot make it identical to the original. Consider when someone falls in love with a dish a friend cooks. If they try to recreate it, it may look similar but it will not taste exactly the same because they do not know every ingredient or the exact method. Even being told the recipe does not guarantee the same result. In the same way, attempting to reproduce or change a first impression rarely leads to the same effect.

Also, first impressions can be based on false information. Someone might lie about their family or personality to appear more attractive to peers, and others may accept that image. Even if the truth comes out later, the initial belief can remain. That shows how strong first impressions are—real or not, they are not easily removed.

We should accept that first impressions are difficult to change. It is better to be true to ourselves than to try to force a new image or copy someone else, because doing so is often painful and will not recreate the original impression.

Some people argue that young students should not choose a specific career path because they are too young to decide. I disagree. I believe it is helpful for students to commit to a career early, since doing so gives them a head start in learning and planning for their future.

When a student knows what they want to do from an early age, they have more time to gain knowledge and skills related to that field. By the time they are older, they will understand their chosen area better than peers who never decided. Having a clear career goal also prevents wasting time trying many unrelated activities just to discover what fits. Instead, students can focus their efforts on experiences and subjects that will support their future job.

Many students already enter high school with an idea of their future career. Once they reach high school, they can take specific classes, join clubs, or look for internships that help them explore and confirm this choice. Those who decide on a path before graduating will likely have a clearer plan for education and work after high school.

Of course, some people worry that children are not mature enough to make such decisions. While it is true that views can change, choosing a direction early does not have to be final. It can be flexible and adjusted as students learn more about themselves.

In conclusion, deciding on a career at a young age can be beneficial because it allows students to gain relevant knowledge and plan ahead, making their transition into adulthood smoother.

People often say that first impressions are very hard to change. Some believe they can control the way they come across whenever they want, but that is not true. First impressions happen so quickly that they leave little room for thinking or changing your reaction — they can occur in less than a second. While some initial judgments can be altered later depending on the situation, others remain fixed no matter what you try. I agree with this idea because impressions are emotional reactions or mental images that stay after an experience.

Certain first impressions have a strong negative impact on our lives. Imagine a moment when the only impression someone can make is the wrong one and they cannot do anything to fix it right away. For example, picture a student in class who accidentally farts loudly and everyone hears it. Although he might try to act as if nothing happened, he cannot really control his response. He feels ashamed, his face turns red, and his heart races — reactions that are not under his conscious control.

The feelings that come with a first impression are often intense because they are not part of everyday life. If embarrassing moments happen constantly, that strange feeling may become familiar. When a situation is unusual, the immediate reaction is usually shame, confusion, or discomfort, and sometimes even physical pain. But when something happens regularly, the reaction can shift toward something more positive. For instance, I often feel happy rather than ashamed when my family teases me with uncomfortable questions. Because it happens so often, it no longer bothers me the way a rare embarrassing event would.

Repeated experiences with similar first impressions can teach people to behave normally in many situations. For those who used to feel intense embarrassment, practice can lead to calmness. Personally, I have had enough situations like this that I now feel comfortable instead of ashamed. If my mother asks whether I have a girlfriend, I simply smile or say I do not — nothing dramatic happens. At school, if friends ask whether I am dating someone I like, I answer honestly like any other student. I no longer feel embarrassed because experience has made these moments feel normal.

I hope that in the future, when someone brings up something embarrassing, my first instinct to feel shame will not show. I want my learned reactions to take over so the moment does not become worse than it already is. I do not want to lose control and make a small incident into the worst moment of my life.

As a student, I think the school should find a balance in its lunch menu. Serving only healthy meals has good intentions but also some drawbacks. Many students do not take care of their diets at home and want to eat their favorite foods at school. For example, in my class when pizza is served, they choose it even though it can upset their stomachs. I remember when Fried Chicken Friday was canceled — it was a favorite, and lots of students didn’t eat that day because they didn’t like the replacement. This shows that banning favorite foods can backfire.

In conclusion, the best solution is a balanced menu. Have some days focused on healthy meals and other days with favorite choices, or offer both at once. That way students can enjoy the food they like while also getting nutritious options, keeping them happy and healthier overall.

People should turn to experts and authorities when faced with important life decisions because individuals acting only on impulse or personal opinion may lack the knowledge needed to choose wisely. Relying solely on instinct can lead people to believe their actions are correct even when they are harmful or illegal. Guidance helps prevent those mistakes and keeps both individuals and the wider community safe.

Laws exist to regulate risky behaviors like using drugs or alcohol, owning firearms, and driving. Many kinds of drugs are illegal in most places, and when they are available legally, you usually need special permission or a prescription. Alcohol is legal in many countries but retailers are required to sell it only to those who are at least 21 years old in some places. Buying a gun also comes with age limits and licensing rules similar to those for controlled substances. Driving requires a license, and young drivers often face additional restrictions: for example, 16-year-olds may get a learner’s permit but must drive with an experienced adult present. These rules are in place so people gain the necessary skills and judgment before they are allowed to act independently.

Workplaces also demonstrate the need for outside guidance. Jobs come with timetables and responsibilities that staff must follow. A fixed schedule tells employees when to start and finish work so the business can operate smoothly. If an employee, such as an accountant, decides to change their hours on a whim—coming in the afternoon instead of in the morning—the company may not have the financial information it needs when required. Ignoring schedules or assigned duties can harm the organization and could lead to disciplinary action or even dismissal. Employers set these rules because following them is essential for the business to function properly.

Living in a community means accepting limits on what you can do in public and private spaces. You cannot set fire to a library simply because you think it would be entertaining, nor can you punch strangers to amuse your friends. Taking a flower from someone’s private garden without permission is also unacceptable. These kinds of actions harm others and break social rules, so authorities and social norms exist to stop people from making such choices.

In conclusion, people should not be left to make every major decision alone. This does not mean individuals lose their rights, but it recognizes that there must be limits and expert advice to prevent harm. Guidance from authorities and knowledgeable people is especially important for minors, who often do not yet have the experience or judgment to know what is right.

The British writer John Lubbock once said, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." This idea raises questions for me because many young people change who they are when they feel insecure or are full of worries. The habits and traits we develop can take strong hold, but I do not think we always fully control them. Often outside forces shape us more than our own free will.

How others see us can make us nervous, and we sometimes alter our behavior to fit what they expect. Parents give us certain values, but society adds many other influences — especially the internet. Online content and popular culture have a huge reach, and they often affect people without anyone being able to manage that effect. Still, there are many kinds of influence, and it is important to find the ones that help you and stick with them. In general, society keeps changing and offers different viewpoints all the time.

Another point is that people can change and grow from their surroundings. I, for example, have changed a lot since I moved to Virginia and I am learning to fit in with how other people live there. There are plenty of influences beyond our control because we often copy what we see online. For example, many rappers talk about relationships and lifestyles that listeners might want to imitate. I used to live in California, where artists and musicians have big audiences; their work can influence many people and also bring them money if they gain attention.

Both children and adults are affected by others. Sometimes we choose which ideas to accept, and other times these choices are made for us by powerful trends. Even so, I feel proud of the world we live in and the chance it gives us to decide some things for ourselves.

There are also risks that appear every year: conflicts, pollution, new viruses and other dangers. News and social media can make these threats feel even more frightening because they spread fast and widely. Despite that, small hopes and friendly gestures keep us moving forward when we feel stuck. That positive feeling helps us continue on.
