Do you think students would benefit from taking classes at home? Some people believe online lessons are a good idea because they save time and seem easier than going to school. I disagree. Learning from home can be harder because students do not get the same explanations and support from teachers. If lessons are only online, many students might not learn much. I believe attending school is better because teachers offer help, many students enjoy being there, and school provides useful activities and distractions.

Some learners can work independently, but others rely on teachers for guidance. For example, my sister often stays after school to get extra help. She says her teachers explain things she does not understand and help her improve. When she fails a test, she meets with a teacher to review the mistakes and learns a lot from those sessions. Teachers often find ways to support students outside of normal class time because they want their pupils to succeed.

Going to school is also important for making friends and taking part in activities. My brother likes to play sports at school and enjoys talking with other students. He thinks playing games and exercising with classmates is fun and helps him feel connected. School gives students a chance to learn about others and to take part in things they cannot do at home. These social experiences are part of education and help prepare people for life after graduation.

Some people argue that online classes suit those who prefer to work alone and that school can be distracting. It is true some students get distracted at school, but many also find it easier to focus when they have structured time, guided activities, and supportive adults around them. For example, a friend of mine gets distracted sometimes, yet she also benefits from sports and group projects that keep her engaged. Talking with teachers and other adults at school can provide advice and perspective that are hard to get through a screen.

In conclusion, teachers play an essential role by explaining material and helping students who struggle, which is difficult to replace with online lessons. Going to school offers social opportunities, enjoyable activities, and resources like books and games that support learning. For these reasons, I believe students should attend school in person rather than studying entirely online. A good school experience helps people get a solid education and prepares them for college and future careers.

Some schools now let students attend lessons from home through online platforms or video calls. I believe this option can be very useful for certain students. In particular, those who work late shifts and young mothers who cannot easily return to the classroom would gain from being able to study remotely.

The first example is a friend of mine who often works after school. Some nights he has a job from about 5 p.m. until midnight, and then he must get up at 5 a.m. to go to school. This schedule is exhausting and he is usually very tired during the morning lessons because he cannot sleep properly. Still, finishing high school is essential for him if he wants a better future. Many high school students hold jobs after class, and a distance-learning option would let them continue working while attending school remotely. If they could study from home, they could rest more and find time to do homework and prepare for tests. This would likely improve their grades, since lack of sleep and limited study time are often reasons for poor academic performance.

The second example concerns pregnant girls in high school. I have seen many young women who do not want to return to school once they become pregnant. They face criticism from others who say negative things because they are too young to have a baby. Even those who try to stay in regular classes sometimes find it impossible to keep up after the child is born, because they must care for the baby. With an at-home learning option, these girls could continue their studies without the pressure and stigma of attending in person. Studying remotely would make it easier for them to complete their courses and graduate, which is important for their future opportunities.

In conclusion, offering distance learning is a positive idea because it supports students who face real challenges. It can help those who work long hours and those who become pregnant to finish high school. By allowing students to learn from home, schools would give them a fair chance to succeed despite difficult personal circumstances.

A positive attitude is essential for success in life. I agree with this idea because people with a constructive outlook can improve their own lives and help society. Although many individuals still have negative attitudes and should change, those who adopt a positive mindset enjoy better family relationships, perform more effectively at work, and can influence others to make improvements.

At home, a positive attitude helps family members create a healthier environment. People who are patient and caring make it easier to solve problems and support each other. For example, many parents or relatives lose patience with children or other family members, which harms relationships. If those people work on becoming more positive and thoughtful, they can make better decisions and be more available to help when someone is in need. In this way, improving personal attitude contributes to a stronger family and a more stable community.

In the workplace, a good attitude also makes a big difference. Employees who are polite, patient, and cooperative get along better with colleagues and serve customers in a friendly way. By contrast, workers with a bad temper or rude behavior often cause conflicts and frustrate clients. When staff keep calm and respond kindly even to difficult customers, the whole job environment improves. Learning to control one’s reactions and remain positive is important for doing well at work.

A person with a positive attitude can also affect others’ lives. Teachers, for example, who encourage students and model respect can help young people develop better behavior and choices. As students grow up with improved attitudes, they are more likely to find good jobs, treat others respectfully, and support their families. Over time, these changes spread and benefit the broader society.

In conclusion, a positive attitude is a key factor for success. It strengthens family ties, enhances job performance, and helps change other people’s lives for the better.

Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." I disagree with this statement. Becoming yourself is not simply a passive resistance to outside influence; it requires actively shaping your life. You should take charge of your choices and steer your path rather than expecting the world to leave you unchanged. True accomplishment comes from deciding who you want to be and working toward it.

The first important step is making your own decisions. If you allow others or society to choose for you, you risk losing direction and feeling exhausted by a life that was not yours. When you make decisions yourself, you understand why you chose a certain path and take responsibility for the results. This awareness makes your achievements more meaningful. People who let outside forces dictate their lives often become unhappy because they did not pick their own goals or values.

The second point is doing what you enjoy. To reach a significant accomplishment, choose activities or a career that match your interests. When you work on something you care about, it rarely feels like a burden. Passion keeps you motivated and prevents burnout, so you are more likely to reach high levels of success. If you follow what others expect instead of what you truly like, you will probably become bored and unsatisfied even if you appear successful to others.

Finally, being yourself means taking responsibility for your future. You are the person who knows your strengths, weaknesses, and dreams best. By making your own choices and following your interests, you can shape a life that fits you. Many people later regret letting the world decide for them because they find themselves stuck in careers or lifestyles that do not match their true selves. Taking control early helps avoid those regrets.

In conclusion, do not let the world dictate who you are. The greatest accomplishment is not only resisting outside pressure but actively choosing and pursuing the life you want. Make your own decisions and follow your passions so you can achieve real satisfaction and avoid a future of disappointment.

I agree that being yourself can be difficult and sometimes lonely. In today’s world most people do not like being alone, though some choose to stay true to themselves. When you accept who you are, you can focus on your goals because you are not wasting energy trying to impress others. You can study, work hard, and also enjoy free time. Being yourself does not mean doing whatever you want without thinking; it means choosing activities that make you happy and staying strong without feeling ashamed.

At first, I found being myself very challenging. During my first year in the United States, I was without my family and I felt very sad. I struggled with English and had no friends, so I did not want to be alone or be myself. I remember how hard it was to face each day by myself. Back then I did not understand how tough being independent could be, and I often wished to return to where I came from.

After a few years, I decided to accept myself and stop being sad all the time. I stopped comparing my life with others and tried not to focus on people who made me feel worse. Ignoring the pressure from friends or family gatherings helped me relax. I learned to breathe deeply and tell myself that everything would be okay. Over time, being true to myself became less frightening and actually helped me become more independent.

Now I take responsibility for my life and my choices, and being myself has changed me. My family encouraged me to learn to do things on my own, and at first I was nervous because I had always relied on them. I had to learn many skills before I turned eighteen. Gradually I learned to take care of myself, manage my work, and plan for my career. I never thought I could do so much without their help, but learning to rely on myself made me stronger.

In short, being yourself is not always easy, but it leads to self-discovery and independence. It taught me how to cope with loneliness, make my own decisions, and become responsible for my future. Don’t be afraid to be who you are — it can bring you long-term happiness and strength.

Technology has made it possible for people to do many things without meeting others face to face. We can borrow books, shop, and play games online without speaking to anyone in person. But limiting human contact through technology has harmed our lives in several ways. We rely on technology every day, every moment, and that dependence brings real problems.

One major problem is how technology affects education. Online lessons can show students information, but they often fail to teach how to complete tasks or solve problems. The personal connection between teacher and student is lost when instruction is only on a screen. When I was young in my country, we had no computers in class. My teacher explained assignments clearly on the board and would help any student who did not understand. That direct help and conversation is what school should be about. Now students learn alone, and the relationship that helps learning is weaker.

Technology also reduces social interaction outside the classroom. I remember sitting with friends in the cafeteria and talking about our days. Today, most students look at their phones during lunch and do not speak to each other. People spend more time inside watching movies, reading digitally, or gaming, and they forget to meet others in person. Instead of going out to eat and enjoying company, many of us order food online and eat alone while using a phone. This change has decreased real human contact.

There are larger dangers too. Advances in technology have made powerful weapons, and the threat of conflict with nuclear tools is more real because of these developments. Technology can make people less aware of what is happening around them; if we are always absorbed by screens, we may ignore serious events outside our doors. Overreliance on devices can weaken human empathy and make people less responsive to the suffering of others.

At work, technology is useful, but it also creates distractions. A person who follows a game or checks social media may stop working and lose focus. Employers may fire distracted workers, and then those people must find new jobs and struggle to support their families. In this way, technology can indirectly cause unemployment and trouble for people who depend on steady work.

Finally, technology increases some risks, especially on the road. Drivers who text or use apps while driving miss important signs or turns, which can lead to accidents. A single mistake can cause deaths, leaving families to grieve and people to be blamed for avoidable harm.

In conclusion, technology has many negative effects on human life. It reduces genuine human contact, makes people lazier and more dependent, weakens empathy, and can even lead to job loss or deadly accidents. While tools can help us, our overdependence on them has made life poorer in important ways.

I agree with Albert Einstein’s idea that imagination is more important than knowledge. Imagination is the starting point for new ideas. It lets you picture things that you have not yet learned and often points you to information you will later acquire. Of course, imagination can sometimes lead you astray if you get carried away and imagine situations your mind cannot handle. For example, thinking too far ahead about a topic can confuse you and make it hard to focus on the facts.

At the same time, knowledge can be more practical in certain situations. When you face a difficult problem, your learned skills and facts help you act sensibly. Think of struggling with a hard math question on a test: the knowledge you have built up helps you solve it. Reading books is another example: it improves your vocabulary and gives you information that makes solving real problems easier.

More often than not, imagination and knowledge work best together. If you want to build something but do not know what to make, your imagination will offer many ideas. Once you choose a design, your knowledge tells you how to construct it and what materials to use. Imagination provides the vision; knowledge supplies the practical steps to make that vision real.

Both imagination and knowledge also have negative sides. When you feel low, your imagination might tell you nothing can make you happy, which makes the mood worse. Children can use their imagination unfairly in games, which can hurt their friendships. Knowledge can also change how people behave: if you do well on a test and then brag while a friend gets a low score, you might damage that friendship. So both can influence relationships for better or worse.

Consider a 16-year-old who needs a job. If he has poor grades and little knowledge, he may not get the position he needs. Other students with better qualifications may be chosen instead. If he cannot find work, he might have to borrow money for food, and owing debts could cause serious problems later. This example shows how lacking knowledge can lead to real hardship even when someone has imagination or desire.

Young children show strong imagination because they do not limit what is possible. At night a child might be sure there are monsters in the closet and call for their parents. The parents may insist there are no monsters, but strange noises can keep the child frightened. Sometimes the sounds turn out to be the parents playing a joke. This shows how imagination can create powerful images that feel very real.

In short, imagination drives new ideas and often points the way to knowledge. Even though knowledge is useful and sometimes necessary, imagination is the spark that makes learning meaningful and creative.

Success is a word we hear all the time, and most people hope to achieve it in their lives. The journey toward success often begins at school, which is one of the most important and memorable parts of childhood. To make learning enjoyable and comfortable, schools and teachers allow students to take part in activities like drama role plays, simple science experiments, and music practice.

Many of the actors, comedians, and performers we admire today were once students sitting in classrooms like ours. They worked hard, joined school plays, and used the opportunities given to them. Because of that practice and confidence-building, they reached where they are now. We can follow a similar path by getting involved in school role plays and starting to improve ourselves early. Role playing is fun, but it also helps students become braver about speaking in public and expressing feelings. Performing can cheer others up, and making people smile is itself a great reward.

Science and technology keep growing quickly, and experiments are being done all the time. To prepare students for this future, schools teach basic experiments that are safe and exciting, such as making a rainbow in a jar, mixing colors, or making a coin seem to disappear. These activities spark students’ curiosity and increase their focus on scientific ideas. They are enjoyable to do and important because children are the next generation of scientists and thinkers.

Every student has some hidden talent—whether it is in music, drawing, or sports—and these gifts often show themselves with time. Music is one of the most common talents seen in schools because it connects directly with our emotions and helps us concentrate. There are many kinds of music—happy, sad, energetic—and each one can change how we feel. We find music everywhere: on TV, in lessons, and during school events. Listening to and making music helps release emotions and lightens the mind.

In conclusion, school is a place for learning and personal growth. If students enjoy their classes and take part in activities, they will always gain something valuable. We should make the most of school, because it is the primary source of our education and a first step toward success.

Some people are unsure how to play basketball, so here are a few tips that can help you play or set up the game. First, consider the environment. While some courts are indoors, many people play outside. I recommend playing outdoors in the summer when the weather is more pleasant. Avoid playing in very hot or very cold conditions because extreme temperatures make it harder to perform. Windy days are also bad for playing outside since strong gusts can change how the ball moves. The best seasons to play are usually summer and spring. Also, daytime is better than night for outdoor play because you can see the ball and the court more clearly.

The court should be wide enough for normal play and have a flat surface so the ball bounces predictably. The hoop needs a sturdy pole at the correct height and a rim wide enough for the ball to pass through easily. The net should hang at a reasonable length so it does not interfere with shots. Finally, make sure the court lines are visible so players can line up for free throws and judge boundaries.

Passing and cooperating with teammates can turn a losing situation into a win, so learn to share the ball. Practice regularly to improve shooting, dribbling, and finding openings in the defense. You and your team should also plan strategies and think of different ways to beat the opponent. Planning ahead gives you backup options and reduces mistakes. In short, practice, fitness, teamwork, and smart planning are the basics for getting better at basketball.

Some schools now let students take classes from home using online lessons or video calls. I believe that distance learning is not helpful for most students. There are several reasons for this: many learners lose focus at home, they miss the personal attention of a teacher, they can cheat or get others to do their work, and they lose important social and emotional support from being at school.

First, many students find it hard to concentrate during online lessons. At home there are more distractions, and without a teacher watching, they may do other things instead of paying attention. Because of this, they learn less than they would in a classroom. Also, when students have a bad day or feel unmotivated, they are even less likely to complete assignments properly at home. Some simply look up answers without trying to understand the topics because they think no one is checking their work.

Second, online classes often mean students do not get enough help when they need it. In school, teachers can give immediate explanations, show examples on the board, or work side by side with students. In contrast, remote learners may struggle to get extra help. They might ask family members to do their homework for them, or hire someone to complete assignments, so they do not truly learn the material. When test time comes, these students can fail because they never gained the necessary skills.

Another important issue is the lack of personal support. Many students go through difficult times and need someone to talk to. At school they can reach out to a teacher, coach, or counselor who notices changes in their behavior and offers guidance. If they stay at home, they may feel lonely and have no one to turn to. This isolation can harm their mental health and affect their studies.

Video conferencing also has limits. Recorded lessons and online explanations do not always cover what students need. Some learners are too lazy to replay videos to understand unclear parts, while in a classroom a teacher can rephrase or give a different example on the spot. Technical problems or a poor internet connection can make it even harder to follow lessons.

Finally, online schooling can take away valuable experiences like school sports and other activities. Students who learn from home may miss opportunities to join teams, develop social skills, and even earn scholarships. Later in life they might regret not having those experiences or finding it harder to communicate with others.

In conclusion, distance learning usually does more harm than good for students. They learn less at home, lack the support and attention they need, and lose important social and emotional benefits from being at school. For these reasons, schools should not replace in-person classes with online learning or video conferencing as the main option.

It tells me that if you don't lose your enthusiasm for something you focus on and keep doing it, you will do it perfectly like you wished.

My other reason is to be audacious and keep trying. When you go from failure to failure, your friends might say, "Stop doing it; you are not going to make it." They are just giving you a suggestion.

If you stop, you will lose your enthusiasm for something that is attracting you just because they said you are not going to make it. Trust yourself; keep trying and don't lose your enthusiasm.

In my opinion, enthusiasm is not easy to have. The only way to have it is someone or something that is attracting me. I would like to focus on having enthusiasm like for video games—I can play for a whole day, but I can't study for a whole day; it would be tough for me. If I had enthusiasm for study, I would be successful too.

Failure is not dreadful; the awful thing is losing enthusiasm, which will be incurable. Believe in yourself; even if you have many failures, continue trying and you will succeed.

Prime Minister Winston Churchill’s remark that “success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm” is an idea I strongly agree with. Some people argue that repeating failure shows you are not talented or cannot finish a task. However, I believe that keeping your enthusiasm alive is the key to eventually succeeding.

A clear example is AiDiSheng, who created the first light blob. He experienced thousands of failures but never gave up or lost his excitement for the project. After many attempts, he finally achieved his goal and produced something no one had made before. This story shows that if you remain passionate about what you are doing and continue to work on it, you can reach the result you hope for.

Another important point is to be brave and keep trying even when others discourage you. When you fail many times, friends or acquaintances may tell you to stop because they think you will not succeed. They offer their opinions, but you should decide for yourself. If you quit just because of what others say, you will let go of the enthusiasm that motivated you in the first place. Trusting yourself and continuing to try is essential.

For me, enthusiasm is not easy to find; it usually comes from something that truly interests me. For instance, I can play video games for hours because I enjoy them, but studying for the same length of time is much harder. If I could feel the same excitement about studying, I believe I would be successful there too.

Failure itself is not terrible. The real problem is losing the enthusiasm that keeps you going. If you believe in yourself and persist through many failures, you increase your chances of success.

Most students look forward to summer vacation because it is one of the nicest times of the year. It is a chance to relax, travel, and spend more time with family and friends. Some teachers argue that the break is too long and that students forget what they learned, but I disagree. Summer is a special period when many young people can reconnect with the people who matter most.

One important reason I value summer is that it allows families to be together. Many parents work long hours—sometimes ten to twelve hours from Monday to Saturday, and occasionally on Sundays too—so during the school year children do not see them much. When summer arrives, parents often have time off as well, and everyone can share meals, trips, and important moments. For students this is a rare opportunity to build stronger relationships with their mothers, fathers, siblings, and grandparents.

For example, my mom is the most important person in my life. She supports me through good times and bad and gives me daily advice to help me avoid mistakes she faced when she was young. During summer we spend more time together, and she helps me become a better person at school, at work, and in my community. Those weeks of shared experiences and conversations make me grow and learn in ways that school alone cannot provide.

My faith is also part of why I value summer. I enjoy using the vacation to attend church activities, reflect, and deepen my relationship with God. These quiet moments teach me important values and lessons that guide my life. Summer offers space not only for fun but for spiritual growth and reflection.

Two months of vacation feels reasonable to me. During the school year students are in class for about nine months, which can be stressful and intense. A longer break is necessary to rest, recharge, and spend time with loved ones. Some educators suggest changing to a year-round schedule with only three or four short breaks in the summer, but I do not agree. Shortening the summer to only one month would not allow enough time for family trips, relaxation, or meaningful rest from schoolwork. Summer should be a time for enjoyment and for being with the people who matter most.

Teachers sometimes worry that students will forget what they learned over the long break, but I think that concern is exaggerated. Important lessons from class—projects, homework, and classwork—stay in our minds. When students go back to school, they usually need only a brief review to remember key ideas. Memory can fade, but the basics remain, and review lessons at the start of the new term can quickly bring students up to speed.

I want to share a personal experience that shows why summer matters. When I lived in Generic_City, I had so much schoolwork—homework, presentations, and projects—that I missed a family outing. My family wanted to spend time together, but I stayed home to finish assignments. Later I realized I had lost a chance to make memories with my relatives because I was too focused on school. My uncle told me it was important to clear my mind and be with the family. That moment taught me that family time is limited and must be prioritized. School deadlines can wait sometimes; family moments cannot.

Education is important and should not be treated merely as an obligation. It is an opportunity to learn about people, animals, the solar system, water, and many useful things that will help us in the future. Still, education should be balanced with time for family, work, and faith. For me, a good routine is to focus on studies Monday to Friday and reserve weekends for God and family. When it is time for school, I dedicate myself to learning; when it is time for family, I fully enjoy those moments.

Being organized helps to make room for everything: family, work, friends, and school. If you plan your time well, you can do your best in class and still have special moments with relatives. No one stays on Earth forever, and we should not miss chances to be with our loved ones. That is why summer vacation is so valuable: it gives students and teachers alike time to rest and to be with family.

Finally, teachers also deserve a break. They work hard all year and use the summer to relax and enjoy time with their own families. When school starts again, a little review is usually enough because many lessons are still remembered. For these reasons I believe two months of summer vacation—plus a couple of weeks for holidays—is an appropriate and important time for students to rest, bond with family, and return to school refreshed. Enjoy your summer and make the most of the time with the people who matter.

Has the limitation of human contact due to the use of technology had positive or negative effects on people's lives?

Technology has a positive effect on people's lives for several reasons.

People have friends and family in other countries or states whom they cannot see, but they can talk with them by technology. Technology is used to meet new people and be more social. It is easy to contact friends and plan to hang out with them.

Some jobs and companies need technology to save information about their customers, such as names and orders, and to organize documents that are important to the company. They also use it to contact workers more quickly or let them know what they have to do the next day by calls or emails.

Now it is more comfortable for students. Some schools allow the use of laptops, whereas in the past students were required to bring all their books every day. Now you only have to bring a laptop that has every book you will need for your classes. You can also turn in assignments and projects by pressing a button, and your teacher will have your work to grade. Technology can also help teachers explain things more clearly with videos.

Technology does not affect people's lives in a negative way. On the contrary, it has a positive effect, and people who say it is negative are possibly older and not accustomed to technology.

The reduction of face-to-face contact caused by technology has brought mostly positive changes to people's lives. First, technology makes it simple to keep in touch with friends and family who live far away. Video calls, messaging apps and social networks allow people to speak and share moments even when they are in different cities or countries. It also helps people meet others and stay socially active, and makes organizing meetups with friends quick and convenient.

In business, many companies rely on technology to operate efficiently. They store customer details and orders electronically, keep important documents organized, and communicate quickly with staff through emails or calls. This speed and organization improve customer service and help teams coordinate their work more effectively.

Education has also become more comfortable thanks to technology. Many schools now permit laptops, so students no longer need to carry many heavy textbooks. Digital devices can hold all course materials, and submitting homework or projects is often as simple as clicking a button. Teachers can also use videos and online tools to explain ideas more clearly.

Overall, technology’s effects are more positive than negative. People who argue that technology harms social life are often older and less familiar with these tools. When used sensibly, technology strengthens relationships, supports work, and makes learning easier.

This program offers many benefits: it helps younger students learn new things, encourages older students to grow by taking teaching seriously, improves younger students’ social and communication skills, trains older students to plan and organize lessons, and allows both age groups to develop different learning techniques.

The main advantage is that younger students gain new knowledge. Teaching children new topics early prepares them for future studies and careers. Through the program, young learners are exposed to interesting subjects that may help them decide what they want to do later in life. When older students explain ideas to younger ones, the younger students can use that information and even pass it on to others. For example, learning basic math now can be useful for everyday tasks like budgeting as they grow up. Overall, the program gives younger students a chance to learn useful and practical skills.

Another important benefit is that the older students mature by teaching younger peers. Acting as a teacher encourages them to think carefully about what to teach and how to explain it. When older students realize younger learners need help in certain areas, they must choose appropriate materials and methods. This responsibility makes older students more focused and thoughtful. Teaching also helps them feel more responsible and grown up, since they must consider whether their lessons are effective and how to improve them.

The program also helps younger students become better communicators. Regular contact with older peers reduces shyness and builds confidence when speaking with new people. As younger students practice talking, asking questions, and presenting ideas, they become more comfortable in front of groups. This increased confidence can make future presentations or class participation less intimidating. In short, the program supports younger students in becoming more social and outgoing.

A further advantage is that older students learn to plan and be organized. Preparing lessons requires them to think ahead about what topics to cover, when to meet, and how to present the material. This planning teaches them to manage time and sequence activities logically. By organizing lessons and materials, older students develop skills in preparation and structure that are useful in school and later life.

Finally, the program brings both age groups together to improve learning techniques. When older and younger students work together, they share different ways of studying and solving problems. They can exchange methods such as using flashcards, repeating readings, or watching tutorial videos, helping each other discover the best approaches for learning. This cooperation makes learning easier and faster for everyone involved.

In conclusion, the program supports both younger and older students: it encourages learning, builds maturity and organization, improves communication, and helps students find effective study strategies for the future.

What should we do if we never take action?

Thomas Jefferson once advised against idleness, observing that steady effort can lead to great results. In the same way, we are more likely to achieve our goals when we keep doing something toward them. Three reasons explain why action helps us accomplish more: we receive support from others, we learn by taking risks, and we stay true to ourselves.

Some people argue that staying inactive can be useful. They claim that God has a plan for each of us, that dreams need time to grow, or that careful thought should come before any action. These points are important, but they do not mean we should do nothing.

First, many people support us. Family and friends often want to see us succeed so we can have a better life. They know our hopes and encourage us to move forward, giving advice or help when we try. This support makes it easier to take steps toward our dreams.

Second, taking risks and acting gives us valuable experience. By trying, we discover our strengths and weaknesses and learn how to handle difficulties. Even when things go wrong, those lessons prepare us to do better next time and build our confidence.

Third, being yourself matters. If you believe in your dreams and act on them, you show your true character and inspire both yourself and your loved ones. Encouraging yourself with thoughts like “I can do this” helps you keep going until you reach your goals.

In short, we accomplish more when we keep taking action. With the help of others, the lessons from risk, and staying true to ourselves, we can work toward our dreams. Without action, we cannot achieve them.

I believe the school should make several changes to the cafeteria because many students are unhappy with the current situation. The food is often the same every week and much of it is low quality. Sometimes the meals are acceptable, but more often they are not, so many students avoid buying food at school.

For example, putting a weekly menu on the cafeteria door or notice board would make this information available to everyone.

Overall, changing the food selection, lowering prices, posting the daily menu, and setting a suitable lunch period would improve the cafeteria for most students. When I think of wisdom, I immediately picture my grandfather. He often shares stories about his life back in his home country. He talks about growing up very poor, sometimes with little food, and how going to school was something special. He also told me about losing his father and brother when he was between six and eight years old, and later about the challenges he faced when he moved to America.

My grandfather was born into a humble family. He had a father, a mother, and one brother. His father worked in construction and his mother took care of the household and prepared meals. The nearest school was about 3.4 miles away, so he had to walk there, but he went anyway because he loved learning. In his town, attending school was rare and considered a great opportunity, so he appreciated every chance to study.

When my grandfather was only five, his father died. His father had been involved with dangerous people and troublemakers. One day, while going to work, he was confronted by four men. He tried to run, but they shot him. He was left with three gunshot wounds and bled out on the ground before anyone could help him. That loss affected the whole family deeply.

His brother became sick and was ill for about two months. My grandfather says his brother was a smart man who helped him improve his reading and writing, and he believes his brother was the reason he did well in school. When his brother fell ill, my grandfather and his mother did everything they could to care for him, but medical care was poor and expensive in their country in 1976. They prayed every night for his recovery, but his brother passed away in his sleep. They buried him, and their mother cried for a long time before slowly accepting the loss.

When my grandfather was older, he married and had two daughters and two sons. He decided to try to move to the United States. He had to pass a difficult test based on a study book; there were 200 possible questions and during the exam they asked 50 random ones. After he passed, he packed his things and said goodbye to his wife and children. He wanted to settle in Virginia, and when he arrived it was very hard at first because his English was limited. He found a job at a restaurant and worked two other jobs as well. As soon as he began earning money, he saved to bring his family over. It took him about eight months to gather what he needed.

After he brought his family to America, I was born soon after. We lived in the same city for as long as I can remember. Now my grandfather works at a school and seems content with how his life turned out. His stories and the lessons he learned from hardship are the kind of wisdom I look up to.

Technology plays a major role in our lives today. It is everywhere — at home, in hospitals, schools, workplaces and on the streets. Overall, I believe technology is very useful, although it can sometimes have negative effects. Because many devices and systems make daily tasks easier, people rely on them constantly. This convenience can also lead to laziness: some people prefer staying indoors playing video games or using apps instead of going outside to meet friends and play sports, which is better for their health.

I support the use of technology because it helps in many important ways. We see it in hospitals where medical machines and equipment assist doctors to treat and save patients. In education, computers and online resources help students learn and complete assignments more efficiently. At work, especially in jobs like construction, tools and machines reduce physical effort and speed up tasks. In short, technology often improves safety, productivity and access to information.

Another big advantage is how technology connects us. No matter where someone lives, it is now easy to keep in touch with family and friends any time through calls, messaging apps and social media. This constant connectivity makes long-distance relationships and teamwork much simpler. However, we must also be cautious because technology can be used for harmful purposes, such as spreading false information or committing crimes.

In conclusion, technology benefits our daily lives in many ways and has become essential. Still, we should be aware of its drawbacks, like addiction and reduced physical activity. As with anything, too much use can be harmful, so it is important to find a balance and use technology responsibly.

I disagree with the idea that failure is better than success. Success matters a lot, and experiencing failure can be one of the hardest things a person faces. When someone keeps failing, it often destroys their motivation and makes them stop doing the activities they enjoy. A person who is unsuccessful may feel powerless and unable to improve their situation, while a successful person usually has more options and the confidence to continue pursuing their goals.

Being successful gives people freedom and stability. When someone is at the peak of their achievements, they can afford to make choices, protect their position, and live comfortably. This security helps them keep going and maintain good conditions in their career or personal life. However, staying successful for a long time can sometimes bring risks. If a person repeats the same routine without change, they may become tired or careless. Complacency can lead to mistakes or a drop in performance, and even a strong career can weaken if the person stops paying attention.

At the same time, early failures can push some people to become stronger. When someone faces setbacks at the beginning, they may gain determination and work harder to improve. Over time, that effort can turn previous failures into future successes. In conclusion, while failure can teach lessons, I still believe success is more valuable overall, and avoiding the discouragement that comes from repeated failure is important.

Students should be expected to choose a career path by the time they start high school. Knowing their intended field helps them understand how long their studies will take and what they must do to graduate. If pupils pick a career early, they can concentrate on the right subjects and move through high school more efficiently. Early choice also allows them to prepare for the college or training they will need later.

First, students can estimate how long they will spend in education when they know their career goal. This helps them plan so they do not stay in school longer than necessary. Many young people prefer to finish their studies quickly because they want to begin working, and having a clear career aim can support that desire. Knowing the graduation requirements for their chosen path prevents wasted time and unnecessary courses.

Second, choosing a career early helps students focus while they are still in school. When teenagers understand what careers they are aiming for, they tend to put more effort into relevant classes. They have the chance to study specific subjects that match their future jobs, which makes learning more purposeful. This focused preparation also means they will be better ready when they enter college or vocational training.

Third, a specific career plan allows high school students to gain skills and knowledge that match their future studies. This preparation benefits them later because they do not have to spend as much time deciding on a direction at college. If a student builds a foundation in high school, they can make faster progress in higher education and may avoid extra semesters.

Some professions require long-term practice and advanced study, but starting that preparation in high school reduces the overall time needed later. Working on skills early can make later training shorter and less difficult.

In conclusion, students are expected to choose a career when entering high school because it clarifies how long they will study, helps them focus, and readies them for further education. For these reasons, deciding on a career at a young age is beneficial.

Summer should be a normal time for people, especially students, to relax and enjoy life. It is a season to spend with family and friends, doing fun activities like shopping, swimming, and going on vacation. Because winter returns after a few months, summer feels short, so it is important to make time for people you care about. Of course, some cannot enjoy summer fully because they must work or handle important responsibilities.

Many people think summer is one of the best seasons because the weather is warm, not cold. The beach becomes a favorite place to play and relax. There are many things to do in summer: you can play in the water, go camping, or take hikes. You might visit another state, spend a night at a friend’s house, or simply hang out with cousins, aunts, and uncles. Children often enjoy the break from school; they stay home, play video games, or spend long days outside with their friends.

Summer can mean staying at home or going out for adventures. Trees and flowers grow more in the warm months, and fruit often appears on trees. In contrast, when winter comes many leaves fall and the weather becomes cold. Summer returns every year, giving us chances to visit relatives or travel out of town to see older family members. Sometimes summer brings heavy rain, since warm weather can also cause storms, though rain can happen in other seasons too.

School closes for the summer so students can have fun and teachers can take a break as well. In some places summer temperatures can get very high, even reaching 100 degrees or more. Many people organize pool parties during the hot days. The warm season allows people to choose activities they enjoy, such as fishing, camping, or diving. Whether summer is good or bad often depends on the decisions you make and how you spend your time.

Fairs and festivals often appear in the summer, with lots of games and rides that families can enjoy together. Public pools and rivers are open for swimming and other water activities. Many families travel to popular destinations like California or Florida to relax and explore. Summer is a special time because it returns each year and gives everyone an opportunity to do things they love, whether that means resting at home or going on new adventures.

Removing students' favorite meals is a bad idea. If popular lunch choices disappear, many kids might lose interest in coming to school or at least in eating there. Offering a wider variety of options could actually make lunchtime more appealing for students instead of taking things away. It seems like a poor decision by the principal.

Some students may dislike school meals because they are not prepared well, or because of visible hygiene problems like hair in the food. Cafeteria staff should wear hairnets during both morning and afternoon shifts to prevent that. Also, fruit such as bananas that look spoiled should be thrown out, and any items past their sell-by date must be removed for safety.

Most children care mainly whether the food tastes good. Snacks like chips are especially popular and should not be banned, since many students prefer them to the main dishes. In short, it would be better to keep the familiar foods available and improve quality and variety so students can enjoy their lunches.

I agree that keeping busy helps us achieve more. People who stay active tend to develop useful routines. Constant effort builds productive habits, and on the path to success there is little room for those who choose laziness.

When we keep our attention on tasks and regularly take action, good habits form naturally. These habits make studying, learning, and working feel more natural and less stressful. Things become easier because the routine supports progress. Others will notice this steadiness and often respond with respect and trust. In short, disciplined habits help shape an effective way of working.

Regular activity is also essential for real achievement. For example, a restaurant cannot serve good food without careful preparation; the same is true for people. No one becomes an excellent doctor, architect, or anything else valuable without focused practice and effort. Hard work is the key that opens the door to success, and steady action is the method that gets you there.

Success and laziness rarely appear together. If we allow ourselves to become idle or content too soon, results will be poor. Employers and colleagues are unlikely to depend on someone who avoids effort, because such a person usually produces little. We should avoid thinking that inactivity has any real purpose; complacency is the enemy of improvement. Instead, we should keep pushing ourselves and stay committed to learning and doing.

A good process leads to good results, and the habit of working consistently creates that process. The road to achievement is not marked by the footprints of those who gave up or did the least. As Thomas Jefferson warned, we should resolve not to be idle, since a great deal can be accomplished when we keep moving.

I think specialized high school programs are a good idea for students because they help us figure out what we want to study before we finish high school. Having extra time to explore different fields lets us make better choices for the future. For example, I want to become a pilot, so attending a school with aviation-related classes would let me pick subjects connected to flying and learn basic skills for handling an airplane.

However, not every school offers these kinds of programs, and many students cannot attend them. Some schools are far away or hard to reach, and not all families have a way to travel there every day. If you drive yourself it is easier, and getting a ride sometimes helps, but not everyone has that option regularly. That makes access a real problem for some students.

I also believe that deciding on a career early can be useful because it may allow students to complete their education more quickly. Being focused on a specific path helps you take the right courses and graduate sooner.

Another advantage is that these schools give you a clearer idea of what to study in college and can open up more chances for internships and practical experience. At the same time, many of these programs require good grades to get in and to keep your place in the classes. If your grades are not high enough, you might not be accepted.

In short, students need to be ready and work hard. If you prepare well and meet the requirements, you can go on to a strong university and follow your dreams.

Thomas Jefferson wrote about his firm decision never to be idle. I agree with this idea because being active and useful matters for people and for society. One problem today is that young people sometimes show little respect for older people. This lack of respect is visible in many places, including schools.

For example, students often become bored or disruptive when a teacher talks about a serious subject. They may laugh or ignore the lesson when it is not meant to be entertaining. Jefferson’s example can encourage people to act differently: instead of wasting time or being cruel, we should help others, especially those who are innocent or vulnerable.

We can reduce these problems if we work together. When people in a community support each other, it becomes easier to stop disrespectful or harmful behavior. If someone tries to put you down, do not pay attention to them; keep working toward your goals. Jealous people may try to block others because they do not want anyone to succeed more than themselves. That is unfair, because everyone has different talents and dreams and must work hard for what they want.

In my opinion, groups of people can stand up against those who put others down and encourage helpful behavior. Some people do not like to help others, and this makes the situation worse. But as a community we can teach cooperation and change those attitudes so that more people follow Jefferson’s idea of not being idle and of helping when it is needed.

Today I want to discuss Ralph Waldo Emerson's idea that remaining true to yourself in a world that often pressures you to be someone else is one of the greatest achievements.

I agree with this statement. Choosing to be yourself is hard, especially when you feel alone. Trying to fit a role that doesn't suit you can become exhausting if you have no one supporting you. On the other hand, having friends or family who encourage you makes staying authentic easier. Still, even with help, it takes effort and courage to keep your identity when so many forces push you to change.

Being yourself becomes even more difficult around negative people. Critics or those who do not accept your choices can make you doubt yourself and try to pull you away from what you truly are. That is why holding on to who you are feels like a real accomplishment: it requires resisting pressure, ignoring negativity, and trusting your own values.

For example, when you follow your own path and succeed, some people may feel threatened or jealous and try to undermine you. In a world like that, not giving in to those attempts to make you conform is an important victory. If your circle accepts you for who you are, life is easier because you don't have to pretend or change to gain approval. But even when acceptance is rare, staying genuine helps you make better decisions. When your choices come from your true self, they are more likely to be right for you.

In short, being yourself despite societal pressure is a significant achievement because it takes strength, support, and clear judgment to remain honest with who you are.

Many families already struggle with timing. Some teachers and students live far from school, sometimes in places like Generic_City, so they spend a long time commuting. If school finishes later, parents may have to wait longer at soccer or football games, and students will get home very late. After a longer day, they still need to do homework, so evenings would become shorter and more stressful. Right now we wake up early and often return home around 5–6 pm; adding more school time would push everything later and make it difficult to keep up with daily tasks.

When I stayed after school, I sometimes didn’t get home until 7–8 pm, which made it hard to finish homework and get enough rest. Making school longer would make this worse for those who live far away and already have tight schedules. It would be much harder to balance classes, activities, and homework.

Adding time to the school day could also mean more homework. If we get only an extra half hour at school, teachers might assign more work, and students would still end up spending additional hours studying at home. Teachers who live far away would also face longer days: they would arrive home late because of rush-hour traffic around 6 pm, then need to grade papers and prepare lessons, and be up early again the next day. That routine would be exhausting for both staff and students.

If the goal is to reduce stress, a better solution would be to adjust school start times instead of lengthening the day. Starting school an hour later, for example, would let everyone wake up later and finish earlier, making evenings more relaxed. This change would help students and parents be less tired and make it easier to attend after-school activities.

Another concern is lunch time. As eighth graders, we eat at 1:40 pm now; if school hours shift later, lunch could be moved to around 2:10 pm, which would leave many students hungry and less able to concentrate. Later dismissal would also affect bus drivers and families who rely on the current schedule. Bus drivers need time for their routes and for their own lives, and parents also depend on fixed pickup times. Making school longer would create problems for them too.

Overall, extending school hours would cause more problems than it solves. It would interfere with family routines, make commutes worse, increase homework pressure, and leave less time for rest and activities. Keeping the current schedule or changing start times would be a better way to support students, families, and teachers.

This text discusses how first impressions often change over time. Its purpose is to explain what makes an initial opinion shift and how that shift can affect us. The essay gives examples and supporting ideas to help the reader understand the topic and shows that impressions are not fixed.

A first impression is the immediate view we form when we meet a person or encounter something new. It is the first judgment our mind produces, but it can be revised as we learn more. When we meet someone for the first time, the image we get might be true or it might be misleading; only time and further contact can reveal the whole truth.

Changes in first impressions can be harmful or helpful. For example, a car may look attractive on the outside, but a mechanic’s inspection might reveal serious problems inside. This is an impression that turns from good to bad. On the other hand, you might hear negative comments about someone and expect them to be unpleasant; after talking to that person, you may find the accusations were wrong and your view improves.

Several factors cause first impressions to change. They include incorrect information, disappointment, strong emotions such as anger, and later reflection. Emotions can make everything seem worse than it really is; when we are angry, small faults catch our attention more. Reflection or rethinking also helps us correct earlier beliefs once we get more facts or calm down.

In conclusion, first impressions are important but not always reliable. Opinions often shift with more experience and information. For that reason, it is better to wait a little before forming a final judgment about a person or thing, because impressions usually change over time.

When someone asks for advice, it is often because they are unsure which way to go or which decision to make.

A bad choice can change a person's life for the worse. It can affect the people closest to them, like a spouse or children. Making the wrong decision or following bad advice can lead to criminal actions and prison. Spending years behind bars can ruin relationships; not being able to see your mom, dad, or kids for a long time is painful and can cause deep sadness.

On the other hand, choosing wisely helps you avoid serious trouble, including federal charges. Good decisions set a better example for your children and improve their chances for a stable future. If you listen to someone who gives sound advice, it can protect both you and your family from hardship, so they do not have to watch you from a prison visiting area.

I say this from experience: I have seen how choosing the wrong friends and listening to the wrong people can harm your family. At the same time, many problems can be fixed if they are small—sometimes it’s just a ticket, a fine, or a minor charge that can be resolved. The key is not to make choices that lead to big trouble. Think about what is best for you and your family, not about what others want you to do.

People you trust can also hurt you by stealing from you, betraying you, or turning against you. My mother used to tell me, “A friend is like a dollar in your pocket, and your pocket has a hole.” That saying reminds me to follow my own judgment and not rely on others who might lead me into trouble.

If you make the right choices, you can go to college, earn a degree in a field you enjoy, and find a good job. That can lead to a stable home, a reliable car, and enough money for emergencies. You may be able to help your parents, give your kids what they need, and avoid the hard struggles many people face just to put food on the table. Choosing carefully matters for you and everyone who depends on you.

Have you ever been told by a teacher to stay after class to finish your work? I believe that offering after-school clubs would be very helpful because they support students’ schoolwork. These clubs can help pupils complete tasks more quickly and understand lessons more clearly. Many children do not enjoy doing homework at home, but if they take part in fun after-school activities, they might be more willing to finish their assignments so they can join the activities.

First, sitting alone doing homework can be boring, but working on tasks during an active club makes learning more interesting. When students are involved and enjoying themselves, they often finish work faster and with less struggle. For example, if a student loves sports and knows they must finish their homework before joining practice, they are likely to hurry and complete it. Today many children prefer learning through games like math challenges, card games, or other interactive exercises. In these settings teachers can also give clearer explanations, which helps students understand the material better.

Second, adults should help students see that schoolwork matters so they will take it seriously and improve their grades. Some young people do not always focus on homework, so a bit of encouragement and structure from teachers or coaches can make a real difference. Having someone check on progress and push students to keep going prepares them for future responsibilities. When learning is part of an engaging activity, students are less likely to give up and more likely to stay motivated than if they were stuck in a quiet room alone.

Finally, putting effort into assignments is essential for understanding and completing them well. If students do not work at their school tasks, they will struggle with harder assignments later. Students should remember to keep trying and not give up on their goals. For these reasons, I think after-school activities would be a good idea for our schools and would help many students succeed.

High school students should be allowed to finish in three years instead of the usual four. With extra effort—such as taking summer classes or evening lessons—many students can complete their requirements sooner. Graduating earlier gives them the option to start working a year sooner or to begin college ahead of schedule. Finishing high school in three years helps students enter the workforce earlier, save money for further study, and reach their life goals sooner.

First, it is realistic for motivated students to complete high school in three years. Some students enroll in summer classes or take additional courses in the evenings to earn the necessary credits more quickly. Others may choose to skip certain elective classes and focus only on required subjects. By using these strategies, students can meet graduation requirements before the fourth year begins. Completing high school early gives them extra time to plan and pursue the next steps in their education or career.

Second, graduating a year early allows students to join the workforce sooner. Many young people want to save money for college fees or personal expenses. If they finish high school in three years, they can spend the extra year working and accumulating savings. This financial cushion can reduce stress when they start college and help them concentrate on their studies rather than worrying about tuition or living costs. In this way, early graduation can make higher education more affordable and manageable.

Third, finishing school early helps students achieve their goals earlier in life. For example, those who aim for a particular career can begin training, internships, or college studies sooner and gain a head start on their professional development. Early success often creates more opportunities: once one goal is reached, students have time and experience to pursue other ambitions. As a result, graduating in three years can lead to a more secure and satisfying future.

Some opponents argue that a three-year plan prevents students from taking elective courses that broaden their knowledge. While this concern is valid, it does not outweigh the benefits. Students who forgo some electives still gain valuable time to work, save money, or start college sooner. They can also pursue broader interests later, after they have achieved their initial goals and have more flexibility.

In summary, completing high school in three years is a sensible option for dedicated students. By taking extra classes or prioritizing required courses, they can graduate early, earn money sooner, and reach their career goals faster. For these reasons, a three-year high school pathway should be available to those who choose it.

Some teachers and adults expect students to choose a career path by the time they start high school. They believe young people should already know what they want to do. However, I think that deciding on a career so early is not realistic for many students, and I will explain why.

First, plenty of teenagers are already responsible for supporting themselves. They may work to pay rent, phone bills, and other living costs. Balancing a job with schoolwork leaves them little time or energy to explore career options. Working students must study, complete homework, and meet their employers’ demands, which is a heavy load. For these young people, adding extra career-focused classes or activities can be overwhelming.

Another important point is that many students lack support. Some cannot afford the materials, courses, or extra help needed to learn about a particular field. While a few are lucky enough to have family, friends, or mentors who offer guidance, others are left without help. Unfortunately, teachers and adults sometimes decide a student is "not ready" and do not give them chances to try. This prevents students from showing they can handle responsibility and make thoughtful choices about their future.

Many teenagers are already struggling with the day-to-day demands of their education and personal life. Some are trying their best even while facing problems at home, and they may become exhausted and think about quitting school. Despite these challenges, many continue to work hard to prepare for their future. Still, asking them to pick a career at such a young age adds pressure when they might simply need time to grow and gain experience.

High school students are still learning about life and responsibility. Expecting them to make a major decision like choosing a career ignores how new many adult tasks feel to them. If they are required to focus on a specific career path, they may have to take more classes and manage more responsibilities than other students, which can be stressful and harmful to their overall learning.

Finally, some teenagers are distracted by social issues and personal image. Instead of concentrating on their studies, they may care more about making friends or fitting in, which can lead to poor choices about their education. Young people need time to mature, improve their attitudes, and understand how hard work and good grades affect their future. Rushing them into a career choice can prevent that natural development.

People may disagree and say some students are ready to decide early. But in my view, it is not a good idea to push most young teens toward a fixed career. It is difficult, stressful, and unfair to expect them to take on such a heavy responsibility before they have had time to grow and gain experience.

A few years ago, before my uncle finished medical school, I watched him suffer frequent anxiety attacks because of the heavy study load. He soon realized that he needed other activities to break up his routine and reduce stress. I believe every student should take part in at least one extracurricular activity, such as playing sports, joining a book club, or doing community service. If more students took part in these kinds of activities, their lives could become richer and less stressful, offering varied experiences and better well-being.

Joining a sport is especially useful for a student's physical health. Many pupils spend most of the day sitting in class and then continue to sit at home doing homework or relaxing. The human body needs regular movement to stay healthy, and exercise supports growth and development in teenagers. Playing sports can change how you feel and improve your fitness, and even short daily activity — as little as twenty minutes — can make a real difference.

Book clubs are another enjoyable option that helps the mind unwind. Sometimes you just need a mental break, and reading is perfect for that. Books can take you to faraway places or into completely imagined worlds without leaving your chair. They offer adventure, drama, romance, and new ideas that you might never encounter otherwise. In a book club, you can share your thoughts about what you read and meet others who feel the same way, which makes reading more social and rewarding.

Taking part in community service benefits both the community and the volunteer. You might wonder how helping others could help you, but volunteering teaches cooperation, builds a sense of responsibility, and brings satisfaction from making a positive impact. It can also be useful academically, because some schools offer credit or scholarships for students who contribute to their communities. If you have never tried volunteering because it seems boring, consider giving it a chance as your extracurricular choice.

All students should pick an activity outside school hours so their minds and bodies get a useful break. Any positive pastime can help you relax and recharge. Find something you enjoy and use the time after school to take part fully in it.

Many people enjoy taking on challenges, including learning new languages. There are about 67 major languages spoken worldwide, and nearly 9% of the population speaks Vietnamese. It is often listed among the ten most difficult languages to learn. I am lucky to speak Vietnamese fluently, and that ability lets me do many useful things: translate between English and Vietnamese, teach friends, and communicate with native speakers.

Because I can switch between Vietnamese and English, I often act as an interpreter. This skill is especially handy on family trips. For example, I usually help my mother whenever we travel because she does not understand English. Being able to translate makes outings much smoother and less stressful for her.

My friends are also interested in Vietnamese and often ask me to teach them. When I enter the classroom, some of them greet me with "Xin chào," which means "hello." I enjoy seeing their enthusiasm. I even taught an American friend who, after some practice, now speaks Vietnamese almost as naturally as his native language.

Knowing Vietnamese is particularly useful in places with many Vietnamese speakers. If you can ask for help in their language, people are more likely to respond and appreciate your effort—sometimes they think it's very impressive. I remember once during a family reunion in Vietnam I got separated from my parents. I tried calling for help in English, but no one understood me. Fortunately, I could speak Vietnamese and asked where the nearest police station was, which helped me find them.

In short, learning Vietnamese is a rewarding challenge. It can open doors when you visit Vietnam and is a valuable skill for helping family and making friends.

Thomas Jefferson once warned against idleness, saying that steady action can accomplish a surprising amount. I agree with this idea because, while some things in life may happen easily, most achievements require effort and persistence. To go far, you must keep working toward your goals instead of waiting for success to come by itself.

First, getting what you want in life usually means putting in the work. Tasks do not finish themselves, and progress rarely happens without effort. Jefferson’s message reminds us that constant activity and focus are key to completing what needs to be done. When you make work a habit, you are much more likely to reach your aims.

Second, avoiding laziness matters for long-term benefits. If you take responsibilities lightly or postpone important tasks, problems tend to build up and become harder to solve later. By staying busy and doing what must be done, life becomes easier over time because you prevent crises and create steady forward movement. Jefferson’s words encourage people to push themselves and stay productive so they can achieve their ambitions.

Finally, the quote also points out a truth about life: things are not free and actions have consequences. The results we enjoy usually reflect the effort we invested. Being thankful for what you have should come with awareness of the work behind it, not from idleness. For someone who needs motivation, this idea can be powerful—reminding them that effort matters and can change their situation.

In conclusion, Jefferson’s warning against idleness is a helpful reminder that steady action leads to real results. It shows that working consistently is often the easiest way to finish tasks and reach goals, while doing nothing rarely brings success. I support this view because it teaches how to live in order to achieve and grow, and it can inspire people who need a nudge to keep going.

"Hey, I had so much fun reading this book with you," a younger student said. Little kids often look up to older students because they make learning exciting and enjoyable. Some schools run a program that pairs younger and older pupils together, and this can be helpful for both partners. They can discover new things, and older students can learn how to support a child and hear honest opinions the younger ones might not share in front of a teacher.

One benefit of the program is that both students can learn things they did not know before. Younger children can show older students how they say certain words or explain the topics they are curious about. Meanwhile, the older students can go over what they are studying in class and help the younger ones understand it better. This kind of exchange becomes a small agreement between them that helps both improve.

Another advantage is that older students get practice that is useful for future jobs. They learn how to guide, teach, and manage a child’s questions and attention. The younger child also teaches the older one in their own way, which builds a strong connection. Sometimes these relationships last many years, and later on the two might meet and recognize each other, remembering who helped whom.

A final way the program helps is by encouraging children to share their thoughts. Many students feel shy speaking up in front of a class, but in a one-on-one setting they are more likely to express their opinions. This helps them explain themselves better and feel more at ease.

I support a midnight curfew for weekends, but I do not agree with a 10 p.m. curfew on weekdays.

Young people under 18 already face many limits, yet they also have real duties to themselves and their families. Teenagers need education, a stable home, and money to meet their needs.

Education is essential, from primary school through high school. In five to ten years these students will be the workers and citizens who help the economy and support the next generation. Interrupting their ability to study or work now could harm their future prospects.

A safe home is also important. Teenagers need a place where they can rest and feel protected. Home should be somewhere they are cared for, where parents or guardians may correct them when necessary, but always with their well-being in mind.

Money matters a great deal for many teenagers. To earn it, they often take part-time or weekend jobs, which means they use their free hours after school to work. This is where a strict 10 p.m. weekday curfew becomes unfair: if a student works from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. there is no problem, but if their shift runs later and overlaps a curfew, they could be wrongly treated as breaking the law. Such interference from the city can be unjust when young people are simply trying to support themselves or their families.

In short, today’s children will become tomorrow’s adults. They need a secure home, time to earn money, and uninterrupted access to education to build a better future.
