People everywhere form quick judgments, and those first impressions are difficult to take back. At a glance someone can create an idea, feeling, or opinion about another person. Those snap judgments often wound people because thoughtless words are said without considering the consequences. Even when someone later tries to apologize, it can be too late. Because first impressions can hurt feelings and change relationships, they are usually very hard to reverse.

First impressions hurt feelings — I have seen this happen to me. Yesterday my sister and I were planning her wedding next April and searching online for dresses. She is like a second mother to me, and I want her to be radiant on her day. When she found a gown I did not like, my immediate reaction was to say it looked ugly and that, because she is slim, it would make her look like a skeleton. I did not mean to be cruel; I only wanted her to wear something beautiful. Still, I spoke without thinking and hurt her. I apologized, but she was upset for a while and stopped talking to me. Eventually she forgave me and we are friends again, but the damage I caused with a single careless comment showed me how hard it can be to undo a first impression.

Another time, at a birthday party for a friend, one of her acquaintances insulted me in front of others, calling me ugly and slow. Her words made me leave the party and feel sad. She later came to my house and apologized, saying she had spoken without thinking, but by then I had already felt the pain of being judged. Although we made up, the initial impression she gave to the group had affected how I felt and how I behaved that night. This shows how quickly a first impression can sting and how an apology does not always erase the hurt.

First impressions can also change people’s behavior toward each other. I once told my best friend that her boyfriend did not love her because I saw him kissing someone at school. She accused me of jealousy and stopped talking to me. In fact, I had been mistaken — it was his twin brother I had seen. My rash judgment harmed our friendship. Even after I explained and apologized, our relationship was not the same; she felt betrayed and kept her distance. This example proves that a single wrong idea can alter a friendship for a long time.

Some people argue that first impressions are easy to fix and that most people do not mind being judged at first. I disagree. Even if someone apologizes, the initial hurt or doubt can remain, especially with people who are sensitive or slow to forgive. First impressions may be corrected in some cases, but often they leave a lasting mark.

In conclusion, first impressions are hard to change because words once spoken are difficult to retract and mistakes are not always forgettable. People have different views about whether failure is part of achieving success. Some believe that failing helps us reach our goals, while others think failure does not contribute to success. I agree with the first view: failure is an important step on the road to success.

When we fail, we learn how to get back up. Trying things we have never done before often involves mistakes, but those mistakes teach us what to change. Big failures can lead to important lessons, and failing once usually means we need to try again with a new plan. Life is full of setbacks, but they do not mean we will never succeed. Instead, each failure gives a chance to correct errors and improve.

Failures also affect our thinking. It is easy to let negative thoughts take over—feeling guilty, useless, or unable to do something. But behind those feelings there is usually an opportunity waiting. We must focus on positive ideas and believe in our skills. Worrying about what others think is not helpful; we are responsible for our own actions. We can ask for support from family, teachers, friends, or other people, but in the end we must lead ourselves toward success.

I had a personal example with a biology SOL exam. I took the test four times before I finally passed. It was difficult and I disliked the process, but I kept going. That experience taught me not to lose determination or avoid responsibility. Instead, I strengthened my approach and kept my goals in mind.

Failing a test can show us what was on the exam, suggest better strategies, and point to useful resources like a dictionary. For these reasons, failure plays a real role in reaching success. Some argue that repeated failure only shows they cannot succeed, but I believe each failure can be used to grow and eventually win.

Success is something many people value most in life. As Winston Churchill observed, real success means moving from one failure to another without losing enthusiasm. I agree with this idea because setbacks often play a crucial role on the path to achievement. True success comes from persistent effort to reach one’s goals, and for most people those goals include doing well at school and finding a dream job.

Finishing school is a major milestone, and for some it is especially difficult to accomplish. Passing exams can be a struggle, so students must study hard to advance and eventually graduate. For example, someone who moves to a new country and does not speak the language may fail subjects such as English, history, or science at first. That person will probably keep trying, learning from each mistake until they improve. When a student gets a poor mark, they can identify what went wrong and prepare differently for the next test. In this way, failure teaches them how to study better and be more ready the next time.

Many people find work they enjoy, but others have to fight longer for their dream career. Some never give up. Take the case of a young man who wanted to be a dancer while his father refused to support him. He left home with almost nothing and no money for training, yet he did not abandon his dream. He opened a small dance workshop to earn money for classes and gradually built a reputation. Today he is known as one of India’s top dance choreographers, Remo D’Souza. Similarly, job seekers often face different paths: some get a position on their first interview, while others must improve their skills and try again until they succeed.

In conclusion, success is what most people want, but it does not come without effort. To become successful, people must learn from their mistakes and use failure as a lesson. Without experiencing setbacks, it is hard to grow and improve. Those who are successful now usually went through failures in the past, and learning from those failures helped them reach their goals.

Is it a good idea for students to finish high school in three years? Some schools let students graduate faster, but whether this is wise depends on the student. For some learners, finishing in three years is a good choice because they already know what they want to do next. For others, a shorter program can mean forgetting important material or not having enough time to decide on a future career. Elective courses and extra time in school can help students become more creative and better prepared for work or further study.

One issue is how well students retain what they learn. Many young people forget subjects quickly, especially after long breaks like summer vacation or when they stop attending classes. Some students are naturally better at remembering lessons, while others need repetition and more time to absorb information. A three-year program might suit students who can learn quickly and keep the knowledge, but it can be risky for those who need more practice to really understand the subjects.

People’s interests and motivation also differ. In some school districts, required programs include classes that students are not interested in, which can make them disengaged. Other students prefer to finish early because they want to start working, avoid interruptions, or go to college sooner. Some believe they are ready to move on, while others prefer the usual length of high school to earn an advanced diploma that could open more opportunities later. In short, the value of a shorter program depends on personal goals and how committed the student is.

More time in high school gives students a chance to think carefully about their future. Those who graduate too quickly sometimes leave school without a clear plan and then struggle to find work or a direction. A few weeks or months after early graduation, they may realize they have no idea what they want to do. On the other hand, students who plan to work right away often know their path regardless of how long they spent in high school. If a student aims to graduate early, they should have a specific plan—whether it is to start a job, save money, or continue studying in college.

Elective classes are another important factor. Choosing electives like art or music can develop different skills and creativity that are useful in the workplace and everyday life. For example, art classes encourage creative thinking, and music classes can lead to performance or production opportunities. Electives give students choices beyond a standard, sometimes boring, curriculum and can help them discover interests that shape future careers.

Summer can be a good time for a break, but it also offers opportunities for additional learning, such as online courses, which may help students who worry about forgetting material. These options can support those who move through school faster and want to keep their skills fresh.

In conclusion, programs that allow high school to be completed in three years can be beneficial for students who already know what they want to do and have the ability to retain learning. However, spending the usual amount of time in high school is not bad either, since it gives students more chances to explore, learn, and plan a future career. The key is that any student choosing a faster path should have a clear plan and be confident about their goals.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea that remaining true to yourself in a world that constantly pressures you to be someone else is one of the greatest achievements. To be yourself requires courage, persistence, and faith in your own path, especially when others try to change or discourage you.

Perseverance is at the heart of staying true to yourself. Life is full of difficulties; no one lives without challenges. People who appear perfect have usually faced many struggles. Success rarely happens overnight. Those who reach their goals keep trying despite obstacles. They accept hardship, adapt, and continue until they overcome it.

Consider a soccer player who wants to score. To reach the goal, he must get past defenders, keep the ball under control, and take the right chance. Scoring requires repeated effort, not a single perfect moment.

When others mock you or tell you to give up, it can be tempting to stop. Words like “You failed,” “You are a loser,” or “Go home and sleep” are meant to hurt. But giving in to them would be accepting someone else’s judgment rather than following your own values. Failure does not mean the end. It only shows that you tried. You still have hands, legs, and a brain — tools to try again. Keep hope alive; with persistence, you can prove the doubters wrong.

Everyone has different strengths. If math is hard for you, that does not make you worthless. You might excel in social studies or another subject. Show your abilities in areas where you are strong. Not being good at one thing does not mean you cannot succeed in another.

Time is more valuable than almost anything. People who think clearly understand how to use time well. If you spend time trying and fail, do not blame time or yourself. Time offers new chances to improve. Keep working. But if you waste time through laziness, you will not get those opportunities back. Time moves forward, and lost time cannot be returned.

For example, if you do not do your homework, you will not receive a good grade. You lost the chance to learn and improve. If you did the homework but made mistakes, your teacher might give you a chance to correct it. That shows the benefit of effort and making use of time.

Inspiration from others who succeeded can guide you. Reading about how people reached their goals can motivate and teach you what to do. Success stories help you see possible paths and organize your own plan.

A well-known story about Robert the Bruce and a spider illustrates this. While hiding in a cave, the king watched a spider trying to climb a wall and failing many times. After several attempts the spider finally reached the top. This small creature’s persistence inspired Robert the Bruce to try again and eventually regain his kingdom.

Obstacles are natural. If you want to be good, you must understand what is bad. If you want to win, you must accept losing sometimes. Failure is common; it means you are trying. Don’t let failure lead to depression. Instead, ask yourself whether one more attempt might change the result. Often, one more effort is all that is needed.

Imagine digging for gold and stopping just before hitting it. If you had dug one more time, you might have found treasure. That is why it is important to keep going and think twice before quitting.

Having clear aims helps you make better decisions. People without goals often do not succeed. Create a routine and follow it. For students, it can be difficult to keep rules, but discipline makes tasks easier. Pay attention in class and finish homework on time. With consistent effort, success becomes more reachable.

Laziness is a major obstacle. Dreaming without working achieves nothing. If you do not act, your dreams will remain wishes. Work hard and use your time well.

Sometimes others try to sabotage your plans. Some people do not want you to succeed and may disturb your work. In such cases, ignore them. Do not engage; they will likely lose interest and move on.

If someone bothers you every day and you consistently ignore them, they will often stop. Your silence and steady work can make them give up.

In the end, success brings satisfaction and pride. When you achieve your goal, those who doubted you may feel ashamed because they judged you wrongly. So do not be lazy: keep working, keep trying, and think carefully about your choices. If you remain persistent and true to yourself, you will likely reach a happy ending and prove your worth to yourself and others.

Second, changing the kind of music you listen to can also help. A lot of popular songs today focus on drugs, violence, or destructive lifestyles, which can reinforce negative feelings. Listening to more encouraging or peaceful music can lift your spirits and shape a healthier outlook.

Third, joining activities that foster positivity is useful. Attending church, spending time at the movies with family, or listening to motivational talks can put you in a better frame of mind and help you forget some of the negative things happening around you.

Being positive has many benefits: it makes you feel better and can lead to success. But positivity is not always the answer. Life can be unfair, and pretending everything is fine when serious problems exist is not realistic. We must face difficulties honestly instead of only pretending that everything is okay.

Looking ahead, I hope the next generation will adopt more positive habits worldwide. If more people engage in positive activities and encourage each other, the world could begin to be seen through a more hopeful and successful lens.

Some students cannot attend school in person for a variety of reasons. They may live far away, lack reliable transportation, or have medical conditions that make regular attendance difficult. For these cases, many schools now offer the option to study from home so students can continue their education without being physically present.

To participate in home-based learning you need a computer or another device and internet access. Without these tools it is very hard to follow lessons remotely. Unfortunately, not everyone can afford the necessary equipment or a stable connection, so access remains a problem for some families.

Learning from home has both advantages and drawbacks. On the positive side, students can study the same subjects as their peers, earn an official diploma, and later apply to colleges. Home study also allows more flexibility: students can work at their own pace and organize their time as they prefer. However, gaining a degree this way does not always replace the experience of attending school in person.

One important disadvantage is the lack of social interaction. Students who study at home may miss the chance to talk and work with classmates, which can affect their communication skills and confidence. This isolation can be stressful and may lead them to feel excluded from their community. In addition, students learning remotely often cannot ask their teachers immediate questions or use the same school resources, so they must be more independent and search for answers on their own.

There are special programs designed for students with long-term health problems or disabilities. Some schools can support these students on campus, while others provide tailored home education. These programs are meant for those with legitimate needs rather than for students who simply do not want to attend school.

If you prefer to study from home, you must usually provide a valid reason and documentation, especially in public schools. Authorities will review your request before approving it. Home learning is a useful option when it is truly necessary, but it should be chosen carefully. Consider the consequences and seek solutions so you can succeed without harming your future.

Failure is a natural part of life, but keeping enthusiasm when you fall is what makes success possible. Life can be difficult and sometimes it feels impossible to get back up. However, if you stay determined and energetic, challenges become easier to handle and your future becomes less complicated. Losing once or twice does not mean the end. With a positive attitude, you will develop patience, reduce stress, and find more joy, which all help you move forward.

When you fail, many negative consequences can follow if you allow pessimism to take over. Life may seem harder than you expected, and without energy and drive it is difficult to reach your goals. For example, if your dream is to go to college, thinking negatively and being lazy will make that dream much harder to achieve. If you do not study, do not work to save money, and avoid looking for a job, you cannot reach your goal. Another example is wanting to buy a car, a house, or travel the world. You might have a job, but if you are lazy and lose your job, you will not earn the money you need. Negativity stops progress and keeps your dreams out of reach.

Enthusiasm changes how we deal with problems. It brings positive thinking, more energy, and greater patience, which reduce stress and make tasks feel less overwhelming. For instance, if your goal is to pass important school exams, a positive and eager attitude will help you study, listen carefully in class, do homework on time, and prepare for tests calmly. Even if an exam is very hard, being enthusiastic helps you focus and manage your time better. If you fail a test, it is not the end. Teachers often offer chances to study more, attend extra sessions, or retake exams, so you can improve and pass later.

Keeping your enthusiasm after setbacks leads to long-term success because you learn from mistakes and look for new possibilities. Suppose you did not graduate because you failed one required class. That is disappointing, but you have options: repeat the year, transfer to a school that supports you better, or find resources to improve in that subject. Another case is losing a job because of an accident at work. You may feel upset, but you can search for other positions, use your experience to find similar work, and show future employers how committed you are. A positive attitude and strong work ethic make employers notice and hire you.

Falling down can bring many difficulties, yet having enthusiasm helps you work hard and keep a good attitude. It is not easy to stay positive in a tough world, but people who do not give up find ways to move forward. If you let negative thoughts control you, stress grows and success becomes harder to reach. Instead, choose to stay enthusiastic, learn from failures, and keep going. This belief is exactly why I agree with Winston Churchill: maintaining enthusiasm in the face of failure is essential for success.

Many people, including pupils and educators, believe that online lessons harm both students and schools. They argue that students often do not take notes during virtual classes and that they become easily distracted from the teacher's instruction. Because of these two problems—poor note-taking and lack of focus—students are less likely to gain from online learning.

One major concern is that students may avoid writing down important information when classes are online. In a physical classroom, pupils usually make notes because the teacher is present and can see them working. When lessons happen over a screen, learners may feel no one is watching, so they might not bother to record key points. If the instructor cannot tell who is taking notes, students can be more careless about doing it. Taking notes helps students remember and understand a subject better: by writing things down, they organize ideas and can review them later. In online lessons, though, teachers have limited ways to check whether students are actually making notes, so many students might skip this helpful habit.

Another problem is that students may not pay enough attention during online lectures. In a classroom, if a student looks away from the teacher, they can miss important statements or demonstrations; the same happens in virtual classes, often to a greater degree. When a learner is distracted—by a phone, a game, or something else at home—they can lose essential information about assignments, instructions, and how to solve problems. Missing these details can be harmful: students may not understand what to do for homework, or they might be unsure how to complete tasks correctly. Attention is necessary to catch the main ideas and to learn how to apply them; without it, students are likely to feel lost and anxious when facing difficult problems.

For these reasons, online classes may not be beneficial for many students. They might neglect to write useful notes because nobody is watching them, and they may fail to concentrate on the teacher’s explanations, causing them to miss important content and instructions. From not taking notes to being easily distracted, these issues make online learning less effective, since teachers cannot always monitor students closely and learners may not take responsibility for following the lesson.

Making your own judgments is one of the most important survival skills. Everyone grows up and eventually takes responsibility for a family and its needs. You become the one who must make decisions not only for yourself but for others too.

Instincts often point your heart toward a path, and sometimes that path is wrong. But mistakes are part of the learning process.

Success is not simple; it involves adventures and setbacks on the way to reaching a goal. You will probably fail more times than you expect before you finally succeed. Achieving things on your own means listening to your instincts and following your ideas.

You might worry about whether you should get advice from experts or authorities about important matters. Life is unpredictable and not the same for everyone, so what helps one person may not suit another. You can consider expert opinions, but they may not always fit your situation.

In the end, you listen to others but make the final choice yourself. You alone are responsible for your decisions. That is why we should make our own choices: to do what feels right and to learn from life’s lessons.

Online schooling can be a good option, but it does not suit everyone. Some students do well being taught at home, while others find it too hard to manage. Virtual classes are not simple; they require self-discipline and motivation, so they are not meant for every learner.

Studying from home is very different from attending a regular school. You do not have to wake up early and you can decide when to do your work, which sounds appealing. However, once you start, you still have to get the tasks done, and that can be stressful—especially if you cannot get the help you need. Not being able to ask questions immediately makes understanding new topics much tougher.

Another problem is making up work or getting extra support after falling behind. In a normal school, teachers can explain things again, offer help, or allow students to redo assignments. At home, those chances are limited, so failing a class can be harder to recover from.

Homeschooled students also miss many parts of school life beyond lessons. They miss hanging out with friends, school dances, fire drills, and even the arguments or conflicts that happen among students. When I struggle at school, I sometimes think about dropping out or switching to online classes. Still, that isn’t the best choice for everyone—many students who try home schooling either stop or return to regular school; I would guess around 60% do.

Overall, regular school often gives a better chance to succeed because you can work with others and receive immediate help. Helping and being helped matters, and doing your best without giving up is what counts. Keep trying, and eventually you will reach your goals.

Dear Mr. Principal,

Today I want to discuss why many employers look for certain personal qualities in job candidates even when they do not have previous experience. I agree with this idea because people who lack specific skills can still be trained and become good workers.

When someone starts a new job, they often do not know everything right away and need guidance from a more experienced person, such as a manager. Employers sometimes hire people who do not have the required experience because they believe those workers can learn while on the job. For example, when I arrived in this country, I worked with my stepfather putting up roofing. At first I did not know how to do it, but I picked up the skills over time by working with him. Another example is when I worked as a cashier last summer. I had trouble with the coin values because they were different from my home country, but my restaurant manager helped me and I worked hard to improve. With support and effort, I became more confident in that role.

Many employees who learn a job are motivated to work hard because they want to understand it more deeply. Even people who already have some knowledge can learn new things from coworkers and managers. In the United States, a lot of people work long hours for the benefit of their families, not just to have a job. They know that by working hard they can give their children better opportunities and set a good example. Parents want their children to learn from their work ethic. Some workers are driven by goals such as saving money, advancing in their careers, or creating a more secure future.

Responsibility is another key quality employers look for. Being responsible helps you get hired and keeps a business running smoothly. Managers notice when employees complete tasks on time and follow instructions. I saw this in my country when a small store failed because the people hired were often late or did not do their duties. The owners could not keep the business open because staff were not reliable. Showing up on time and doing your work well is one of the simplest ways to prove you are responsible and helpful to an employer.

Patience, especially from managers, is also important. Training new people takes time, and some managers are too impatient to teach. They may feel they have other tasks and think training someone new will not be worth the effort. In contrast, many managers in restaurants and shops have a positive attitude and enjoy helping new staff learn. A patient manager can make a big difference in a new employee’s success.

In conclusion, I believe that not knowing all the tasks for a job is not a barrier if a person is responsible and willing to learn. Experience is something you gain through facing challenges and making mistakes, so being open to learning is more important than being perfect from the start.

John Lubbock, a British naturalist and politician, once wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." Does our character come from choices we make, or is it shaped by forces beyond our control? I believe we can decide what kind of people we become. We can pick traits such as being quiet, outgoing, or confident, and steer ourselves toward those qualities. Here are a few reasons I hold this view.

First, consider being quiet. Quietness is not inherently good or bad; it depends on when and how it is used. You can choose to be quiet in some situations and speak up in others. I experienced this myself in middle school. In sixth and seventh grade I hardly talked to anyone and had very few friends. That made me feel lonely, so I began to try talking to classmates more often. As a result, I made friends and felt less isolated. That change showed me that I could alter a quiet nature by making different choices in social situations.

Second, being social is another trait we can develop. Being friendly and willing to talk helps you meet people, learn new things, and broaden your view of the world. Between seventh and eighth grade I became very talkative. At times I worried I might be annoying because I talked a lot, but I also learned how to start conversations and approach others. I discovered that people change in different ways—some who were nice became moody, some who were mean became kinder, and others stayed the same. Learning this came from interacting with many people, which was something I chose to do. That experience convinced me that we can choose to become more social.

Third, consider confidence or being "over yourself." Confidence is useful, but taken too far it becomes arrogance. Some people dislike cocky behavior and call such people boring or unpleasant. I admit I was a bit cocky and overly competitive in sports. When I scored or won, I sometimes shouted with excitement without thinking. Looking back, I realize I could have controlled those reactions, but I often acted on impulse. Even so, I believe that with effort we can shape how confident we are and control when confidence turns into overconfidence.

In conclusion, when John Lubbock wrote that line, he was pointing to the idea that people can make choices about who they are. Based on my experiences—becoming less quiet, more social, and learning about confidence—I agree that we have the power to choose our character traits.

John Lubbock once said that your character will be what you choose to make it. I agree with this idea. People are able to shape their own character because they control how they behave, which environments they stay in, and how they react to good or bad events. Ultimately, everyone has the freedom to decide who they want to be.

No matter how difficult a situation becomes, we still have choices about our responses. We can decide to smile or to cry, to look for the positive or to focus on the negative. This ability to choose our response is central to forming our character. Even when faced with strong pressure or hardship, people can choose the attitude they adopt and the kind of person they become.

My grandmother is a clear example of this. She is 78 years old and has always been very independent. She used to say, “If I don’t do it, nobody will do it as well as I can,” and she kept a very active, energetic life. Then she suffered a severe stroke that left half of her body paralyzed and took away her voice. The doctors told us she would likely be in a wheelchair for the rest of her life. It was painful for the family to see someone so full of life suddenly so limited. For a while we were shocked and upset, but my grandmother refused to give in to despair. Even after the stroke, she kept a positive attitude and worked to make the best of her situation. Her choice to stay hopeful and to keep trying taught me that people can decide their character even in very hard times.

We also control the environments we live in to some extent. People can choose who they spend time with and can recognize when relationships are harmful. A negative environment can certainly influence behavior, but we can also change it or leave it. Knowing how surroundings affect us is part of shaping our character. We are responsible for choosing what we accept from others and how much we let their mood shape ours.

How we react to other people reveals a lot about our character. Responses can show our strengths and weaknesses, and they determine whether we seem calm or quick-tempered. Some people copy others’ behavior, but that is not truly building their own character. In the end, everyone has the right to choose the character traits they want, and it will be those choices that define them.

Requiring students to take summer classes to finish high school in three years is not a good plan. I believe this because many students may not have enough credits, some need summer jobs and would be stressed balancing work and school, and others prefer to take a year off after graduation.

First, many students simply do not have the necessary credits to graduate early. To complete all requirements in three years, they would often need to take extra courses during regular semesters or overload their schedules. That kind of pressure can cause stress and reduce their ability to do well in class. Four years gives students time to join clubs, play sports, and manage a normal class load. Those activities also help when applying to college, since they show commitment and well-roundedness. Trying to fit everything into a shorter period could leave students overwhelmed and less prepared.

Second, summer is a common time for students to work. Teenagers often rely on summer paychecks to save for a car, college, or other expenses. If summer hours are replaced with classes, students lose that chance to earn money and gain work experience. Juggling a job and summer school would leave them with less free time and more stress. For many, the summer is the only opportunity to focus on saving or supporting their families without the distraction of regular classes.

Finally, some students value a break after high school. A gap year can provide time to rest, reflect on future plans, or work full time to save money. Taking a year off can help young people recharge before the demands of college or a career. Forcing everyone to complete high school in three years removes that option and may lead to tired, less motivated students entering higher education.

In conclusion, shortening high school to three years with summer classes is not a good idea. Students might lack credits and become overloaded, lose the ability to work during the summer, and miss the chance to take a useful break before moving on to the next stage of life.

Students can gain from having the option to take classes from home because there are several valid reasons why some may prefer it. Personally, if given the choice I would rather attend school so I can meet more people, but I understand why online learning suits others.

My first reason is that some students do not feel comfortable with their school community. They might believe that classmates are unfriendly, rude, or disrespectful. In these cases, parents may support home-based learning because they worry about how outside influences could affect their child. Families sometimes fear that a child could pick up bad habits or be led into trouble if they spend time with the wrong people.

The second reason is that many learners simply prefer the routine of studying at home. They may feel judged by others at school or worry that they do not fit in, so staying home can reduce anxiety. For some students, a typical school day is overwhelming; online classes give them a quieter environment where they can focus without constant social pressure.

The third reason involves health and emotional issues. Some students have medical conditions that make attending school difficult or risky, and they might fear being mocked because of their illness. Others have experienced upsetting events at school and feel embarrassed or hurt, which makes going back to the classroom painful. Online education offers these students a way to continue their studies while avoiding situations that might worsen their condition or make them uncomfortable.

Even though I would choose to go to school, I would try to support those who pick online learning. I believe it is important to encourage people who are worried or ashamed, and to explain why being in school can be helpful when they are ready. At the same time, we should respect anyone’s decision to learn from home because both options allow students to study and progress.

In conclusion, students should be free to choose online classes if they have good reasons. Everyone has different needs, and no one should let other people’s opinions stop them from learning.

Depending on where you are, there could be deer. There are lots of dangerous things in the night that no one can see, or even some dangerous people that might harm us in the night. There are a lot of bad things on the road at night. You as the driver could, of course, grow tired from your long drive and maybe crash. In conclusion, I see why you don't want us to go driving at 10 P.M. or even past midnight because of there being dangerous things in the night, but I do also hope that you know that we don't stay up because of random things. We're actually staying up for important things like our jobs or after school activities, and we will be very careful in the night because we know of the dangers of the night.

To the city council: I appreciate that you are trying to keep our streets safe, but I disagree with imposing a 10 P.M. weekday curfew for teenagers. Many of us have commitments after school — sports practices, club meetings, volunteer work — and others hold part-time jobs that end later in the evening. Sometimes travel delays, like traffic, mean we get home much later than planned. I understand the concern that driving late can be risky because people are tired and may not be as alert. Still, teenagers often stay awake later than many adults and are capable of managing their responsibilities. We are not out late just for fun; a lot of us are driving to important activities or returning from work, and we want to show that we can be responsible.

At the same time, I do support keeping teens off the road after midnight. Late-night hours bring particular dangers: impaired drivers are more likely to be on the road, wild animals such as deer can appear unexpectedly, and there is a greater chance of encountering people who might cause harm. Long drives can also make anyone grow sleepy and increase the risk of accidents. For these reasons, a curfew that prevents teenage driving starting at 12 A.M. seems reasonable to reduce nighttime hazards.

In conclusion, while a strict 10 P.M. weekday rule would unfairly limit many teenagers who have legitimate obligations, a midnight cutoff better balances our need to get to important evening activities with the city’s goal of protecting young drivers and others on the road. We will continue to be cautious and recognize the dangers of driving late at night.

Failure is something many of us try hard to avoid. Most people arrange their lives to stay away from situations where they might fail, while a smaller group deliberately faces challenges and treats mistakes as ways to learn. Those who choose the latter often gain more from life.

Fear affects a large part of our decisions. We worry about how we appear, whether we made the right choice, and what will happen if things go wrong. Because of this uncertainty, people tend to split into two camps: those who play it safe and those willing to take risks. Each approach has its advantages and disadvantages.

People who prefer safety rely on what they already know and avoid new experiences that might lead to failure. Calling them “shy” is not always accurate; they simply do not want to risk making mistakes. This attitude prevents failure because they do not try new things, but it also reduces the chances of success. Examples include staying silent in class, avoiding a new sport, or not trying a new style of clothing. Their reluctance often comes from past negative experiences: saying something silly in front of others, failing at a sport, or feeling awkward at the gym. They learn to protect themselves from embarrassment, but as a result they miss many opportunities for growth.

On the other hand, people who try new things and gain experience are often remembered for their achievements. Winston Churchill is a strong example. His path to becoming Prime Minister was not smooth; his life shows many attempts and failures before success. Those who follow this approach view failure as a lesson that helps improve ideas and actions. When a mistake happens, they do not hide from it. Instead, they correct it, learn from it, and use that knowledge to avoid repeating the same error. This learning process builds confidence and enthusiasm, and in the long run it usually leads to success.

Ambition and enthusiasm push people toward their goals. For Churchill, his determination helped Britain during World War II; he kept going because he felt responsible for his country. Enthusiasm can appear in many forms: the duty of a leader, the joy of a musician, or the love of a parent. Keeping this energy depends on the person, not the size of the goal. Whether the aim is small or large, it is the person’s persistence that matters. Someone who truly wants to become president can work toward it, but a person without motivation will not even go to the gym regularly. Failures can either weaken enthusiasm or make it stronger, depending on how the individual responds.

My own experience with martial arts shows how useful failure can be. I taught myself to use two nunchaku at once. Because I am right-handed, training my left hand was painful. I hit my forearm many times until the skin was red after an hour of practice. People asked why I kept going instead of giving up, but my goal—to master the nunchaku—kept me working. After months of practice, my control improved. I am not a master yet, but now I rarely hurt myself during practice.

Some failures are more serious and can make it impossible to try again, such as situations where people are seriously injured or die. But even after tragedies, people can recover and become stronger. I remember a boy who loved doing bike tricks. After a car accident he lost a leg and spent months in a wheelchair. Doctors fitted him with a prosthetic leg and after long rehabilitation he wanted to ride again. He failed many times at first and felt angry, but he did not give up. Eventually he returned to performing tricks and now rides like he did before the accident. His determination inspired me.

I agree with Winston Churchill: we must fail in order to learn and enjoy our achievements. We should practice not until we can sometimes get it right, but until we cannot get it wrong. Having a clear goal and the enthusiasm to pursue it helps us grow stronger after each failure. We can stay comfortable and avoid mistakes, or we can face failure and gain the experience that leads to real success.

To begin with, some companies have moved to a four-day workweek with longer days, and now there are plans for schools to provide only two hours of classes per week. This change would bring several problems: lesson time would be cut drastically, teachers’ pay would be reduced and based on hours worked, and the wider economy could suffer.

I believe schools should not shorten the school day just to save energy. Students need a full day of lessons—about eight hours—to cover the required material. With only two hours of instruction each week, teachers would not have enough time to teach the curriculum properly, and students’ learning would be seriously disrupted.

A second concern is teachers’ income. If pay is shifted to an hourly system tied to such small amounts of classroom time, many teachers would see much smaller paychecks. Those teachers might have to find extra work to make ends meet, which could reduce the quality of education even further because they would have less time to prepare and mark work.

Finally, cutting working hours across schools and businesses to save energy could hurt the economy. Many people rely on steady pay to meet expenses like loans, insurance and food. Reducing hours could leave families struggling to afford basics and could push up prices for necessities.

In conclusion, while saving energy is important, reducing school hours and cutting people’s work time in this way would damage both education and the economy. Employers and policymakers should seek solutions that do not harm students or workers.

I believe a youth curfew is a good idea and should be put in place for several reasons. First, most teenagers attend school on weekdays and only stay out late when it is a holiday or they are sick. Setting a reasonable bedtime on weeknights would help keep many young people off the streets late at night, where there is no need for them to be. A 10 p.m. curfew on weekdays seems sensible: it encourages students to be home at a safe hour, reduces the chance of running into trouble, and lowers the risk of becoming victims of crimes that often happen late at night.

Another important point is that many crimes, including violence and drug-related activity, tend to happen after dark. If teenagers are required to be home earlier, the opportunity for them to encounter criminals would decline. There are a lot of people who sell drugs at night, and keeping youths off the streets would reduce their chances of being exposed to or drawn into drug use. An earlier curfew could therefore protect them from dangerous influences and situations.

If a curfew law were adopted, the times I suggest are reasonable: Monday through Friday a 10 p.m. limit, and on Saturday and Sunday a midnight limit. These hours are fair and allow young people time to socialize without staying out too late. If someone is out past curfew, there should be a clear and serious reason for it, such as an emergency. The rule would not stop normal activities but would set a sensible boundary to improve safety. I agree that the law should target those under 18 rather than adults; once people are legally adults they should be responsible for their own choices and able to decide right from wrong.

The purpose of a curfew is not to punish, but to protect the community and keep teenagers safer. Of course, laws cannot change the behavior of every individual; some teens will still make poor choices regardless of rules. Still, the curfew would reduce the number of young people in risky situations. It is not meant to prevent friends from meeting; rather, it aims to lower the number of youths exposed to street dangers at night. Many harmless accidents and violent incidents happen when it is dark, and by limiting nighttime presence on the streets we can decrease these chances.

There should be allowances for common activities like parties or sleepovers, but clear limits are necessary. I understand concerns about practical issues: for example, if teenagers attend a party on a Saturday night (when curfew is midnight) and lose track of time, arriving home at 1 a.m. could lead to police involvement. The consequences of being found out should start gently, with a warning, and increase only if disobedience continues. A fair system of penalties would avoid ruining a teenager’s future over a single mistake.

One serious worry is that breaking curfew might create a record that could affect college applications or other opportunities. Many parents and teens fear that a small legal infraction could show up on records and hurt chances of getting into a good university. That outcome would be regrettable, especially if the infraction was minor. Lawmakers would need to consider how to handle records for curfew violations so that a youthful mistake does not permanently damage a student’s prospects.

It is also worth noting that there are already restrictions for young drivers with permits, which prevent them from driving late at night. That shows there is precedent for limiting certain freedoms for safety reasons. Like any law, a curfew has pros and cons, but I believe the advantages are stronger: fewer teens in dangerous places, less chance of encountering criminals or drugs, and a safer community overall. The main downside I can think of is the risk of a permanent record for breaking curfew, which should be addressed by fair policies.

In summary, a curfew for minors would likely reduce thefts, assaults, and other crimes like sexual violence that happen more often in the dark. By keeping teenagers off the streets at risky hours, we would decrease the likelihood of harm and make communities safer. With reasonable hours, clear exceptions, and fair enforcement, such a law could protect many young people without unfairly limiting their lives.

As a student, I prefer working in a group rather than doing tasks alone. There are several reasons why group work suits me better. First, we can finish the assignment much faster because tasks are shared. Second, each person can focus on a different part, so the work is divided. Third, teammates help one another when someone struggles, which makes solving problems easier.

Working in a group does have downsides. It can be distracting at times, and people often have different ideas about how the assignment should look or what to include. These disagreements can slow progress if the team does not agree.

Now consider the benefits of working alone. The main advantage is fewer distractions, so it may be easier to concentrate. Also, the final product will follow only your ideas and style. Another plus is you can ask the teacher directly about how they want the assignment completed, which increases the chance of meeting the requirements exactly.

However, working alone has negative sides too. It usually takes more time because one person must do everything. You must rely on yourself for all parts, which can be tiring and stressful.

In the end, whether you choose group work or solo work, you will face similar issues like how much work needs to be done and how to present the ideas. For me personally, group work is better because I know I might not finish everything by myself. In a team I can be responsible for one section, and even if I do less, the assignment gets completed. That is why I prefer working in a group—teamwork makes the dream work.

I don’t think changing school lunches to healthier choices would make much difference. Even now the menu rarely becomes truly healthy, despite students asking for changes. When the cafeteria offers both healthy and unhealthy options, many pupils still pick the less nutritious choice. For example, if the two choices are pizza or rice with chicken, most students will choose pizza every time.

On the other hand, switching the lunch menu to healthier meals could be a good idea in theory. We must remember students’ different eating habits — some don’t eat at all and may go hungry during the day. If the school did decide to replace the unhealthy items, it should remove foods like pizza, hot dogs, and chicken nuggets and offer alternatives such as rice and chicken instead of fried potatoes, or a fresh pasta salad with tomatoes, onions, and spinach. There should also be options for vegans, like a vegetable burger or other plant-based meals.

However, the school should think carefully about how it spends money. Funds used for cosmetic projects, like replacing floor tiles, might be better used for more important needs than cleaning up the lunch menu. Many people seem indifferent about how poor the food quality is — it’s unpleasant but not the worst problem the school faces. Because of that, students often solve the issue themselves by bringing food from home.

In practice, changing the menu may not fix the situation. Even when students complain about the taste or quality, they still eat the school food, and many don’t take the step of bringing a meal even if they dislike it. At the same time, a lot of students already bring their own lunches so they do not have to rely on the cafeteria. So rather than spending time and money on overhauling the menu, it might be simpler for students to pack their own food if they want healthier choices.

Attending classes from home is not a good idea. I believe students do better when they go to school in person for several reasons I learned from my own experience. Online lessons are not enjoyable because you do not have a teacher right beside you to explain things when you are confused. Although a teacher may be available virtually, they are not there in person, and if you are taking courses online you often do not get immediate help. Also, many students fall off track at home — instead of studying, they wander around the internet. I strongly disagree with the idea that students benefit from taking classes at home.

Having a teacher in the classroom makes a big difference. There are times when you will have many questions about the topic the class is discussing. At school, teachers explain ideas and give examples during the lesson, which helps students understand better. In an online course it can be much harder to grasp the main point because we do not have a teacher standing next to us. We must work alone without classmates who can help. In class you can ask a friend for a quick explanation and they will usually help, but online that support is missing. To follow online lessons I had to do a lot of extra work: I watched three to five lessons each day, wrote notes for every lesson, and took many quizzes. I often read the same material three times to catch the important facts. Because of that experience I learned to be more organized and independent, but I still think students should attend school in person. Online classes should not mean taking so many notes just to understand the basic ideas.

Teachers at school also control behaviour, such as using electronics during lessons. At home, many students are on their phones or laptops while supposed to be studying, and they are not fully focused. Without a teacher’s supervision, it feels like you have the freedom to do what you want, which leads to little learning. If we pay more attention to our phones than to the course, we will not learn and might fail. Then we would have to retake the class.

I agree that online classes have some advantages for students who want to wake up later or have more time for breakfast. I am the kind of person who likes to sleep, too. But it is still our responsibility to finish work and submit it before the deadline. If you do not manage your time, you risk failing, so you must set aside time for both school and personal life.

In conclusion, I do not believe students gain from attending classes at home. It requires a lot of self-discipline to attend lessons, complete work, and meet deadlines without a teacher physically present. For these reasons, I think studying at school is better.

It feels good when someone says "thank you" or "you're welcome." Using polite words and showing good manners makes everyday life nicer for both you and the people around you. Whenever someone helps you or gives you something, always say thank you and respond with you're welcome. When you are kind and polite, others are more likely to be kind in return. Being friendly and caring spreads happiness — make others feel good, and they will often do the same for you. Also, be ready to help someone when they need it.

If you treat people with kindness and use polite phrases, they will often do the same for you. Saying thank you or yes, sir shows respect, and these small actions encourage others to respond politely. If you want others to say thank you or you're welcome to you, start by saying those words to them. Being nice is the basic rule of getting nice treatment back.

Always try to be cheerful and say something pleasant. Good manners can help you make friends. When someone helps you, tell them thank you — a few kind words might have made their whole day. For example, if someone thanks you after you help them, respond with you're welcome. Nobody likes dealing with rudeness, so if you want polite behavior from others, model it yourself. If you want help or kindness, offer it first — that encourages people to return the favor. If someone drops their things, help pick them up; they will likely thank you, and you can simply say you're welcome.

Manners and kindness tell others something positive about you. When you are paying for your groceries or making a purchase, take a moment to ask the cashier how their day is going. Small gestures, like showing interest in someone’s day, can make them feel better and more respected. Even if you do not know the person, a polite "thank you" or "you too" when someone wishes you a good day makes a difference. Avoid saying things that could hurt someone, because then they might not respond politely.

When you eat out, remember to thank the staff and consider leaving a tip if you can — this is another way to show appreciation. If a worker seems to be having a rough day, you might invite them to join you for a meal or buy them something small to brighten their mood. Little acts of kindness can matter a lot.

Always say something nice because kindness often comes back to you. Politeness and good manners improve your relationships and make life better for everyone. The more you practice them, the more you will receive them in return.

Who wants to tackle a project alone when working with others is an option? Teamwork offers many advantages: tasks often get finished faster and with better organization. Being part of a group also gives you the chance to talk things over with classmates, get useful feedback, and improve the final result.

Of course, some people prefer to work alone, and that has one clear advantage — there are no interruptions from teammates. For example, a group can be slowed down if one person does very little and spends time goofing off. That kind of distraction doesn’t happen when you handle everything yourself.

Still, there are strong reasons to choose a group. First, a team can complete assignments more quickly than a single person. Imagine you have a short-answer task due in a week plus a slideshow to prepare. Given the choice, I would pick a group every time because you can split the work and meet the deadline more easily.

Second, working with others creates opportunities to discuss ideas and receive comments from peers. Group members can point out strengths and weaknesses in each other’s work, helping everyone improve their contributions.

Another major benefit is the variety of ideas a group brings. Instead of relying on only your own thoughts, you get many perspectives. Even when opinions differ, combining them often leads to stronger, more creative outcomes.

Whether it's a school assignment or a project in a business setting, working with a group is generally more advantageous than working alone. The shared effort, feedback, and range of ideas usually lead to better and faster results.

Keeping teenagers off the streets at night is important for several reasons. Implementing a rule that requires young people to be home by 10 pm would benefit them academically, socially, medically and economically.

First, such a curfew would likely improve school performance. When teenagers are not allowed to roam the streets late at night, they can get more rest and be more alert in class. If they use those hours for schoolwork instead of staying out, their grades should improve. Overall, limiting late-night outings would support their learning and help them recover energy for the next day.

Second, curfews can make it easier for teenagers to build better social relationships. Young people seen on the streets late at night may be viewed with suspicion, and others might avoid them because they seem risky or involved in trouble. By staying at home during night hours, teens are less likely to be judged or feared by neighbors and peers. This could lead to more positive interactions in safe settings, where it is easier to meet people and communicate without the stigma of hanging around at night. In this way, reducing late-night street presence can help teens form healthier social connections.

Third, there are clear health and safety advantages. Being out late increases the chance of encountering dangerous situations, including fights or assaults that may cause serious injuries. If teenagers are required to stay home after a certain hour, they will be less exposed to potential violence and less likely to end up in emergency care. A curfew can therefore reduce the risk of harm and protect teenagers from avoidable medical problems.

Finally, curfews can have economic benefits. If teens want to be out late, they might look for legitimate nighttime work or other lawful activities that keep them occupied and help them earn money. Having a job or taking part in productive evening programs offers a constructive alternative to idling on the streets and can teach responsibility. Earning and saving money also prepares young people for future needs and emergencies, which is an important part of becoming independent.

For all these reasons, imposing a nighttime curfew for teenagers is a sensible measure. It can help them do better at school, improve their social life by reducing negative perceptions, protect them from physical harm, and encourage productive economic habits. Overall, keeping teens off the streets after 10 pm supports their well-being and development.

Do people gain confidence from their successes or from praise? Some believe students must already be self-assured to learn, while others argue confidence grows after accomplishments. I agree with the first view: confidence should come before achievement. Without a basic sense of self-belief, it is hard to try new things, work steadily, or face challenges. I will explain this with a few examples.

First, having confidence is necessary to keep learning and improving. Many careers require continuous study; take doctors, for instance. Medical professionals must keep updating their knowledge because new illnesses and treatments appear all the time. Similarly, learning a new language is difficult and never truly finished. A Spanish speaker studying English will find that words do not always match neatly between languages. Knowing you will keep learning day by day builds confidence, even if you will never know every word. That inner assurance motivates you to study and improve, which eventually leads to real progress.

Second, a positive and confident attitude helps you complete tasks and perform under pressure. Anger or panic makes it hard to focus, but calm confidence keeps you working toward a goal. For example, when final exams or standardized tests like the SOL approach, students who keep coming to class and preparing, even on tough days, are more likely to remember what they studied. Long-term preparation makes exam day feel manageable. If you have studied consistently, you will feel ready when the test arrives and be more likely to succeed.

Third, confidence means feeling sure about how you will act in new situations. When going to a job interview, you cannot predict everything that will happen, but showing self-assurance helps others believe you can do the work. Employers prefer candidates who appear ready and composed. If you let fear control you, interviewers will notice, and you may lose the opportunity even if you could have done the job well.

Some people argue the opposite: confidence grows after you achieve something. They say that success brings satisfaction and increases self-belief. There is truth in this. Passing an important test after months of study gives a strong sense of accomplishment. Teachers may spend many weeks preparing students for exams, and when the tests are over, students often feel relieved and proud. Passing a driving test is another example: if you pass on the first try, your confidence rises because you proved to yourself that you can do it. Even when people fail, the act of trying and eventually succeeding can strengthen confidence. Positive people often think they will learn and improve and keep trying until they succeed. The story of learning to walk shows this clearly: as a child you fall many times, but persistence leads to independence and belief in yourself.

Despite these valid points, I still believe confidence must come first. It gives people the courage to face the unknown and to keep working when things are hard. Without some initial self-trust, it is difficult to start the learning process or to handle stressful situations. My advice is to build your confidence so it can cover your doubts and push you to act. Achievements will follow, and those successes will only strengthen the confidence you chose to develop at the start.

First, a lot of students hold part-time jobs to help their parents or to save money for future studies. Juggling work and school is tiring and leaves little energy for studying, so these students may miss chances to prepare for quizzes or finish assignments. Even if schools offered study halls, working students often cannot participate in many extracurricular programs because their schedules are already full. For them, working is a responsibility and an investment in their future, so they should be allowed to prioritize it over school-run activities.

Second, many students return home straight after school because they need to look after younger brothers or sisters. Families that cannot afford a babysitter rely on older children to help with meals, cleaning, and laundry. These duties make it hard for the student to join after-school clubs every day, though they might attend occasionally when a parent is available. They often combine taking care of siblings with doing homework, which is why imposing extra school activities would be unfair.

Third, some students simply want to choose their own interests. Many enjoy exercising or playing sports like basketball, tennis, or gymnastics; others prefer art, environmental projects, or learning a new language. These students get involved in extracurriculars by their own choice, and the school does not need to tell them what is best. Personal choice helps them stay motivated and enjoy their free time.

For these reasons, I believe schools should not control students’ after-school activities. Understanding each student’s situation and goals will help us respect their efforts and support their path to success and happiness.

Some people argue that repeating tasks you already do well is the best way to reach your goals, while others believe you should attempt harder challenges to go beyond what you planned. I agree with the latter view: pushing yourself past familiar limits can help you achieve more than you imagined.

Trying to exceed your goals can move you forward in life. It often makes work or hobbies more interesting, and it widens your knowledge. If you limit yourself to only what you already know, you miss chances to grow and discover new strengths. On the other hand, when you accept difficult tasks, you learn and improve in ways that staying comfortable never allows.

A key part of this process is believing in yourself. If you convince yourself that you cannot do something, you will not even try. To reach your goals and feel satisfied, start by trusting your own abilities. Give yourself the chance to attempt more than you think is possible.

Success and progress depend on how you act and what you choose to do. Not everyone has the same opportunities, so when you have the chance to push further, take it. For example, a student once challenged herself by taking chemistry even though she doubted her abilities at first. In the end she passed the course and proved to herself that she could do more than she expected.

Many people dislike their jobs and do only the minimum. But you can make work more enjoyable. First, find an aspect of your job that interests you. Then set a small challenge each week and treat it like a game. This approach keeps you motivated and makes progress feel rewarding. Most people respond well to challenges because they enjoy overcoming them.

Education plays a large role in personal growth and will continue to do so. You can learn in many ways — by studying, watching others, or practicing new skills. Be prepared for whatever comes: be mentally ready, emotionally steady, and physically able. Life brings surprises, both good and bad, and each experience teaches something valuable.

In conclusion, Emerson’s advice to “do something beyond what you already mastered” is wise. Push yourself, aim higher than your current goals, and believe in your ability to improve a little each day. Life is full of challenges meant to make you stronger.

Summer projects would be much more successful if students were allowed to choose them. When learners pick topics that match their interests, they are more engaged, more likely to complete the work, and often enjoy the process.

Often teachers spend a lot of time planning a single assignment for the whole class, only to find that many students put in little effort or lose interest. That outcome wastes teachers’ energy and fails to help students learn. If instead students proposed their own project ideas, they would be more invested and more willing to do the work.

When students choose a subject they care about, their curiosity motivates them to explore and learn more. Curious students dig deeper, try new approaches, and often produce more creative work. Letting them select projects opens the door to unique ideas and experiments they might not attempt if given a fixed topic. Personal choice encourages original thinking and helps students discover new strengths.

Summer projects can also help improve grades. A student who struggles during the year might benefit from working at their own pace over the summer, revisiting concepts without the pressure of keeping up with classmates. For those who do not learn well in crowded or noisy classrooms, independent summer work is a chance to study in a way that suits them. With the whole summer available, students have time to finish thoughtfully; if they still fail to complete their project, it is a sign of poor time management that will likely affect their grade.

The subject itself matters a lot. If a student is assigned a topic that does not interest them, they are more likely to procrastinate or ignore the task. For example, a student who prefers history may avoid a science assignment about gene mutation, even if the topic seems important. Allowing choice means students can pick areas they are genuinely curious about rather than forcing them to work on subjects that do not engage them.

In short, students should be able to design their own summer projects. This approach reduces the burden on teachers, encourages creative thinking, and gives students a better chance to succeed and feel proud of their work. That positive experience can also lead to a stronger start to the next school year.

Some schools run programs that pair older pupils with younger ones so the older students can support the younger with classwork and activities. This arrangement benefits both age groups in several ways. I will explain three main reasons why these programs are valuable for students and the wider community.

First, younger children gain from the knowledge and experience of older students. When a consistent mentoring program exists, more pupils join and they can form small groups to focus on different subjects or projects. This group structure makes learning more personal and helps younger students feel comfortable asking questions.

Second, the program can assist students who are struggling academically. Mentors can offer extra explanations and practice to pupils getting low grades or poor test scores. The initiative can also collect classroom supplies like books, binders, pencils, crayons and paper to support those in need. Older students might organize simple fundraisers, for example selling homemade food, to buy materials or run tutoring sessions.

Finally, this kind of program strengthens the whole community. It encourages cooperation among students and involves adults who help organize donations and events. For these reasons, mentoring programs are important and useful for both younger and older students as well as their families.

In conclusion, when older students help younger ones with homework and activities, everyone benefits academically and socially, making these programs worthwhile.

Is it difficult to remain true to yourself in a world that pushes you to be someone else? Too often we try to fit in instead of living honestly and finding happiness in our own way. In this essay I will explain how society pressures us constantly, how we absorb those influences and change, and why it seems each year our generation faces more problems.

Every day the world around us encourages change. We rarely pause to ask ourselves what we really want for our lives. Do we want to follow the crowd? Do we want money and status? Do we want to fulfill our real goals? These are important questions we should consider carefully. If we simply copy others, we may end up somewhere we did not choose. To be successful in a meaningful way, we must be true to ourselves; no one else will live our lives for us.

Society affects many parts of who we are: our hobbies, speech, style, beliefs and more. If we do not conform to what is popular, we can be seen as uncool. Clothing is a clear example. If we do not wear the latest brands or trends, people might judge us. Sometimes the reason is practical — we cannot afford those clothes, we do not have access to them, or we simply prefer different styles. Yet others may think we are not attractive or fashionable because of that. This unfair pressure can lead to teasing and even bullying. For some, the exclusion and shame go deeper and cause depression. It is painful that fitting in depends so much on what we wear or buy.

Worse, the negative influences around us are growing. Many problems seem to intensify each year, and our generation feels the impact. Drug use is a serious issue that harms lives. Conflicts between countries create fear and suffering. Popular culture often promotes harmful messages — some music focuses on drugs, violence and casual sex, which can shape young people’s attitudes in unhealthy ways. If we do not find our own values and act on them, following these trends could lead us into trouble.

Some people claim the world is solely to blame for these bad influences. But that is not completely true. We also make choices about what to accept and how to behave. It is easier to blame society than to admit we were influenced by it. In truth, responsibility lies both with the world and with ourselves. We must learn to resist harmful trends and make better decisions.

I hope things can change. There is still time to improve our society, and it is not impossible. I wish the coming generation will be brave enough to stand up for positive values and to shape a kinder, more supportive world. If more people choose authenticity and respect, we can make a better future for everyone.

I agree that a positive attitude is essential for success in life. Being friendly and upbeat matters in any workplace, and it also makes social situations better — you rarely meet someone who is having fun with a bad attitude at a party. Personally, I am thankful that I usually stay positive. In my job at a restaurant I notice the difference: when I am in a bad mood the shift feels long and tiring, but when I stay cheerful the hours fly by. A good attitude creates a strong first impression and can quickly change a tense moment into a pleasant one, which helps in the long term.

I also believe that a positive outlook can open doors over time. You might meet your future partner, connect with someone important, or find chances you never expected. Many people do not realize how much an optimistic manner can help them get a good job, earn promotions, and move up to higher positions where they can earn more. Lots of people want to be successful and wealthy, but they do not always think about how their attitude affects that goal. Of course, many are negative because life is hard for them and they face real difficulties, but keeping your head up can make a big difference.

Finally, being kind and smiling at others can lift their spirits and make the world a little better. People prefer company and care about being treated well, so small acts of friendliness matter. Workplaces would improve if more people focused on having a positive environment. A good attitude is not only important for success at work, it also helps with personal wellbeing. I imagine many people who are pleasant and many who are not, but overall, aiming to be positive will benefit both you and those around you.
