Distance learning can benefit students in many important ways. With internet access, learners can attend classes online and keep in touch with teachers from home. They can gain the same knowledge as in a traditional classroom, but in a more comfortable and flexible setting. One major advantage is reducing exposure to bullying. When schools offer an online option, teachers and parents can protect students from peers who pressure others to drink, smoke, or use drugs. Many students also have significant responsibilities after school—taking extra courses online, looking after younger siblings, or working a job—and remote learning can make it easier to balance those duties.

Although teachers try to prevent bullying, it is hard to control every student’s behavior. Some young people ignore rules, act lazy, or simply do not care about others. Many students face difficult home lives, lack parental attention, or suffer from overwhelming schoolwork; adding peer harassment can lead to serious consequences. In extreme cases, the pressure and isolation push students toward self-harm or suicide. Sometimes schools are aware of bullying but fail to treat the situation as urgent, leaving victims feeling unsafe. Teenagers often do not realize how much harm their actions can cause: teasing, physical fights, or threats may have lasting effects on someone else’s life and could even lead to legal trouble for the bully.

Peer pressure is another strong reason to consider distance learning. Some students are forced into risky behaviors by friends who say things like “if you don’t do this, you’re not my friend,” or threaten to reveal secrets. This fear of losing relationships can push teens to make choices that damage their health, reputation, or future. High school teachers may be strict, but many students attend school mainly to socialize or to disrupt others, harming the learning environment. Instead of only giving referrals or suspensions to disruptive pupils, offering a home-based study option could prevent problems and protect other students’ education.

Online learning can also help students who are saving money for college or juggling work. Studying while working can be stressful and exhausting, and attending school with a job makes time management difficult. Traditional school routines include breaks and activities that take time; at home, a student could complete assignments more efficiently and then handle other responsibilities. Working from home allows students to take the time they need on assignments and avoid rushing tests. Not having to wake up very early can also improve rest; better sleep helps concentration, prevents falling asleep in class, and reduces the risk of skipping school or dropping grades.

In conclusion, offering a homeschooling or distance learning option can have many positive effects on students’ education and wellbeing. It provides a flexible way to learn the same material as classroom students while avoiding harmful peers and distractions. With many online tools and apps available, learning at home can be engaging and efficient, and it gives vulnerable students a safer and more manageable way to succeed.

To reach important goals you must be willing to work harder and use the lessons from failure to keep going.

I tried different foot positions and angles until I found ways to kick with more power or more accuracy. Those early mistakes showed me there were several techniques to try, not just a single right way.

Failure also builds strength of character. When you are knocked down and then return with more determination, you become someone who does not give up after one setback. That renewed confidence helps you avoid repeating the same errors and keeps you moving forward.

Thomas Edison was asked how it felt to fail many times while inventing the light bulb. He answered that he did not fail; rather, he discovered many steps that would not work on the way to a working design. In short, mistakes teach us, open new options, and make us stronger. People should not fear failing — trying and failing is part of the path to a greater satisfaction when success finally comes.

Many hardworking people keep searching for jobs and hope for a better future. They are responsible, confident, and willing to do their best to improve any workplace. Yet too often they are turned away because they lack prior experience, and employers refuse to hire them for that reason.

Some will say experience is necessary to get a job, but I disagree. There are many examples of people who succeeded without previous experience; what matters is persistence and self-belief. My father struggled to find work when I was young. His mother was ill and the family needed money, but he had no relevant experience. He kept applying and learning from each rejection, and he never gave up. Today he is one of the best-known journalists in Morocco, despite starting without experience and becoming better than many who had years of it.

To begin with, a candidate does not always need experience to be valuable. Employers often look for loyalty, a strong work ethic, and honesty. A person who works hard, shows respect, and tries to improve the workplace can contribute more than someone who only has past experience. Positive attitude and dedication can lift a team and win the trust of colleagues and managers.

Secondly, this idea applies beyond office jobs — it is true for acting, sports, or any field you want to enter. As many well-known figures say, everyone starts as a beginner. For job seekers, showing motivation and proving you deserve a position can be enough. You should prepare so you do not appear uninformed, but preparation is different from having years of experience. My father pointed out that inexperienced workers often bring new ideas and energy that push a business forward. Their fresh perspective and enthusiasm can make them stand out.

Third, employers should be willing to give candidates a chance. Many talented people never get the opportunity to demonstrate their skills simply because they lack a resume. A friend of mine from France wanted to work as a teaching assistant for French classes in the United States, but schools rejected her because she had little formal teaching experience. That was unfair: as a native speaker, she could have been an excellent teacher and helped students learn more naturally. Employers who refuse to look beyond experience lose out on capable applicants.

In conclusion, not having experience should not stop someone from getting a job. Confidence, hard work, and a positive attitude can take you far. I am sure that people without experience can succeed and even outperform those with experience if they keep trying, prepare well, and stay optimistic — just as my father and my French friend did.

There are a lot of reasons why I don't think working from home or working online is a good idea. You never know who you're going to meet online. Some kids don't have internet access, so they wouldn't be able to work online. When you're at school, you have all kinds of resources to help you.

My opinion is that working at school is better than working at home. Kids actually have a chance to get stuff done at school, while at home they would just sleep and not do their school work because, well, they're at home. Learning at school is way more helpful than learning online. You always have someone there to help. Yes, there will be some kids that will learn online, and there will be some people who do work better with the person right in front of them.

I do not agree with the idea of students learning entirely from home. Many young people would likely exploit that freedom. Given the choice, some students would prefer to stay in bed rather than get up for a seven o’clock class. There are different types of students: some are self-disciplined and make the effort to attend school, while others find it hard to motivate themselves without the structure of a school day. For those reasons, sending all students to learn from home would not work well.

Some students struggle to focus at home, while others avoid school for social or personal reasons. When I say they would take advantage, I mean that instead of doing assignments at the right time, some would simply sleep or put their work off until later. School can be hard, but teachers, school staff and parents provide support that helps students keep up. Even online classes offer help when needed, but many learners benefit from being physically present. Visual learners or those who understand better through face-to-face instruction often find it easier to learn when the teacher is in front of them. Also, some students do better working alone, while others succeed through group work or partner activities; those group experiences are easier to arrange at school.

I am not denying that remote learning can be useful for some students. However, for many, learning at home would lead to procrastination or distraction instead of study. There are several practical reasons I prefer in-person schooling: students do not always have reliable internet access at home, and schools provide resources that many families lack. Another concern is the uncertainty of online environments — you do not always know who you will encounter when classes move to the internet.

In my view, school buildings offer a more effective setting for most students to complete their work. At home, the temptation to delay tasks is strong, and without immediate help nearby, progress can stall. While remote learning suits a number of students, many more benefit from being in a classroom where teachers and classmates are present to support learning.

Kindness is a word everyone recognizes, but what exactly does it mean and why does it matter so much to other people?

At its core, kindness is doing something for someone else without expecting anything in return. It can be a large gesture, like giving money to a charity, or a tiny one, like holding a door or offering a sincere compliment. These acts may seem ordinary, yet they come from a choice to help. We often act kindly because we hope the favor will be passed on: when someone is treated well, they are more likely to treat others the same. In this way, simple gestures become part of a chain that makes the world a little more caring.

Why do these small actions have such powerful effects? People remember how others made them feel. A brief moment of warmth or respect can lift someone’s mood and change the rest of their day. Over time, those memories influence how they behave toward others and what they teach their own children. We want a kinder world not only for ourselves but for the next generation, so our actions matter beyond the immediate moment.

In short, kindness creates real change. Even the smallest kindnesses can leave a strong impression and inspire more kindness. By choosing to help, we can brighten someone’s life and, through them, help improve the lives of many more.

Technology makes it possible to do many things without meeting other people in person. We can borrow books, buy groceries, or play games online without ever speaking to another human being.

I believe this reduction in face-to-face contact is harming our society, especially as phones and other devices become more powerful. In the future, technology may control many parts of life, and this could weaken real human connections.

For example, two students might start talking on social media and feel comfortable confessing their feelings through messages. If they later meet, the first meeting can be awkward, but it can also lead to a genuine friendship or a romantic relationship. Meeting someone in person helps build trust and emotion in a way that messages alone often cannot. Being committed to someone is more than words. It is about supporting each other and being present, not only sharing short declarations online.

Saying “I love you” repeatedly over a chat can feel warm, but we should ask whether it has the same meaning as saying it face to face. Ending a relationship by text also shows a lack of courage and respect. People who rely only on screens miss out on the depth of real conversations and the small moments that create strong bonds.

If we do not change, our dependence on phones could grow into an unhealthy obsession. Some people think we should take strong action to reduce device use and encourage direct interaction. If we come together and choose to spend more time in person, relationships will be richer—like a flower opening when it receives sunlight.

Overall, the shift toward isolated, screen-based communication has negative effects on human life. I hope that someday people will reconnect directly and restore the importance of being with one another.

Some schools are thinking about offering distance learning so students can join lessons from home through online classes or recorded videos. While this approach could help some learners, many others oppose it. I personally disagree with allowing students to attend classes from home.

My first concern is that home environments create many distractions. When students are surrounded by food, it is easy for them to snack instead of concentrating on the lesson. Television programs can catch their attention and pull them away from studying. The biggest distraction, however, is usually the mobile phone. At home there is no one to enforce rules about putting phones away, so students may spend class time texting or browsing social media. In addition, homes may have several family members moving about and making noise, which makes it difficult to focus on the material being taught.

Another problem is that many students would not treat online lessons seriously. Being in a familiar, relaxed space can make them feel too free and reduce their sense of responsibility. Some days they might attend and other days they might skip lessons, since no teacher is physically present to check their participation. In a classroom, teachers set clear rules that guide behaviour and learning. These rules help students stay disciplined and make the most of their time. Without this structure at home, students are likely to miss out on important content and practice.

Finally, learning at home often leads to less effective education. In class, students can ask questions and receive immediate explanations, extra examples, and personalized help. Online videos and virtual sessions do not always offer the same level of interaction or teacher attention. If a student does not understand something, waiting for an answer or finding help later may slow their progress. As a result, they may not learn as deeply as they would in a regular classroom.

I do recognize why some people support distance learning. It can save travel time and be helpful during bad weather when schools might otherwise close. It is also useful for students who lack reliable transport and would otherwise struggle to get to school. These are valid advantages that make online classes appealing for certain situations.

Nevertheless, I believe students should continue attending school in person. The classroom environment, teacher supervision, and immediate support lead to better concentration and stronger learning. For these reasons, I do not think replacing school attendance with home-based online classes is a good idea for most students.

In Virginia, for instance, many public schools teach the same material and give the same exams year after year. This uniform system has not changed much over a decade and can hold back students with different goals or talents.

In conclusion, the examples of those who have achieved great things show that communities should encourage individuality instead of relying only on standard systems like government-run schools. Success comes from self-confidence and from being true to yourself, not from simply following what others tell you to do.

Do you attend classes from home? If not, you might want to consider the advantages of learning through online lessons or video calls. Many students and parents choose homeschooling for several reasons, and it can offer real benefits.

People often say that studying at home helps students learn better. I agree: homeschooling can improve concentration, increase safety, and reduce exposure to negative influences. These are three strong reasons why some students prefer classes delivered remotely.

First, learning from home can help students focus. In traditional classrooms, attention is sometimes lost because of disruptive classmates. When other students act out or refuse to follow rules, it can interrupt lessons and make it hard for everyone to concentrate. In some cases, arguments or on-purpose misbehavior can even cause students to leave the classroom out of frustration. At home, with fewer interruptions, a learner can spend more time on schoolwork and follow lessons at their own pace.

Second, studying at home is often safer. There are worrying incidents in society, including violent attacks at schools, that make parents and students uneasy. For many families, the home environment feels more secure than commuting to and being inside a large school building. Online classes remove the daily risks that can come with crowded public places and long journeys.

Third, homeschooling can prevent harmful peer influences. Schools bring together young people from many backgrounds and with different habits. Some students may encourage risky behavior—skipping classes, bullying, fighting, or hanging out in unsafe places after school. By learning at home, students can avoid some of these pressures and stick to a more positive routine.

While traditional schools have their own strengths, attending classes online from home has clear advantages. It can create a safer learning space, help students concentrate better, and limit exposure to negative peer pressure. For these reasons, many families find homeschooling a better option.

Many people ask whether working in groups is better than working alone, and whether group work helps you concentrate or makes tasks easier and more enjoyable. I believe group work is more beneficial than working by yourself for several reasons: we can share ideas, finish tasks on time by organizing responsibilities, and it is often more fun and less stressful because we work with others.

First, group work encourages sharing ideas. When people work together they can pool their knowledge and suggest different approaches to the same problem. Group discussion helps everyone understand the task more clearly because members explain points to each other and ask questions. This exchange of opinions and information means each person contributes something useful, which improves the overall result and helps everyone learn.

Second, working in a group usually makes it easier to stay organized and meet deadlines. When you work alone, projects can take a long time and you may struggle with parts you do not understand. In a team, tasks can be divided among members so that each person focuses on a specific part. With three or four people sharing the work, the project moves faster and is more likely to be finished before the deadline. Assigning roles also prevents confusion and helps the group support each other until the job is done.

Finally, group work is often more enjoyable and less lonely. Some students prefer to work alone because they do not like talking to new people, and that is fine. Still, being part of a group gives you a chance to meet classmates you might not usually speak with. Working together can feel more relaxed — someone may tell a joke or share a friendly comment, which can lighten the mood. Although small distractions sometimes happen, they also bring laughter and make the process more pleasant. For many people, this social side makes group projects easier and more motivating.

In conclusion, I think group work has clear benefits over working alone. Teams allow us to share and develop ideas, organize tasks so we finish on time, and make the experience more enjoyable and engaging. Working in groups also teaches cooperation, responsibility, and support, which help the whole team succeed.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea that success often follows failure, because nothing will be achieved without trying and making mistakes along the way. If a person never attempts anything new, they cannot develop abilities, and without those abilities it is difficult to reach success.

People should learn more than one skill because life can be unpredictable and challenging. Sticking to only one thing keeps you from growing. As Emerson suggests, you cannot develop if you never push yourself to learn new things.

Imagine someone who only knows their job but nothing else. Would life be easy for them? Probably not. Everyday life brings many different demands, and to handle them we must explore beyond our main profession. Trying different activities helps us acquire new skills.

For example, an engineer who cannot find work may want to start a business. If they have no experience in running a company, it will be hard at first. But by trying and learning step by step, they will gain the necessary business skills. Practical effort turns a weakness into competence.

Having skills in several areas also improves how others see you and makes you more responsible. Being skilled in more than one field increases your chances of success and recognition. Life changes constantly, and people grow older every day, so we must keep developing ourselves to meet whatever comes next.

Skills are also important for the next generation. Parents and adults should know how to guide children by showing the right and wrong ways. A skillful person can teach others and becomes a source of knowledge people want to approach. That respect and recognition can lead to greater opportunities.

Knowledge is endless, like the sea; learning never stops. But knowledge from books alone is not enough. We do not gain many practical skills simply by reading. To become truly capable, we must work, investigate, and try things beyond what textbooks show. Practice is the most effective path to improvement.

In the end, knowledge without practical ability has little use. Skills form when we perform tasks and face challenges, so without trying new things it is hard to succeed or expand the mind. I agree with Emerson: life is difficult, and mastering more than one skill will help us become successful. Work hard, stay active, and do not be afraid—progress and success come from effort and trying different paths.

Some people argue that a positive attitude is not essential for success, but I disagree. In today’s fast-paced world people often hurry through tasks and rush to reach their goals, and this rush can harm how they treat others. I believe a positive outlook is very important for success for several reasons.

First, a positive manner can open doors in your career. When you are friendly and optimistic, others are more likely to respect and trust you. That could lead to job offers, partnerships, or opportunities you did not expect. Employers and colleagues notice someone who brings energy and cooperation, and that impression can change the direction of your career.

Second, having a positive attitude can brighten someone’s day and create a chain reaction. If a person is feeling down and you approach them with kindness and encouragement, you might lift their spirits. That person may then treat others better, spreading a more positive atmosphere around them. Small acts of positivity can therefore affect many people, not just the person you first helped.

Finally, positivity improves communication and relationships. When you speak to people in a positive way, conversations are smoother and trust grows. This makes it easier to form strong friendships and professional connections, which are often crucial for success in life.

In conclusion, because a positive attitude can bring career opportunities, cheer up others and encourage goodwill, and help build solid relationships, I believe it is a key factor in achieving success.

I feel lazy and unproductive when I do nothing. I believe we can achieve more when we keep ourselves busy and active. Staying busy helps the mind stay alert and gives a sense of purpose. For example, going to school, having a job, and helping other people are ways to stay engaged. If you keep doing things regularly, you will develop a habit of being active. Thomas Jefferson once said to "never be idle," which means we should avoid becoming the kind of people who prefer to do nothing.

First, going to school helps you accomplish more because it keeps your mind occupied. For instance, I wake up on time, attend classes every day, and complete my homework after school. These routines make me feel productive. When I don’t understand a topic, I ask the teacher for clarification, and I also try to help classmates by sharing what I know. Keeping my mind busy not only improves my learning but also gives me chances to talk and cooperate with others, which makes me feel good.

Second, having a job provides important experience for the future. In my first job I learned many things, such as how to use a computer. At first I thought I would never learn it, but I did, and it now helps me in my studies. I also discovered that interest is necessary to achieve something. If you are not interested or you prefer to do nothing, you will not reach your goals. In my second job I did not know how to use a cellphone, but I put effort into learning so I could help customers take orders. By my third job I had gained skills like answering the phone, taking orders, and giving good customer service.

Third, helping other people is another way to accomplish things. When you help homeless people, you can talk to them and learn why they are without a home or family support. Some choose to leave home because they don’t like their parents’ rules, but running away is not the best solution since everyone needs someone to support them. It is also important to listen to older people because they often have useful advice from their experience. I remember a time when I was homeless with my two brothers and we had no food. Seeing their hungry faces made me cry. That experience helps me feel compassion when I see others asking for food now.

I chose this topic because I believe we accomplish more when we are always doing something. Going to school, working, and helping others are ways I stay active and achieve things. I also understand that doing nothing can lead to problems, and although there are other ways to succeed, I prefer to help myself and others through action. By living this way, I consider myself to have accomplished many things.

Their surroundings may encourage them to remain where they are.

Have you ever wondered whether studying from home really helps students? Many young people want a good education and a bright future, but problems at school can stop them from doing well. For some, traditional public or private schools are not the right fit. They switch to online schooling and find it makes a big difference. Students who were failing or struggling at regular school sometimes do much better when they learn from home, and many stories show how online school has improved their lives.

I have seen this in my own family and heard it on radio shows and interviews with public figures. One example is my cousin, Generic_Name. She could not keep up with her classes or arrive at school regularly because she was fighting an eating disorder. That kind of illness makes school very hard. Her family decided to try online schooling, and it helped her a lot. Being at home allowed her to manage meals and attend doctor appointments while keeping up with assignments. Sometimes teachers even visited to help her with homework. With that support, she slowly recovered and kept improving her grades. Years later, after many challenges, she became a lawyer. It may sound unbelievable to some, but online education gave her the flexibility she needed to succeed.

Some people think stories like this are exceptions or that online school cannot lead to real success. But I have heard similar accounts on radio podcasts. In one program a mother talked about her son, also named Generic_Name, who was often bullied in high school and even threatened with fights. The mother enrolled him in online school, where he attended video classes and met with teachers by video conference every few days. He found it easier to focus when it was just him and his laptop, without other students causing problems. Because he could keep up with both his studies and his activity on social media, he felt more comfortable and less stressed. Critics might say he should face bullies instead of avoiding them, but everyone has a limit. If harassment is constant, moving to online school can be the right choice to protect a young person’s mental health.

Celebrities have mentioned similar experiences. A well-known girl on social media, Generic_Name, described how constant online criticism and being targeted by other people ruined her confidence. She fell into depression and struggled to continue at public school. Teachers suggested she try homeschooling, and she did online school through the rest of high school and even for college courses. She says this changed her life: she became more confident and decided to attend a public college later when she felt ready. Some doubt that switching to online school helped her, but for her it reduced fear and gave space to grow. Afterward, she could return to regular college life and continue her social media career.

It is important for people facing similar difficulties to read and listen to other people’s experiences. These stories can help students and families decide whether online schooling might be a better option. Looking back at what others went through also shows how things have changed and what choices worked for them. One clear solution is to offer online schooling as an option for those who find public school too hard for any reason. Another solution is for people to stop spreading hate online. For students, especially those who are popular on social media, escaping constant negativity can make a big difference. Online school is not the right answer for everyone, but for many it provides a safer, more flexible way to succeed.

Many schools now allow students to join classes from home through online platforms or video calls. I believe this option should be available because it helps students who struggle with social interaction, those who have had negative experiences at school, and learners who concentrate better in familiar surroundings. Although some people worry about distractions or lack of social life, the advantages for these groups are significant.

First, remote learning can support students who find it hard to socialize or approach teachers and classmates. People develop in different ways, and some young people are naturally shy or carry emotional scars that make face-to-face interaction difficult. Letting them study from home gives them a safe space where they can participate without feeling pressured to be social. This freedom often allows them to show their true abilities, especially when they have few other opportunities to demonstrate their strengths in a regular classroom.

Second, online classes can be a refuge for students who have suffered bad experiences at school, such as bullying. Being targeted by classmates can destroy confidence and make it hard to continue attending in person. For these students, learning from home removes the daily source of fear and stress, so they can focus on education again. In many cases, moving away from a hostile environment is an important step toward recovering motivation and pursuing long-term goals.

Third, some students learn best when they are comfortable and free from classroom distractions. A familiar environment, such as home, can help them concentrate and maintain high standards. When family members are supportive, students often feel encouraged to keep working even when lessons are challenging. This emotional support can be a strong factor in academic success.

Critics say that home learning leads to distractions, poor time management, and missed social experiences. While these concerns are real for some, they do not apply to every student. For those who struggle in traditional settings, online options offer a practical alternative that can improve their performance and well-being.

For these reasons, I strongly believe schools should offer online or video-based classes as a choice. It would help students who have trouble socializing, those who have been hurt by past school experiences, and learners who thrive in a comfortable setting, increasing their chances of doing well.

Technology lets people do many things without meeting others in person. For instance, people can borrow books from machines, buy items online, or play video games without talking to anyone face to face. While these innovations bring advantages, they also cause problems. Some argue that technology is valuable for emergencies, but many believe it has changed people’s behaviour and made screens more important than the people around us.

Supporters of technology emphasize its role in urgent situations. Imagine a family living far from the city with no neighbours nearby; in an emergency, a phone or internet connection can be the only way to get help. I remember in my country there were families in remote areas who had no devices to contact others. When they became sick they could not call for assistance, and some suffered serious consequences because they did not have access to communication tools at a critical time. In these cases, technology can save lives.

On the other hand, many people think technology negatively affects attitudes and behaviour. In the past, people often showed more respect to one another even if they had less formal education. Today, critics blame films, music, books, and cartoons delivered through devices for changing young people’s values. Constant use of screens can cause mental health issues or make users less aware of real life. For example, I know a family whose fifteen-year-old daughter watches a lot of television. She behaves as if she is more mature than her peers and often disobeys her parents. Her behaviour is poor, and I feel partly the parents are responsible because they keep buying electronic devices and do not supervise how she uses them. Letting children use technology too early can be harmful because they may learn bad habits that are hard to correct later. Instead of leaving children with screens, parents could spend time with them and guide their activities.

Many people are also worried that screens have become more important than human relationships. A psychologist I read argued that face-to-face conversations are better for clear communication, and I agree. Online, people can hide their true selves and even lie about who they are. I read a book about a teacher who was messaging someone she did not know; the other person pretended to be a man but was actually a woman. When the teacher suggested a video call, the stranger refused, proving the online identity was false. Incidents like this happen frequently and make people less trusting.

In conclusion, technology can be both helpful and harmful depending on how it is used. It keeps advancing, so people must learn to use it responsibly and at the right times. Technology has the power to improve lives, but only when it is managed wisely.

Nowadays people seem more divided about how to live and behave. Life is not always simple, and everyone has their own ideas, so it's understandable that situations get complicated. I believe individuals should make their own choices because doing so helps them learn from experience, understand how life operates, value themselves, and become more capable and independent.

Others may try to tell you how to live, but real understanding comes from personal experience. There will be times when you fall or face unexpected difficulties, and only by going through these moments will you learn how tough life can be. Making mistakes is part of being human; no one is perfect. Life can surprise you without warning, so you need to be prepared to handle both easy and hard situations. When you decide for yourself, you build the skill to choose what is best for you.

Life can be difficult to grasp at times, but it is part of everyday existence and worth learning about so small problems don’t cause too much stress. Challenges are given to you as the person responsible for your own life, and the outcomes often depend on how you respond. As we grow, life can either strengthen or weaken us depending on our choices and attitude. It is important to remember that events may come at inconvenient moments, but dealing with pain and setbacks can make you stronger and show that you are truly living.

Also, if you do not love yourself, it is unlikely someone else will do that for you. Relying on others for your happiness is risky; happiness starts with you. Not everything you do will please other people, so learning to act independently is more effective. The more capable and self-reliant you are, the more positive results you will achieve. Appreciate yourself and the things around you, but keep in mind that life is not easy and surprises can happen at any time.

In conclusion, making your own decisions helps you understand life better and prepares you for what comes. Self-love leads to the ability to love others, and recognizing that life centers around your choices—not other people’s opinions—can guide you toward growth and resilience.

Character refers to the way you behave and respond to the world, and I believe that each person can build their own character by choosing the traits they want to develop. While some people think that our character is shaped mainly by those around us — for example parents or friends — I maintain that nobody can force a particular personality on you.

Deciding who you want to be is important. If you never make conscious choices about your behavior and values, you may feel uncertain about yourself and struggle to know what direction to take in life. Choosing your character helps you feel confident and makes it easier to recognize who you really are.

Having an individual character matters because many people copy the behavior of others, whether it is their parents or popular figures. But when you form your own way of acting, you stand out as unique. A recent study at the University of Virginia found that people who consciously select how they behave and which traits to adopt tend to be happier than those who simply copy others’ personalities.

You are your own person. From early childhood you begin to develop your character, and over time you can guide it through the experiences you have and the decisions you make. Some will argue that parents determine a child’s personality, but I believe that personal experience plays the larger role. As John Lubbock put it, your character becomes what you choose to make it.

In conclusion, you can become whoever you wish; your character grows from your own choices and life experiences. Others will always form opinions about you, but you should follow your own sense of what is right and be content with who you are. Don’t allow other people, even your parents, to decide how you should act — shape your own character and behave in the way that feels true to you.

I do not agree with the school board’s plan to add an extra hour and a half to the school day. This change would increase students’ classwork and homework, create more conflicts and drama during school, and interfere with other important activities outside class. Because of these problems, students would probably be less focused and less willing to attend school.

First, extending the school day would mean more lessons and assignments for students. With longer days, teachers might give additional projects and homework, and pupils would have to spend extra time studying. Many students would find it hard to concentrate on long stretches of work, and they would become tired or frustrated. After a full day, most young people want a break, so asking them to study more right away would reduce their motivation. For these reasons, an added hour and a half could make learning less effective rather than better.

Second, the longer day could increase tension and drama at school. When students are tired or stressed, they are more likely to argue or act out. Extra unsupervised time between classes or before lessons could lead to more gossip, fights, or distractions around the building. This kind of behavior would make concentrating in class even more difficult and could cause overall grades to fall. In short, a longer day might bring more social problems that get in the way of learning.

Finally, extending school hours would clash with students’ other responsibilities and interests. Many students have sports practices, games, family events, or jobs that take place after school. Adding time to the schedule could force them to miss these activities or leave them with less time for friends and relaxation. That would upset students and their families and reduce the time they have for important non-school activities. As a result, students would feel their day became less balanced and enjoyable.

In conclusion, increasing the school day by an hour and a half would likely make students less eager to attend. It would create more coursework and homework, raise the chance of drama and distractions at school, and interfere with family time and extracurriculars. For these reasons, the school board’s proposal is not a good idea.

Imagine a world drained of color, cold and joyless, where many people live with sadness. That bleak reality could become true if we keep believing that small, kind gestures don't matter. In fact, tiny acts of kindness can make a big difference, both for individuals and for society as a whole.

One clear benefit of being kind is the way it builds your own reputation. There are many ways to earn a positive image, but a simple and effective one is treating others kindly. Small, friendly actions help form and sustain all kinds of relationships. Often, kindness is returned: when you are considerate to others, they sometimes respond in kind. I have seen this happen personally. A short compliment I gave once brightened someone's mood, and on days when I felt low and it showed, people offered me warmth in return. Being consistently kind makes you more visible in a positive way; people begin to see you as someone who cares, and they may seek your company or ask for encouragement. In that sense, kindness can make your presence more meaningful to others.

Kindness also spreads outward and can improve communities. Our world has many problems, but if more people practiced simple kindness, it could create a chain reaction. Someone who receives friendliness often feels happier and wants to pass that feeling on, so they act kindly toward others. That ripple effect can reach far: as one person influences another, more people adopt nicer behavior, and the atmosphere improves. I experienced this in school. After I made a conscious effort to be kind to classmates, I became more noticeable in a positive way, and others began to act more warmly toward each other. It felt like everyone benefited.

Finally, small acts of kindness can help people feel better about themselves. As Aesop reminded us, no kind deed, however small, is ever wasted. A compliment or a friendly word can lift someone’s spirits, and when others notice that kindness, it creates a wholesome mood around them. Kindness can change someone's life. I remember being about eleven years old and struggling at school and at home. The friends I found then made a huge difference — they brightened my year and became people I trusted to be there for me. For someone facing trouble, a little support can shift their path toward greater happiness.

For these reasons, no matter how small, acts of kindness really can change lives and help create a more hopeful world.

Second, influencing people can make them pay attention to your message and pass it on to others. When someone listens to you and then shares the same advice, more people can benefit. This process can lead to better decisions in everyday life, such as knowing when to make purchases or how to act in new situations, so they are less likely to be confused when facing them.

Giving practical advice prepares people for the future and prevents them from staying stuck on past problems. Later, they can teach their own children what they learned, giving the next generation a useful advantage.

For these reasons, I think influencing others in a positive way is valuable and important.

Can you picture how satisfying it would be to live by deliberately choosing the best version of yourself? Deciding on your own character is something you are unlikely to regret later.

People pick their character because they believe this choice will help them succeed. At first, making that decision can feel very difficult because we cannot be sure it will work out. But nothing valuable comes easily. If we want real success, we must stick to the character we choose.

When we adopt a character intentionally, we gain confidence to carry out our plans. With that confidence, handling whatever life brings becomes much simpler. We do not choose our character without understanding ourselves first, and that is why it is important to know what suits us. For example, life often brings many problems, but if we decide to face them calmly by using the character traits we value, those difficulties feel less stressful and life becomes easier.

Take relationships: when planning to marry, people do not just guess whether they fit with a partner. They choose a way of being that will go well with the other person. Sometimes you fall in love with someone who seems to have better qualities than you, and you may decide to adopt some of their good habits. This shows why choosing your character matters.

Many people begin shaping their character at school. They see many kinds of behavior there and start to notice which ones suit them. Teachers also play a role by teaching good conduct, so students often form their characters during their school years.

Choosing the character you want also helps you find the right people, because you will feel happier with those who share similar traits without pretending. You cannot live well by acting like someone you are not; that is a false life. Life becomes easier and more joyful when you follow the rules of the character you have chosen. So choose your character and live by it.

Many people believe that having a positive attitude is essential for success. I agree with this view because a good outlook helps in work, shows your background, and supports learning.

A constructive attitude often makes a strong impression during job searches. For instance, if two candidates attend the same interview and one answers politely and shows enthusiasm while the other seems rude or uninterested, the employer is more likely to choose the first person. Employers value people who come across as cooperative and motivated, so a pleasant manner can be the deciding factor.

The way someone behaves can also reflect their upbringing. People who treat others with respect usually give the impression that they were raised with good manners and values. On the other hand, someone who speaks rudely or insults people gives a poor impression and may be judged as lacking proper guidance. In this way, attitude communicates personal background and character.

Attitude is important in education too. Students who listen attentively and participate actively show teachers that they are committed to learning. Teachers are more willing to help learners who demonstrate a sincere interest, while those with a negative approach may receive less support. A positive attitude therefore helps students make the most of educational opportunities and improve their chances of future success.

Some argue that attitude is not always under our control because mood can change or make us act poorly. While it is true that everyone feels down sometimes, making an effort to stay positive most of the time is still useful. Small changes in behavior can have big effects on how others respond to us and on our own progress.

In conclusion, maintaining a positive attitude supports success by helping in job situations, reflecting good upbringing, and enhancing learning. Even though moods vary, a generally positive approach benefits both personal and professional life.

I agree with Churchill’s view that failure is part of the path to success. Failure teaches us lessons we would not learn if everything worked out on the first try. It reveals what went wrong and points to what we must change for the next attempt. Failures also help us understand our reasons for doing something — whether we really want the goal and how much effort it will take.

Many people fail often, and there is no reason to feel ashamed about that; each setback gives us new knowledge. As my father used to say, going through many failures does not mean everything is over. Failure may explain why life can be difficult or why we are not yet successful, but it also clarifies our aims and pushes us to try harder. Through mistakes we gather more detail and experience, improving our judgment and skills. For these reasons I believe Churchill was right: failure plays a crucial and positive role in the pursuit of success.

Some schools now give students the choice to join lessons from home using online platforms or video calls. Schools often present this option as helpful for pupils who do not want to attend in person or who are unable to go because of illness. While studying at home can bring some of the same advantages as being in class, it is not entirely better overall.

I believe remote learning does offer useful benefits in certain situations, especially for students with health or mobility problems. However, it is not a full replacement for school because many students do not learn as well at home as they do in the classroom.

First, taking classes from home can be very useful for learners who have physical difficulties or medical conditions. For example, a student with arthritis or another mobility issue may find it hard or impossible to travel to school every day. Online lessons or video meetings with a tutor allow them to continue their education without the physical strain. This can help them complete their studies and obtain a diploma, which is important for their future job opportunities. Remote learning can also help students who have problems at school, such as those who have been involved in fights or who feel unsafe. Studying from home with support from an adult or online teacher gives these students a chance to keep learning without being in a harmful environment.

On the other hand, studying from home can be a disadvantage for students who simply do not want to go to school. Without teachers present to guide and supervise them, these students may skip work or become distracted and learn less. This is especially true for people learning a new language. I am an example: I am not a native English speaker, and if I studied at home it would be much harder for me to improve. In school I hear English many times each day from teachers and classmates, and this constant exposure helps me learn faster. I can also make friends who speak English and who support me. For me, attending school is better, even though it is sometimes difficult. The teacher and classmates help me improve, and I can see steady progress in my language skills.

In conclusion, studying from home is not completely beneficial for everyone. It has real advantages for some students, such as those with health issues or safety concerns, but it can be harmful for others who need the structure and social environment of school. Overall, whether at home or in the classroom, learning depends on the student’s motivation. For me, going to school helps me improve every day, learn new things, and become more confident because I have people who help me and I practice English regularly.

This essay discusses a proposal some schools are considering: switching to a four-day week by extending each school day by two hours. I will explain why I do not support applying this change to my high school. I will outline the main benefits and drawbacks and suggest steps the school should take before making a final decision.

Picture receiving a notice from the school saying students will attend classes only four days per week, with longer hours each day. I oppose this plan because it would harm rather than help my high school. One immediate effect would be on after-school programs and activities. If each school day lasts ten hours, students will be much more tired, and fewer of them will want to take part in clubs, sports, or other extracurriculars. As a result, the school might have to suspend some of these programs. This change would especially hurt juniors and seniors who work after school; many would find it difficult to keep their jobs and might be forced to quit.

There are a few advantages and disadvantages to this proposal. A clear advantage is that longer school periods would give us more time to complete classwork and cover material during the day. Another possible benefit is that operating school one less day a week could reduce energy use and save resources for the school. However, the downsides are significant: extracurricular opportunities could disappear, fewer students would participate, and the extended hours could conflict with part-time jobs held by older students. Changing work schedules is often difficult, and some students might have no choice but to leave their employment.

Before implementing such a change, the school should follow a careful process. First, the staff should hold internal meetings to examine the idea and raise concerns. Next, the school should bring parents into the discussion and explain exactly how the new schedule would work. After that, the administration should send a detailed letter home asking parents to indicate whether they agree or disagree, ideally by signing and returning the form. Only after gathering feedback from both staff and families should the school make a final decision.

In conclusion, I do not think my school should adopt a four-day week with two extra hours each day. Although there are some benefits, the negatives outweigh them for our situation. The change could lead to canceled after-school activities, cause some students to lose their jobs, and make everyone more tired. Our current schedule allows students to play sports, join clubs, and work when needed, so I believe we should keep it as it is.

I want to talk about the advantages of working in a group. I believe group work makes tasks easier and more enjoyable because students can share ideas and learn from one another. It also helps us understand issues from several different perspectives.

First, collaborating in a group makes assignments less difficult because members can split the work. One person might gather information, another writes the text, and someone else finds charts or images needed for the project. This division of labor speeds up the process and reduces pressure on each student. Working together is also more enjoyable: students can talk while they work and even laugh about small mistakes, which makes the experience more pleasant.

Second, group work gives students a chance to learn beyond the topic of the assignment. When people exchange ideas and opinions, everyone gains new knowledge and ways of thinking. Hearing classmates’ viewpoints helps us see problems from angles we may not have considered. In addition, group members can support one another: if one student is unsure about an answer, others might explain it and help them understand.

Finally, some students feel more at ease in a group setting. This comfort encourages them to share their thoughts and try out different positions without fear. Working together and discussing ideas often leads to better results because the group can combine strengths and correct weaknesses. Through conversation and shared tasks, students also practice listening and respecting different opinions.

In conclusion, group work offers many benefits. It helps students learn more, achieve stronger results, and understand a variety of viewpoints. Group projects also teach respect for others’ ideas and improve communication and teamwork skills.

I can see the reason behind wanting to add an extra hour and a half to the school day to give students more learning time. However, many children would not welcome this change, and I agree with them.

First, students already spend a long time at school and most do not want to stay even longer. Many take part in after-school programs—sports, volunteer work, music lessons, or other clubs—that start at specific times. Extending the school day would clash with these activities and make it harder for students to attend them. Some young people also have responsibilities at home, like chores or caring for family members, which would be squeezed if their school day increases. Even if adults think these things are unimportant, they matter to the students and contribute to their personal development alongside formal education.

Extra school hours would also reduce the time available for homework and studying at home. If students finish later, they may have less time in the evening to prepare for tests or complete assignments. This could lead to worse grades, which would be harmful to both the students’ futures and their families. Poor academic performance may be the opposite of what the longer school day is intended to achieve.

Families are likely to resist a longer school day because it cuts into time they could spend together. Evening routines—dinner out, family walks, or simply relaxing before bedtime—would be harder to keep. Some parents, if extra hours are added, might at least want the school day to start 20 minutes later so children can get more sleep and not be so tired the next morning. That would be a reasonable compromise, but it would not solve the problem of reduced free time overall.

On weekends, families often travel or take part in activities far from home. If students come home later on weekdays with extra homework and larger projects, these family trips and quality time could suffer. Over time, students who feel overloaded may stop doing homework or studying properly, which harms their learning.

If many families are unhappy, some students may transfer to schools with shorter days or switch to homeschooling. A drop in enrollment could force a school to cut programs or even close, which would lead to job losses for teachers and staff. That outcome would be damaging for the whole community and is another reason to rethink the idea of lengthening the school day.

Students might promise to keep phones on silent, but that does not stop them from using the device or creating disruptions. For these reasons, banning phones at school is the better choice.

Dear Principal,

I think changing the rule is a good idea. A lot of students have a C average now, and if they play sports that requirement could drop even more. Schoolwork should come before extracurriculars, because playing sports can make it harder for some students to keep up with their classes. For that reason, keeping the minimum at a B average to join sports or other activities would encourage students to focus on their grades first.

If the school raises the standard to a B, many students will work harder to reach it. When they get report cards or progress reports and see low averages, they will realize they spent too much time on activities and not enough on studying. The principal can try the change and watch how students respond; if it doesn’t help, the policy could be adjusted. But making the goal a B gives learners something clear to aim for. It doesn't have to be an A for everyone, but a B is reasonable and achievable.

Some students will argue that it is hard to study while also playing sports, but I believe the rule will help them in the long run. If the whole school moves from a C average to a B average, our school’s academic reputation will improve. Students who want to succeed will push themselves until they reach that level. Those who are unwilling to put in the effort and who fall asleep in class or skip assignments will not see their grades improve; that is their responsibility.

There may be cases where a student has tried everything—attended tutoring, completed all homework, and turned in assignments on time—but still falls short of a B. In those situations it would be fair for the principal to speak with the student’s teachers and consider allowing participation. Teachers can give guidance about whether the student truly did their best. Still, most students can reach a B with a good plan and some effort.

Another reason to support this change is that if students do not have good grades at the end of the year, they might not pass. Raising the standard will help prevent that by making academic performance a priority from the start. Even if some students only try harder because they want to play sports, those better habits can carry over into other parts of their lives.

For these reasons, I would like the school to require at least a B average for participation in sports and activities. Everyone is capable of improving, even if they don’t believe it at first. Trying harder in class won’t hurt, and doing it for sports can be the motivation some students need to succeed for themselves.

This essay examines the pros and cons of switching to a four-day school week with ten-hour days. Some people think this schedule would save energy and resources, but after considering both sides, I do not support lengthening each school day by two hours.

As a student, I understand why a longer weekend might appeal to some, yet I believe eight hours at school is already enough for many pupils. Sitting in class for ten hours would be exhausting. In every class there are students who fall asleep or lose focus because homework, part-time jobs, or sports leave them worn out. Adding two extra hours each day would only make it harder for them to stay attentive. The idea of a three-day weekend sounds good, but only if the in-school time does not damage learning and well-being.

People also claim the four-day week saves energy, but that is misleading. If Monday through Thursday are each two hours longer, those extra hours add up to the same amount of time lost on a traditional five-day schedule. In other words, the total number of hours students spend in school over the week does not necessarily drop, so any supposed energy savings are doubtful.

Personal situations show how this change could be unfair. For example, a friend of mine loves the thought of a four-day week because it would give him more time for homework and to see his girlfriend. For him, the new schedule would be ideal. But others would suffer. My boyfriend, who trains with the basketball team for about two hours after school and then works four hours to help his family, would not get enough sleep if school ended later. After his shift he must still do homework, or assignments would be late. Many students make sacrifices to support their families, and longer days would make their lives harder.

Teachers must be considered as well. They will be responsible for ten straight hours of instruction and planning, and they are not machines. Their fatigue could affect teaching quality, and they may oppose a schedule that is more demanding.

For these reasons, my school should not adopt a ten-hour, four-day model without careful study. Any decision must take into account students, teachers, and office staff. What works for some companies may not suit a high school, since schools have different activities and responsibilities. There is no guarantee this change would benefit our community.

Working alone often has advantages because you can set your own rhythm and avoid clashes over ideas. While some people argue that group work is superior, I believe working independently is usually more helpful.

One main benefit of working alone is being able to go at the pace that suits you. Moving at your own speed matters because it reduces pressure and allows you to learn from any mistakes. Maybe you prefer to spread tasks over several evenings rather than finish everything in one session. If you work by yourself, you do not have to worry about friends interrupting you or turning your study time into social time. When you are the only person responsible for the project, you control how and when the work gets done.

Working alone also helps develop independence and prepares you for real-life situations. When you complete tasks on your own, you make decisions about what is correct and how to present your ideas without constantly checking with others. This can build confidence and time-management skills, since you are the one keeping track of deadlines and pacing your work. If someone tends to rush you, you do not have to accept that pressure when you are working alone; you simply follow the schedule that works best for you.

Some people argue in favor of group work, but groups often introduce distractions and complications. Studies have shown that many students complain about group projects and would rather work alone. Another common problem is uneven commitment: you might not know if your teammates are at the same level or will complete their parts on time. That means you may need to check up on others or even finish their share yourself, because the whole group receives one grade.

Isn’t it nicer to focus without these concerns? By working alone you avoid disagreements about ideas, control your timetable, and take full responsibility for your results. Group work can be complicated and sometimes frustrating. For these reasons, I believe working independently is more beneficial.

This process can be stressful and may include refusals. Yet you keep trying, learning from each interview, adjusting your approach, and not losing faith. That patient persistence is exactly how people eventually find success.

Finally, we are all responsible for our actions, words, and choices. Mistakes can affect others, so we must accept accountability and keep improving. Staying motivated is essential; if we give up, someone else might take the opportunity we wanted. In short, failure is not the opposite of success but part of the journey toward it.

I disagree with adding an extra hour and a half to the school day. First, students already spend about eight hours at school doing classes and other activities, which is tiring. Extending the day would make it even more exhausting for both children and adults.

Second, longer school hours would reduce time for childhood activities. If students are at school for nine and a half hours, they have less opportunity to play, relax, or enjoy hobbies after class. For example, when you come home exhausted, you might want to have fun or hang out with friends, but long school days leave little energy for that.

Third, homework takes up a lot of time. After a long day at school, many students still have hours of assignments to finish. If you get out of school late and then spend two or three more hours doing homework, there is rarely time left to go out because it is already dark and parents often won’t allow it. This means students miss out on social and leisure time.

Fourth, longer days make scheduling appointments harder. If school ends at 2:45 and you have an appointment at 3:00, staying later at school could cause you to miss it. Leaving early sometimes feels like wasting valuable learning time, so parents and students face a difficult choice.

I understand that schools might want longer days to improve learning and future job prospects, but children and adults also need time for themselves. For these reasons, I am against adding extra hours to the school day.

All students should take part in at least one extracurricular activity. The principal is right to require this because these activities bring benefits both now and in the future.

I believe every student ought to join one or more activities. They support mental and emotional health, improve physical fitness, and strengthen college applications. Many studies show that regular participation in sports lowers the risk of heart disease and breathing problems. Being active through athletics reduces the chance of serious health issues later in life.

Sports and other physical activities also help you stay in shape. Playing basketball, baseball, running track, or cheering are great ways to burn calories and build stamina. People who exercise regularly are generally healthier and feel better day to day. The physical benefits are obvious, but the advantages go beyond fitness.

Extracurriculars provide emotional relief, too. They give you a break from the pressures of school and a chance to focus on something enjoyable. Taking part in a club or team distracts you from constant stress and helps you relax. Activities are not limited to sports: working on the yearbook, joining student council, or volunteering around the school are all ways to get involved. When students work together, they stop being isolated and start forming friendships and support networks.

Participation also matters for college. Colleges look for applicants who do more than just earn high grades. Being involved in activities shows commitment, leadership, and the ability to manage responsibilities. It can make your application stand out and increase your chances of receiving scholarships. Colleges want students who are independent and can contribute to campus life, so extracurricular experience is a strong advantage.

Requiring every student to join at least one activity would help them in many ways. It is a low-risk way to gain new skills, improve health, and build a stronger college profile. I fully support the principal’s decision—sometimes you need to be nudged into something new, and trying an activity won’t hurt.

Technology plays a major role in our lives today and will become even more important in the future. People always try to find ways to make life easier and more comfortable. While many welcome these changes, others worry about their negative effects. I agree with the view that modern technology has harmed our social life because it reduces face-to-face contact, keeps people stuck in one place, and sometimes causes aggressive reactions when use is restricted.

In the past, people met on the streets, visited neighbors, and spent time together in public places. Now we can call or message friends with a single tap, seeing them only on small screens. This shift has made many prefer staying home instead of enjoying the city or meeting friends in person. Some argue that talking to strangers online is not different from talking to strangers on the street, but online contact is riskier. People can use fake profiles to steal personal information or lie about who they are. When we met someone in person, we could judge how they behaved and decide whether to trust them. Online friendships often start without that real-world context, so it is harder to know if they are genuine.

Childhood has changed a lot because of technology. Before, kids played outside in the streets, visited friends’ houses, or went to parks. Today many prefer video games, which are easily set up on a TV or device. Some children spend all day playing and avoid sports or going out to play with others. At school, conversations often focus on games rather than on studies, which can hurt their learning and homework performance. When the first game consoles appeared, they were exciting but expensive; families often chose to spend money on simple treats or outings instead. Now it seems many children and teenagers would rather stay where technology is and miss real-life experiences.

Another problem is the aggressive behaviour that appears when parents limit technology use. Families often have conflicts because children react strongly if devices are taken away. Some doctors say this happens because young people live in a virtual world where they feel powerful and lose it when parents remove that space. It can be very hard to make a child stop using technology, and in extreme cases teenagers break things, including the devices themselves.

Some people point to the positive effects of technology and the useful tools it provides. Still, I believe its negative impact on social interaction, children’s habits, and family life shows that we must control how we use technology to protect our society’s future.

Music, drama, and art classes should remain electives rather than mandatory courses. These subjects are not something people use every day in most careers or daily tasks, so forcing every student to take them does not fit everyone's needs. Since students have different interests and future plans, requiring arts classes limits their ability to focus on what matters to them.

Schools teach practical skills like basic math that students will use in adult life, for example to manage bills and taxes. In contrast, knowing how to compose a song, perform on stage, or paint well is often more of a hobby than a necessity for maintaining a stable life. Most employers are not going to hire someone because they can draw or act, unless the job is directly related to those talents. Only a small number of people manage to turn art, music, or drama into a reliable profession; success in those fields usually depends on exceptional talent or strong dedication from the start. That is why these subjects are better offered as options for students to explore, not as required parts of the curriculum.

Colleges and universities also do not treat art skills the same way they treat core academic subjects when deciding admissions or majors. Abilities in painting or theater are rarely part of the standard tests or prerequisites that determine whether a student is accepted. As young people grow and refine their goals, they often change direction—someone who plans to become a doctor might later choose research instead. Science-related majors share many courses, so switching between them is relatively easy. But art, music, and drama are specialized areas with little overlap with other fields, so requiring them would not help students who later change their plans.

It is true that studying the arts can lead to fulfilling careers—writing music, acting, and creating visual art can be rewarding and profitable for those who succeed. However, this applies to a minority, and it is not a dependable path for most students. Making these subjects compulsory would reduce the choices available to young people and force them to spend time on topics that may not suit their aims. For these reasons, music, drama, and art should remain elective options, allowing students to decide whether they fit their future goals.

I disagree with making the school day longer. I would not want to stay an extra hour at school, and I think most students would feel the same. 

First, we already spend most of the day at school. An eight-hour day is long enough, and adding another hour would be too much for many of us. 

Second, extra time at school would leave less time after classes for homework and rest. Teachers already assign a lot of homework, so if we have to stay later, we will likely end up finishing assignments late into the evening. That means less sleep and more stress. 

Third, a longer school day would reduce our free time even more. With more hours at school and heavy homework loads, there would be little time left for hobbies, family, or relaxation. 

For these reasons—being at school almost the whole day already, having less time to complete homework, and losing free time—I believe we should not add another hour to the school day.

Some schools now let students take classes from home through online lessons or video conferencing. I believe this choice is very useful for many learners. It helps those who cannot follow the regular school timetable because of limited time, money, or personal circumstances, and it makes it possible for them to complete their studies.

Online courses are a good solution for students who want to finish school but cannot be present in a classroom. With online lessons, students can study from home and organize their learning around the hours they have available. Time is often a major obstacle: many students leave school because they must work after classes and have no time for homework or school activities. As school performance falls, they decide to drop out and keep working to support themselves or their families. For some young people who moved here alone, this is their only way to send money home. Online learning allows them to continue their education while holding a job.

Video conferencing is another useful option. Like online courses, it can be taken from home and can fit different schedules. The important difference is that video classes happen in real time, so students and teachers see and speak to each other through a camera. This live interaction is helpful because students can ask questions immediately and practice with the teacher, much like in a regular classroom.

A big advantage of both methods is that students can keep working and handling personal responsibilities while studying. These programs are not only for teenagers; adults who left school earlier can also take these courses and finish their education. Often people stop studying because they think they are too old for high school, but distance learning removes that barrier and welcomes learners of all ages.

Today, more teenagers are leaving school for different reasons—some have no alternatives, others are not motivated. By offering remote learning options, schools give a second chance to those who dropped out and make it easier for many students to complete their education and improve their future prospects.

I believe that if more schools provide distance learning as an option, more people will be able to study and benefit from it. With these programs, students will have fewer excuses for not finishing school and will gain better opportunities in life.
