Many students look forward to summer vacation, but some teachers worry that long breaks make it harder for pupils to remember what they learned and think the holidays are too long. Still, educators must consider how students feel about time off. Students need extended breaks, so schools should not switch to year-round calendars. Instead, there should remain a 3–4 week summer holiday and short week-long breaks in spring and autumn.

One important reason is that students need time with their families. During the school year, much of a young person’s time is spent on classes, homework, and preparing for the next day. Some have large projects that take up evenings and weekends. As a result, students often give less attention to their parents and miss chances to talk about their lives. Losing this family time can harm relationships and reduce the support students receive at home. Because of this, abolishing longer summer breaks would make it harder for many families to reconnect.

A second reason is that students have other responsibilities and interests outside school. Holidays are when many young people help at home, work part-time jobs, or simply use their free time in ways that suit them. Breaks give them a chance to relax and recover from academic pressure without constant homework or projects. Also, many students feel that some school lessons are not always relevant to their daily lives, which can make it easy to forget material when they return. Time off allows them to balance school with personal and family duties.

Although some argue that summer breaks are too long and lead to learning loss, the benefits for family life and personal responsibilities make a strong case against year-round schooling. Therefore, schools should keep a 3–4 week summer break and short breaks in spring and fall.

Some schools in the United States now let students take classes from home because they think it can be a good choice. For example, offering remote lessons has helped reduce bullying in some middle and high schools, so some students prefer not to return to the building and want to study from home. However, learning at home often causes problems. Many students become distracted, find it hard to concentrate, and do not learn as well as they would in a classroom. Although distance learning can be done online or through video calls, it can make the learning environment weaker. At the same time, some students do feel more relaxed when studying at home.

A big reason students lose focus at home is the easy access to phones and other devices. Staying at home more often can lead to boredom and habits that hurt studying. If students are used to sleeping in class, they may also sleep during online lessons. Some students work part time and arrive tired, so they cannot pay attention or participate much.

Paying attention in online lessons is difficult for many young people. They are more tempted to listen to music, play games, or check social media instead of following the teacher. Because it is less formal than a classroom, students may put less effort into concentrating and do not gain as much from the lesson.

Learning through a screen often makes it harder to understand new material. When teachers explain ideas in class, students can ask questions right away and get clearer answers. Online, it can be challenging to follow explanations and receive help. As a result, some students fall behind and struggle to learn the content fully.

Schools offer home-based classes because of the potential benefits: students may feel safer and more comfortable at home, have more time for homework, and get better rest so they have energy for lessons. Still, being close to family and household distractions can also reduce attention.

In conclusion, while online classes have some advantages, many students who study from home are more easily distracted and learn less. They may not understand lessons as well, feel frustrated, and spend time on phones or entertainment instead of studying. For these reasons, distance learning is not the best option for all students.

Some students who live far from school or struggle with learning are not doing well in their classes. Teachers are concerned about these students and try many methods to help them. After checking test scores and seeing lower marks, teachers reported the problem to the principal. They needed a solution, so they met and suggested that those students complete their assignments at home through a program called home school.

Home school is a system that lets students finish homework, quizzes, assignments, and even tests at home. This approach can help students improve because they can work at their own pace. Many students say that home school is easier than attending regular classes. One advantage is the comfort: you can stay at home, eat lunch whenever you want, watch TV during breaks, and still finish assignments on time.

However, other students do not like being home schoolers because they feel lonely or bored. They miss making friends and the social life of school. They may also need help with schoolwork that is harder to get at home, and sometimes they worry about not receiving all the information they would have learned in class. Often families choose home school because there are no nearby schools, but parents usually choose it because they want their children to have a good education and a better future.

You keep your friends, who can help with homework, and teachers are available to explain things and prepare you for college. While home school can be a useful program and can help students in the short term, regular school is generally a better choice for long-term success. People should take school seriously if they want the best opportunities for their future.

Dear Principal,

I believe students should be permitted to bring cell phones to school during the day. The main reason is safety: phones allow students to get help quickly in an emergency. If someone is injured or feels unsafe, they can call 911 or other local services right away. Having a phone also lets students contact the school office or their parents if something serious happens at school.

Phones are useful for more everyday problems too. Students sometimes spill food on their clothes or need to go home because they feel unwell. In those situations, a quick call to a parent or guardian can solve the problem without causing extra worry. Phones can also help if a student is being bullied; they can call the school, a trusted adult, or their family to report the incident and get support.

Another reason to allow phones is that they help students stay in touch during free time. Breaks between classes or lunchtime are times when many students want to communicate with family or coordinate rides after school. This is especially important at the end of the day when students are going home; having a phone makes it easier to arrange safe transportation or call for help if plans change.

For these reasons, allowing cell phones at school would improve students’ safety and give families a reliable way to stay connected throughout the day.

When people seek guidance, they often ask more than one person. Why does this happen? If you are someone who rarely follows others’ advice, learning to accept it can be useful. Listening to different people can help you make wiser decisions, understand situations more quickly and clearly, and learn from other people’s experience. Getting many viewpoints is especially important in roles like a city mayor, who must consider the concerns of the whole community. If a city’s leaders ignored the voices of residents, the place could suffer, so taking in advice is essential.

Throughout life we face many choices—some small, some life-changing—and these choices shape our future. Advice from others can make your decisions smarter. For example, Abraham Lincoln became aware of the injustices faced by African Americans and, after hearing from others and reflecting on the issue, took steps that contributed to ending slavery. If he had not listened to the right counsel and opinions, history might have been different. This shows how thinking carefully and accepting advice can lead to important changes.

At various times we all receive guidance from people we respect. Whatever advice they give adds to our understanding and can influence our behavior for years. For instance, if a parent tells you not to give up when things get hard, that lesson can stay with you and help you handle challenges. Such guidance builds wisdom, perseverance, and a mindset that supports success. Over time, advice from role models, teachers, or family members helps you tell right from wrong and prepares you for difficult choices.

Having multiple opinions is like sampling food from different cooks: by trying different dishes you might find something you like that you would never have discovered otherwise. The difference with advice is that it provides ideas and knowledge to guide your choices.

In conclusion, advice exists to support us. Opinions can help steer us toward better thinking and smarter choices in life. Not every suggestion will suit you, but it’s worth listening. By hearing others out, you can become the best version of yourself—more aware and wiser in facing life’s decisions.

I understand this is a big change, but it would bring many benefits to students. Below are some reasons why the menu should be changed and how it would help our school community.

Second, students would become healthier, stronger, and more active. Eating nutritious food helps children stay awake and focused in class, instead of feeling tired or sluggish after eating unhealthy snacks. This would also help parents save money on doctor visits and medicine. In addition, serving healthy food at school can teach students the importance of good eating habits that will benefit them throughout life.

These are my main reasons for changing the school menu. Please consider this idea so we can become healthier, think more clearly, and build good habits while spending much of our time at school. Doing this would be an investment in our future and in the well-being of the whole school.

A city council is discussing a proposal to set a curfew for teenagers: 10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight on weekends. Some people support this idea, while others—especially many young people—oppose it. Opinions are divided, but I believe introducing a curfew for teenagers is a sensible measure. In my view, it would encourage better sleeping patterns, reduce unhealthy eating and drinking habits, and give teens more opportunities to spend time with their families.

One clear benefit of a curfew is that it helps teens get enough sleep. If young people are required to be home earlier, they will usually go to bed sooner than when they stay out late. Teenagers need about seven to eight hours of sleep because their bodies and brains are still growing. When they sleep well, they feel more energetic and focused. Staying out late often disrupts normal bedtime routines, making teens tired, sluggish, and less active during the day. Poor sleep also increases the risk of accidents. Drowsy driving can cause dizziness and reduced attention, which has led to many crashes involving young drivers. Late nights can also be linked to drinking and driving, another dangerous outcome of staying out. I have noticed that when I do not sleep enough, I cannot concentrate in class and my schoolwork suffers. Being awake while others are asleep separates me from daily routines and makes it harder to stay involved in what is happening around me.

Curfews can also influence teenage eating and drinking choices. Being out late often means eating fast food or junk food, which is harmful to young people’s health. Combined with lack of sleep, poor diet leaves teens feeling sluggish and less able to take part in school and sports. Early unhealthy habits can lead to illnesses at a young age and weaken the immune system. In addition, late-night outings increase the chance of underage drinking, which is dangerous for developing bodies. Junk food can cause weight gain, which affects teenagers socially, mentally, and physically. If teens spend evenings at home, they are more likely to eat meals prepared by their parents, which tend to be healthier and less greasy. From personal experience, eating too much unhealthy food makes me feel unwell, and when I am in places where people do not know me, I sometimes feel isolated. I also know a family member who became very overweight after often eating junk food; he now struggles with daily tasks and faces teasing, which hurts his confidence. To avoid these problems and negative comments, teens should be encouraged to eat home-cooked, nutritious meals.

Beyond sleep and diet, curfews promote family time. When teenagers are home in the evenings, they have more chances to talk and connect with family members instead of always being out with friends. Many family misunderstandings and the generation gap appear because family members do not spend enough time together. Having dinner as a family helps people share what is happening in their lives, discuss new experiences, and support each other. For example, when my family comes together we talk about things we tried recently and important topics like staying healthy. We also share problems and joys, which strengthens our relationships and helps everyone feel understood.

There are many reasons to believe curfews would help direct teenagers toward healthier, more positive lives. Better sleep, healthier eating, and closer family relationships are all likely outcomes if these rules are put in place. To build a healthier future generation that can contribute positively to society, such measures are worth considering. If teens are well-rested and well-nourished, they will be more alert and able to pursue their goals. Greater family interaction will also improve emotional support at home. Teenagers should view a curfew not as a restriction on their freedom but as a way to protect their health and future. Limiting harmful habits now can give young people a better chance at a long, active, and fulfilling life.

One major problem with phones in class is that they can stop students from paying attention. If pupils rely on their devices, they may become lazy about doing assignments, which is why schools provide computers and libraries where accurate information can be found. When phones are allowed, many students will not use them for learning; instead they will be on social media or texting friends. School is meant to be a place for learning, and constant access to phones can get in the way of listening to teachers and completing tasks.

Students also get upset when teachers take their phones away because they are used to having them all the time. But learning usually happens when students read, think, and work through problems themselves. If phones are available during class or tests, some pupils will look up answers instead of trying, which is a form of cheating. To avoid this, teachers could collect phones at the start of class and return them at the end so students focus on the lesson without distractions.

On the other hand, phones can be useful tools. They are often quicker and easier to use than a computer, and students can search for information they do not understand or find new ways to learn. For some tasks people type faster on a phone than on a PC, and phones can give access to helpful educational resources and different ideas.

In conclusion, phones in school have both benefits and drawbacks. They provide fast access to information and flexible ways to learn, but they can also distract students, encourage cheating, and reduce attention in class. A balanced approach—allowing phones for learning when supervised, and removing them during lessons or tests—seems the most sensible.

Everyone has the capacity to make good choices, but the important part is to name those choices clearly and plan how to act on them. Many famous people started out as ordinary individuals; their stories show that by being themselves and choosing a direction, they became remarkable. They did not wait for life to make decisions for them — they planned their own path.

The world will not pick you for you; instead, you need to choose how you will face the world.

I believe that your character is largely shaped by the choices you make. The decisions you take every day influence who you become. Three important factors that affect character are the people you spend time with, the environment you grew up in, and your own motivation. Being aware of these can help you develop positive qualities for the future.

First, the friends and acquaintances you choose have a strong impact on your behavior and attitudes. People tend to adopt habits and values from those they are close to, so the company you keep matters. If you surround yourself with hardworking, kind people, you are more likely to act in similar ways. On the other hand, spending time with friends who are lazy or uninterested in improving themselves can make it harder to stay motivated. That old saying, “you are who you hang out with,” holds true: your social circle can encourage either good or bad habits.

Second, the way you were raised and the household you grew up in also shape your character. The atmosphere at home is a constant influence. For example, children who live with parents who argue a lot may feel sad or anxious and this can affect their schoolwork and social life. The negative mood at home can become a habit that is hard to break. Conversely, growing up in a supportive and cheerful household usually helps people develop confidence and a positive outlook. A stable, encouraging home can make it easier to do well at school and to build healthy relationships.

Finally, I think motivation is the most important factor in forming good character. When you have a clear purpose or goal, it gives you direction and energy to change your life. Motivation lets you overcome difficult backgrounds or past mistakes. For instance, someone who has faced hardship in their family might use that experience as a push to work harder and succeed. Struggles can become a reason to improve, and in the process you develop persistence, responsibility, and other lasting traits.

In conclusion, your character is something you can shape through your choices. Who you spend time with, the home you grew up in, and what drives you are all key influences, but none of them are completely outside your control. If you are unhappy with your friends or your surroundings, you can make changes. If you lack motivation, you can find goals that matter to you. Ultimately, everyone makes decisions—good or bad—and those choices determine who you become.

People naturally enjoy recognition, and praise can make practicing more enjoyable. Repeating an activity helps us improve, and feeling good about progress often motivates continued effort. However, if learners receive only compliments and never hear how to do better, what incentive remains to keep learning? Constantly hearing "this is perfect" or getting an A+ for every piece of work removes the need to grow. Students may become unable to accept criticism and come to expect constant attention and approval.

Consider artists as an example. Many creators are never fully satisfied with their own work; that dissatisfaction pushes them to refine their skills. They may receive praise, but their real drive comes from noticing flaws and trying to correct them. Criticism, even when hard to hear, is useful when taken constructively. From this perspective, only offering praise would be harmful, because education should prepare students for the real world, where people will evaluate and sometimes criticize what they do. If someone cannot handle feedback, they risk failing at jobs where improvement and adaptation are necessary.

To be clear, I am not claiming that praise is always bad or that students should be made to feel miserable about their efforts. Rather, praise should be paired with honest, respectful feedback. Balancing positive comments with constructive criticism helps learners understand both their strengths and the areas they need to work on. It teaches them that successes often come alongside shortcomings, and that the world outside school will not be nothing but praise.

I believe students achieve more when they stay active and keep doing things. Being busy with productive tasks is more useful than sitting idle. When students take action, they learn more, move ahead in life, and grow into more responsible adults. For these reasons, I think a student who consistently works toward goals will accomplish more over their lifetime than someone who does nothing.

One reason I hold this view is simple: you cannot reach a goal without taking steps toward it. When you are engaged in activities, you gain knowledge and skills. For example, in fourth grade I struggled with math and felt frustrated, but I decided to practice every day after school for the rest of the year. After I studied each night, my grades improved. I would not have made that progress if I had not put in the effort. Also, research and reports often show that students who keep working on tasks at home or after school tend to perform better than those who remain inactive. Finally, being busy helps students learn to manage their time more effectively.

Students who do things tend to go further in life than those who do not. My aunt is a good example: she became a doctor because she focused on her goals and prepared for many important exams. She often handled several tasks at once and stayed committed to her studies. In the same way, people who face many challenges learn that success usually requires doing something — taking risks, studying, or practicing — rather than waiting for things to happen.

Another important effect of staying active is increased maturity. When students balance schoolwork and a job or other responsibilities, they begin to understand what it means to be an adult. For instance, a student who works after school and still has homework must find time to complete assignments, sometimes using breaks at work or free hours in the evening. This builds planning skills and responsibility. Also, having a good role model or example in life can help students become wiser and more capable.

In conclusion, students who keep themselves occupied with meaningful tasks gain knowledge, travel farther in life, and grow up more quickly than those who do nothing. Being active teaches practical life skills and helps students reach greater achievements than inactivity ever would.

Some students get distracted by phones, while others use them to their benefit. Although many people argue that mobile phones should be banned from classrooms, I believe they should be allowed, especially for research and class projects. With a smartphone we can quickly find information, examples, and explanations that help us understand topics the teacher is covering.

People who oppose phones in class usually say they cause distractions and are addictive, making it hard for students to concentrate. While this can happen, I think it is a matter of self-control and responsible use. If students agree to use their phones only for learning, they can not only find useful information but also develop skills that will help them professionally in the future.

I remember a moment in my English class that shows why phones are useful. I was absent for two days because I was sick and worried I had missed a lot. When I returned, the teacher explained our next assignment and offered extra help after school, but I preferred not to stay. Instead, I asked for the vocabulary list and promised to look the words up myself. With my phone I quickly searched each term, read examples, and wrote down the meanings while the lesson continued. If phones were not allowed, I would not have been able to catch up so easily. Using the internet on my phone helped me improve my language skills by finding good, reliable information—something that would have been harder without it.

Phones are also very helpful for group work. In a government class my friends and I had to create an imaginary country: choose its name, location, and set rules. The teacher brought a few computers, but there were not enough for every group. We asked whether we could use our phones for research and the teacher agreed, on the condition we used them only for the project. We used our phones to find facts, maps, and ideas, worked together efficiently, and finished the assignment on time. This experience showed how phones can act like portable computers and prevent delays when technology resources are limited.

In conclusion, mobile phones should be allowed in classrooms for research and projects. Although some will disagree, when used correctly they are powerful learning tools. Technology is part of our world, and students should be able to take advantage of it to improve understanding and complete classwork effectively. Each school and class can set rules to ensure phones are used responsibly.

A current discussion in many places is whether schools should copy the four-day workweek that some companies use to save energy and resources. Under this idea, each school day would be lengthened by two hours, making a ten-hour school day and giving students a three-day weekend.

Many people oppose this change because longer days would be exhausting for students, teachers, and other school staff. Spending ten hours at school for four days in a row could be more draining than attending shorter classes spread across five days. There is also a concern that schools might add more graduation requirements or expect students to finish additional work, which would demand extra time and increase pressure on everyone.

I am against extending the school day because it would cause real problems outside the classroom. A lot of students have jobs after school, and some work nearly full time. If school days went on later or extended the week, those students might not be able to meet their work obligations. In addition, using energy more carefully during the regular schedule could make a meaningful difference without changing school hours. Simple measures such as switching off lights when rooms are empty or letting in fresh air by opening windows are easy and effective ways to reduce energy use. Getting suggestions from community members outside the school could also generate practical ideas for saving energy.

Longer daily schedules would likely harm learning for many students. When classes run for ten hours, it becomes harder to stay focused and absorb new information. Waking earlier and returning home much later would make students more tired, and fatigue reduces the ability to learn. The total energy used by a four-day school week might not be much lower than five shorter days; the difference could be only slight, so the trade-off does not seem worth the cost in well-being and learning quality.

To make a fair decision, we need an open discussion that includes students, parents, teachers, and other community members. Not every student learns at the same pace; many need more time to understand new subjects. From my own experience, new material can be difficult, and cutting the number of school days or extending each day could make learning harder for those students. Because there are many easy ways to save energy without changing school schedules, keeping five shorter days seems the better option while we explore other conservation methods.

Having technology on our side has improved life and reduced many daily stresses. Imagine if Ford had to hire thousands of workers to build one car every five hours, or if restaurants needed twenty rude or slow employees, or if Walmart relied only on slow cashiers. Life would be harder without the great technology we now have.

I do not agree with students taking classes from home or using video conferencing. I think online lessons cause many problems. From my experience as a student, I believe some pupils will not join lessons properly, may sleep through them, and will not complete their own work. These issues can make many students fall behind or even fail. Here are the reasons I feel this way.

First, many students will put off joining classes. They might tell themselves, "I'll join the next session," and keep postponing until they stop trying. Instead of logging on, they could go outside to play with friends or spend time on other things. Sometimes parents have to keep reminding them to get online, but children do not always listen. Others will simply switch on their game console or phone instead of attending the lesson.

Second, students can easily fall asleep during an online class. When this happens, the teacher often cannot do anything about it. In a real classroom, teachers can notice who is dozing off and wake them up or bring their attention back to the lesson. Being physically present makes it easier for teachers to check that students are paying attention and doing what they are supposed to do.

Finally, many students will not do their own work when studying from home. Even if they appear online, there is no guarantee they are the ones completing assignments. They could ask someone else to do the work or even pay another person to do it. Teenagers can be lazy but also clever at finding ways to avoid doing their tasks.

Some people argue that home lessons are better because they save time in the morning and students can join from their computers. While this is true for some, others need a teacher nearby to explain things and keep them focused. For these reasons, I disagree with students attending school from home.

I agree with this prompt. Many people claim it is impossible to change the world, but I believe change begins with our minds. Too often we let doubts block us; we tell ourselves that nothing we do will matter. The first thing we must do is change our priorities and how we look at the environment and society around us.

People must open their eyes to what is really happening. Even a small action can start a larger change. It does not matter how minor the first step is — once it begins, it grows. Think about our lives: are they safe when the planet is warming and natural systems are failing? I would say no. Global warming affects us all, yet many wait for someone else to act. What we have been doing so far is not enough, but change is possible if we decide to act.

Changing ourselves is not easy. Many say they cannot change because it is too hard or because they believe no one will notice. People feel tired after a long day or discouraged by their routines, and that becomes an excuse not to try. I will not give up. Like a tree whose leaves change color, people can change too. I can change myself, and together with others we can make a much bigger difference. Teamwork multiplies the impact: when people join, the change becomes stronger and may even inspire other countries to follow.

On a personal level, I want to improve my own behavior. Many people need help to become more courteous, kind, responsible, and punctual. Changing myself is my top priority because I know that if I act correctly, I can influence others. Knowing the difference between right and wrong helps me decide what to do. Nothing in this world is perfect, but we must support each other. We should feel proud of the good things we do now and of the improvements to come.

I am interested in technology and electricity, and these fields are important to me. I would like to study technology and build a personal robot to help with household tasks. Many people would welcome such help, though robots can be risky if updates fail or they behave unpredictably. Still, these innovations could improve life for many and allow people to rest more. I also dream of a smartphone that charges by sunlight, reducing the need for other energy sources. These ideas could change daily life and support a cleaner environment.

Mistakes are part of learning. It is never too late to try many things, and making errors is not failure. On the contrary, mistakes teach us and lead to success. If you never make mistakes, you miss valuable lessons. My mother tells me that you can change the world — or at least the world inside your head — and build many things to help others. Even a small change can be more powerful than a single grand action. Change is coming, and it can begin with small steps.

Of course, not everyone will change. Some people will keep believing wrong ideas, and it is sad to see them ignore the reality of our environment. First impressions and deep beliefs are hard to change, and many impressions remain fixed. Still, others can be persuaded, and I focus on those who are open. Sometimes I do not know exactly what to write, so I share what I see, hear, and feel. My own changes may be small, but dreams can become real in time. If I can help someone achieve a dream, they will thank me because I changed their life. Now it is my turn to give back after others helped me.

Behavior in school, at home, in the neighborhood, and in the wider community is part of the change. Teachers and parents shape how we study and prepare for the future. The most important thing is to get started. If no one begins, nothing will change. My teacher says it is important to change how things are built and to aim for the goals you want. I love the idea of changing things, but I need some help. One practical plan I have is to make a short video or an animation and share it on social media. A good video can reach many people and inspire them to act. If viewers identify with the message, they might say, "This is what I needed," and the idea could spread around the world.

This topic is not difficult: change is possible if we refuse to give up. The changes you make may become reasons for others to feel proud of you. I will finish with this thought: if you believe you are doing the right thing, continue; if you are mistaken, learn and keep going. If everyone does their part, things will improve. I make mistakes and so do you, but if we correct them, we can turn our goals into reality. Life passes quickly, so live it as if each day matters and never give up. I will do my best — change is near.

Why should you have a good attitude? First, a positive attitude helps you succeed in life, and there are several reasons for this. Second, a negative attitude will hold you back. People with bad attitudes often struggle to find work, miss out on good opportunities, and may even create problems in serious situations like a court case. Below are the main ways a good attitude benefits you: it makes others like you, it earns respect, and it makes finding a job easier.

1. People will like you

When you show a positive and respectful attitude, others are more likely to enjoy being around you. Respecting people leads them to return that respect and to treat you well. This kind of behavior opens doors and can help you progress in your career and personal life. During a job interview, for example, a friendly and professional attitude can improve your chances of being hired, while a rude or negative manner can cost you the position.

2. Respect

Earning respect from others helps you become more successful because people who respect you will support you rather than try to undermine you. Respect is not given automatically; you gain it by treating others well and helping them when you can. Building respect will create more opportunities and assistance from others, which supports your long-term success.

3. Finding a job

Looking for a job is much harder if you have a poor attitude. Employers and college admissions officers prefer candidates who show good behavior and a cooperative spirit. If you want your dream job or to get into a desired college, a positive attitude can make acceptance far more likely. With a negative attitude, you risk being rejected or removed.

In conclusion, having a good attitude makes life easier. It helps people like you, brings respect, and increases your chances of getting a job, all of which lead to greater success.

Do you know how many people are unhappy because they pretend to be someone else? Today there are millions who do not live the life they truly want. It can be hard to be yourself in a society that often judges anyone who is different, but the greatest achievement for any person is to keep their individuality. Being true to yourself leads to real happiness. Fighting society’s prejudice and accepting who you are can feel like a battle when it seems the whole world wants to change you.

Many people believe success means having lots of money, fame, or possessions. But those things do not help you be yourself. A person can own everything yet still feel empty, because material things do not define who you are and do not bring lasting happiness. If you are not happy, all the success in the world feels pointless. It is said that about sixty percent of people are unhappy with their lives, but studies suggest this can change if people are honest with themselves and remove unwanted parts from their lives. The first step to happiness is being genuine. Living a lie leads to a miserable life. You must accept your personality and your interests based on what you truly think and feel. One serious consequence of not being honest with yourself is mental illness like depression. This problem is common and dangerous, and often connected to not accepting who you are. For these reasons, being yourself is difficult but it is one of the most important rewards in life.

Throughout life you will face many choices, and it is important to listen to your own voice. People must not let others decide for them when those decisions affect their identity. First, you need to know what you want, because that is what being happy with yourself means. Always put your own opinion first; that is the key to real happiness. It is easy to follow others’ views or to be influenced by a world that tries to turn you into someone you are not. In the end, what you want is the answer to being truly happy.

Everyone is trying to find their path in life, and being honest about feelings and desires can help reach that goal. Right now the world seems like a constant struggle because many people are fighting for the right to be themselves and for acceptance. This is not an easy task. The only person whose opinion should really matter is you. You do not need to worry about what others think; care about what you think. Unfortunately, not everyone understands this. Many still expect acceptance based only on being human, not on being different. It is hard to be yourself when millions want to change you and refuse to accept that difference is natural. Diversity is part of balance; differences in race, color, language, traditions and customs should be respected. People should learn from each other, not demand uniformity. Today, many work to create a world with less prejudice, where everyone can be themselves and receive the rights they deserve. This is a hard fight, but the result would be a great accomplishment. If people accept themselves, with both strengths and flaws, others cannot easily harm them; they reach a point where criticism no longer brings them down.

Many philosophers and researchers believe the social problem of rejecting difference comes from long ago, when people hid their true feelings out of fear of rejection. In part it is our fault because we have often stayed quiet when something was wrong. But it is not too late: many are trying to change how the world views what is acceptable. That is why accepting yourself can seem like a war if everyone tries to change you. We must be strong and not let others question our decisions. Another reason being yourself is hard is that sometimes we are our own harshest critics. If everyone were honest with themselves, authenticity would be normal in society, but we find it so difficult that uniqueness often looks wrong. We need to change this way of thinking and make being ourselves the norm.

We still have a lot to learn, but I believe we are moving in the right direction. People must overcome many obstacles to claim their individuality and always remember where they are and where they want to go. Being yourself is very difficult when society says you cannot be different, because how can you discover who you are if no one gives you the chance? Yet finding that answer is the greatest achievement a person can have. Living as your true self is the best way to live a full life.

I believe schools should not add two extra hours to each school day. Many students already follow busy routines that include jobs, sports, or extracurricular clubs, and longer days would clash with those commitments. If a district switches to a four-day week but lengthens the remaining days, students could end up with very little free time and might need to start school earlier, which would be difficult for many families.

There are some clear advantages to a four-day week, however. Students would enjoy three-day weekends year-round, giving them more time to relax and recharge. They would also have extra hours to finish homework or turn in missing assignments, which could help improve grades. Schools could use the change to shorten the overall school year or extend holiday and spring break periods, which some families would welcome.

But extending the school day has downsides. Longer classes can make it harder for students to stay focused, and many might become tired or even fall asleep in class. If I had to sit through two additional hours, I would probably lose concentration or doze off until the day ended. In my view, a four-day school week can be a good idea if it does not mean much longer school days, because students need that extra day to rest and handle other responsibilities. Overall, this is my opinion on the four-day school week.

Should students choose a career at a young age? I believe it is a good idea for young people to start focusing on a career earlier, even though there are some difficulties for those who have many responsibilities outside school. Overall, committing to a career path while still in school can help students gain useful knowledge and practical experience that will benefit them later.

First, when students begin training early, they become better prepared for working in that field. If they study something they enjoy, they will practice regularly and learn important skills over time. This steady practice helps them concentrate on their chosen profession and builds confidence. By the time they finish their studies, they should be able to show what they have learned and perform tasks without much trouble.

Second, in many societies schools expect students to identify a career direction during high school, and this can be helpful. Choosing a special subject gives students a clearer idea of their strengths and what kind of job fits them. It also lets teachers and employers see whether a student did well in that area. Knowing a specialty early can make it easier to decide future steps and avoid wasting time trying many different things without real progress.

I also think it is important for people to know what they want to become. Some young people are unsure about their dreams, but others already have a clear goal. Taking relevant courses while young can make those goals realistic. I remember my father encouraging me to take classes in English, computing, guitar, and dance when I was a child. At the time I refused and only wanted to play. Later I understood why learning these skills matters. They helped me grow and showed me that I could achieve more than I thought.

Another advantage is that schools often offer chances to work during the summer or after classes, which gives practical experience. In my country many schools do not provide vocational options, so students leave school without practical skills and are not ready for work. There, parents usually do the working while young people only study. When schools support career learning, students have more opportunities to earn and to prepare for the job market.

In conclusion, students should consider taking a career path while they are young because it helps both themselves and society. Early career training teaches useful skills, prepares students for real work, and reduces uncertainty about the future. Even if they continue studying afterward, these courses give them an advantage in life and increase their chances of success.

Some people believe students should choose a career by the time they start high school. I agree with this view because deciding early gives young people more time to prepare, learn about their chosen field, and avoid wasted effort later.

First, picking a career in or before high school helps students gain knowledge and experience related to that field. When teenagers decide on a path early, they can focus on the subjects and activities that build relevant skills. This commitment also encourages them to take responsibility for their future and set clear goals. For example, a student who wants to study engineering can begin taking math and science courses, join related clubs, or find internships, which makes them better prepared for university.

Second, choosing a career sooner allows students to research their options and change their minds without losing much time. High school gives a safe period to explore different professions and test preferences. If a student realizes a chosen career is not a good fit, they can switch direction before enrolling in a college program, saving money and avoiding unnecessary university study. For instance, a student who starts with interest in medicine but later prefers graphic design can adjust their plans while still in high school.

In conclusion, expecting students to identify a career by the start of high school is useful. Early decisions help them build relevant experience, develop responsibility, and provide time to investigate and, if needed, change their plans so they do not waste time or resources on an unsuitable university course.

I understand why some people accept Emerson’s idea, but I disagree with it. In many families and communities, people are pushed into careers they do not love. Parents or society may say, “You should be a doctor or an engineer,” and young people accept that path even if it does not match their interests. I believe everyone can choose what they are passionate about rather than simply following other people’s expectations.

Loving your work or studies makes a big difference in life. When you enjoy what you do, every small success feels meaningful and keeps you motivated to learn more and improve. Whether someone is excited about a profession, learning a language, writing, making discoveries, or helping others, that passion gives them energy and focus. Forcing someone into a different role can harm their mental and physical well-being because they lack the inner drive that makes difficult tasks bearable.

I can explain this from my own experience. Back home I studied business for most of my life because I wanted a career in that field. After I moved to the United States last year, my parents and many people around me told me I should train to be a nurse. I did not have any real interest in nursing, but without support, I agreed to try it. Since then I have felt unsure and unhappy. Thinking about the future often brings me down. I know that if I were following a path I loved, I would accept challenges more easily, stay determined, and work hard until I succeeded.

For these reasons I oppose the idea that society determines who you become. Some will argue that our surroundings shape us, but I think people can resist that pressure. Every day people try to enjoy life and also try to bring joy to others. For example, when I lived in Italy, every year people celebrated a religious holiday by gathering in the town center. They would talk, eat, laugh and enjoy each other’s company. You could have a great time there whether you had much money or very little. This showed me that happiness often comes from being with people who make you feel good, not from having a lot of money.

In life, I believe you should not follow others blindly or rely completely on other people’s approval. Do what you enjoy and trust yourself. Some people are jealous and may try to discourage you or damage your dreams with negative words or actions. If you let them control you, you could stop trying to reach your goals. That is why it is important to live your own life and make decisions based on what you believe is right, not on what others tell you to do.

I often think about how different the world could be if more people tried to help others, especially young people. One day in Italy, I went to the supermarket with my dad and a friend. When we reached the checkout, I noticed a man who could not afford the sandwich he wanted. He only had fifty cents, and the sandwich cost around two euros. He was about to put it back, and I felt I had to do something. I bought the sandwich for him. He smiled and said, “My friend, you made my day better.” That moment made me very happy. It reminded me that small acts of kindness do not require a lot of money but can still make a big difference to someone.

In conclusion, I think we accomplish more when we try to help others and when we believe in ourselves. Live your life, never give up, and trust your own abilities. Giving up usually means you have lost faith in yourself, and that is never a good thing.

Some people argue that praising a student's work, even when it is not their best, helps build self-esteem. They claim that confidence is essential for learning and personal growth. I agree with this view. Self-assurance encourages students to move forward instead of staying stuck. Without faith in their own abilities, learners are less likely to take on challenges or complete tasks during their lives. Praise can help create a positive attitude that motivates students to continue improving and to aim for success.

When students doubt what they can achieve, they tend to remain at the same level and miss chances to develop. A lack of confidence lowers their self-worth and can prevent them from trying new things. On the other hand, believing in their potential gives students the courage to practice more and to push beyond their comfort zone. If a student thinks they can do better, they will keep working and gradually get stronger in their skills. Failing or submitting imperfect work the first time should not be the end; with encouragement and effort, they can do better next time. Therefore, a belief in oneself influences future outcomes and should be supported from early on.

To build this forward-looking mindset, students need clear goals and a plan. Writing down objectives helps them see what they want to achieve and decide which steps to take first. They also benefit from having supportive friends or family who encourage them. Even if a student does not give their best effort every time, praise can remind them that improvement is possible and worth pursuing. Rather than discouraging them for imperfect work, we should offer recognition so they keep trying. In this way, praising students—even for less-than-perfect work—can strengthen self-esteem and help them grow throughout life.

Learning from home through distance education is not the best choice. The main reason is that it is different from being at school. In a classroom we have more learning opportunities. If we do not understand something, we can ask the teacher and they can explain it again. In contrast, studying at home can make it harder to get immediate help. Still, sometimes taking classes at home is necessary — for example when you are ill or have another urgent reason. If learning is important to you, online lessons are better than skipping school, as long as you keep the energy to reach your goals.

Distance learning at home can also bring some benefits. It can help some students feel more positive and focused because they can study at times that suit them. When classes are recorded, you may have more opportunities to listen carefully. Studying from home also lets you do other tasks you want while managing your time.

Some schools allow regular remote lessons, and that can be useful. However, going to school is still very important because it gives more chances to take different classes and to graduate together with other students. Video lessons are somewhat like real classes because you can see the teacher, but often you cannot get the same immediate support.

In conclusion, attending school in person is more helpful than distance learning. From my point of view, being at school is necessary to have better opportunities to learn and to keep working toward your goals.

People who value self-reliance believe in following their own instincts and making decisions independently. I think that these people should rely mostly on themselves rather than always turning to experts or authorities for important life choices. Learning by doing, earning what you want, and making practical choices helps build responsibility and teaches the real value of things.

Different people value different things: some care most about clothes, shoes, or phones; others value family, friends, or a home and money. When someone spends their own money on an expensive item, they tend to care for it more. For example, if a girl buys a pair of shoes that cost $100, she will likely be upset if they get dirty or damaged because she worked for that money. The same goes for young men who pay several hundred dollars for name-brand sneakers; they usually do not want those shoes ruined and will avoid messy work while wearing them.

That is why it is important to make sensible choices based on your plans. If you know you will be doing outside or physical work, it makes sense to buy cheaper shoes that you will not worry about ruining. People who want to be independent should think ahead and choose items that fit their lifestyle. Buying expensive goods without considering how they will be used often leads to regret and constant worry about protecting them.

Teenagers, especially, should start working so they understand the cost of things. If young people always ask their parents for items, they will not learn how much those items truly cost or how much effort is needed to earn them. Working part-time helps teens appreciate what they buy and encourages better spending decisions. When you buy something with your own money, you are more likely to take care of it and not waste it on things you do not need.

I speak from experience: I work and save money so I can buy things I want or need. When someone gives me a gift, I value it because they chose it and spent their time to get it. Once I bought a pair of AirPods for a friend as a Christmas gift. He was very happy, and it made our relationship stronger. Acts like that show how much people care for one another, and receiving a gift bought by someone else also feels special.

In my life, my sister and my friend RJ mean a lot to me. RJ helped me find true love and supports me every day. Because of people like him, I feel happy and valued. In short, self-reliant people learn more by doing and earning; this independence teaches them to value possessions and relationships more than constantly seeking advice from others.

Many students prefer a long summer vacation because it gives them plenty of free time to relax and see friends. I understand this view, especially for those whose families live in another country; a long break allows them to travel home and visit parents, relatives, and old friends. However, I believe a year-round school calendar would be better: a short 3–4 week summer break, a longer winter holiday, and one-week breaks in spring and autumn.

Long uninterrupted school and then a single long break can make learning feel repetitive. When students study the same subjects for months without regular rests, they can become bored and stressed. Short, more frequent breaks would help them refresh their minds and avoid the burnout that comes from doing the same tasks over and over.

In addition, long summer vacations often make it harder for students to return to school. After several weeks away, many feel lazy or unmotivated, and it takes time to get back into study routines. With shorter breaks spread through the year, students keep a steady rhythm of work and rest. This reduces the pressure on their memory and concentration because they are not required to absorb or relearn large amounts of material all at once.

In conclusion, while long summers have benefits like allowing travel to visit family, a year-round schedule with a short summer break, a longer winter holiday, and brief spring and fall breaks would help students avoid boredom, reduce stress, and maintain better study habits.

Some schools allow cell phones in class for educational uses. While supporters argue that phones can help students find information quickly, I believe they should not be permitted during lessons. My reasons are that students already spend too much time on their phones and fail to pay attention, phones are used for many non-educational activities, and they create constant distractions.

First, many students are on their phones all day and do not focus on class. School should be a place for learning, but when pupils are busy with their devices they miss important explanations from the teacher. Even if a phone could be helpful for looking something up, it does not replace being present in class. When tests or quizzes arrive, students who spent lessons on their phones often discover they do not know the material because they were not listening.

Second, cell phones are easily used for things unrelated to schoolwork. Students text friends, play games, watch videos, or listen to music instead of following the lesson. They also take pictures and make videos that they post on social media for fun. Sometimes this behavior can even lead to bullying, for example when someone records or shares embarrassing images of a classmate. These activities take time and attention away from learning.

Third, phones interfere with completing homework, projects, and classroom tasks. Although people say phones can help with assignments or clarify confusing topics, they often prove distracting. Apps, social media, and calls can interrupt students while they work, and they may forget to finish classwork or homework. This can cause grades to drop, especially if students miss important instructions or fail to submit assignments because they were distracted by their phones.

In conclusion, even if some schools use cell phones for educational purposes, they should not be allowed during class. Students are likely to remain on their devices instead of paying attention, use them for entertainment or social purposes, and become distracted from their schoolwork. For these reasons, phones do more harm than good in the classroom.

If a shop looks nice but most reviews are poor and only a few are positive, you will likely choose somewhere else. In conclusion, first impressions stick with us and are not easy to reverse. The first time we see something or meet someone often shapes our lasting opinion.

Do you set ambitious goals?

Many people have aims in life; some choose ambitious ones while others prefer easier, smaller targets. Ambitious goals are harder to reach, but we should not trade them for low ones simply because they seem simpler.

Even if you complete a hundred small tasks, you cannot say they are the same as one big ambition. A major goal can lead to true success, while doing many minor things makes it unlikely you will achieve something comparable. That is why aiming high matters if you want to accomplish something significant.

First, having a big goal helps you become a remarkable person. For instance, Keanu Reeves is known not only for his acting but also for his modest lifestyle, showing that ambition is not always about money. Ambitious aims can be personal and moral as well as professional, and they shape your character.

Second, high goals make you stand out from others. Kobe Bryant reached the top of basketball because he set out to be the best and worked relentlessly toward that aim. If you dedicate yourself to what you love, you can excel in any field; small goals rarely inspire the same level of commitment.

Finally, focusing on low ambitions prevents real growth. Someone who only sets easy targets will miss lessons from failure and lose chances to develop. Ambitious goals can be very difficult or even seem impossible, but giving up is the only true defeat. Believe in yourself and say, “I can do it,” and you will take the first step on the path to success.

Ralph Waldo Emerson argued that being true to yourself in a world that pressures you to change is one of the greatest achievements. I disagree with this idea because, in reality, many people never reach that level of self-expression. Most fail to accomplish their goals, give in to outside expectations, and hide who they really are.

Many accept ambitions that are not truly theirs because they believe those goals will please family or fit social standards. As a result, they either lose sight of what they really want or never set authentic goals at all.

Second, a lot of people try to become someone else to fit in rather than being themselves. They make choices to match the roles expected of them, not because those choices reflect their inner identity. This leads to unhappiness for many, since pretending to be someone else usually does not bring real satisfaction. People may appear successful or well-adjusted outwardly, but inside they feel disconnected from their true self.

Finally, some people simply do not know who they are. They have not discovered their values and desires, so they cannot show their real character in public. Instead of living honestly, they hide or copy others because it seems safer.

For these reasons, Emerson’s claim does not match many people’s experience. Rather than achieving genuine selfhood, many remain uncertain, follow external pressures, and disguise their true identities.

I fully agree with the idea that success often means moving from one failure to another without losing enthusiasm. Failure is a necessary part of progress, but today the environment is less forgiving than it used to be. Companies, churches, and governments no longer offer the same support they once did; when someone fails now, others are quick to judge and doubt that person’s ability to reach their goals. Despite that, I believe that setbacks can push us forward if we respond correctly.

A clear example is the first day at a new job. Many of us have felt insecure and unsure about tasks at the beginning. Sometimes coworkers laugh or point out mistakes instead of guiding you. They may wait until you do something wrong before offering help, which makes the situation more difficult. This reaction can be discouraging, but it also reveals an important truth: life can be harsh, and people will not always be kind. What matters is how you react to those blows. You must keep going, learn from errors, and not let criticism stop you from improving.

Know your value and work for it, but be prepared to endure setbacks along the way. Avoid blaming others for your failures; taking responsibility helps you grow. That attitude is what separates those who succeed from those who give up.

In conclusion, failures and criticism are part of the path to success. They can give you the push you need to improve, but only if you maintain your enthusiasm and resilience. If you cannot handle the criticism, your motivation will fade and your efforts will be wasted.

Some people value self-reliance and believe each person should follow their own instincts and ideas. But when it comes to important life choices, should individuals rely solely on themselves or seek advice from experts and experienced people? I believe that consulting guidance and authorities is the better approach.

First, experts and advisers usually have more experience than those who make decisions without help. They have faced similar problems before and can offer practical solutions. Listening to their insights lets people learn useful lessons and avoid common mistakes.

Second, while some prefer to decide alone and others like to discuss choices with friends, it is helpful for everyone to share their situation with knowledgeable people. Explaining your background and goals to an adviser helps them give tailored suggestions, and this exchange helps the decision-maker gain new information and understanding.

Third, people who always act independently may think life is simple for them, but that is often not true. Making well-informed choices usually requires meeting and learning from those who have better judgment.

In conclusion, people should study more about decision-making and seek out experienced individuals to guide them when facing important life matters.

Both public and private schools should offer menus that reflect students’ preferences, and one simple way to do that is to use a website where pupils can vote or answer short surveys about lunch options. If schools collect students’ choices and information about allergies through an online form, they can plan meals that more students will enjoy and can eat safely. Right now many pupils dislike the cafeteria food and bring meals from home or skip eating, which harms their energy and attention in class.

A practical plan is to update the school menu every year based on the results of the online survey. When students feel the food is tasty and varied, they are more likely to eat well and to be alert during lessons. For example, mornings could begin with fruit or a light drink, and lunch can include different choices like tacos or other popular items so students do not eat the same dishes every day. Changing the menu annually keeps meals interesting and lets the school try new recipes that better match what students want.

Schools should also promote healthy routines around mealtime. A short ten-minute exercise break before lunch would help students feel hungrier and more ready to eat. After that, they should have enough time to get their food and sit down comfortably. Long lines and slow service discourage students from eating at school, and half of pupils may avoid the cafeteria for that reason. Providing faster service, more menu variety, and natural drinks like water and fruit juices would support healthier choices.

When children eat food they like and that gives good nutrition, their concentration and mood in class improve. Students involved in sports especially need meals that fuel their activity; good school food helps them maintain energy and recover from practice. If students and teachers both have appealing options, the whole school community benefits: attendance at lunch increases, behavior and focus during lessons get better, and people generally feel happier.

To make this change work, schools need a clear process for gathering opinions. An easy-to-use website or online form that students fill out before each school year would let food services see what is popular and what needs to change. Administrators can compare responses from year to year and update the menu accordingly. This approach makes the choice democratic and practical, allowing cafeterias to offer more attractive meals while still managing costs and logistics.

In summary, creating an annual menu review based on student surveys and improving mealtime routines would reduce the number of pupils skipping school meals, raise their energy and concentration, and make meals more enjoyable. Small changes—like more variety, quicker service, natural drinks, and a short exercise break—can have a big positive impact on students’ health and school life.

I prefer working in a group to working alone because group work offers more advantages. When people work together, they bring different ideas and perspectives to a project. This variety helps the team choose better topics, decide what to include, and plan how to present the work. Also, dividing tasks among members makes the job easier and keeps everyone focused on the goals set by the teacher.

Working in a team encourages everyone to take part and support each other. Group members can explain parts of the assignment that others do not understand, so the whole group learns more about what the teacher expects. When students share their opinions, they can combine the best parts of each idea to make stronger work. Teamwork also helps students practice expressing themselves and listening to others, which improves communication skills.

Another important benefit is that group work can help improve grades for students who are struggling. Some students do not always get perfect scores when they work alone, but being part of a group gives them a chance to improve. Classmates can give feedback and help complete tasks, so weaker students can learn from stronger ones. If someone is unsure about how to present or write something, the group can help them find a better way.

It is true that some students prefer working alone and feel more comfortable doing so. Working by yourself can sometimes be simpler because you do not need to agree with others. But often, working alone limits the range of ideas and can make it harder to stay motivated. In contrast, group members can encourage each other and make choices together, which usually leads to better results.

Teams do have problems sometimes, for example when a member does not complete their part, it can affect everyone’s grade. Even so, working with others gives a chance to correct mistakes and learn from each other. For these reasons, I believe group work is generally more beneficial than working alone.

This teen manual is about expectations and whether students can gain from studying at home. I think allowing students to attend classes from home is a good idea. Many young people would benefit from flexible learning because their life situations make it hard to go to school every day.

First, some students need to work or help their families, so they cannot spend all day at school. If they can join lessons from home, they will not miss important classes while earning money or supporting relatives. Also, some learners face unfair treatment or other barriers that stop them from going to school regularly. In these cases, home-based or online classes give them a chance to continue learning without feeling excluded. In some places teachers even visit students’ houses to teach when the students cannot come, and online lessons are another way to avoid losing study time.

Responsibility is another reason to support home study. In the area where I was born, many children must walk long distances to reach school. Sometimes teachers travel to homes to teach a few students. Transport can be expensive or simply not available, so attending school every day is difficult for some families. If students take responsibility and use the option of home study, they can keep learning and increase their chances of graduating. Students who are committed can also win scholarships that help them and their families, so flexible learning can be a key to their future success.

Another important point is that online classes suit different kinds of students. Many adults who need to work find it easier to study remotely. Some young people attend school only a few days a week because they need to work or have other duties. For them, studying from home or at times like evenings makes it possible to continue their education. Night or late classes are useful for people who cannot attend morning lessons, and online options increase those possibilities.

In conclusion, letting students study from home gives them valuable choices. It helps those who work, who live far from school, or who lack transport. It also supports people who need flexible hours, like evening study. Personally, I would choose to finish high school online because it would allow me to share my experience and manage other responsibilities. Overall, offering home-based learning is a positive opportunity for many students.

Adding extra hours would leave them exhausted from sitting and concentrating for so long. As a result, some students might lose interest in learning or even become depressed. They would have less time and energy left to do homework or to review what they learned at school. Second, lengthening the day would delay many school programs and cause practical problems for families. Clubs, sports, and other after-school activities would have to start later, and some students might stop attending them because it becomes too late. This is especially difficult for students who travel a long distance to school. That leaves little time for homework, family time, or rest. For these reasons, delaying the schedule could reduce participation in valuable extracurriculars and create hardship for students and their families.

Schools already spend large sums on electricity every year, and adding extra hours of lighting, heating or cooling, and staff presence would raise these expenses further. Money spent on higher utility bills would mean less funding available for important things like updating classrooms, buying supplies, or improving technology. The school board must consider whether the benefits of extra class time are worth the extra financial burden.

Choosing nutritious school meals over junk food will make it easier for us to take part in sports and physical activities. Heavy, greasy meals often leave our stomachs feeling full and slow, while lighter, healthier options give us the energy to move. Even professional athletes keep fit by eating well, which helps them perform better.

Healthier food can also help us avoid depression. If we often eat unhealthy food and gain weight, it can lead to low self-esteem and sadness. Many students feel unhappy about their appearance when they become overweight, and this can contribute to depression. Reducing the amount of junk food at school may lower the risk of students becoming overweight and help them feel better about themselves.

Obesity is a serious health problem. In extreme cases, it can limit a person’s mobility and make everyday activities difficult. Preventing weight gain through better school meals is an important step in protecting students’ long-term health.

Finally, nutritious food helps students stay active and mentally alert. After a healthy lunch we are less likely to feel tired and lazy, so we can concentrate on classes and join in after-school activities. A good diet also supports brain function in a similar way that exercise strengthens the body.

In conclusion, I think changing the school menu to include healthier options is an excellent idea. It will improve our physical health, reduce the chance of depression, and make students more active. Offering healthy food is one of the best things the cafeteria can do to help us stay well.

Keeping your body moving is very important because regular activity helps you stay healthy and gives you more energy. People who keep active are less likely to become ill, since movement supports overall wellbeing.

Most of us have daily tasks or goals, whether at work or elsewhere, and many enjoy staying busy throughout the day. This constant activity is beneficial: when your muscles are used regularly they become stronger and more accustomed to work. After a long day of activity, what your body usually needs most is time to rest and recover.

An active lifestyle generally leads to better health and a lower risk of sickness. If you are someone who likes to be busy all the time, getting sick can be especially difficult because you are used to being on the move. Often, people who stay active manage to remain energetic even as they grow older.

It is also important to eat well and take in enough vitamins if you want to keep doing a lot every day. Your body requires nutrients to function and recover; without proper nourishment you will be weaker and less able to cope with physical demands. Therefore, be careful and look after your nutrition while you stay active.

Many people are naturally busy and rarely stay in one place for long, but some others spend most of their time sitting and should try to add more activity to their routine. Being active can clear your mind and improve how your body feels. At the same time, remember that there are limits: it is wonderful to do the things you enjoy, but do not push your body beyond what it can handle.

Do you think technology is helpful? I believe it is. Technology makes many everyday tasks easier and more convenient. For instance, instead of going to the shop, you can order groceries online. My sister does this when she is ill or too busy; the delivery arrives at our house, which saves her time and effort. Also, many jobs now allow people to work from home using a laptop, which is a big advantage for those who need flexibility.

Another useful feature of modern technology is ride-hailing apps like Uber. If you do not drive or need a quick ride somewhere, you can request a car with a few taps on your phone. Shopping for clothes is simpler too: when you cannot visit stores, you can browse online shops and buy what you want. Books are available digitally as well, so you can read or borrow books on the internet without going to a bookstore. You can also pay bills and make purchases online, which reduces the need to handle cash or visit offices.

Technology helps families stay connected across long distances. My grandmother lives in Generic_City, and we are able to video call her from another country. That has made keeping in touch much easier. When we travel, online check-in is useful because my older sister completes it in advance, so we do not have to wait in long lines at the airport and we already have our seats. Mobile payment options such as Apple Pay are helpful too if you forget your wallet; you can still buy what you need.

However, there are some downsides. If people order everything online and avoid going out, they may not get enough physical activity and could become lazy. Another problem is that technology can reduce face-to-face interaction. For example, when I visit my grandmother for holidays, my cousins often sit together but spend the time on their phones instead of talking to each other.

Overall, I think technology has brought many positive changes to daily life, but it is important to balance its use to avoid the negative effects on health and personal relationships.
